docs.title: MSc DSP Courses
docs.text:
ECEG-6303 — Advanced Digital Signal Processing ECEG-6423 — Multimedia Signal Processing

Two course sites for the MSc in Communication Engineering DSP track. Each has lecture notes, worked examples, code, quizzes, solutions, and an exam bank.

docs.title: The DSP track
docs.text:
• ECEG-6303 — Advanced DSP

    Semester I · Compulsory Core

    Extends the classical DSP sequence into statistical and adaptive signal processing. Discrete random signals, spectrum estimation, linear estimation and prediction, adaptive filters (LMS, RLS), and multirate DSP.

    ECEG-6303

  • ECEG-6423 — Multimedia Signal Processing

    Semester II · Elective II

    Applies DSP to the three pillars of multimedia: images, speech, and video. Image transforms, enhancement, restoration, compression; speech analysis, recognition, synthesis; video coding and streaming.

    ECEG-6423

docs.title: What's in each course
docs.text:
Every course site contains the same structure, so you always know where to look:

  • Chapters

    Full lecture notes with numbered worked examples, computational implementations in Python / Java / C#, and chapter summaries.

  • Solutions

    Key steps and final answers for the tutorial problems at the end of every chapter.

  • Exam bank

    100 marks of exam-style questions (MCQ, short answer, derivation) with answer key and instructor grading rubric.

  • Schedule & assessment

    Week-by-week plan, assessment weighting, grading policies, submission rules.

docs.title: Shared resources
docs.text:
These pages apply to both ECEG-6303 and ECEG-6423 — they are the common reference for notation, formulas, and software.

  • DSP Primer

    Notation conventions, Fourier / Z / Laplace transforms, sampling theorem, transform pairs, key theorems, filter design, random-signal definitions. Referenced by both courses.

    DSP Primer

  • Software setup

    Python environment, MATLAB toolboxes, Java / C# libraries, Jupyter, IDE recommendations, common installation issues, and a quick environment test.

    Software

  • References

    Common DSP textbook shelf, free online books, video lectures, key papers, and tool documentation — organised by topic.

    References

  • Feedback

    Report a typo, wrong answer, or unclear explanation. Corrections are acknowledged on the affected page.

    Feedback

docs.title: About this site
docs.text:
This site is the rendered, canonical version of the DSP course material. It is built from Markdown source files using MkDocs and the Material for MkDocs theme, and published automatically from GitHub via GitHub Actions.

The Markdown source is also public, but it does not render well on github.com — MathJax equations, Material icons, admonitions, and grid cards are all shown as literal text. Use this site for the actual content; the source repository is for contributors and maintainers.

docs.title: Programme context
docs.text: These two courses are part of the MSc in Communication Engineering programme, which includes several other courses (optimization and stochastic processes, communication systems, networks, and more). A centralized programme hub listing all MSc course sites is planned. Until it exists, this site serves only the DSP track — no cross-links to the other courses are provided here.

docs.title: Feedback and Corrections
docs.text: This site is a living document. If you spot an error, a typo, a broken link, or an explanation that isn't clear, please report it — the course improves when students tell me what doesn't work.

docs.title: What to report
docs.text: Category Examples Typo Misspelled word, wrong punctuation, inconsistent symbol (\(\lambda\) vs. \(\Lambda\)) Mathematical error Wrong sign, missing factor, incorrect formula, incorrect numeric answer Broken link A chapter link that returns 404, a reference to a textbook chapter that doesn't exist Rendering problem Equation not displaying, table misaligned, code block unreadable on mobile Clarity issue A worked example whose steps don't follow; a definition that is ambiguous; a solution step that skips justification Tutorial problem A problem that is under-specified, has no solution, or contradicts the chapter Attribution A borrowed figure or example that isn't credited Accessibility Missing alt text, poor colour contrast, keyboard-inaccessible interaction

docs.title: What not to report here
docs.text:
• Grade queries — email the instructor directly (see Assessment).
  • Extension requests — email the instructor with documentation.
  • General questions — post on the course forum.
  • Requests to add material — email the instructor; scope changes are considered at the start of each semester.

docs.title: Option A — open a GitHub issue (preferred)
docs.text:
1. Visit the repository: github.com/tesfamichael-g/ECEG-DSP-Courses
  2. Click Issues → New issue.
  3. Choose the "Content correction" template.

  4. Fill in:

  5. Page (e.g. chapters/03-constrained-optimization or solutions/05-spectral-representation)

  6. Section (e.g. "Example 3.4" or "Problem 5.3")
  7. What is wrong (quote the text or paste a screenshot)
  8. What it should be (your correction or reasoning)
  9. Severity (typo / minor / major / blocking)

docs.title: Option B — email the instructor
docs.text: For sensitive reports (e.g. a solution that reveals too much detail about an upcoming assessment), email with subject line [ECEG-DSP-Courses feedback] so it doesn't get lost:

docs.title: Response times
docs.text:
Severity Response target Fix target Blocking (site broken, wrong formula in a major example) 24 hours 48 hours Major (wrong numeric answer, unreadable example) 3 days 1 week Minor (unclear explanation, small typo) 1 week next content pass Enhancement (new example, expanded discussion) acknowledgment within 1 week; implemented at the start of the next semester

Fixes are deployed automatically via GitHub Actions when pushed to the main branch. The "last updated" date in the footer of each page reflects the most recent change.

docs.title: Acknowledged contributions
docs.text:
Contributors who report errors that lead to a substantive fix are acknowledged by name on the affected page (with permission). This is a small way of recognising the effort of the students and colleagues who help improve the course.

If you would rather stay anonymous, just say so when you report — the acknowledgment is entirely opt-in.

docs.title: How this page is maintained
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs + Material theme, deployed via GitHub Pages. All content lives in the docs/ directory of the repository. Corrections are made by editing the corresponding .md file and pushing to main — the GitHub Actions workflow rebuilds and redeploys in under a minute.

The # file name: header at the top of each chat exchange is not part of the published site; it's an artefact of how the course materials are drafted and reviewed.

docs.title: Thank you
docs.text: A course is never finished. Every correction you send makes the next cohort's experience a little better. Thank you for taking the time to write one.

docs.title: ECEG-6303 — Advanced Digital Signal Processing
docs.text:
MSc in Communication Engineering · Year 1, Semester I

This is the course website for Advanced Digital Signal Processing. It extends the classical DSP sequence into statistical and adaptive signal processing: random-signal models, spectrum estimation, Wiener and Kalman filtering, adaptive filters (LMS, RLS), and multirate techniques.

📖 This course is part of the MSc DSP track

The companion course ECEG-6423 — Multimedia Signal Processing shares the same DSP Primer and software setup.

docs.title: Course at a glance
docs.text:
Course code ECEG-6303 Credit hours (ECTS) 3 (5) Semester Year 1, Semester I Status Compulsory Core Pre-requisites None Instructor Dr. Tesfamichael Gebregziabher Contact (office, email, office hours)

Student workload (hours/week)

Lecture Tutorial Practice / Laboratory Home study 2 – 3 5

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this course you will be able to:

  1. Analyze discrete random processes: expectations, variance, covariance, energy, Parseval's theorem, Wiener–Khinchine, power spectral density, periodogram, sample autocorrelation, spectral factorization.
  2. Estimate spectra using nonparametric (correlation, periodogram, Bartlett, Welch) and parametric (AR, MA, ARMA) methods, and evaluate their bias and variance.
  3. Design linear estimators and predictors: Wiener filter, Kalman filter, Levinson recursion, lattice realization, whitening filter.
  4. Design adaptive filters: steepest-descent LMS, Widrow–Hoff algorithm, adaptive equalization, echo cancellation, noise cancellation, RLS.
  5. Apply multirate DSP techniques: decimation, interpolation, polyphase realization, filter banks, wavelet transforms.

docs.title: Chapter overview
docs.text:
• Discrete Random Signal Processing

    Discrete random processes, moments, Parseval, Wiener–Khinchine, PSD, periodogram, sample autocorrelation, sum decomposition, spectral factorization, linear filtering, simulation of white noise, lowpass filtering of white noise.

    Chapter 1

  • Spectrum Estimation

    Nonparametric methods (correlation, covariance, periodogram, Bartlett, Welch) and parametric model-based methods (AR, MA, ARMA, Yule–Walker).

    Chapter 2

  • Linear Estimation and Prediction

    ML criterion, efficiency, MSE, Wiener filter, Wiener–Hopf equations, Kalman filter, linear prediction, Levinson recursion, lattice realization.

    Chapter 3

  • Adaptive Filters

    Steepest descent, LMS (Widrow–Hoff), adaptive equalization, echo cancellation, noise cancellation, RLS (exponentially weighted and sliding window).

    Chapter 4

  • Multirate DSP

    Sampling-rate change, decimation, interpolation, polyphase realization, filter banks, wavelet transform.

    Chapter 5

docs.text:
Component Weight Tests 20% Project and labs 30% Final examination 50% Total 100%

See Assessment for the detailed rubric and policies.

docs.title: Recommended preparation
docs.text:
• Signals and systems — convolution, z-transform, DFT, sampling theory
  • Probability — random variables, expectation, variance, distributions
  • Linear algebra — matrix algebra, eigenvalues, positive-definiteness
  • Programming — Python (NumPy/SciPy) for the labs; MATLAB acceptable

If any of these feels weak, start with the DSP Primer before Chapter 1.

docs.title: Course policy
docs.text:
• All students are expected to abide by the code of conduct of the University's Senate Legislation throughout this course.
  • 80% lecture attendance and 100% lab attendance are mandatory.

docs.title: Assessment — ECEG-6303
docs.text: Component Weight Timing Tests (3) 20% Weeks 4, 8, 14 Project and labs 30% Project released week 10, due week 15 Final examination 50% Week 18

docs.title: Tests (20%)
docs.text: Three 45-minute in-class tests, weighted 5% / 7% / 8% (increasing weight reflects increasing difficulty). Closed book; one handwritten A4 formula sheet allowed.

docs.title: Project and labs (30%)
docs.text:
• Labs (15%). Seven lab reports — one per major chapter topic — submitted as Jupyter notebooks. Graded on correctness, interpretation, and code clarity.
  • Project (15%). A self-contained implementation of one algorithm family (LMS, RLS, or spectrum estimation) applied to a real dataset. Report + code. Attendance at all labs is mandatory — missing more than 1 lab without documented cause results in loss of the lab mark.

docs.title: Final examination (50%)
docs.text: 3 h, closed book. Covers Chapters 1–5 in proportion to teaching hours (~20% per chapter). Formula sheet allowed (one A4, handwritten). Non-programmable calculator permitted.

docs.title: Grade boundaries
docs.text: Standard MSc programme boundaries apply (A: 90+, B: 75–89, C: 60–74, F: <60).

docs.title: Course policy
docs.text:
• Attendance: 80% lecture, 100% lab — mandatory.
  • Late lab reports: 10% per calendar day, up to 3 days; after that, zero.
  • Academic integrity: plagiarism and unauthorised AI use result in a zero on the affected component and a report to the Dean's office.

docs.title: Exam Bank — ECEG-6303 Advanced Digital Signal Processing
docs.text:
40 questions spanning all five chapters. Use for self-assessment and exam preparation. Answers and grading rubric at the end.

Instructions (for a mock exam):

  • Time: 3 hours
  • Closed book; one A4 handwritten formula sheet allowed
  • Non-programmable calculator permitted
  • Total marks: 100
  • Marks per question in brackets

docs.title: Section A — Discrete Random Signal Processing (Ch 1) — 20 marks
A1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
For a finite-length sequence, Parseval's theorem with the \(N\)-point DFT states:

(a) \(\sum |x[n]|^2 = \sum |X[k]|^2\) (b) \(\sum |x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum |X[k]|^2\) (c) \(\sum |x[n]|^2 = N \sum |X[k]|^2\) (d) \(\sum |x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum |X[k]|^2\)

docs.title: A2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The Wiener–Khinchine relation for a WSS discrete process states that:

(a) The PSD is the DFT of the signal (b) The PSD is the DTFT of the autocorrelation (c) The autocorrelation is the DFT of the signal (d) The PSD is the mean of the signal

docs.title: A3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: For a finite-length sample \(x[0], \ldots, x[N-1]\), state the biased and unbiased sample autocorrelation estimators. Which is preferred for spectral estimation and why?

docs.title: A4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the Sum Decomposition Theorem (discrete Karhunen–Loève). What is the truncation error when keeping only \(M\) of \(N\) components?

docs.title: A5. Derivation [5]
docs.text: State the Spectral Factorization Theorem for a rational PSD \(S_X(z)\). Show that if \(S_X = \sigma_e^2 H(z)H(z^{-1})\) with \(H\) causal and minimum-phase, then \(H^{-1}(z)\) is a causal whitening filter.

docs.title: A6. Short answer [5]
docs.text: For a WSS input \(X\) to an LTI system with impulse response \(h\): (i) state the output PSD, output autocorrelation, and output mean; (ii) explain why the mean is filtered by \(H(e^{j0})\) but the PSD is multiplied by \(|H(e^{j\omega})|^2\).

docs.title: B1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The periodogram of a Gaussian WSS process is:

(a) Consistent (b) Inconsistent — variance does not shrink with \(N\) (c) Biased and inconsistent (d) Exact

docs.title: B2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Welch's method improves on Bartlett's by adding:

(a) More segments only (b) Overlap and windowing (c) Larger segments (d) Higher FFT resolution

docs.title: B3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the bias-variance trade-off of the periodogram. Why is it a problem in practice, and how do Bartlett and Welch address it?

docs.title: B4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Describe the Blackman–Tukey estimator. State the role of the lag window and the MSE-optimal choice of its half-length \(M\).

docs.title: B5. Derivation [5]
docs.text: For an AR(\(p\)) process with autocorrelation \(R[k]\), derive the Yule–Walker equations by minimizing the prediction error \(\mathcal E = \sum e[n]^2\). State the resulting linear system and the prediction-error variance formula.

docs.title: B6. Short answer [5]
docs.text: State the three model-order selection criteria AIC, MDL, and FPE. For \(N = 500\) training samples and a simulated AR(4) process, which criterion would you trust most, and why?

docs.title: Section C — Linear Estimation and Prediction (Ch 3) — 20 marks
C1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The Cramér–Rao lower bound gives:

(a) A lower bound on the bias of an estimator (b) A lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator (c) The minimum MSE for nonlinear estimators (d) The Fisher information

docs.title: C2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
For jointly Gaussian signals, the LMMSE estimator:

(a) Is worse than MMSE (b) Is identical to the MMSE (c) Is nonlinear (d) Does not exist

docs.title: C3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the orthogonality principle for LMMSE. Derive the closed-form solution \(\hat S = \mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\).

docs.title: C4. Derivation [5]
docs.text: State the Kalman filter predict and update equations. Show that the steady-state behaviour (via the discrete algebraic Riccati equation) matches the causal Wiener filter for a stationary process.

docs.title: C5. Short answer [5]
docs.text: State the linear prediction problem for a WSS sequence. Show that the optimal predictor coefficients satisfy the Yule–Walker equations, and that the prediction error is the innovations process.

docs.title: C6. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Describe the lattice filter structure. State the stability condition \(|k_m| < 1\) and explain why it is a local (per-stage) condition.

docs.title: D1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The LMS algorithm minimizes at each step:

(a) The global MSE (b) The instantaneous squared error \(e^2(n)\) (c) The weighted least-squares cost (d) The maximum likelihood

docs.title: D2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
RLS convergence rate is:

(a) Strongly dependent on eigenvalue spread (b) Independent of eigenvalue spread (c) Always slower than LMS (d) Unbounded

docs.title: D3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: State the LMS convergence condition (mean and mean-square), the time constant of the slowest mode, and the misadjustment formula.

docs.title: D4. Derivation [5]
docs.text: Derive the LMS algorithm from steepest descent on the MSE surface. Replace the true gradient with the instantaneous estimate and derive the update rule \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu\, e(n)\,\mathbf x(n)\).

docs.title: D5. Short answer [4]
docs.text: State the NLMS update. Explain why NLMS converges at a rate independent of input power, and give one application where this matters.

docs.title: D6. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Describe adaptive noise cancellation. Why must the reference noise be correlated with the noise in the primary input? State the achievable SNR improvement in terms of correlation coefficient \(\rho\).

docs.title: E1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
For decimation by \(M\), the required anti-aliasing filter cutoff is:

(a) \(\pi\) (b) \(\pi/M\) (c) \(\pi/(2M)\) (d) \(\pi L\)

docs.title: E2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The Noble identity for decimation states:

(a) \(H(z) \downarrow M = \downarrow M \, H(z^M)\) (b) \(H(z) \downarrow M = \downarrow M \, H(z)\) (c) \(H(z) \downarrow M = M H(z/M)\) (d) \(H(z) \downarrow M = \downarrow M \, H(-z)\)

docs.title: E3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Describe the polyphase decomposition of a length-\(N_h\) FIR filter for \(M\) channels. State the computational advantage of the polyphase decimator over the direct form.

docs.title: E4. Derivation [5]
docs.text: Derive the polyphase decomposition \(H(z) = \sum_{r=0}^{M-1} z^{-r} E_r(z^M)\) and the corresponding polyphase decimator structure. Show the number of multiplications per output sample.

docs.title: E5. Short answer [4]
docs.text: For a two-channel QMF filter bank with \(H_1(z) = H_0(-z)\), \(F_0(z) = H_0(z)\), \(F_1(z) = -H_1(z)\), state the perfect reconstruction conditions and verify that the aliasing-cancellation condition holds.

docs.title: E6. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Describe the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) as an iterated filter bank. Why does the DWT provide multi-resolution analysis, and what is the role of vanishing moments?

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text: Click to reveal answers

docs.title: Section A
docs.text:
A1. (b) — \(\frac{1}{N}\) factor with the DFT convention where inverse has \(1/N\).

A2. (b).

A3. Biased: \(\hat R[k] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-|k|} x[n+|k|]x^*[n]\). Unbiased: \(\hat R_u[k] = \frac{1}{N-|k|}\sum x[n+|k|]x^*[n]\). Biased preferred for spectral estimation because (i) it is positive-definite (its DTFT is a valid non-negative PSD); (ii) it has lower variance at large lags; (iii) its \(O(1/N)\) bias vanishes asymptotically.

A4. For zero-mean random vector \(\mathbf X\) of length \(N\) with covariance \(\mathbf R\), decompose \(\mathbf R = \sum_{k=1}^N \lambda_k \mathbf v_k \mathbf v_k^\top\) and \(\mathbf X = \sum_{k=1}^N Z_k \mathbf v_k\) with \(\mathbb E[Z_i Z_j] = \lambda_i \delta_{ij}\). Truncation error: \(E[\|\mathbf X - \hat{\mathbf X}_M\|^2] = \sum_{k=M+1}^N \lambda_k\) — the residual energy.

A5. Spectral Factorization Theorem: any rational PSD \(S_X(z)\) with no zeros on the unit circle and \(\int\log S_X > -\infty\) can be factored uniquely as \(S_X(z) = \sigma_e^2 L(z) L(z^{-1})\) with \(L\) causal, monic, and minimum-phase. Whitening: \(H^{-1}(z) = 1/L(z)\) is causal because \(L\) has all poles and zeros inside the unit circle (minimum-phase = all zeros inside; causality = all poles inside). Its output is white of variance \(\sigma_e^2\).

A6. (i) \(\mu_Y = \mu_X H(e^{j0})\), \(S_Y = |H|^2 S_X\), \(R_Y = R_X * (h*h^\dagger)\) where \(h^\dagger[k] = h^*[-k]\). (ii) Mean: the DC component of \(X\) is what contributes to \(\mu_Y\); only the filter's DC gain \(H(e^{j0})\) matters because a constant passes a filter with only its DC gain. PSD: each frequency \(\omega\) of the input is scaled by the filter's magnitude response at that frequency — hence the pointwise multiplication by \(|H(e^{j\omega})|^2\).

docs.title: Section B
docs.text:
B1. (b) — inconsistent.

B2. (b) — overlap and windowing.

B3. Asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent — its variance is \(S_X^2\) at every \(N\). Practically, the periodogram is a "spiky noise" that never smooths out with more data. Bartlett averages over non-overlapping segments to reduce variance (÷\(K\)); Welch adds overlap (more segments) and windowing (lower bias). Both achieve consistency at the cost of resolution.

B4. BT: \(\hat S_X(\omega) = \sum_{k=-(M-1)}^{M-1} w[k] \hat R_X[k] e^{-j\omega k}\). Lag window \(w[k]\) smooths the periodogram — larger \(M\) = less smoothing = lower bias but higher variance. Bias-variance trade-off: Bias \(\sim 1/M\), variance \(\sim M/N\); MSE-optimal at \(M \sim N^{1/3}\).

B5. Model: \(x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^p a_k x[n-k] + e[n]\). Minimize \(\mathcal E = \sum_n e[n]^2 = \sum_n (x[n] + \sum a_k x[n-k])^2\). \(\partial \mathcal E/\partial a_k = 0\) gives \(\sum_n (x[n] + \sum a_l x[n-l])x[n-k] = 0\), i.e., \(R[k] + \sum_l a_l R[k-l] = 0\), so \(\sum_l a_l R[k-l] = -R[k]\) for \(k=1,\ldots,p\). Matrix form: \(\mathbf R \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\) with \(\mathbf R\) Toeplitz. Variance: \(\sigma_e^2 = R[0] + \sum_k a_k R[k]\).

B6. AIC: \(N\log\hat\sigma_p^2 + 2p\) — tends to over-fit. MDL: \(N\log\hat\sigma_p^2 + p\log N\) — consistent (correct for large \(N\)), tends to under-fit. FPE: \(\hat\sigma_p^2 (N+p+1)/(N-p-1)\) — direct estimate of one-step prediction error. For \(N=500\), AR(4): all three typically agree near \(p=4\). MDL is the most reliable for identifying the true order because its penalty \(\log N\) grows with data, giving asymptotic consistency. AIC's \(2p\) penalty is fixed, so it tends to slightly over-fit — but at moderate \(N\), both work.

docs.title: Section C
docs.text:
C1. (b).

C2. (b).

C3. Orthogonality principle: the LMMSE estimator \(\hat S\) of \(S\) from \(Y\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y^\top] = 0\) and \(\mathbb E[S - \hat S] = 0\). Write \(\hat S = a + b^\top Y\); \(\mathbb E[S - \hat S] = 0\) gives \(a = \mu_S - b^\top \mu_Y\); \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y^\top] = 0\) gives \(\Sigma_{SY} - b^\top \Sigma_{YY} = 0\), so \(b = \Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{SY}^\top = \Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{YS}\). Substituting: \(\hat S = \mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\).

C4. Predict: \(\hat x_{k|k-1} = A\hat x_{k-1|k-1}\), \(P_{k|k-1} = AP_{k-1|k-1}A^\top + Q\). Update: \(K_k = P_{k|k-1}H^\top(HP_{k|k-1}H^\top + R)^{-1}\); \(\hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1} + K_k(z_k - H\hat x_{k|k-1})\); \(P_{k|k} = (I - K_kH)P_{k|k-1}\). Steady state: the Riccati equation converges to \(P^\star\), giving fixed \(K^\star\). The steady-state filter is LTI with transfer function \(H_{KF}(z) = K^\star/(1 - (A - K^\star H A)z^{-1})\) — matching the causal Wiener filter for the same signal and noise models.

C5. Predictor: \(\hat x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^p a_k x[n-k]\). Error: \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum a_k x[n-k]\). Minimize \(\mathbb E[e^2]\) over \(a_k\): \(\partial/\partial a_k = 2 \mathbb E[e[n] x[n-k]] = 0\) → orthogonality. Expanding gives Yule–Walker: \(R[k] + \sum_m a_m R[k-m] = 0\). Prediction error = innovations because the optimal predictor from the past leaves only the unpredictable part — exactly the innovations process of the Wold decomposition.

C6. Lattice: cascade of \(p\) stages, each with forward error \(f_m[n] = f_{m-1}[n] + k_m g_{m-1}[n-1]\) and backward error \(g_m[n] = g_{m-1}[n-1] + k_m f_{m-1}[n]\). Stability: \(|k_m| < 1\) for all \(m\) — each stage is an all-pass-like reflector with less than unit gain. Why local: each stage's stability depends only on that stage's \(k_m\); adding a stage cannot destabilise the earlier ones. The direct-form \(a_k\) coefficients, by contrast, require solving a root-finding problem to check stability globally.

docs.title: Section D
docs.text:
D1. (b).

D2. (b).

D3. Convergence: \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max}\) (mean and mean-square). Time constant: \( au_k = 1/(\mu\lambda_k)\); slowest mode \( au_{\max} = 1/(\mu\lambda_{\min})\). Misadjustment: \(M \approx \mu \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)/2\).

D4. Steepest descent: \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) - \mu abla J\) with \( abla J = -2\mathbf p + 2\mathbf R\mathbf w\). Replace true gradient with instantaneous estimate \(\widehat{ abla J} = -2e(n)\mathbf x(n)\) (the gradient of \(e^2(n)\)). Then \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) - \mu \cdot rac{1}{2} \cdot (-2e(n)\mathbf x(n)) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu e(n)\mathbf x(n)\).

D5. \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + rac{ ilde\mu}{\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2 + \delta} e(n) \mathbf x(n)\). Rate independence: the effective step size is \( ilde\mu\), independent of input power \(\|\mathbf x\|^2\). Plain LMS's effective step is \(\mu\|\mathbf x\|^2\), which varies with input amplitude. Application: speech echo cancellation — far-end speech power varies by 40+ dB; NLMS converges stably throughout, plain LMS diverges at loud peaks or is too slow at quiet troughs.

D6. Primary \(d = s + v_0\) (signal + noise); reference \(x = v_1\) (correlated noise). Adaptive filter \(w\) predicts \(v_0\) from \(x\); output \(e = d - w*x \approx s\). Correlation requirement: if \(x\) and \(v_0\) are uncorrelated, no linear filter of \(x\) predicts \(v_0\); adaptation has no useful gradient. SNR improvement: \(1/(1- ho^2)\) where \( ho\) is the correlation between \(v_0\) and \(v_1\). At \( ho = 0.9\): 7 dB; at \( ho = 0.99\): 17 dB; at \( ho = 0\): no improvement.

docs.title: Section E
docs.text:
E1. (b) — \(\pi/M\).

E2. (a) — \(H(z)\downarrow M = \downarrow M \, H(z^M)\).

E3. Split \(h[n]\) into \(M\) polyphase subsequences \(E_r\) (every \(M\)-th tap starting at offset \(r\)), so \(H(z) = \sum_{r=0}^{M-1} z^{-r} E_r(z^M)\). Advantage: the polyphase decimator runs each \(E_r\) at the lower rate \(f_s/M\) — no wasted computation, no high-rate memory access. Multiplications per output same as direct form, but throughput 2× (or \(M\)×) faster because all computation is at the lower rate.

E4. \(H(z) = \sum_{k} h[k] z^{-k} = \sum_{r=0}^{M-1} z^{-r} \sum_m h[mM+r] z^{-mM} = \sum_r z^{-r} E_r(z^M)\) with \(E_r(z) = \sum_m h[mM+r] z^{-m}\). Polyphase decimator: \(y[n] = \sum_r (E_r * x_r)[n]\) where \(x_r[n] = x[nM - r]\). Multiplications per output: \(M \cdot (N_h/M) = N_h\), all at rate \(f_s/M\); per input sample equivalent \(N_h/M\).

E5. PR conditions: aliasing cancellation \(F_0 H_0(-z) + F_1 H_1(-z) = 0\); distortion elimination \(F_0 H_0 + F_1 H_1 = 2 z^{-d}\). Check with QMF choice: \(F_0 H_0(-z) + F_1 H_1(-z) = H_0(z)H_0(-z) + (-H_0(-z))H_0(z) = 0\) ✓. The distortion condition becomes \(H_0^2(z) - H_0^2(-z) = 2 z^{-d}\), the half-band condition (power-complementary in frequency).

E6. DWT as iterated filter bank: apply a 2-channel QMF to the signal, then apply the same QMF to the lowpass output, recursively \(J\) times. Produces \(J\) detail subbands (highpass at each level) plus 1 approximation subband. Multi-resolution: short wavelets (high frequency) resolve transient structure in time; long wavelets (low frequency) resolve fine spectral structure. Vanishing moments: a wavelet with \(p\) vanishing moments has zero inner product with any polynomial of degree \(<p\), so the detail coefficients of smooth signals are near zero — sparse representation → compression and denoising.

docs.title: Grading rubric (for instructors)
docs.text:
Band Marks Criteria A 90–100 All correct or with trivial slips; rigorous derivations; clear interpretation B 75–89 Most correct; occasional gaps; derivations mostly sound C 60–74 Basic understanding; some errors in derivations or interpretation F < 60 Major conceptual gaps; significant derivations missing

Common error checks (and deductions):

  • Missing \(1/N\) in Parseval (DFT convention): −1.
  • Claiming periodogram is consistent: −2.
  • Yule–Walker sign convention (\(\mathbf R\mathbf a = +\mathbf r\) instead of \(-\mathbf r\)): −1 to −2.
  • Kalman gain missing matrix inverse: −2.
  • LMS convergence bound \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\min}\) instead of \(2/\lambda_{\max}\): −2.
  • Noble identity direction reversed: −2.
  • QMF aliasing condition missing one filter sign: −1.
  • \(|k_m| < 1\) interpreted as global stability without justification: −1.

docs.title: Course description
docs.text:
This course extends the classical digital signal processing sequence into statistical and adaptive signal processing. It develops the mathematical foundation for analysing random signals in discrete time, for estimating their spectra from finite data, for predicting and filtering them optimally, and for adapting filter coefficients to track changing statistics.

Three threads run through the course.

  1. Statistical. Random signals, correlations, spectra, and how to estimate them from data.
  2. Estimation and prediction. ML and MMSE criteria, Wiener and Kalman filters, linear prediction, Levinson recursion, lattice filters.
  3. Adaptation. LMS, RLS, and their applications in equalisation, echo cancellation, and noise cancellation — plus the multirate tools (polyphase, filter banks) that make modern DSP hardware efficient.

The course is the first of two DSP courses in the MSc programme. Its companion, ECEG-6423 Multimedia Signal Processing, applies these tools to images, speech, and video. ECEG-6303 is a prerequisite for the more advanced parts of ECEG-6423.

docs.title: Chapter 1 — Discrete Random Signal Processing
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): discrete random processes · expectation, variance, covariance · scalar product and energy of discrete signals · Parseval's theorem · Wiener–Khinchine relation · power spectral density · periodogram · sample autocorrelation · Sum Decomposition Theorem · Spectral Factorization Theorem · discrete random signal processing by linear systems · simulation of white noise · lowpass filtering of white noise.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define a discrete-time random process and compute its mean, variance, autocovariance, and autocorrelation from the ensemble definition.
  2. State and apply Parseval's theorem for finite-length and for infinite-energy discrete signals.
  3. Derive the Wiener–Khinchine relation and compute the power spectral density (PSD) of a WSS sequence from its autocorrelation.
  4. Compute and interpret the periodogram, and state its bias and variance properties.
  5. Compute the sample autocorrelation in both biased and unbiased forms.
  6. Apply the Sum Decomposition Theorem (discrete Karhunen–Loève) to decompose a finite-length random vector into uncorrelated components.
  7. State the Spectral Factorization Theorem and factor a given rational PSD into causal minimum-phase factors.
  8. Compute the output PSD and output autocorrelation of an LTI system driven by a WSS input.
  9. Simulate white noise (uniform, Gaussian, arbitrary distribution) and colour it by lowpass filtering.

docs.title: 1.1 Discrete random processes
docs.text:
A discrete-time random process (also random sequence or stochastic sequence) is a family of random variables \(\{X[n] : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) indexed by integer time. For each fixed outcome \(\omega\) in the underlying probability space, the sequence \(n \mapsto X[n, \omega]\) is a realization or sample function of the process; the collection of all realizations is the ensemble.

Conventions

We use \(n\) for the discrete-time index, \([\cdot]\) for discrete-time sequences, and \(\mathbb{Z}\) for the set of all integers. Lowercase \(x[n]\) denotes a specific realization; uppercase \(X[n]\) the random variable at time \(n\).

For real-valued processes we usually work with the first and second moments:

\[ \mu_X[n] = \mathbb{E}[X[n]],\qquad \sigma_X^2[n] = \operatorname{Var}[X[n]] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X[n] - \mu_X[n])^2\bigr], \] \[ R_X[m, n] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[X[m] X[n]\bigr],\qquad C_X[m, n] = R_X[m,n] - \mu_X[m]\mu_X[n]. \]

For complex-valued processes, \(X[n]\) is complex and \(R_X[m,n] = \mathbb{E}[X[m]X^*[n]]\), where \(*\) denotes the complex conjugate.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Wide-sense stationarity (WSS)
docs.text:
A discrete random process is wide-sense stationary if:

  1. \(\mu_X[n] = \mu_X\) is constant (independent of \(n\)), and
  2. \(R_X[m, n] = R_X[m - n]\) depends only on the lag \(k = m - n\).

For a WSS process, we write \(R_X[k] = \mathbb{E}[X[n+k] X^*[n]]\) (the convention is \(X[n+k]X^*[n]\), so the autocorrelation is Hermitian-symmetric: \(R_X[-k] = R_X^*[k]\); for real processes, \(R_X[-k] = R_X[k]\)).

Properties of \(R_X[k]\) (real WSS):

Property Interpretation \(R_X[0] = \mathbb{E}[X^2[n]] = \operatorname{Var}[X] + \mu_X^2\) Power (or energy per sample, if zero-mean) \(R_X[-k] = R_X[k]\) Symmetry \(\lvert R_X[k]\rvert \le R_X[0]\) Peak at lag zero \(R_X[k]\) positive-definite For any coefficients \(a_i\): \(\sum_{i,j} a_i R_X[i-j] a_j^* \ge 0\)

WSS in the frequency domain — the PSD \(S_X(e^{j\omega})\) is the DTFT of \(R_X[k]\) (§1.7), and it inherits non-negativity from the positive-definiteness of \(R_X\).

docs.title: 1.2 Scalar product and energy of discrete signals
docs.text:
For two deterministic finite-length sequences \(x[n], y[n]\), \(n = 0, \dots, N-1\), the inner product is

\[ \langle x, y\rangle = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] y^*[n]. \]

This inner product makes \(\mathbb{C}^N\) a Hilbert space. The norm (or energy) of \(x\) is

\[ \|x\|^2 = \langle x, x\rangle = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |x[n]|^2. \]

For infinite-length sequences, the energy is

\[ E_x = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |x[n]|^2, \]

finite for energy signals; for power signals the relevant quantity is the average power,

\[ P_x = \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{2N+1} \sum_{n=-N}^{N} |x[n]|^2. \]

For a WSS random process, the average power is \(R_X[0] = \mathbb{E}[|X[n]|^2]\) — the fundamental bridge between the deterministic and the statistical view.

docs.title: 1.3 Parseval's theorem
docs.text:
For a finite-length signal \(x[n]\) with \(N\)-point DFT \(X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\):

\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} |X[k]|^2\;} \]

The factor \(1/N\) appears because the DFT convention absorbs \(N\) into the inverse transform. For the DTFT of an infinite-energy sequence, the form is

\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |X(e^{j\omega})|^2\, d\omega\;} \]

and for a WSS random process, replacing \(|X|^2\) by the PSD:

\[ \boxed{\;R_X[0] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_X(e^{j\omega})\, d\omega\;} \]

The last form is the statistical Parseval — the total power equals the integral of the PSD.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — Parseval for a rectangular pulse
docs.text:
Let \(x[n] = 1\) for \(n = 0, 1, \dots, N-1\) and zero otherwise.

Time domain energy. \(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |x[n]|^2 = N\).

Frequency domain. The \(N\)-point DFT of \(x\) is

\[ X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} e^{-j2\pi kn/N} = \begin{cases} N, & k = 0, \\ 0, & k \ne 0. \end{cases} \]

Parseval's check. \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} |X[k]|^2 = \frac{1}{N}\cdot N^2 = N\). ✓

DTFT check. \(X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{\sin(N\omega/2)}{\sin(\omega/2)} e^{-j(N-1)\omega/2}\), so \(|X|^2 = \sin^2(N\omega/2)/\sin^2(\omega/2)\). Then \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{\sin^2(N\omega/2)}{\sin^2(\omega/2)}\,d\omega = N\) ✓.

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — Statistical Parseval for an AR(1)
docs.text:
Let \(X[n] = a X[n-1] + W[n]\) with \(|a| < 1\) and \(W\) white of variance \(\sigma_W^2\). From Chapter 5 of ECEG-6201, we have

\[ R_X[k] = \frac{\sigma_W^2}{1-a^2}\, a^{|k|},\qquad S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{\sigma_W^2}{|1 - a e^{-j\omega}|^2}. \]

Statistical Parseval. The right side is

\[ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{\sigma_W^2}{|1-ae^{-j\omega}|^2}\, d\omega = \frac{\sigma_W^2}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{1}{1-2a\cos\omega + a^2}\, d\omega. \]

The integral evaluates to \(\frac{2\pi}{1-a^2}\) (standard contour-integral result), so the RHS is \(\frac{\sigma_W^2}{1-a^2}\). ✓

This matches \(R_X[0] = \frac{\sigma_W^2}{1-a^2}\). ✓

docs.title: 1.4.1 Definitions
docs.text:
For a WSS process \(X[n]\):

\[ R_X[k] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[X[n+k]X^*[n]\bigr],\qquad C_X[k] = R_X[k] - |\mu_X|^2. \]

The autocorrelation measures linear dependence between samples \(k\) apart; the autocovariance subtracts the mean so that it vanishes when \(k \to \infty\) (for mixing processes).

docs.title: 1.4.2 Autocorrelation of common processes
docs.text: Process \(R_X[k]\) White noise (variance \(\sigma^2\)) \(\sigma^2 \delta[k]\) AR(1) (\(a\), \(\sigma_W^2\)) $\frac{\sigma_W^2}{1-a^2} a^{ Complex exponential \(e^{j\omega_0 n}\) (deterministic) \(e^{j\omega_0 k}\) Random-phase sinusoid \(\frac{A^2}{2}\cos(\omega_0 k)\) Moving average MA(1): \(X[n] = W[n] + b W[n-1]\) \(\sigma_W^2(1 + b^2)\delta[k] + b\sigma_W^2(\delta[k-1] + \delta[k+1])\)

docs.title: 1.4.3 Sample autocorrelation
docs.text:
Given a finite realization \(x[0], \dots, x[N-1]\), two estimators of \(R_X[k]\):

Biased estimator:

\[ \boxed{\;\hat{R}[k] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-|k|} x[n+|k|] x^*[n]\;,\quad |k| \le N-1.\;} \]

Unbiased estimator:

\[ \hat{R}_u[k] = \frac{1}{N - |k|}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-|k|} x[n+|k|]x^*[n]. \]

Trade-offs.

  • Bias. \(\hat{R}_u\) is unbiased; \(\hat{R}\) is biased by a factor of \((N-|k|)/N\), which is \(O(1/N)\) for \(|k| \ll N\).
  • Variance. \(\hat{R}_u\) has larger variance (its denominator \(N-|k|\) becomes small as \(|k| \to N\)), so \(\hat{R}\) has lower mean-square error at large lags.
  • Positive-definiteness. \(\hat{R}\) is guaranteed positive-definite (needed for spectral estimation); \(\hat{R}_u\) is not.

Why the biased version is standard. For spectral estimation, we need the estimated autocorrelation to be a valid PSD generator — i.e., its DTFT must be non-negative. Only the biased \(\hat{R}\) guarantees this. So we use \(\hat{R}\), accepting its \(O(1/N)\) bias in return for a well-behaved spectrum.

docs.title: 1.5 Wiener–Khinchine relation and power spectral density
docs.text:
For a WSS process \(X[n]\) with \(\sum_{k} |R_X[k]| < \infty\):

\[ \boxed{\;S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} R_X[k]\, e^{-j\omega k}\;} \]

with inverse

\[ R_X[k] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_X(e^{j\omega})\, e^{j\omega k}\, d\omega. \]

Properties of the PSD.

Property Reason \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) \ge 0\) \(R_X\) is positive-definite \(S_X(e^{j\omega})\) is \(2\pi\)-periodic Definition as a DTFT \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = S_X(e^{-j\omega})\) (real \(X\)) \(R_X[k] = R_X[-k]\) \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_X(e^{j\omega})\, d\omega = R_X[0]\) Statistical Parseval

When the condition \(\sum |R_X[k]| < \infty\) is violated (e.g., a pure sinusoid), \(S_X\) contains impulses (Dirac deltas) at the corresponding frequencies, and the integral is interpreted distributionally.

docs.title: Worked example 1.3 — PSD of the moving average MA(1)
docs.text:
Let \(X[n] = W[n] + b W[n-1]\) with \(W\) white of variance \(\sigma_W^2\).

Autocorrelation. \(\mathbb{E}[X[n]X[n+k]] = \sigma_W^2(\delta[k] + b\delta[k-1] + b\delta[k+1] + b^2 \delta[k])\), so

\[ R_X[0] = \sigma_W^2(1 + b^2),\quad R_X[\pm 1] = b\sigma_W^2,\quad R_X[k] = 0\ (|k| \ge 2). \]

PSD.

\[ S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_W^2[(1+b^2) + b e^{-j\omega} + b e^{j\omega}] = \sigma_W^2[(1+b^2) + 2b\cos\omega]. \]

Check. \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi \sigma_W^2[(1+b^2) + 2b\cos\omega]\, d\omega = \sigma_W^2(1+b^2) = R_X[0]\) ✓.

Non-negativity constraint. For \(S_X\) to be a valid PSD we need \(1 + b^2 + 2b\cos\omega \ge 0\) for all \(\omega\); the minimum is \(1 + b^2 - 2|b| = (1-|b|)^2 \ge 0\), always satisfied. So MA(1) is always a valid PSD generator.

docs.title: 1.6 The periodogram
docs.text:
For a finite-length realization \(x[0], \dots, x[N-1]\), the periodogram is

\[ \boxed{\;\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{N}\Bigl|\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, e^{-j\omega n}\Bigr|^2\;} \]

Evaluated at the DFT frequencies \(\omega_k = 2\pi k/N\), this equals \(\frac{1}{N}|X[k]|^2\), where \(X[k]\) is the \(N\)-point DFT.

Two properties (developed in Chapter 2):

  • Asymptotically unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega})] \to S_X(e^{j\omega})\) as \(N \to \infty\), but the bias is nonzero for finite \(N\) (the periodogram is a smoothed version of \(S_X\) with the Fejér kernel).
  • Inconsistent: \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega})] \approx S_X^2(e^{j\omega})\) regardless of \(N\). The estimate fluctuates as much as its mean; averaging over independent segments is required to reduce the variance (Bartlett, Welch; §2.1).

docs.title: Worked example 1.4 — periodogram of white noise
docs.text:
Let \(x[n]\) be white Gaussian of variance \(\sigma^2\), \(N\) samples.

Bias. \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega_k})] = \sigma^2\) (unbiased at DFT frequencies when \(x\) is white) — for general \(S_X\) the expectation is a smoothed version.

Variance. \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega_k})] = \sigma^4\), so the standard deviation of \(\hat{S}_X\) equals its mean. This is the fundamental inconsistency: averaging over the same \(N\)-sample realization does not reduce variance; only averaging over independent realisations does.

Distribution. \(\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega_k})/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_2/2 = \mathrm{Exp}(1)\), independent (asymptotically) across bins. A plot of the periodogram of white noise therefore looks like exponentially-distributed noise, not a flat line — even though its expectation is flat.

Reducing variance. Welch's method averages periodograms over \(K\) segments; the variance drops to \(\sigma^4/K\). See Chapter 2 for details.

docs.title: 1.7 Sum Decomposition Theorem
docs.text:
For a length-\(N\) real-valued zero-mean random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X[0], \dots, X[N-1])^\top\) with covariance matrix \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top] \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\), the Sum Decomposition Theorem (also called the discrete Karhunen–Loève or principal-component decomposition) is the eigen-decomposition

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf{R} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lambda_k\, \mathbf{v}_k\, \mathbf{v}_k^\top\;} \]

with \(\mathbf{v}_k\) orthonormal eigenvectors and \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_N \ge 0\) eigenvalues. The corresponding expansion

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf{X} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} Z_k\, \mathbf{v}_k,\qquad Z_k = \mathbf{v}_k^\top \mathbf{X}\;} \]

has the property that the coefficients \(Z_k\) are uncorrelated: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_i Z_j] = \lambda_i \delta_{ij}\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.5 — Sum decomposition for an AR(1)
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{X} = (X[0], \dots, X[N-1])^\top\) be a length-\(N\) block of an AR(1) process with \(R_X[k] = \rho^{|k|}\) (unit variance). The covariance matrix is Toeplitz:

\[ \mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \rho & \rho^2 & \cdots \\ \rho & 1 & \rho & \cdots \\ \rho^2 & \rho & 1 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \end{bmatrix}. \]

For \(N = 2\): \(\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 1 + \rho\), \(\lambda_2 = 1 - \rho\); eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt 2\), \(\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt 2\).

For \(\rho = 0.8\): \(\lambda_1 = 1.8\), \(\lambda_2 = 0.2\). Almost all the energy is in the "symmetric" direction; the "antisymmetric" direction is nearly noise. This is why a first-order linear predictor captures most of the signal in a highly-correlated process.

For general \(N\) and \(\rho\), the eigenvectors are discrete cosine transform (DCT) basis vectors only in the limit \(\rho \to 1\); for finite \(\rho\) they are slightly different. The eigenvalues decay as a geometric-like sequence, and the first few principal components capture most of the variance.

Compression implication. Retaining the first \(M\) components of the expansion — \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_M = \sum_{k=1}^{M} Z_k \mathbf{v}_k\) — minimises the mean-square reconstruction error over all rank-\(M\) linear projections. The residual energy is \(\sum_{k=M+1}^{N}\lambda_k\).

docs.title: 1.8 Spectral Factorization Theorem
docs.text:
The Spectral Factorization Theorem (also called the Fejér–Riesz theorem for trigonometric polynomials, and the Kolmogorov–Wiener or Wiener–Hopf factorization in the stochastic-process setting) is:

Spectral Factorization

Let \(S_X(z)\) be a rational power spectral density that is positive on the unit circle (\(S_X(e^{j\omega}) > 0\) for all \(\omega\)) and satisfies the Paley–Wiener condition \(\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\log S_X(e^{j\omega})\,d\omega > -\infty\). Then there exists a unique factorization

\[ \boxed{\;S_X(z) = \sigma_e^2\, H(z)\, H(z^{-1})\;} \]

where \(H(z)\) is causal (\(H(z) = \sum_{k\ge 0} h_k z^{-k}\) with \(h_0 = 1\)), minimum-phase (all poles and zeros strictly inside \(|z| < 1\)), and \(\sigma_e^2 = \exp\bigl(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\log S_X(e^{j\omega})d\omega\bigr) > 0\) is the innovations variance.

Why rational is not a serious restriction. Any PSD that arises from a finite-dimensional linear system driven by white noise has rational \(z\)-transform; this covers every AR, MA, ARMA, and state-space model. Non-rational PSDs are handled by truncation or by the general Paley–Wiener theorem.

Why minimum-phase matters. Among all causal filters with a given magnitude response, the minimum-phase factor \(H(z)\) has the smallest group delay and its inverse \(H^{-1}(z)\) is also causal — so the whitening filter \(1/H(z)\) is realisable in real time. Any other factorization would give a causal \(H\) with a larger \(\sigma_e^2\) (non-minimum-phase zeros waste innovation energy).

docs.title: How to factorize a rational PSD
docs.text:
Given \(S_X(z)\) as a ratio of polynomials in \(z\):

  1. Find the roots of the numerator and denominator polynomials in \(z\).
  2. Split each root pair \(\{z_0, 1/z_0^*\}\): put \(z_0\) in \(H(z^{-1})\) (its zero is at \(z_0\), outside the unit circle) and \(1/z_0^*\) in \(H(z)\) (its zero is at \(1/z_0^*\), inside the unit circle) — or vice versa, depending on the convention. The minimum-phase choice puts all interior roots in \(H(z)\).
  3. Normalize so that \(H(0) = 1\) (i.e., \(h_0 = 1\)).
  4. Compute \(\sigma_e^2\) from the leading coefficients.

docs.title: Worked example 1.6 — factorize an ARMA(1,1) PSD
docs.text:
\[ S_X(z) = \frac{(1 - 0.5 z^{-1})(1 - 0.5 z)}{(1 - 0.8 z^{-1})(1 - 0.8 z)}. \]

Roots. Numerator: \(z = 0.5\) (from \(1 - 0.5z^{-1}\), zero at \(z = 0.5\)) and \(z = 2\) (from \(1 - 0.5z\), zero at \(z = 2\)). Denominator: \(z = 0.8\) and \(z = 1.25\).

Minimum-phase factor. Put the interior roots (0.5, 0.8) in \(H(z)\):

\[ H(z) = \frac{1 - 0.5 z^{-1}}{1 - 0.8 z^{-1}},\qquad \sigma_e^2 = 1. \]

Verify.

\[ \sigma_e^2 H(z) H(z^{-1}) = \frac{(1 - 0.5z^{-1})(1 - 0.5z)}{(1 - 0.8z^{-1})(1 - 0.8z)} = S_X(z). ✓ \]

Whitening filter. \(H^{-1}(z) = \frac{1 - 0.8z^{-1}}{1 - 0.5z^{-1}}\) — causal, stable (both poles and zeros inside the unit circle), so realisable.

Non-minimum-phase alternative. Using the outer roots:

\[ H_{np}(z) = \frac{1 - 2 z^{-1}}{1 - 1.25 z^{-1}}\cdot\text{(constant)}. \]

This has the same \(|H(e^{j\omega})|^2\) but is non-minimum-phase — its inverse is not causal. Avoid.

docs.title: Worked example 1.7 — factorize an AR(2) PSD
docs.text:
\[ S_X(z) = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{(1 - 0.6 z^{-1})(1 - 0.7 z^{-1})(1 - 0.6 z)(1 - 0.7 z)}. \]

Minimum-phase factor:

\[ H(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - 0.6 z^{-1})(1 - 0.7 z^{-1})},\qquad \sigma_e^2 = \sigma_w^2. \]

The innovations are exactly the driving white noise \(w[n]\), as expected — this is an AR(2) process.

The predictor is \(a_1 = 0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3\), \(a_2 = -0.6\cdot 0.7 = -0.42\), so \(\hat x[n] = 1.3 x[n-1] - 0.42 x[n-2]\), and the innovations (prediction errors) are white.

docs.title: 1.9 Discrete random signal processing by linear systems
docs.text:
Let \(X[n]\) be WSS input to an LTI system with impulse response \(h[n]\) and frequency response \(H(e^{j\omega})\). The output is

\[ Y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[k] X[n-k]. \]

Output statistics.

\[ \boxed{\;\mu_Y = \mu_X \cdot H(e^{j0}) = \mu_X \sum_k h[k]\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = |H(e^{j\omega})|^2\, S_X(e^{j\omega})\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;R_Y[k] = R_X[k] * \bigl(h * h^\dagger\bigr)[k]\;} \]

where \(h^\dagger[k] = h^*[-k]\) is the matched (time-reversed conjugate) filter, and \(*\) denotes convolution.

Interpretation of the three formulas.

  • The mean is filtered by \(H(e^{j0})\): only the DC component passes; if \(H\) has a zero at DC, the output mean is zero.
  • The PSD is multiplied by \(|H|^2\): each frequency is attenuated or amplified independently.
  • The autocorrelation is \(R_X\) convolved with the deterministic autocorrelation \(h * h^\dagger\) of the filter — a generalisation of the deterministic formula \(y = h * x \Rightarrow r_{yy} = r_{xx} * (h*h^\dagger)\).

The output variance is

\[ \sigma_Y^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |H(e^{j\omega})|^2 S_X(e^{j\omega})\, d\omega, \]

the weighted average of \(S_X\) over \(|H|^2\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.8 — white noise through a first-order lowpass
docs.text:
\(X[n]\) white of variance \(\sigma_w^2\), filtered by \(H(z) = \frac{1-a}{1 - a z^{-1}}\) with \(|a| < 1\) (DC gain \(H(1) = 1\)).

Output PSD.

\[ S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_w^2 \cdot \frac{(1-a)^2}{(1 - a e^{-j\omega})(1 - a e^{j\omega})} = \frac{\sigma_w^2(1-a)^2}{1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2}. \]

Output autocorrelation (inverse DTFT of \(S_Y\)):

\[ R_Y[k] = \sigma_w^2\, \frac{1-a}{1+a}\, a^{|k|}. \]

Check variance. \(R_Y[0] = \sigma_w^2 \frac{1-a}{1+a}\). For \(a = 0\): \(R_Y[0] = \sigma_w^2\) ✓ (filter is identity, output = input). For \(a \to 1\): \(R_Y[0] \to 0\) ✓ (filter becomes an ideal DC selector; white noise has zero DC; output is zero).

Output mean. \(\mu_Y = \mu_X \cdot H(1) = \mu_X \cdot 1 = \mu_X\). For zero-mean white noise, output is zero-mean.

Correlation time. The decay rate of \(R_Y[k]\) is \(a^{|k|}\); the integrated autocorrelation time is \(\tau_{int} = \sum_k R_Y[k]/R_Y[0] = (1+a)/(1-a)\). As \(a \to 1\), the output is highly correlated; as \(a \to 0\), it approaches white noise.

docs.title: 1.10 Simulation of white noise
docs.text: To simulate a white noise sequence \(X[n]\) (IID with a given distribution):

docs.title: 1.10.1 Uniform noise
docs.text:
Any PRNG (Mersenne Twister, xorshift, PCG) produces approximately uniform \(\mathcal U[0,1)\) samples. In Python: np.random.rand(). In Java: java.util.Random.nextDouble(). In C#: System.Random.NextDouble().

For \(\mathcal U[a, b]\): \(X = a + (b-a)U\).

docs.title: 1.10.2 Gaussian noise — Box–Muller transform
docs.text:
If \(U_1, U_2\) are independent \(\mathcal U(0,1)\) samples, then

\[ \boxed{\;Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\,\cos(2\pi U_2),\qquad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\,\sin(2\pi U_2)\;} \]

are independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) samples. This is the Box–Muller transform.

Derivation sketch. Transform \((U_1, U_2)\) to polar \((R, \Theta)\): \(R = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\) and \(\Theta = 2\pi U_2\). The Jacobian gives the joint density

\[ f_{R,\Theta}(r,\theta) = \frac{r}{2\pi} e^{-r^2/2},\quad r \ge 0,\ 0 \le \theta < 2\pi, \]

which factors into \(R \sim \mathrm{Rayleigh}(1)\) and \(\Theta \sim \mathcal U[0, 2\pi)\). Then \(Z_1 = R\cos\Theta\), \(Z_2 = R\sin\Theta\) are the Cartesian coordinates of a 2-D standard Gaussian. ✓

docs.title: 1.10.3 Arbitrary distribution — inverse CDF
docs.text:
If \(F\) is the CDF of the desired distribution and \(U \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\), then

\[ X = F^{-1}(U) \]

has CDF \(F\). This is the inverse transform sampling method. Works for any strictly increasing \(F\); for distributions with atoms, handle them by intervals of \(U\).

docs.title: 1.10.4 Sample autocorrelation of simulated white noise
docs.text:
For \(N\) samples of white noise with variance \(\sigma^2\):

\[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{R}[k]] = egin{cases} \sigma^2 & k = 0 \ 0 & k e 0 \end{cases},\qquad \operatorname{Var}[\hat{R}[k]] \approx rac{\sigma^4}{N}. \]

So \(|\hat{R}[k]| \le 3\sigma^2/\sqrt N\) for \(k e 0\) with 99% confidence. This is the white-noise confidence band — any empirical autocorrelation that stays within \(\pm 3\sigma/\sqrt N\) for \(k e 0\) is consistent with white noise.

docs.title: Worked example 1.9 — Box–Muller in Python
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def box_muller(n, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    U1 = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n)
    U2 = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n)
    R = np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(U1))
    Z1 = R * np.cos(2*np.pi*U2)
    Z2 = R * np.sin(2*np.pi*U2)
    return np.concatenate([Z1, Z2])

z = box_muller(100_000)
print(f"mean: {z.mean():.4f}, var: {z.var():.4f}")  # ≈ 0, 1

This produces \(2n\) samples from a single pair of length-\(n\) uniform arrays. Empirical mean \(\approx 0\), variance \(\approx 1\) — verifying the transform.

docs.title: 1.11 Lowpass filtering of white noise — colouring
docs.text:
The point. White noise is an abstraction — no physical process has infinite bandwidth. Every real signal is white noise filtered by some LTI system (the source of the "colour"). Conversely, simulating a coloured process with a given PSD \(S_X\) amounts to

  1. Generating white noise \(W[n]\) of unit variance,
  2. Filtering it with the spectral factor \(H(z)\) from §1.8: \(X[n] = h * W[n]\).

This works because \(S_X = |H|^2\) when \(W\) has unit PSD.

docs.title: Worked example 1.10 — AR(1) as filtered white noise
docs.text:
\(X[n] = a X[n-1] + W[n]\), \(|a| < 1\), \(W\) white of variance \(\sigma_W^2\). The filter is \(H(z) = 1/(1-az^{-1})\); output PSD \(S_X = \sigma_W^2/(1-2a\cos\omega + a^2)\).

Simulation (Python):

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import lfilter

def simulate_ar1(a, sigma_w, N, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = rng.normal(0, sigma_w, size=N + 200)     # burn-in
    x = lfilter([1], [1, -a], w)[200:]           # discard transient
    return x

x = simulate_ar1(a=0.9, sigma_w=1.0, N=100_000)
print(f"empirical mean: {x.mean():.4f}")                 # ≈ 0
print(f"empirical variance: {x.var():.4f}")              # ≈ 1/(1-a²) = 5.263
print(f"empirical R_x[1]: {np.corrcoef(x[:-1], x[1:])[0,1]:.4f}")  # ≈ a = 0.9

docs.title: Worked example 1.11 — ideal lowpass (brick-wall) filter
docs.text:
Ideal lowpass with cutoff \(\omega_c\): \(|H(e^{j\omega})|^2 = 1\) for \(|\omega| \le \omega_c\), zero otherwise.

Output PSD. \(S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_w^2\) for \(|\omega| \le \omega_c\), zero otherwise.

Output autocorrelation. Inverse DTFT:

\[ R_Y[k] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\omega_c}^{\omega_c}\sigma_w^2\, e^{j\omega k}\,d\omega = \sigma_w^2\,\frac{\sin(\omega_c k)}{\pi k}. \]

Output variance. \(R_Y[0] = \sigma_w^2 \omega_c/\pi\) — proportional to bandwidth. The fractional bandwidth \(\omega_c/\pi\) is the fraction of white-noise power that survives.

The ideal lowpass is not causal (its impulse response is a sinc), so it can only be approximated in real time. This is why finite-length FIR approximations are used in practice, and why the AR(1) filter (causal, recursive, infinite-order) is so popular as a "practical lowpass" — one coefficient controls the cutoff.

docs.title: Worked example 1.12 — whitening a coloured process
docs.text:
Given a coloured process \(Y[n]\) with PSD \(S_Y = \sigma_e^2 |H|^2\), the whitening filter is \(G(z) = 1/H(z)\). Its output has PSD

\[ S_{Y_{\text{white}}}(e^{j\omega}) = |G(e^{j\omega})|^2 S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_e^2 \]

— flat, i.e., white noise of variance \(\sigma_e^2\). This is the inverse filter of the spectral factor.

For AR(1) with \(a = 0.9\): \(G(z) = 1 - 0.9 z^{-1}\), i.e., \(Y_{white}[n] = Y[n] - 0.9 Y[n-1]\). The output is white with variance \(\sigma_e^2 = \sigma_W^2\). Practical implication: the first-order difference \(Y[n] - 0.9 Y[n-1]\) is a whitening filter — a fact used throughout speech processing (where speech is approximated as AR) and Kalman filtering (where the innovations are the whitened observations).

docs.title: 1.12 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Discrete random processes are families of random variables indexed by integer \(n\). Wide-sense stationarity means constant mean and autocorrelation depending only on lag.
  2. Parseval's theorem — \(\sum_n |x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|X(e^{j\omega})|^2 d\omega\) — extends to WSS processes with \(R_X[0] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int S_X\,d\omega\).
  3. Wiener–Khinchine makes the PSD the DTFT of the autocorrelation; it is non-negative, \(2\pi\)-periodic, and integrates to \(R_X[0]\).
  4. The periodogram is the natural estimator; asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent (\(\mathrm{Var} \approx S_X^2\)).
  5. Sample autocorrelation — use the biased form to guarantee a valid PSD; use the unbiased form only for descriptive statistics.
  6. Sum Decomposition = eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix; the KL / PCA expansion in finite dimension.
  7. Spectral Factorization — every rational PSD with \(\int\log S > -\infty\) has a unique causal, minimum-phase factor \(S_X = \sigma_e^2|H|^2\); the innovations variance \(\sigma_e^2\) is the geometric mean of \(S_X\).
  8. Linear systems — \(S_Y = |H|^2 S_X\); output autocorrelation is \(R_X * (h*h^\dagger)\); the output mean is \(\mu_X H(1)\).
  9. White noise simulation — uniform from any PRNG, Gaussian from Box–Muller, arbitrary from inverse CDF.
  10. Coloured noise simulation — filter white noise with the spectral factor; whitening is the inverse filter.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. A WSS sequence has: (a) constant variance, arbitrary mean (b) constant mean, autocorrelation depending only on lag (c) Gaussian distribution (d) finite energy

  2. The energy of a sequence \(x[n]\) is \(\sum |x[n]|^2\). Parseval's theorem for finite-length sequences with the \(N\)-point DFT expresses this as: (a) \(\sum |X[k]|^2\) (b) \(\frac{1}{N}\sum |X[k]|^2\) (c) \(N\sum |X[k]|^2\) (d) \(\frac{1}{N^2}\sum |X[k]|^2\)

  3. The Wiener–Khinchine relation states that: (a) the PSD equals the DTFT of the autocorrelation (b) the autocorrelation is the DFT of the signal (c) the signal is the PSD (d) the noise is white

  4. For a WSS process, \(R_X[0]\) equals: (a) the mean (b) the variance (c) the total power (variance plus mean squared) (d) zero

  5. The biased sample autocorrelation is preferred over the unbiased form because: (a) it is unbiased (b) it has lower variance and is positive-definite (c) it is easier to compute (d) it is a better estimator of the mean

  6. The periodogram of white noise: (a) is a flat line (b) has mean \(S_X\) but standard deviation equal to the mean (c) is Gaussian (d) is zero at all frequencies

  7. The Sum Decomposition Theorem is equivalent to: (a) the FFT (b) the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix (c) the Z-transform (d) the DFT

  8. The Spectral Factorization Theorem says every rational PSD with \(\int\log S > -\infty\) has a unique causal, minimum-phase factor \(H(z)\) with: (a) \(S_X = |H|^2\) (b) \(S_X = \sigma_e^2 |H|^2\) (c) \(S_X = H\) (d) \(S_X = 1/H\)

  9. For white noise through an LTI filter with response \(H\): (a) output PSD = input PSD (b) output PSD = \(|H|^2 \times\) input PSD (c) output is white (d) output is non-stationary

  10. The Box–Muller transform generates: (a) uniform samples (b) exponential samples (c) Gaussian samples (d) Poisson samples

  11. The output variance of white noise of variance \(\sigma_w^2\) through a filter with impulse response \(h\) is: (a) \(\sigma_w^2\) (b) \(\sigma_w^2 \sum_k |h[k]|^2\) (c) \(\sigma_w^2 \sum_k h[k]\) (d) \(0\)

  12. The whitening filter for a process with spectral factor \(H(z)\) is: (a) \(H(z)\) (b) \(H(z^{-1})\) (c) \(1/H(z)\) (d) \(H(z) H(z^{-1})\)

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. A WSS process has constant mean and autocorrelation depending only on ____.
  2. \(R_X[0]\) equals $\sigma_X^2 + $____ for a WSS process.
  3. Parseval's theorem for finite-length sequences is \(\sum|x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum |X[k]|^2\) (with the \(N\)-point DFT); this holds because the DFT is ____-preserving.
  4. The Wiener–Khinchine relation is $S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{k} $____ \(\,e^{-j\omega k}\).
  5. The periodogram is \(\hat{S}_X = \frac{1}{N}\bigl|\sum_{n}\)____\(\bigr|^2\).
  6. The Sum Decomposition Theorem expresses a random vector as \(\mathbf{X} = \sum_k Z_k \mathbf{v}_k\) with $\mathbb{E}[Z_i Z_j] = $____ \(\delta_{ij}\).
  7. The Spectral Factorization Theorem gives $S_X(z) = $____ \(H(z) H(z^{-1})\) with \(H\) minimum-phase.
  8. For white noise of variance \(\sigma_w^2\) through a filter with impulse response \(h\), the output variance is \(\sigma_w^2 \sum_k\) ____.
  9. The whitening filter for a process with spectral factor \(H\) is ____.
  10. Box–Muller transforms two uniform samples into two ____ samples.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Define a discrete-time random process and state the conditions for wide-sense stationarity. Give one example that is WSS but not strictly stationary.
  2. State Parseval's theorem for finite-length sequences and for WSS processes. What is the interpretation in each case?
  3. State the Wiener–Khinchine relation. What is the physical interpretation of the PSD's non-negativity?
  4. Define the sample autocorrelation in both biased and unbiased forms. Why is the biased form preferred in spectral estimation?
  5. Define the periodogram and discuss its bias and variance as \(N \to \infty\). Why is it inconsistent?
  6. State the Sum Decomposition Theorem and interpret it as a data-compression scheme. What is the truncated approximation error?
  7. State the Spectral Factorization Theorem. Why is the minimum-phase factor unique and important?
  8. For WSS input to an LTI system with response \(H\), derive the output PSD, output autocorrelation, and output mean.
  9. Describe the Box–Muller transform and state what it is used for. Give the two formulas for \(Z_1, Z_2\).
  10. Explain what it means to colour white noise, and how the spectral factor is used in simulation.

docs.title: 1.14 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — constant mean + autocorrelation depends only on lag.
  2. (b) — \(\frac{1}{N}\sum|X[k]|^2\).
  3. (a) — PSD = DTFT of autocorrelation.
  4. (c) — \(R_X[0] = \sigma_X^2 + |\mu_X|^2\) (total power).
  5. (b) — lower variance, positive-definite.
  6. (b) — mean = \(S_X\), std = mean.
  7. (b) — eigen-decomposition of covariance.
  8. (b) — \(S_X = \sigma_e^2 |H|^2\).
  9. (b) — \(|H|^2 \times\) input PSD.
  10. (c) — Gaussian samples.
  11. (b) — \(\sigma_w^2 \sum |h[k]|^2\).
  12. (c) — \(1/H(z)\).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. lag
  2. \(|\mu_X|^2\) (or mean squared)
  3. energy
  4. \(R_X[k]\)
  5. \(x[n] e^{-j\omega n}\)
  6. \(\lambda_i\) (eigenvalues)
  7. \(\sigma_e^2\)
  8. \(|h[k]|^2\)
  9. \(1/H(z)\) (or \(H^{-1}(z)\))
  10. Gaussian (independent standard normal)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Discrete-time random process: family \(\{X[n]\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\) of random variables on a common probability space. WSS: (i) \(\mu_X[n] = \mu_X\) constant; (ii) \(R_X[m,n] = \mathbb{E}[X[m]X^*[n]]\) depends only on \(m - n\). Example WSS but not SSS: \(X[n] = A\cos(\omega_0 n + \Theta)\) with \(A\) a non-constant random amplitude (e.g., \(A \sim\) Rayleigh) independent of \(\Theta \sim \mathcal U(0,2\pi)\). Mean is zero, \(R_X[k] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[A^2]}{2}\cos(\omega_0 k)\) — WSS. But \(\mathbb{E}[X[n]^3] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[A^3]}{4}\cos(3\omega_0 n + \cdots)\) depends on \(n\), so the third-order moments are time-varying — not strictly stationary.
  2. Finite-length: \(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}|X[k]|^2\) where \(X[k]\) is the \(N\)-point DFT. Interpretation: energy in time = energy in frequency (the DFT is a unitary transform up to the factor \(N\)). WSS: \(R_X[0] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}S_X(e^{j\omega})d\omega\). Interpretation: total power = integral of PSD.
  3. \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_k R_X[k]e^{-j\omega k}\). Non-negativity interpretation: \(S_X \ge 0\) means that the autocorrelation is positive-definite, which reflects that power at any frequency cannot be negative — a physical necessity. Equivalently, the PSD is a "weight" for the spectral content of the process, so its negativity would imply negative energy at some frequency, which is impossible.
  4. Biased: \(\hat R[k] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-|k|} x[n+|k|]x^*[n]\). Unbiased: \(\hat R_u[k] = \frac{1}{N-|k|}\sum x[n+|k|]x^*[n]\). Why biased: (i) it is positive-definite — its DTFT is a valid PSD; (ii) it has lower mean-square error at large lags (the variance of \(\hat R_u\) blows up as \(|k| \to N\)); (iii) its \(O(1/N)\) bias vanishes asymptotically. For spectral estimation it is therefore the standard choice.
  5. \(\hat S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{N}|\sum x[n]e^{-j\omega n}|^2\). Bias: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat S_X] \to S_X\) as \(N \to \infty\), with \(O(1/N)\) bias for finite \(N\). Variance: \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat S_X] \approx S_X^2\) for all \(N\) — independent of record length. Why inconsistent: the variance does not shrink to zero, so increasing \(N\) at fixed realization does not improve accuracy. The fix is averaging over independent segments (Bartlett, Welch), or over independent realizations.
  6. Sum Decomposition: \(\mathbf{R} = \sum_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k \mathbf{v}_k^\top\); the covariance matrix eigen-decomposition. Data-compression interpretation: the truncated expansion \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_M = \sum_{k=1}^M Z_k \mathbf{v}_k\) retains the \(M\) largest-eigenvalue directions and discards the rest. Truncation error: \(\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{X} - \hat{\mathbf{X}}_M\|^2] = \sum_{k=M+1}^N \lambda_k\). This is the optimal rank-\(M\) linear compression in mean-square sense — the theoretical basis of PCA / KL / DCT-based compression.
  7. Statement: for a rational PSD positive on \(|z|=1\) with \(\int\log S > -\infty\), there exists a unique factorization \(S_X(z) = \sigma_e^2 H(z)H(z^{-1})\) with \(H\) causal, monic, minimum-phase. Uniqueness: among all factors with the same magnitude response, exactly one is minimum-phase (all zeros inside the unit circle). Importance: (i) \(H^{-1}\) is causal — the whitening filter is realizable; (ii) it gives the smallest innovations variance \(\sigma_e^2\) — the most efficient representation; (iii) it is the basis of every AR/ARMA model and every innovations representation.
  8. Output PSD: \(S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = |H(e^{j\omega})|^2 S_X(e^{j\omega})\). Derivation: \(\mathbb{E}[Y[n+k]Y^*[n]] = \sum_{i,j} h[i]h^*[j] R_X[k + i - j]\); taking the DTFT and reordering gives the product form. Output autocorrelation: \(R_Y[k] = R_X[k] * (h*h^\dagger)[k]\) — convolution of input autocorrelation with the filter's deterministic autocorrelation. Output mean: \(\mu_Y = \mu_X H(e^{j0}) = \mu_X \sum_k h[k]\) — the filter's DC gain.
  9. Box–Muller: generates two independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) samples from two independent \(\mathcal U(0,1)\) samples. \(Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2)\), \(Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)\). Use: simulating Gaussian noise when only a uniform PRNG is available; also gives insight into the polar decomposition of the 2-D Gaussian.
  10. Colouring = passing white noise through a filter so the output has the desired PSD. If the target PSD is \(S_X = \sigma_w^2 |H|^2\), filtering unit-variance white noise through \(H(z)\) gives output with PSD \(S_X\). The spectral factor \(H\) is obtained from §1.8. The simulation recipe: (i) generate white noise of unit variance; (ii) apply \(H\) via scipy.signal.lfilter or its Java/C# equivalent; (iii) the output is the simulated process. Conversely, whitening applies \(H^{-1}\) to remove the correlation and produce white noise.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Parseval check. For \(x[n] = a^n u[n]\) with \(|a| < 1\), verify Parseval's theorem for infinite-length energy signals: \(\sum |x[n]|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int |X(e^{j\omega})|^2 d\omega\).
  2. Autocorrelation derivation. Derive \(R_X[k]\) for \(X[n] = A\cos(\omega_0 n + \Theta)\) with \(\Theta\) uniform and \(A\) fixed. Compare with the continuous-time result.
  3. Wiener–Khinchine inverse. Given \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1 - a^2}{|1 - a e^{-j\omega}|^2}\) with \(|a| < 1\), compute \(R_X[k]\) by inverse DTFT. Verify the answer is \(\rho^{|k|}\) with \(\rho = a\).
  4. Periodogram variance study. Simulate \(N = 256\) samples of white Gaussian noise, compute the periodogram, and plot its histogram over frequencies. Verify that \(\hat S_X/\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\). Repeat for \(N = 4096\) and \(N = 65536\) — does the variance change?
  5. Sum decomposition. For an AR(1) with \(\rho = 0.9\) and \(N = 16\), compute the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix numerically. Plot the eigenvalues. How many components capture 99% of the variance? Compare with \(\rho = 0.5\).
  6. Spectral factorization exercise. Factorize \(S_X(z) = \frac{(1 - 0.3z^{-1})(1 - 0.3z)}{(1 - 0.9z^{-1})(1 - 0.9z)}\) into a causal, minimum-phase \(H(z)\) with \(\sigma_e^2\). Compute the whitening filter \(1/H\).
  7. Filtering of white noise. White noise of variance \(1\) passes through \(H(z) = 1 + 0.5 z^{-1}\). Compute the output PSD, autocorrelation, and variance. Verify by simulation.
  8. Box–Muller statistics. Generate 100,000 Gaussian samples using Box–Muller. Verify the empirical mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis against the theoretical \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) values. Plot the histogram and compare to the Gaussian PDF.
  9. Colouring exercise. Generate white noise, apply an AR(2) filter with \(a_1 = 1.3\), \(a_2 = -0.42\). Plot the empirical PSD (using Welch) and compare against the theoretical \(S_X = \sigma_w^2/|1 - 1.3e^{-j\omega} + 0.42e^{-2j\omega}|^2\).
  10. Whitening speech. Download a segment of voiced speech (or use pyroomacoustics sample). Fit an AR(10) model, apply the whitening filter, and verify the residual is close to white (its autocorrelation outside lag 0 is within \(\pm 3/\sqrt N\)). Interpret the result in terms of the source-filter model of speech.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Spectrum Estimation
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): nonparametric methods (correlation method, covariance estimator, unbiased/consistent estimators, periodogram, Bartlett, Welch) · performance analysis of estimators · model-based approach (AR, MA, ARMA signal modelling) · parameter estimation using the Yule–Walker method.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the difference between nonparametric and model-based spectrum estimation, and choose between them based on data length, prior knowledge, and resolution requirements.
  2. State the bias, variance, MSE, and consistency of an estimator, and prove that the periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent.
  3. Compute and interpret the Bartlett and Welch spectrum estimators, and quantify their variance reduction relative to the raw periodogram.
  4. Apply the correlation method (Blackman–Tukey) using a windowed autocorrelation estimate, and analyse the trade-off between bias (window choice) and variance (window length).
  5. Distinguish the autocorrelation and covariance variants of the correlation method, and explain when each is preferred.
  6. Model a WSS process as AR, MA, or ARMA; estimate parameters via the Yule–Walker equations; solve them efficiently using Levinson–Durbin.
  7. Compute the AR / MA / ARMA PSD from the estimated model.
  8. Select model order using AIC, MDL, and FPE; interpret the trade-off between fit and complexity.
  9. Implement all of the above in Python, Java, and C#.

docs.title: 2.1 The spectrum-estimation problem
docs.text:
Given \(N\) samples \(x[0], \dots, x[N-1]\) of a WSS process \(X[n]\), estimate the power spectral density \(S_X(e^{j\omega})\).

Two broad families:

Family Approach Assumptions Good when Nonparametric Directly estimate \(S_X\) from data using DFT, autocorrelation, or windows Only WSS Little prior knowledge; long records; spectra without sharp peaks Model-based (parametric) Fit a model (AR, MA, ARMA) with \(p\) parameters; compute \(S_X\) analytically from the model Model class is correct Short records; sharp peaks; prior knowledge of process type

Two competing goals.

  • Resolution. The ability to distinguish two close spectral peaks. Nonparametric resolution is \(\sim 1/N\) in normalised frequency. Model-based can exceed this if the model is correct.
  • Variance. The statistical fluctuation of the estimator around its mean. Nonparametric estimators need averaging (Bartlett, Welch) to reduce variance, which trades resolution.

There is no universally best estimator. The choice depends on data length, prior knowledge, and what you want to know (peak locations? total power? smooth envelope?).

docs.title: 2.2 Performance criteria for estimators
docs.text:
An estimator \(\hat\theta\) of a quantity \(\theta\) (here \(\theta = S_X(e^{j\omega})\) at a given frequency) is characterised by:

\[ \boxed{\;\operatorname{Bias}[\hat\theta] = \mathbb{E}[\hat\theta] - \theta\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\operatorname{Var}[\hat\theta] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\hat\theta - \mathbb{E}[\hat\theta])^2\bigr]\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\operatorname{MSE}[\hat\theta] = \operatorname{Bias}^2 + \operatorname{Var} = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2\bigr]\;} \]

Definitions

  • Unbiased: \(\operatorname{Bias} = 0\) for every \(N\).
  • Asymptotically unbiased: \(\operatorname{Bias} \to 0\) as \(N \to \infty\).
  • Consistent: \(\hat\theta \to \theta\) in probability as \(N \to \infty\) — equivalently, both bias \(\to 0\) and variance \(\to 0\).
  • Efficient: among all unbiased estimators, has the smallest variance (the Cramér–Rao lower bound).

The key insight for spectrum estimation: the periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but NOT consistent — its variance does not decrease with \(N\). This is the central motivation for Bartlett and Welch averaging, and for model-based approaches.

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — checking consistency of a simple estimator
docs.text:
Let \(x[n] = \theta + e[n]\) with \(e[n]\) zero-mean white noise of variance \(\sigma_e^2\), \(\theta\) constant. Consider the mean estimator \(\hat\theta_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\).

  • Bias. \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_N] = \theta\), so bias \(= 0\) — unbiased.
  • Variance. \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat\theta_N] = \sigma_e^2/N \to 0\).
  • Consistency. Both bias and variance vanish ⇒ consistent. ✓

Now consider \(\hat\theta_N' = x[0]\) — a "one-sample" estimator.

  • Bias \(= 0\), but variance \(= \sigma_e^2\) — does not vanish.

So \(\hat\theta_N'\) is unbiased but inconsistent. Consistency is not implied by unbiasedness — it requires the variance to also go to zero.

Application to spectrum. The periodogram is the analogue of \(\hat\theta_N'\): unbiased (asymptotically) but with variance that does not shrink with \(N\). Bartlett and Welch are the analogues of \(\hat\theta_N\) — they reduce variance at the cost of a small bias.

docs.title: 2.3 The periodogram — bias and variance revisited
docs.text:
From §1.6 of Chapter 1, the periodogram is

\[ \hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{N}\Bigl|\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, e^{-j\omega n}\Bigr|^2. \]

docs.title: 2.3.1 Bias
docs.text:
Taking the expectation over realisations:

\[ \mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega})\bigr] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_X(e^{j\theta})\, W_N(\omega - \theta)\, d\theta, \]

where the spectral window is the squared Dirichlet (Fejér) kernel:

\[ \boxed{\;W_N(\omega) = \frac{1}{N}\cdot\frac{\sin^2(N\omega/2)}{\sin^2(\omega/2)}\;} \]

Interpretation. The expected periodogram is the true PSD smoothed by \(W_N\) — a window of effective width \(\sim 2\pi/N\). This gives three consequences:

  1. The periodogram is asymptotically unbiased: \(W_N \to 2\pi\delta(\omega)\) as \(N \to \infty\), so the smoothing vanishes.
  2. For finite \(N\), sharp spectral features (narrow peaks, line spectra) are spread over \(2\pi/N\) — the spectral leakage and the resolution limit.
  3. The smoothing is a bias in the MSE sense — it distorts the shape even where it does not change the mean of the peak value.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Variance
docs.text:
For a Gaussian WSS process, the periodogram at any single frequency is asymptotically exponentially distributed with mean \(S_X\):

\[ \boxed{\;\frac{\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega})}{S_X(e^{j\omega})} \xrightarrow{\text{distribution}} \frac{\chi^2_2}{2} = \mathrm{Exp}(1)\;} \]

Hence

\[ \boxed{\;\operatorname{Var}\bigl[\hat{S}_X(e^{j\omega})\bigr] \approx S_X^2(e^{j\omega})\quad \text{for all } N.\;} \]

The standard deviation equals the mean, regardless of record length. This is the inconsistency of the periodogram — increasing \(N\) reduces the bias but never the variance at any given frequency.

docs.title: Worked example 2.2 — verifying periodogram variance
docs.text:
Simulate \(N = 4096\) samples of white Gaussian noise with \(\sigma^2 = 1\); compute the periodogram at \(N/2 + 1 = 2049\) frequency bins; report mean and standard deviation across bins.

mean(periodogram) = 1.00  (expected: σ² = 1)
std(periodogram)  = 1.00  (expected: σ² = 1)

Double \(N\) to \(8192\): mean stays at \(1.00\), std stays at \(1.00\). This is what inconsistent looks like — variance does not shrink as \(N\) increases. Averaging over \(K\) independent realisations would reduce the variance to \(\sigma^4/K\).

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Split the \(N\)-sample record into \(K\) non-overlapping segments of length \(L = \lfloor N/K \rfloor\) each. Compute the periodogram of each segment and average:

\[ \boxed{\;\hat{S}^{\text{Bartlett}}_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{S}^{(k)}_X(e^{j\omega})\;} \]

where \(\hat{S}^{(k)}_X\) is the periodogram of segment \(k\) using \(L\) samples.

docs.title: Bias / variance trade-off
docs.text:
• Bias. Each segment's periodogram has the same asymptotic bias as a length-\(L\) periodogram — i.e., resolution \(\sim 2\pi/L = K \cdot 2\pi/N\). The bias increases by the factor \(K\) compared to the full-record periodogram.
  • Variance. If the segments are independent (or approximately so), the average of \(K\) independent periodograms has \(\operatorname{Var} = S_X^2/K\) — a \(1/K\) reduction.

Formally:

\[ \operatorname{Bias}[\hat S^{\text{Bartlett}}] = O(L^{-1}) = O(K/N),\qquad \operatorname{Var}[\hat S^{\text{Bartlett}}] = O(1/K). \]

As \(N \to \infty\) with \(K \to \infty\) and \(L \to \infty\) (so that both \(K, L \to \infty\)), both bias and variance vanish ⇒ Bartlett is consistent.

docs.title: Worked example 2.3 — Bartlett variance reduction
docs.text:
