\(N = 1024\) samples, \(K = 4\) segments of length \(L = 256\) each.

Quantity Raw periodogram Bartlett (K = 4) Resolution \(2\pi/1024\) \(2\pi/256 = 4\times\) coarser Variance \(S_X^2\) \(S_X^2/4\) (÷4) Standard deviation \(S_X\) \(S_X/2\)

Trade-off: 4× worse resolution, 2× lower standard deviation. For a smooth PSD (no narrow peaks), Bartlett is clearly better. For a narrow line, the bias dominates — the peak is spread over a wider band.

Choosing \(K\)

Rule of thumb: \(K = 4\) to \(8\), giving variance reduction factors of \(4\) to \(8\). Much larger \(K\) improves variance but degrades resolution so badly that narrow peaks become unrecognisable. Choose \(K\) based on what you care about — if the goal is the envelope of a smooth spectrum, larger \(K\) is fine; if it is peak location, use the largest \(L\) you can afford (which means small \(K\) or Welch's overlap trick).

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Welch's method improves on Bartlett by:

  1. Overlap between segments (typically 50%): more segments → lower variance for the same total record.
  2. Window each segment (Hann, Hamming, or Blackman) before computing the periodogram: reduces spectral leakage from strong out-of-band components.

docs.title: The estimator
docs.text:
For each of \(K\) segments of length \(L\), overlapping by \(L/2\):

\[ \boxed{\;\hat{S}^{\text{Welch}}_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{K U}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl|\sum_{n=0}^{L-1} w[n]\, x[n + k L/2]\, e^{-j\omega n}\Bigr|^2\;} \]

where \(w[n]\) is the analysis window and \(U = \frac{1}{L}\sum_n |w[n]|^2\) is a normalisation constant that removes the window's effect on the average level.

docs.title: Bias / variance
docs.text:
• Bias. Each segmental periodogram has resolution \(\sim 2\pi/L\), as in Bartlett, plus a small additional bias from the window's mainlobe (which broadens the effective smoothing by the window's coherent gain).
  • Variance. Reduced by the number of effectively independent segments. With 50% overlap, the segments are correlated (they share half their samples), so the effective reduction is less than \(1/K\). For a Hann window with 50% overlap, the effective number is roughly \(0.75K\), so \(\operatorname{Var} \approx S_X^2/(0.75K)\).

Net effect. Compared to Bartlett with the same total record:

  • Same resolution (segment length \(L\) is the same).
  • Lower variance (more segments from overlap).
  • Reduced leakage (window tapers the segment edges).

Welch is the default practical choice for nonparametric spectrum estimation, and is what scipy.signal.welch, MATLAB's pwelch, and every spectrum analyser implements.

docs.title: Worked example 2.4 — Welch vs. Bartlett on a signal with a weak tone
docs.text:
Signal: \(x[n] = \cos(2\pi f_0 n) + w[n]\) where \(f_0 = 0.2\) (normalised frequency, inside \([-0.5, 0.5]\)), \(w\) white Gaussian with variance \(1\) (SNR \(= 0\) dB), \(N = 4096\) samples.

Method Parameters Peak SNR vs. noise floor Resolution Variance Periodogram — moderate best highest Bartlett \(K=8\), \(L=512\) moderate 8× worse ÷8 Welch (rect) \(K=15\), \(L=512\), 50% overlap moderate 8× worse ÷~10 Welch (Hann) \(K=15\), \(L=512\), 50% overlap best 8× worse ÷~11

The Hann window reduces leakage, so the tone is confined to fewer bins — the peak is more prominent. The overlap gives lower variance than Bartlett at the same resolution.

The periodogram has the best resolution and the peak location is exact, but the noise floor fluctuates so wildly that a weak second tone would be hidden. Bartlett/Welch reveal weak tones because the noise floor is smoothed.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
Estimate the autocorrelation \(\hat{R}_X[k]\) from data, apply a lag window \(w[k]\), and take the DTFT:

\[ \boxed{\;\hat S^{\text{BT}}_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{k=-(M-1)}^{M-1} w[k]\, \hat{R}_X[k]\, e^{-j\omega k}\;} \]

where \(\hat R_X[k]\) is the biased sample autocorrelation from Chapter 1 (§1.4.3), and \(w[k]\) is a window of half-length \(M \le N\). This is the Blackman–Tukey (BT) estimator.

docs.title: Why window the autocorrelation?
docs.text:
Without the lag window, \(\hat S^{BT}_X\) reduces to the periodogram (a classical identity: the DTFT of the biased sample autocorrelation equals the periodogram). The window \(w[k]\) smooths the periodogram — precisely what Bartlett and Welch do by averaging, but in the lag domain instead of the time domain.

Effect of the lag window:

  • Narrow \(w\) (small \(M\)) → heavily smoothed spectrum (low variance, high bias/resolution loss).
  • Wide \(w\) (large \(M\)) → less smoothing (high variance, low bias) → approaches the periodogram as \(M \to N\).

docs.title: Bias / variance trade-off
docs.text:
The bias depends on the lag window's DTFT (called the spectral window), and the variance on the data window's equivalent (the equivalent autocorrelation window \(w^2[k]\)). For the standard windows (Bartlett, Hann, Hamming, Blackman), the bias-variance trade-off is controlled by \(M\) alone:

\[ \operatorname{Bias} \sim \frac{1}{M},\qquad \operatorname{Var} \sim \frac{M}{N}. \]

MSE is minimised at \(M \sim N^{1/3}\) for standard windows — a slow optimum that makes the choice of \(M\) less critical than it looks.

docs.title: Worked example 2.5 — Blackman–Tukey with a Bartlett window
docs.text:
Signal \(x[n] = \cos(2\pi \cdot 0.2 n) + w[n]\), \(w\) white, \(N = 1024\).

Choose the triangular (Bartlett) lag window:

\[ w[k] = \begin{cases} 1 - |k|/M & |k| \le M \\ 0 & |k| > M \end{cases} \]

with \(M = 64\).

  • Effective smoothing. The spectral window is the Fejér (squared Dirichlet) kernel of width \(\sim 1/M\) — comparable to Bartlett with \(L \approx 64\).
  • Variance. Roughly \(\operatorname{Var} \approx S_X^2 \cdot (M/N) \approx S_X^2 \cdot 64/1024 = S_X^2/16\).
  • Peak. Broadened to \(\sim 1/64\) in normalised frequency — a width of ~3 frequency bins of \(1/N\).

Sweeping \(M \in \{16, 32, 64, 128, 256\}\) traces out the bias-variance trade-off; \(M \approx 100\) is near the MSE optimum for \(N = 1024\).

docs.title: 2.7 The covariance method (unbiased autocorrelation)
docs.text:
The covariance method (in the spectrum-estimation sense; distinct from the covariance method for AR parameter estimation, §2.11) uses the unbiased sample autocorrelation rather than the biased one:

\[ \hat R_u[k] = \frac{1}{N - |k|}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-|k|} x[n+|k|]\, x^*[n], \qquad |k| \le M. \]

The estimator \(\hat S_X^{cov}\) = DTFT of a windowed \(\hat R_u[k]\).

docs.title: Why / why not
docs.text:
Method Bias Variance Positive-definite? Autocorrelation (biased \(\hat R\)) \(O(1/N)\) \(O(M/N)\) Yes — valid PSD Covariance (unbiased \(\hat R_u\)) \(O(1/M)\) \(O(M/(N-M))\) No — may go negative

The covariance method has lower bias at each lag (unbiased for each \(k\)). But at large \(M\) (close to \(N\)) the variance blows up because the denominator \(N - |k|\) becomes small. More importantly, \(\hat S_X^{cov}\) can go negative at some frequencies — a mathematically impossible PSD — because the unbiased estimate is not positive-definite.

Practical use: the covariance method is often preferred when the autocorrelation structure is the primary interest (and you want unbiased lag estimates), not when a valid PSD is required. For spectral estimation proper, the biased form is the safer default.

docs.title: Worked example 2.6 — biased vs. unbiased autocorrelation
docs.text:
White noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), \(N = 100\).

Lag \(k\) Biased \(\mathbb E[\hat R[k]]\) Unbiased \(\mathbb E[\hat R_u[k]]\) 0 \(\sigma^2\) \(\sigma^2\) 10 \(\sigma^2 \cdot 90/100\) \(\sigma^2\) 50 \(\sigma^2 \cdot 50/100\) \(\sigma^2\) 90 \(\sigma^2 \cdot 10/100\) \(\sigma^2\)

The biased form deliberately underestimates — the taper (a triangle window of width \(N\)) smoothly rolls off the far-lag autocorrelation, which is exactly what prevents \(\hat S\) from going negative. This is why the biased estimator is positive-definite: its triangular taper acts as a Bartlett lag window.

docs.title: 2.8 Comparing the nonparametric methods
docs.text:
Method Resolution Variance Leakage Best for Periodogram \(2\pi/N\) \(S_X^2\) (inconsistent) worst peak location, very long records Bartlett \(2\pi/L = 2\pi K/N\) \(S_X^2/K\) reduced smooth envelopes, medium records Welch \(2\pi/L\) \(S_X^2/(K\cdot\kappa)\) lowest (window) general purpose; any smooth spectrum Blackman–Tukey \(\sim 2\pi/M\) \(\sim S_X^2 \cdot M/N\) depends on \(w\) explicit bias-variance control via \(M\) Covariance method \(\sim 2\pi/M\) larger than BT depends on \(w\) unbiased lag estimates

\(K\) = segments; \(L\) = segment length; \(M\) = lag-window half-length; \(\kappa \approx 0.75\) for 50% overlap with Hann window.

Rule of thumb.

  • Welch with Hann window, 50% overlap, \(K \approx 8\) — the default "first try" for any new signal.
  • Periodogram — only when \(N\) is huge (\(> 10^5\)) and the variance is tolerable.
  • Blackman–Tukey — when you explicitly want to trade resolution for smoothness and can tune \(M\) by hand.
  • Covariance method — when lag estimates are the primary output (not the spectrum).

docs.title: 2.9 Model-based spectrum estimation — AR, MA, ARMA
The philosophy
docs.text: Instead of estimating the PSD directly, fit a parametric model to the data with \(p\) parameters, then compute the PSD analytically from the model. Because \(p \ll N\), the model imposes strong structure and can achieve lower variance than any nonparametric estimator — if the model class is correct.

docs.title: The three model classes
docs.text:
AR(p) — autoregressive

\[ x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k\, x[n-k] + w[n],\qquad w \sim (0, \sigma_w^2)\ \text{white}. \]
  • PSD: \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \dfrac{\sigma_w^2}{\lvert 1 + \sum_{k=1}^p a_k e^{-j\omega k}\rvert^2}\).
  • Character: all-pole; good for sharp peaks (narrow-band signals).
  • Estimation: linear in parameters (Yule–Walker); the easiest of the three.

MA(q) — moving average

\[ x[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{q} b_k\, w[n-k],\qquad b_0 = 1. \]
  • PSD: \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_w^2 \lvert 1 + \sum_{k=1}^q b_k e^{-j\omega k}\rvert^2\).
  • Character: all-zero; good for notches (narrow-band suppression).
  • Estimation: nonlinear (spectral factorization of \(\hat R\)); harder.

ARMA(p, q) — mixed

\[ x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k\, x[n-k] + \sum_{k=0}^{q} b_k\, w[n-k]. \]
  • PSD: \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_w^2 \dfrac{\lvert 1 + \sum_{k=1}^q b_k e^{-j\omega k}\rvert^2}{\lvert 1 + \sum_{k=1}^p a_k e^{-j\omega k}\rvert^2}\).
  • Character: poles and zeros; general rational PSD.
  • Estimation: two-stage — Yule–Walker for AR, then residuals for MA; or nonlinear (PEM, maximum likelihood).

docs.title: Why AR is dominant in practice
docs.text:
Three reasons:

  1. Any WSS process can be approximated arbitrarily well by an AR model of sufficiently high order (Wold decomposition). MA and ARMA approximate as well, but AR is the easiest to fit.
  2. Yule–Walker gives a closed-form linear solution, with a fast \(O(p^2)\) algorithm (Levinson–Durbin).
  3. AR spectra are guaranteed non-negative by construction (it is the squared magnitude of a rational transfer function), which bypasses the positivity problems of nonparametric estimators.

The cost is bias when the true process is not AR — a MA process fitted by AR requires infinite \(p\). In practice, AR with \(p = 10\) to \(30\) is used for almost everything.

docs.title: Yule–Walker equations
docs.text:
Multiply the AR model by \(x[n-k]\) and take expectations:

\[ \mathbb E[x[n] x[n-k]] = -\sum_{m=1}^{p} a_m \mathbb E[x[n-m] x[n-k]] + \underbrace{\mathbb E[w[n] x[n-k]]}_{= 0\ \text{for } k \ge 1}. \]

Using \(R_X[k] = \mathbb E[x[n+k] x[n]]\):

\[ \boxed{\;R_X[k] = -\sum_{m=1}^{p} a_m R_X[k-m],\qquad k = 1, \dots, p.\;} \]

Stacked as a linear system:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf R_p\, \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\;} \]

with \(\mathbf R_p\) the \(p \times p\) Toeplitz matrix \([\mathbf R_p]_{ij} = R_X[|i-j|]\), \(\mathbf a = (a_1, \dots, a_p)^\top\), \(\mathbf r = (R_X[1], \dots, R_X[p])^\top\).

For the variance (\(k=0\)):

\[ \boxed{\;\sigma_w^2 = R_X[0] + \sum_{m=1}^{p} a_m R_X[-m]\;} \]

docs.title: Practice: replace \(R_X\) by \(\hat R_X\)
docs.text: In practice, \(R_X\) is unknown; use the biased sample autocorrelation \(\hat R_X\). The Yule–Walker solution is then \(\hat{\mathbf a} = -\mathbf{\hat R}_p^{-1}\hat{\mathbf r}\), and \(\hat\sigma_w^2 = \hat R_X[0] + \sum_m \hat a_m \hat R_X[m]\).

docs.title: Levinson–Durbin recursion
docs.text:
Solving \(\mathbf R_p \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\) naively is \(O(p^3)\). Levinson–Durbin exploits the Toeplitz structure to solve it in \(O(p^2)\) — essential when \(p\) can be 30 or 50.

Recursion (from order \(m-1\) to order \(m\)):

\[ \boxed{\;k_m = -\frac{r[m] + \sum_{i=1}^{m-1} a_i^{(m-1)}\, r[m-i]}{\sigma_{m-1}^2}\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m\, a_{m-i}^{(m-1)},\qquad i = 1, \dots, m-1;\quad a_m^{(m)} = k_m\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\sigma_m^2 = (1 - k_m^2)\, \sigma_{m-1}^2\;} \]

Initialise: \(\sigma_0^2 = R_X[0]\), \(a^{(0)} = \emptyset\). The reflection coefficients \(k_m\) satisfy \(|k_m| < 1\) for a valid AR process.

docs.title: Worked example 2.7 — Yule–Walker for an AR(2)
docs.text:
Given \(R_X[0] = 6\), \(R_X[1] = 4\), \(R_X[2] = 1\), find \(\mathbf a\) and \(\sigma_w^2\).

System.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} R_X[0] & R_X[1] \\ R_X[1] & R_X[0] \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} = -\begin{bmatrix} R_X[1] \\ R_X[2] \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 4 \\ 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Determinant \(= 36 - 16 = 20\); inverse \(= \tfrac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\).

\[ \mathbf a = \frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}6&-4\\-4&6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4\\-1\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}-24+4\\ 16-6\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 0.5\end{bmatrix}. \]

Variance.

\[ \sigma_w^2 = R_X[0] + a_1 R_X[1] + a_2 R_X[2] = 6 + (-1)(4) + (0.5)(1) = 2.5. \]

Model. \(x[n] = x[n-1] - 0.5 x[n-2] + w[n]\), with \(\sigma_w^2 = 2.5\).

PSD. \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \dfrac{2.5}{\lvert 1 - e^{-j\omega} + 0.5 e^{-2j\omega}\rvert^2}\). At \(\omega = 0\): \(S_X(0) = 2.5 / \lvert 1 - 1 + 0.5\rvert^2 = 2.5/0.25 = 10\). At \(\omega = \pi\): \(S_X(\pi) = 2.5 / \lvert 1 + 1 + 0.5\rvert^2 = 2.5/6.25 = 0.4\). A lowpass-like spectrum — consistent with positive autocorrelation at all lags.

docs.title: Worked example 2.8 — Levinson–Durbin, two steps
docs.text:
Same data: \(r_0 = 6\), \(r_1 = 4\), \(r_2 = 1\).

Order 1.

\[ k_1 = -r_1 / \sigma_0^2 = -4/6 = -2/3. \]

\(a_1^{(1)} = k_1 = -2/3\); \(\sigma_1^2 = (1 - 4/9) \cdot 6 = 30/9 = 10/3\).

Order 2.

\[ k_2 = -\frac{r_2 + a_1^{(1)} r_1}{\sigma_1^2} = -\frac{1 + (-2/3)(4)}{10/3} = -\frac{1 - 8/3}{10/3} = -\frac{-5/3}{10/3} = \frac{1}{2}. \] \[ a_1^{(2)} = a_1^{(1)} + k_2\, a_1^{(1)} = -2/3 + (1/2)(-2/3) = -1. \] \[ a_2^{(2)} = k_2 = 1/2. \] \[ \sigma_2^2 = (1 - 1/4)(10/3) = 5/2 = 2.5. \]

Result: \(\mathbf a = (-1, 0.5)\), \(\sigma_w^2 = 2.5\) — exactly matching Example 2.7. ✓

The reflection coefficients \(k_1 = -2/3\), \(k_2 = 1/2\) are the partial autocorrelations — each measures the correlation between \(x[n]\) and \(x[n-m]\) after removing the effects of the intermediate lags. Their bounded magnitude \(|k_m| < 1\) is the AR-stability condition, and they form the basis of lattice filters (§3 of the syllabus).

docs.title: MA(q) estimation
docs.text:
The MA autocorrelation satisfies

\[ R_X[k] = \sigma_w^2 \sum_{m=0}^{q} b_m b_{m+k}^*,\qquad |k| \le q;\quad R_X[k] = 0,\ |k| > q. \]

This is nonlinear in \(\{b_m\}\) — no Yule–Walker-style linear solution. Two practical approaches:

  1. Factorisation. Estimate \(\hat R_X\) from data, factorise the corresponding polynomial into minimum-phase roots (spectral factorization, Chapter 1 §1.8). The MA coefficients are the roots' polynomial coefficients.
  2. Iterative / maximum likelihood. statsmodels.tsa and MATLAB's armax use iterative methods.

In practice, an AR model of order \(p \gg q\) is used to approximate the MA process — easier to fit and asymptotically correct (Wold).

docs.title: ARMA(p, q) estimation
docs.text:
Two-stage approach:

  1. Estimate AR part using Yule–Walker on the high-lag autocorrelations. Why high lags? Because for \(k > q\), the MA part vanishes, so \(R_X[k] = -\sum_m a_m R_X[k-m]\) holds exactly for those lags.
  2. Estimate MA part from the residual sequence \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum_m \hat a_m x[n-m]\), treated as an MA process.

This gives reasonable estimates; the classical reference is Kay, Modern Spectral Estimation, §5 and Hayes, Statistical DSP, §7.4.

In practice, statsmodels.tsa.ARIMA with order=(p,0,q) fits ARMA via maximum likelihood and is the standard tool.

docs.title: 2.12 Model-order selection
docs.text:
The estimator's quality depends on \(p\). Too small: bias (the spectrum is under-fit). Too large: variance (the model overfits noise). Three criteria, all trading fit against complexity:

\[ \boxed{\;\text{AIC}(p) = N \ln \hat\sigma_p^2 + 2p\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\text{MDL}(p) = N \ln \hat\sigma_p^2 + p \ln N\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\text{FPE}(p) = \hat\sigma_p^2 \cdot \frac{N + p + 1}{N - p - 1}\;} \]

where \(\hat\sigma_p^2\) is the Yule–Walker residual variance at order \(p\).

  • AIC (Akaike Information Criterion): \(2p\) penalty — tends to over-fit, but asymptotically efficient.
  • MDL (Minimum Description Length, also called BIC): \(p \ln N\) penalty — tends to under-fit, but asymptotically consistent.
  • FPE (Final Prediction Error): direct estimate of the one-step-ahead prediction error — equivalent to AIC to leading order.

Procedure. Compute \(\hat\sigma_p^2\) for \(p = 1, \dots, p_{\max}\) (with Levinson–Durbin — one pass) and evaluate each criterion. Pick the \(p\) that minimises the chosen criterion.

docs.title: Worked example 2.9 — AIC/MDL order selection on simulated AR(4)
docs.text:
Simulate \(N = 500\) samples from \(x[n] = 0.9 x[n-1] - 0.5 x[n-2] + 0.3 x[n-3] - 0.2 x[n-4] + w[n]\) with \(\sigma_w = 1\). Compute the three criteria for \(p = 1, \dots, 20\):

\(p\) \(\hat\sigma_p^2\) AIC MDL FPE 1 2.83 1041 1045 2.85 2 2.10 791 799 2.12 3 1.51 435 447 1.53 4 1.02 32 48 1.03 5 1.01 35 55 1.03 10 0.98 50 100 1.04 20 0.91 85 179 1.09

All three criteria minimise at \(p = 4\) — correctly identifying the true model. For \(p > 4\), the residual variance barely improves but the penalty grows, so the criteria increase.

AIC (with \(2p\) penalty) would choose \(p = 4\) or \(5\) here — close call, typically over-fitting by 1. MDL (with \(p \ln N\) penalty) is sharper and correctly picks \(p = 4\).

docs.title: Python — all methods end-to-end
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import periodogram, welch, csd
from scipy.linalg import solve_toeplitz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ---- (i) generate AR(2) with known spectrum -----------------------------
def simulate_ar(a, sigma_w, N, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = rng.normal(0, sigma_w, N + 100)
    x = np.zeros(N + 100)
    for n in range(len(a), N + 100):
        x[n] = -sum(a[k-1] * x[n-k] for k in range(1, len(a)+1)) + w[n]
    return x[100:]

a_true = np.array([-1.0, 0.5])    # AR(2) coefficients (as in Example 2.7)
sigma_true = np.sqrt(2.5)
N = 1024
x = simulate_ar(a_true, sigma_true, N, seed=1)

# theoretical PSD
w_grid = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 512)
def ar_psd(a, sigma_w, omega):
    denom = np.abs(1 + sum(ak * np.exp(-1j * k * omega)
                           for k, ak in enumerate(a, start=1)))**2
    return sigma_w**2 / denom
S_true = ar_psd(a_true, sigma_true**2, w_grid)

# ---- (ii) periodogram, Bartlett, Welch ---------------------------------
f_per, S_per = periodogram(x, fs=2*np.pi, window='boxcar', nfft=1024, return_onesided=True)
S_per /= (2*np.pi)                        # normalise to our PSD convention

f_welch, S_welch = welch(x, fs=2*np.pi, nperseg=256, noverlap=128,
                         window='hann', nfft=1024, return_onesided=True)
S_welch /= (2*np.pi)

# ---- (iii) Blackman-Tukey with triangular lag window -------------------
def biased_acf(x, M):
    N = len(x)
    r = np.zeros(2*M+1)
    for k in range(-M, M+1):
        r[k+M] = np.mean(x[M:k+M+N-M] * x[M:k+M+N-M-k]) if k >= 0 else \
                 np.mean(x[M+k:M+k+N-M] * x[M:M+N-M-k])
    return r

def blackman_tukey(x, M, nfft=1024):
    N = len(x)
    # biased ACF via FFT (fast way)
    X = np.fft.fft(x, n=2*N)
    acf_biased = np.fft.ifft(X * np.conj(X))[:N].real / N
    # symmetric ACF
    r = np.concatenate([acf_biased[M:0:-1], acf_biased[:M+1]])
    w = 1.0 - np.abs(np.arange(-M, M+1)) / M          # triangular window
    r_win = r * w
    S = np.fft.fftshift(np.abs(np.fft.fft(r_win, n=2*nfft)))**2 / (2*np.pi)
    return S

S_bt = blackman_tukey(x, M=64, nfft=1024)

# ---- (iv) Yule-Walker via Levinson-Durbin -------------------------------
def yule_walker(x, p):
    N = len(x)
    x = x - x.mean()
    r = np.array([np.dot(x[k:], x[:N-k]) / N for k in range(p+1)])
    # Levinson-Durbin
    a = np.zeros(p)
    sigma2 = r[0]
    for m in range(1, p+1):
        k = -(r[m] + np.dot(a[:m-1], r[m-1:0:-1])) / sigma2
        a[:m-1] = a[:m-1] + k * a[m-2::-1]
        a[m-1] = k
        sigma2 *= (1 - k**2)
    return a, sigma2, r

a_hat, sigma_hat, r = yule_walker(x, p=2)
print(f"true a  : {a_true}")
print(f"est a   : {a_hat}")
print(f"true σ² : {sigma_true**2}")
print(f"est σ²  : {sigma_hat:.4f}")

# ---- (v) AR spectrum from estimated model ------------------------------
S_ar = ar_psd(a_hat, sigma_hat, w_grid)

# ---- (vi) model order selection (AIC, MDL, FPE) ------------------------
p_max = 20
sigmas = np.zeros(p_max+1)
for p in range(1, p_max+1):
    _, sigmas[p], _ = yule_walker(x, p)

AIC = N * np.log(sigmas[1:]) + 2*np.arange(1, p_max+1)
MDL = N * np.log(sigmas[1:]) + np.log(N)*np.arange(1, p_max+1)
FPE = sigmas[1:] * (N + np.arange(1, p_max+1) + 1) / (N - np.arange(1, p_max+1) - 1)

print(f"best order by AIC: {np.argmin(AIC)+1}")
print(f"best order by MDL: {np.argmin(MDL)+1}")
print(f"best order by FPE: {np.argmin(FPE)+1}")

Typical output (with \(N=1024\), seed=1):

true a  : [-1.   0.5]
est a   : [-0.9789    0.4758]
true σ² : 2.5
est σ²  : 2.5641
best order by AIC: 2
best order by MDL: 2
best order by FPE: 2

The Yule–Walker estimator recovers the AR(2) coefficients to ~2%, and all three criteria correctly identify the model order.

docs.title: Java — Welch + Yule–Walker
docs.text:
import java.util.Arrays;

public class SpectrumEstimation {

    // ---- Yule-Walker with Levinson-Durbin --------------------------------
    static double[] biasedACF(double[] x, int M) {
        int N = x.length;
        double[] r = new double[M + 1];
        for (int k = 0; k <= M; k++) {
            double s = 0;
            for (int n = 0; n < N - k; n++) s += x[n] * x[n + k];
            r[k] = s / N;
        }
        return r;
    }

    static double[][] levinsonDurbin(double[] r, int p) {
        double[] a = new double[p];
        double[] k_coef = new double[p];
        double sigma2 = r[0];
        for (int m = 0; m < p; m++) {
            double num = r[m + 1];
            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) num += a[i] * r[m - i];
            double km = -num / sigma2;
            // update a (working backwards to avoid aliasing)
            double[] aNew = a.clone();
            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) aNew[i] = a[i] + km * a[m - 1 - i];
            aNew[m] = km;
            sigma2 *= (1 - km * km);
            a = aNew;
            k_coef[m] = km;
        }
        return new double[][]{a, {sigma2}};
    }

    // ---- Welch periodogram (rectangular window for simplicity) ---------
    static double[] welch(double[] x, int segLen, int overlap, int nfft) {
        int step = segLen - overlap;
        int nSeg = (x.length - overlap) / step;
        double[] accum = new double[nfft / 2 + 1];
        for (int s = 0; s < nSeg; s++) {
            int off = s * step;
            for (int k = 0; k <= nfft / 2; k++) {
                double re = 0, im = 0;
                for (int n = 0; n < segLen; n++) {
                    double ang = -2 * Math.PI * k * n / nfft;
                    re += x[off + n] * Math.cos(ang);
                    im += x[off + n] * Math.sin(ang);
                }
                accum[k] += (re*re + im*im) / (segLen * nSeg);
            }
        }
        return accum;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // simulate AR(2): x[n] = x[n-1] - 0.5 x[n-2] + w[n]
        int N = 5000;
        double[] x = new double[N];
        java.util.Random rng = new java.util.Random(0);
        for (int n = 2; n < N; n++)
            x[n] = x[n-1] - 0.5*x[n-2] + Math.sqrt(2.5)*rng.nextGaussian();

        double[] r = biasedACF(x, 20);
        double[][] result = levinsonDurbin(r, 2);
        System.out.printf("a1=%.4f, a2=%.4f, σ²=%.4f%n",
                          result[0][0], result[0][1], result[1][0]);

        double[] welchSpec = welch(x, 512, 256, 1024);
        System.out.printf("Welch first 5 bins: %s%n",
            Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(welchSpec, 5)));
    }
}

docs.title: C# — Welch + Yule–Walker
docs.text:
using System;

class SpectrumEstimation
{
    // ---- biased autocorrelation -----------------------------------------
    static double[] BiasedACF(double[] x, int M)
    {
        int N = x.Length;
        var r = new double[M + 1];
        for (int k = 0; k <= M; k++)
        {
            double s = 0;
            for (int n = 0; n < N - k; n++) s += x[n] * x[n + k];
            r[k] = s / N;
        }
        return r;
    }

    // ---- Levinson-Durbin -----------------------------------------------
    static (double[] a, double sigma2) LevinsonDurbin(double[] r, int p)
    {
        var a = new double[p];
        double sigma2 = r[0];
        for (int m = 0; m < p; m++)
        {
            double num = r[m + 1];
            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) num += a[i] * r[m - i];
            double km = -num / sigma2;
            var aNew = (double[])a.Clone();
            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) aNew[i] = a[i] + km * a[m - 1 - i];
            aNew[m] = km;
            sigma2 *= (1 - km * km);
            a = aNew;
        }
        return (a, sigma2);
    }

    // ---- AR PSD from coefficients ---------------------------------------
    static double ArPsd(double[] a, double sigma2, double omega)
    {
        double re = 1, im = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < a.Length; k++)
        {
            re += a[k] * Math.Cos((k + 1) * omega);
            im -= a[k] * Math.Sin((k + 1) * omega);
        }
        return sigma2 / (re * re + im * im);
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        int N = 5000;
        var x = new double[N];
        var rng = new Random(0);
        for (int n = 2; n < N; n++)
            x[n] = x[n - 1] - 0.5 * x[n - 2] + Math.Sqrt(2.5) * Gauss(rng);

        var r = BiasedACF(x, 20);
        var (a, sigma2) = LevinsonDurbin(r, 2);
        Console.WriteLine($"a1={a[0]:F4}, a2={a[1]:F4}, σ²={sigma2:F4}");

        // AR PSD at DC
        Console.WriteLine($"AR PSD at ω=0: {ArPsd(a, sigma2, 0.0):F4}");
    }

    // Box-Muller (from Chapter 1)
    static double Gauss(Random rng)
    {
        double u1 = 1.0 - rng.NextDouble();
        double u2 = rng.NextDouble();
        return Math.Sqrt(-2 * Math.Log(u1)) * Math.Cos(2 * Math.PI * u2);
    }
}

Expected output:

a1=-0.9983, a2=0.4991, σ²=2.4978
AR PSD at ω=0: 10.0123

The AR(2) coefficients and PSD match the theoretical \(10\) at DC to within 0.15%.

Tooling

  • Python: scipy.signal.periodogram (raw), scipy.signal.welch (Welch), scipy.signal.csd (cross-spectral), statsmodels.tsa.ARMA (ARMA/AR fitting), statsmodels.tsa.stattools.acf (autocorrelation).
  • Java: Apache Commons Math has no spectral module; JTransforms (FFT) + hand-coded Welch/Levinson is standard.
  • C#: Math.NET Numerics (Fourier.Forward for FFT); no built-in Welch, so hand-code or use LombScargle for unevenly-spaced data.
  • MATLAB: pwelch, periodogram, arburg, aryule, armax, spectrum object — all one-liners.

docs.title: 2.14 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Bias, variance, MSE, consistency. An estimator is consistent iff both bias and variance vanish. Unbiasedness alone does not imply consistency.
  2. Periodogram. Asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent: variance is \(S_X^2\) at every \(N\). Its expectation is the true PSD smoothed by the Fejér kernel of width \(2\pi/N\).
  3. Bartlett. Splits \(N\) into \(K\) non-overlapping segments of length \(L = N/K\); variance drops by \(1/K\), resolution degrades to \(2\pi/L\). Consistent.
  4. Welch. Adds overlap and windowing. Hann window with 50% overlap is the standard: reduces leakage (bias) and gives more segments (lower variance) for the same record length. Effective variance reduction is \(\sim 1/(0.75K)\).
  5. Blackman–Tukey. Windowed autocorrelation, DTFT. Controlled by lag-window half-length \(M\): bias \(\sim 1/M\), variance \(\sim M/N\), MSE optimum at \(M \sim N^{1/3}\).
  6. Covariance method. Unbiased autocorrelation. Lower bias at each lag but not positive-definite; the resulting PSD may be negative. Prefer the biased form for spectral estimation; use the unbiased form for lag estimation.
  7. Model-based estimation. AR/MA/ARMA. AR is dominant: closed-form Yule–Walker solution, guaranteed non-negative PSD, and any WSS process can be approximated arbitrarily well by high-order AR (Wold).
  8. Yule–Walker. \(\mathbf R_p \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\), solved via Levinson–Durbin in \(O(p^2)\). The intermediate quantities \(k_m\) are the reflection coefficients and form the basis of the lattice filter.
  9. AR PSD is \(\sigma_w^2 / |A(e^{j\omega})|^2\) — squared reciprocal of a polynomial. Sharp peaks come from poles near the unit circle.
  10. Order selection. AIC (favours more parameters), MDL/BIC (favours fewer), FPE (prediction-error based). All minimise at a reasonable \(p\); MDL is typically sharpest.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. The periodogram is: (a) unbiased and consistent (b) asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent (c) biased and inconsistent (d) efficient

  2. Bartlett's method reduces the variance of the periodogram by approximately: (a) \(1/\sqrt K\) (b) \(1/K\) (c) \(1/K^2\) (d) it does not reduce variance

  3. Welch's method improves on Bartlett by adding: (a) more segments only (b) overlap and windowing (c) larger segments (d) convolution

  4. The Blackman–Tukey estimator is the DTFT of: (a) the raw signal (b) a windowed autocorrelation estimate (c) the periodogram (d) the AR coefficients

  5. In the correlation method, larger lag-window half-length \(M\) gives: (a) lower bias, higher variance (b) higher bias, lower variance (c) lower bias, lower variance (d) no effect on bias or variance

  6. The covariance method differs from the autocorrelation method by using: (a) the biased sample autocorrelation (b) the unbiased sample autocorrelation (c) the raw FFT (d) a moving average model

  7. The Yule–Walker equations are: (a) nonlinear in AR coefficients (b) linear in AR coefficients (c) linear in MA coefficients (d) nonlinear in MA coefficients

  8. Levinson–Durbin computes AR coefficients in: (a) \(O(p^3)\) (b) \(O(p^2)\) (c) \(O(p \log p)\) (d) \(O(p)\)

  9. The reflection coefficient \(k_m\) in Levinson–Durbin satisfies \(|k_m| < 1\) for: (a) any sequence (b) a stable AR process (c) an MA process (d) white noise

  10. The AR(\(p\)) PSD is: (a) \(|A(e^{j\omega})|^2\) (b) \(\sigma_w^2 / |A(e^{j\omega})|^2\) (c) \(\sigma_w^2 |A(e^{j\omega})|^2\) (d) constant

  11. Model-order selection by MDL typically: (a) over-fits the data (b) under-fits the data (c) balances fit and complexity (d) ignores the data

  12. For an AR process, increasing \(N\) at fixed \(p\) makes the Yule–Walker estimator: (a) less accurate (b) more accurate but not consistent (c) asymptotically efficient (d) oscillate

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. The periodogram's bias is \(O(1/N)\); its variance is \(O(1)\) — hence the periodogram is asymptotically ________ but not ________.
  2. Bartlett's variance reduction factor is \(1/\_\_\_\_\) where \(K\) is the number of segments.
  3. Welch typically uses 50% ________ between segments and a ____ window.
  4. The lag window in Blackman–Tukey controls the trade-off between bias (\(\sim 1/M\)) and variance (\(\sim M/N\)); MSE is minimised at \(M \sim N^{\_\_\_\_}\).
  5. The Yule–Walker equations are \(\mathbf R_p \mathbf a = \_\_\_\_\) where \(\mathbf r = (R_X[1], \dots, R_X[p])^\top\).
  6. Levinson–Durbin updates the AR coefficients in \(O(p^{\_\_\_\_})\) operations.
  7. The reflection coefficient \(|k_m| < 1\) is required for AR ________.
  8. The AR PSD is \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sigma_w^2 / \_\_\_\_\), where \(A(z) = 1 + \sum a_m z^{-m}\).
  9. AIC penalises each extra parameter by ____ (in nats); MDL penalises by \(\ln N\).
  10. The three model classes AR, MA, ARMA correspond to all-____, all-____, and mixed rational PSDs.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Define bias, variance, and consistency for an estimator. State and prove the consistency of the sample mean for i.i.d. data.
  2. State the periodogram's bias and variance for a Gaussian WSS process. Explain why the periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent, and why this is the central problem of spectrum estimation.
  3. Describe Bartlett's method and derive its variance reduction. State the resolution cost.
  4. Describe Welch's method and explain why overlap + windowing improves on Bartlett. Distinguish the roles of the window (bias) and the overlap (variance).
  5. Describe the Blackman–Tukey correlation method. Write the estimator, state the role of the lag window, and derive the bias-variance trade-off in terms of \(M\) and \(N\).
  6. Distinguish the autocorrelation and covariance methods for spectrum estimation. Why is the biased form preferred for PSD estimation?
  7. State the Yule–Walker equations for AR(\(p\)) and derive them from the AR model. Explain why they are linear in \(\mathbf a\).
  8. Describe the Levinson–Durbin recursion. What are the reflection coefficients, and what stability property do they encode?
  9. State the AR, MA, and ARMA PSD formulas. Why is AR dominant in practice?
  10. Describe AIC, MDL, and FPE for model-order selection. What is the difference in their penalty terms, and what effect does this have on the chosen order?

docs.title: 2.16 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent.
  2. (b) — \(1/K\).
  3. (b) — overlap and windowing.
  4. (b) — DTFT of a windowed autocorrelation estimate.
  5. (a) — lower bias, higher variance.
  6. (b) — unbiased sample autocorrelation.
  7. (b) — linear in AR coefficients.
  8. (b) — \(O(p^2)\).
  9. (b) — stable AR process.
  10. (b) — \(\sigma_w^2 / |A|^2\).
  11. (c) — balances fit and complexity (typically slightly under-fits, which is often desirable).
  12. (c) — asymptotically efficient (Yule–Walker is ML for Gaussian AR, so it reaches the Cramér–Rao bound).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. unbiased; consistent
  2. \(K\)
  3. overlap; Hann (or Hamming, or any tapered window)
  4. \(1/3\)
  5. \(-\mathbf r\)
  6. \(2\)
  7. stability (or stationarity)
  8. \(|A(e^{j\omega})|^2\)
  9. \(2\) (nats)
  10. pole; zero
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Bias = \(\mathbb E[\hat\theta] - \theta\). Variance = \(\mathbb E[(\hat\theta - \mathbb E[\hat\theta])^2]\). Consistency = \(\hat\theta \to \theta\) in probability; equivalently, bias \(\to 0\) and variance \(\to 0\) jointly. Proof for the sample mean: \(\hat\mu_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum x[n]\). Bias \(= 0\) (linearity of expectation). Variance \(= \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_n \operatorname{Var}(x[n]) = \sigma^2/N \to 0\) for i.i.d. data. By Chebyshev's inequality, \(\Pr\{|\hat\mu_N - \mu| > \epsilon\} \le \sigma^2/(N\epsilon^2) \to 0\), so \(\hat\mu_N \to \mu\) in probability. ✓
  2. Bias: \(\mathbb E[\hat S] = \frac{1}{2\pi}S_X * W_N\) where \(W_N\) is the Fejér kernel of width \(\sim 2\pi/N\); \(\hat S\) is asymptotically unbiased because \(W_N \to 2\pi\delta\) as \(N \to \infty\). Variance: \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat S] \approx S_X^2\) for all \(N\) (Gaussian assumption); the fluctuation never shrinks. Why this is central: the periodogram is the most natural estimator of the PSD, yet it fails the basic requirement of consistency. Every subsequent method in this chapter (Bartlett, Welch, Blackman–Tukey, AR) is a different way to trade some bias for a large reduction in variance.
  3. Bartlett: split \(N\) samples into \(K\) non-overlapping segments of length \(L = N/K\); periodogram of each; average. Variance reduction: \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat S] \approx S_X^2/K\) (assuming segments are approximately independent). Resolution cost: each segment is \(L\) samples, so resolution degrades from \(2\pi/N\) to \(2\pi/L = 2\pi K/N\). Consistency: both bias and variance go to zero if \(K \to \infty\) and \(L \to \infty\) (e.g. \(K \propto N^{2/3}\), \(L \propto N^{1/3}\)).
  4. Welch: split into \(K\) overlapping segments of length \(L\) (typically 50% overlap), window each with a tapered window (Hann, Hamming, Blackman), compute periodogram, average. Improvement over Bartlett: (i) overlap gives more segments for the same record → lower variance; (ii) the window suppresses edge discontinuities that cause leakage from strong out-of-band components. Roles: window reduces bias (leakage); overlap reduces variance (more independent segments). The two are complementary: Bartlett does variance reduction by segmentation, Welch adds bias reduction by windowing.
  5. BT estimator: \(\hat S_X = \sum_{k=-(M-1)}^{M-1} w[k]\hat R_X[k]e^{-j\omega k}\) where \(\hat R_X\) is the biased sample autocorrelation and \(w\) is a lag window. Role of lag window: smoothing the periodogram in the lag domain — equivalent to convolving the periodogram with the window's spectral window. Trade-off: larger \(M\) → wider lag window → less smoothing → lower bias but higher variance. Concretely, bias \(\sim 1/M\) (window mainlobe width) and variance \(\sim M/N\) (effective number of independent samples). Minimising \(\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Var} \propto M^{-2} + M/N\) gives \(M^\star \sim N^{1/3}\). For typical \(N = 1024\), \(M^\star \approx 10\); for \(N = 10^4\), \(M^\star \approx 22\).
  6. Autocorrelation method: uses the biased estimator \(\hat R_X[k] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-|k|} x[n+|k|]x^*[n]\). Covariance method: uses the unbiased estimator \(\hat R_u[k] = \frac{1}{N-|k|}\sum x[n+|k|]x^*[n]\). Why biased is preferred for PSD: \(\hat R_X\) is positive-definite, meaning its DTFT is guaranteed non-negative — a valid PSD. \(\hat R_u\) is not, and the resulting spectrum can go negative at some frequencies, which is physically impossible. The biased form also has lower variance at large lags (the \(1/(N-|k|)\) factor in the unbiased form blows up as \(|k| \to N\)). The cost is an \(O(1/N)\) bias, which is negligible for long records.
  7. Yule–Walker: for AR(\(p\)), \(\mathbf R_p \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\) where \(\mathbf R_p\) is \(p \times p\) Toeplitz with \([\mathbf R_p]_{ij} = R_X[|i-j|]\), \(\mathbf a = (a_1, \dots, a_p)^\top\), \(\mathbf r = (R_X[1], \dots, R_X[p])^\top\). Derivation: multiply the AR equation \(x[n] + \sum_m a_m x[n-m] = w[n]\) by \(x^*[n-k]\) and take expectations. For \(k \ge 1\), the right side vanishes (white noise orthogonal to past). The left gives \(R_X[k] + \sum_m a_m R_X[k-m] = 0\), i.e., \(R_X[k] = -\sum_m a_m R_X[k-m]\). Why linear: the unknown coefficients \(a_m\) appear linearly — the equations are a linear system in \(\mathbf a\). That is the crucial advantage of AR over MA and ARMA, both of which give nonlinear systems.
  8. Levinson–Durbin: an \(O(p^2)\) recursion for solving the Toeplitz Yule–Walker system. At each order \(m\), one new reflection coefficient \(k_m\) is computed, and the AR coefficients of order \(m\) are updated from order \(m-1\) by \(a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m a_{m-i}^{(m-1)}\) and \(a_m^{(m)} = k_m\), with the residual variance \(\sigma_m^2 = (1-k_m^2)\sigma_{m-1}^2\). Reflection coefficients: \(k_m\) is the partial autocorrelation at lag \(m\) — the correlation between \(x[n]\) and \(x[n-m]\) after removing the linear effect of intermediate lags. Stability property: \(|k_m| < 1\) for all \(m\) is necessary and sufficient for the AR model to have all poles inside the unit circle (a stable filter). This is what makes the lattice structure of §3 inherently stable.
  9. PSD formulas: AR: \(S_X = \sigma_w^2 / |1 + \sum a_k e^{-j\omega k}|^2\). MA: \(S_X = \sigma_w^2 |1 + \sum b_k e^{-j\omega k}|^2\). ARMA: ratio of the two. Why AR dominates: (i) it is linear to fit (Yule–Walker), while MA/ARMA require nonlinear methods; (ii) it is guaranteed non-negative by construction (squared magnitude of rational); (iii) Wold's theorem says every WSS process can be approximated arbitrarily well by an AR model of sufficiently high order; (iv) the O(p²) Levinson–Durbin algorithm makes high-order AR cheap. In practice, AR with \(p = 10\) to \(30\) is the default, and it works well for most real signals (speech, ECG, spectra with sharp peaks).
  10. AIC: \(\text{AIC}(p) = N\ln\hat\sigma_p^2 + 2p\) — penalises each parameter by \(2\) nats. Tends to over-fit. MDL/BIC: \(\text{MDL}(p) = N\ln\hat\sigma_p^2 + p\ln N\) — penalises each parameter by \(\ln N\), which grows with record length. Tends to under-fit but is consistent (correctly identifies the true order for large \(N\)). FPE: \(\text{FPE}(p) = \hat\sigma_p^2 (N+p+1)/(N-p-1)\) — estimates the one-step prediction error; to leading order equivalent to AIC. Effect of penalty: larger penalty (MDL) → smaller chosen \(p\); smaller penalty (AIC) → larger chosen \(p\). Choose AIC if under-fitting is worse than over-fitting (the true PSD might have more peaks than the AR model can capture); MDL if you want the sharpest estimate of the true model order. In signal-processing practice, AIC is more common when the purpose is spectrum estimation; MDL when the purpose is model identification.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Hayes, Statistical Digital Signal Processing and Modeling, Wiley, 1996 — Chapters 5–7. This chapter is essentially a guided tour of Chapters 5–7 of Hayes, which is the textbook closest to the syllabus.
  • Proakis & Manolakis, Digital Signal Processing, Pearson, 2007 — Chapter 14 (spectrum estimation). Basic treatment, good for background.
  • Kay, Modern Spectral Estimation: Theory and Application, Prentice-Hall, 1988 — the definitive reference for nonparametric and parametric methods. Excellent on the periodogram's variance.
  • Stoica & Moses, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Prentice-Hall, 2005 — modern, rigorous; covers subspace methods (MUSIC, ESPRIT) not touched in this chapter.
  • Percival & Walden, Spectral Analysis for Physical Applications, Cambridge University Press, 1993 — the standard reference for Welch and multitaper methods.
  • Haykin, Adaptive Filter Theory, Pearson, 5th ed., 2014 — Chapter 1 for the Yule–Walker and Levinson material.
  • Marple, Digital Spectral Analysis, Dover, 2019 — comprehensive practical reference.
  • scipy.signal documentation: periodogram, welch, csd.
  • statsmodels.tsa documentation: ARMA, AR, acf, pacf.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Periodogram variance study. For \(N \in \{256, 1024, 4096, 16384\}\), simulate white Gaussian noise and compute the standard deviation of the periodogram across frequency bins. Confirm that it is \(\sigma^2\) regardless of \(N\).
  2. Bartlett bias trade-off. For \(N = 4096\), compute the periodogram and Bartlett estimators with \(K = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\). For a signal with two tones at \(0.20\) and \(0.22\) (normalised frequency), determine the largest \(K\) that still resolves the two peaks.
  3. Welch vs. Bartlett. With the same \(N\) and the same segment length \(L = 512\), compare the variance reduction of Bartlett (non-overlapping) and Welch (50% overlap, Hann window). Quantify the effective reduction factor.
  4. Blackman–Tukey tuning. For a white-noise signal with \(N = 1024\), compute the MSE between \(\hat S^{BT}_X\) and the true flat spectrum for \(M = 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256\). Find the empirical \(M^\star\) and compare with \(N^{1/3} \approx 10\).
  5. Biased vs. unbiased autocorrelation. For \(N = 200\) samples of white noise, plot both \(\hat R_X[k]\) and \(\hat R_u[k]\) over \(k \in [0, N-1]\). Verify the theoretical mean biases. Where does the variance of \(\hat R_u\) diverge?
  6. Yule–Walker exercise. Given \(R_X[0] = 10\), \(R_X[1] = 5\), \(R_X[2] = 1\), solve for the AR(2) coefficients and \(\sigma_w^2\) by hand, then verify with scipy.linalg.solve_toeplitz.
  7. Levinson–Durbin vs. matrix inverse. Implement Levinson–Durbin from scratch and compare against numpy.linalg.solve for \(p = 1, \dots, 20\). Plot the timing difference and confirm \(O(p^2)\) vs. \(O(p^3)\).
  8. AR spectrum. Fit an AR model of order 10 to a recorded segment of voiced speech (e.g., from pyroomacoustics's sample data). Plot the AR PSD and identify the formants (spectral peaks). Compare with a Welch estimate.
  9. Model-order selection. For a simulated ARMA(1,1) process with \(a_1 = 0.8\), \(b_1 = 0.5\), \(\sigma_w = 1\), and \(N = 500\), compute AIC, MDL, and FPE for \(p = 1, \dots, 15\). Do they agree? Which is closest to the true order (2 for AR part, 1 for MA)?
  10. Consistency demonstration. Simulate a Gaussian AR(1) process with \(a_1 = 0.9\) at increasing \(N \in \{100, 1000, 10000, 100000\}\). Compute the Bartlett estimator with \(K \propto N^{2/3}\) and \(L \propto N^{1/3}\). Plot the MSE between the estimate and the true AR(1) PSD vs. \(N\) on a log-log axis. Verify that the MSE decreases with \(N\) — this is the practical manifestation of consistency.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Linear Estimation and Prediction
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): maximum likelihood criterion · efficiency of estimator · least-mean-squared-error criterion · Wiener filter · discrete Wiener–Hopf equations · recursive estimators · Kalman filter · linear prediction · prediction error · whitening filter · inverse filter · Levinson recursion · lattice realization · Levinson recursion for Toeplitz systems.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State and apply the maximum likelihood (ML) criterion; derive the ML estimator of a scalar parameter in Gaussian noise; compute the Cramér–Rao lower bound (CRLB) and check whether an estimator is efficient.
  2. State the least-mean-squared-error (MMSE) criterion; distinguish the optimal (possibly nonlinear) MMSE from the linear MMSE (LMMSE).
  3. Derive the orthogonality principle and use it to solve LMMSE problems for random vectors and random processes.
  4. Formulate and solve the Wiener–Hopf equations for the FIR Wiener filter; derive the causal IIR Wiener filter via spectral factorization.
  5. Derive and apply the discrete Kalman filter (scalar and vector form); interpret the predict-update recursion and the Riccati equation.
  6. Derive the forward and backward linear prediction equations; interpret prediction error and the prediction-error filter.
  7. Design the whitening filter and the inverse filter as an application of spectral factorization and prediction-error filtering.
  8. Apply Levinson–Durbin (recap from Chapter 2) to solve the Toeplitz normal equations of linear prediction; state its \(O(p^2)\) complexity.
  9. Derive the lattice filter from the reflection coefficients and explain its numerical and structural advantages (stability, modularity, order adaptation).
  10. Implement all of the above in Python, Java, and C#.

docs.title: 3.1 Overview — what estimation problems look like
docs.text:
Every estimation problem has three ingredients:

  • A parameter or signal to be estimated (scalar \(\theta\), vector \(\boldsymbol\theta\), or a random process \(S[n]\)).
  • Observations \(Y\) (a vector of samples, or a full observation record).
  • A criterion to optimise — what makes one estimate "better" than another.

The three criteria we will develop, in increasing generality:

Criterion Optimises Requires Maximum likelihood Probability of observations Full probabilistic model of \(Y \mid \theta\) MMSE (optimal) \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)^2]\) over all estimators Joint distribution of \((S, Y)\) LMMSE \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)^2]\) over linear estimators Only second-order statistics (means and covariances)

The LMMSE criterion is the workhorse of digital signal processing: it requires only first and second moments, it is linear — hence computationally tractable — and for jointly Gaussian signals it coincides with the true MMSE.

The Wiener filter is the LMMSE estimator for stationary processes (frequency-domain solution); the Kalman filter is the LMMSE estimator for state-space models (recursive time-domain solution). They are two views of the same problem.

docs.title: 3.2.1 The ML criterion
docs.text:
Given \(N\) observations \(Y = (y[0], \dots, y[N-1])^\top\) with joint density \(p_Y(y; \theta)\) indexed by a parameter \(\theta\), the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is

\[ \boxed{\;\hat\theta_{\text{ML}} = \arg\max_\theta p_Y(Y; \theta)\;} \]

equivalently, maximising the log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta) = \ln p_Y(Y; \theta)\):

\[ \hat\theta_{\text{ML}} = \arg\max_\theta\, \ell(\theta). \]

For an i.i.d. sample, \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_n \ln p_y(y[n]; \theta)\).

docs.title: 3.2.2 Properties of the MLE (under regularity conditions)
docs.text: Property Statement Consistency \(\hat\theta_{\text{ML}} \to \theta\) in probability as \(N \to \infty\) Asymptotic normality \(\sqrt N (\hat\theta_{\text{ML}} - \theta) \to \mathcal N(0, I^{-1}(\theta))\) Asymptotic efficiency Attains the CRLB asymptotically (smallest possible variance) Invariance If \(\hat\theta\) is MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat\theta)\) is MLE of \(g(\theta)\)

docs.title: 3.2.3 The Cramér–Rao lower bound (CRLB)
docs.text:
For any unbiased estimator \(\hat\theta\) of a scalar parameter \(\theta\),

\[ \boxed{\;\operatorname{Var}[\hat\theta] \ge \frac{1}{I(\theta)},\qquad I(\theta) = -\mathbb E\Bigl[\frac{\partial^2 \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta^2}\Bigr] = \mathbb E\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta}\Bigr)^2\Bigr]\;} \]

where \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher information. The bound is achieved (equality) iff the log-likelihood has the exponential-family form \(\ell(\theta) = a(\theta)\hat\theta + b(\hat\theta) + c(\theta) + d\).

An estimator is efficient if it achieves the CRLB at finite \(N\); the MLE is asymptotically efficient under regularity.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — estimating amplitude in Gaussian noise
docs.text:
Observations \(y[n] = A + w[n]\), \(n = 0, \dots, N-1\), with \(w[n] \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) i.i.d. Estimate the constant amplitude \(A\).

Log-likelihood.

\[ \ell(A) = -\frac{N}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(y[n] - A)^2. \]

MLE.

\[ \frac{d\ell}{dA} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_n (y[n] - A) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\;\hat A_{\text{ML}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} y[n] = \bar y\;} \]

the sample mean — as expected for a Gaussian.

CRLB.

\[ \frac{d^2\ell}{dA^2} = -\frac{N}{\sigma^2} \;\Longrightarrow\; I(A) = \frac{N}{\sigma^2}. \]

So \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat A] \ge \sigma^2/N\).

Efficiency. \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat A_{\text{ML}}] = \operatorname{Var}[\bar y] = \sigma^2/N\). The sample mean attains the CRLB for every finite \(N\) — it is an efficient estimator. This is the finite-\(N\) exception; in general only asymptotically efficient.

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — estimating frequency in complex Gaussian noise
docs.text:
Observations \(y[n] = A e^{j(\omega_0 n + \theta)} + w[n]\), \(w\) complex white Gaussian with variance \(\sigma^2\) per real dimension, estimate \(\omega_0\) with \(A\), \(\theta\) known.

Log-likelihood. The dominant term for large \(N\) is proportional to the real part of the correlation between observations and the assumed signal:

\[ \ell(\omega) \approx \frac{2 A}{\sigma^2}\,\Re\Bigl\{e^{-j\theta}\sum_n y[n]e^{-j\omega n}\Bigr\}. \]

MLE. Maximising \(\ell(\omega)\) is equivalent to maximising \(\bigl|\sum_n y[n]e^{-j\omega n}\bigr|^2\) — the periodogram! The MLE of a sinusoidal frequency is the peak of the periodogram. This connects Chapter 2 (spectrum estimation) and Chapter 3 (ML estimation) into one framework.

CRLB. The Fisher information is

\[ I(\omega_0) = \frac{2 A^2}{\sigma^2}\sum_n n^2 \sim \frac{2 A^2 N^3}{3\sigma^2}, \]

so \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat\omega_0] \ge \frac{3\sigma^2}{2 A^2 N^3} \propto 1/N^3\) — faster than the usual \(1/N\) rate. Frequency estimation is unusually accurate.

The CRLB is only tight in the high-SNR regime (\(\text{SNR} = A^2 N / \sigma^2 \gg 1\)); below the threshold SNR (typically ~10 dB for periodogram-frequency estimation), the MLE loses lock and the actual variance is much larger than the CRLB.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Problem statement
docs.text:
Given observations \(Y\) and a target \(S\), the MMSE estimator is

\[ \boxed{\;\hat S_{\text{MMSE}} = \arg\min_{\hat S(Y)}\, \mathbb E\bigl[(S - \hat S)^2\bigr]\;} \]

where the minimisation is over all functions \(\hat S : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb R\). The optimal solution is the conditional mean:

\[ \boxed{\;\hat S_{\text{MMSE}}(Y) = \mathbb E[S \mid Y]\;} \]

with minimum MSE \(\operatorname{Var}[S \mid Y]\) (the conditional variance).

Consequences.

  • The optimal estimator is generally nonlinear (except when \((S, Y)\) are jointly Gaussian).
  • It depends on the full joint distribution of \((S, Y)\) — much stronger information than the second moments alone.
  • In practice, the conditional mean is often hard to compute, motivating the linear restriction.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Linear MMSE (LMMSE)
docs.text:
Restrict the estimator to affine functions of \(Y\):

\[ \hat S_{\text{LMMSE}} = a + b^\top Y. \]

Then the solution is given by the orthogonality principle:

Orthogonality principle

The LMMSE estimator \(\hat S\) satisfies $$ \boxed{\;\mathbb E\bigl[(S - \hat S)\, Y^\top\bigr] = 0\;} $$ and (by the affine structure) \(\mathbb E[S - \hat S] = 0\). The estimation error is orthogonal to the observation space.

docs.title: 3.3.3 Closed form
docs.text:
Let \(\mu_S = \mathbb E[S]\), \(\mu_Y = \mathbb E[Y]\), \(\Sigma_{SY} = \mathbb E[(S - \mu_S)(Y - \mu_Y)^\top]\), \(\Sigma_{YY} = \mathbb E[(Y - \mu_Y)(Y - \mu_Y)^\top]\). Then

\[ \boxed{\;\hat S_{\text{LMMSE}} = \mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\,\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\,(Y - \mu_Y)\;} \]

with minimum MSE

\[ \boxed{\;\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{min}} = \Sigma_{SS} - \Sigma_{SY}\,\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\,\Sigma_{YS}\;} \]

where \(\Sigma_{SS} = \operatorname{Var}[S]\) (scalar) and \(\Sigma_{YS} = \Sigma_{SY}^\top\).

docs.title: 3.3.4 Gaussian case
docs.text:
Linear = optimal for Gaussian

If \((S, Y)\) are jointly Gaussian, then the conditional mean is affine in \(Y\), so the LMMSE estimator is the MMSE estimator. This is the fundamental reason Kalman filtering is optimal for linear Gaussian systems, and why LMMSE is so useful in practice — Gaussianity makes it exact.

docs.title: Worked example 3.3 — LMMSE of a random signal in additive noise
docs.text:
Let \(S \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_S^2)\) and \(V \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_V^2)\) be independent, with \(Y = S + V\). Estimate \(S\) from \(Y\).

Second moments. \(\Sigma_{SY} = \mathbb E[SY] = \mathbb E[S(S+V)] = \sigma_S^2\); \(\Sigma_{YY} = \sigma_S^2 + \sigma_V^2\).

LMMSE.

\[ \hat S = 0 + \frac{\sigma_S^2}{\sigma_S^2 + \sigma_V^2}\, Y = \frac{\text{SNR}}{1 + \text{SNR}}\, Y, \quad \text{SNR} = \sigma_S^2/\sigma_V^2. \]

Interpretation.

  • Large SNR (\(\sigma_V^2 \to 0\)): \(\hat S \to Y\) — trust the observation.
  • Small SNR (\(\sigma_V^2 \to \infty\)): \(\hat S \to 0\) — trust the prior mean (zero).

Minimum MSE.

\[ \operatorname{MSE}_{\text{min}} = \sigma_S^2 - \frac{\sigma_S^4}{\sigma_S^2 + \sigma_V^2} = \frac{\sigma_S^2 \sigma_V^2}{\sigma_S^2 + \sigma_V^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma_S^{-2} + \sigma_V^{-2}}. \]

Notice the harmonic sum form: the posterior precision is the sum of the prior precision (\(1/\sigma_S^2\)) and the measurement precision (\(1/\sigma_V^2\)). This is exactly the information form of the Kalman filter update — a preview of §3.7.

Since the model is jointly Gaussian, this LMMSE equals the MMSE. No nonlinear estimator can do better.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Problem statement
docs.text:
Let \(X[n]\) be a WSS desired signal, \(Y[n]\) an observed WSS process, both jointly WSS. We want a linear time-invariant filter \(h[n]\) such that

\[ \hat X[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[k]\, Y[n-k] \]

minimises \(\mathbb E[(X[n] - \hat X[n])^2]\).

No causality requirement — the filter may use future observations. This is the non-causal (or smoothing) Wiener filter.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Orthogonality in the time domain
docs.text:
By the orthogonality principle applied at every lag \(m\):

\[ \mathbb E\bigl[(X[n] - \hat X[n])Y^*[n-m]\bigr] = 0,\quad \forall m. \]

This gives the normal equations (Wiener–Hopf equations in infinite form):

\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[k]\, R_Y[m-k] = R_{XY}[m],\quad \forall m \in \mathbb Z.\;} \]

docs.title: 3.4.3 Solution in the frequency domain
docs.text:
Take the DTFT of both sides. The convolution becomes a product:

\[ H(e^{j\omega})\, S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = S_{XY}(e^{j\omega}), \qquad \boxed{\;H_{\text{nc}}(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{S_{XY}(e^{j\omega})}{S_Y(e^{j\omega})}\;} \]

where \(S_{XY}\) is the cross-power spectral density, \(S_{XY}(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_k R_{XY}[k]e^{-j\omega k}\).

For the signal-in-noise case with \(Y[n] = X[n] + V[n]\), \(X \perp V\):

\[ S_{XY} = S_{XX},\qquad S_Y = S_{XX} + S_{VV} \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\;H_{\text{nc}}(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{S_{XX}(e^{j\omega})}{S_{XX}(e^{j\omega}) + S_{VV}(e^{j\omega})}\;} \]

docs.title: 3.4.4 Interpretation
docs.text:
The non-causal Wiener filter shapes the passband according to the local SNR:

  • Where \(S_{XX} \gg S_{VV}\) (high SNR): \(H \approx 1\) — pass the signal.
  • Where \(S_{XX} \ll S_{VV}\) (low SNR): \(H \approx 0\) — reject the noise.
  • Where \(S_{XX} = S_{VV}\): \(H \approx 1/2\) — half pass, half reject.

The minimum MSE is

\[ \operatorname{MSE}_{\text{min}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_{XX}(e^{j\omega})\bigl(1 - H_{\text{nc}}(e^{j\omega})\bigr)\, d\omega = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{S_{XX} S_{VV}}{S_{XX} + S_{VV}}\, d\omega. \]

docs.title: Worked example 3.4 — non-causal Wiener filter for AR(1) + white noise
docs.text:
\(X[n]\) is AR(1): \(X[n] = a X[n-1] + W[n]\), \(|a| < 1\), \(\sigma_W^2 = 1\). \(V[n]\) is white, \(\sigma_V^2 = 0.5\), independent of \(X\).

Spectra.

\[ S_{XX}(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{|1 - a e^{-j\omega}|^2} = \frac{1}{1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2}, \quad S_{VV} = 0.5. \]

Wiener filter.

\[ H_{\text{nc}}(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2 + 0.5(1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2)} = \frac{1}{1.5(1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2)}. \]

Not a low-pass — it is a notch-rejecting filter that attenuates the frequencies where \(S_{XX}\) is small (high frequencies when \(a > 0\)).

MSE reduction. For \(a = 0.7\), numeric integration gives \(\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{min}} / \operatorname{Var}[X] \approx 0.31\) — the Wiener filter eliminates ~70% of the estimation error, using future observations.

The causal filter (§3.6) cannot use future observations, so it does not achieve the same MSE. The gap between the non-causal and causal MSEs quantifies the "cost of real-time".

docs.title: 3.5.1 Setup
docs.text:
In practice, \(h[n]\) is finite-length: \(h[0], \dots, h[M-1]\). The estimation is

\[ \hat X[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} h[k]\, Y[n-k], \]

and the orthogonality principle gives \(M\) linear equations:

\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{k=0}^{M-1} h[k]\, R_Y[m-k] = R_{XY}[m],\quad m = 0, \dots, M-1.\;} \]

Matrix form (Toeplitz):

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf R_Y\, \mathbf h = \mathbf r_{XY}\;} \]

where \(\mathbf R_Y\) is the \(M \times M\) Toeplitz matrix with \([\mathbf R_Y]_{ij} = R_Y[i-j]\), and \(\mathbf r_{XY} = (R_{XY}[0], \dots, R_{XY}[M-1])^\top\).

The solution is \(\mathbf h = \mathbf R_Y^{-1}\mathbf r_{XY}\), computed via Levinson–Durbin if \(\mathbf R_Y\) is Toeplitz (which it is, for WSS data).

docs.title: Worked example 3.5 — 3-tap Wiener filter
docs.text:
\(Y[n] = X[n] + V[n]\), \(X \perp V\). Known:

\[ R_X[0] = 4,\quad R_X[1] = 2,\quad R_X[k] = 0\ (|k| \ge 2);\qquad R_V[0] = 1,\quad R_V[k] = 0\ (k \ne 0). \]

Design a 3-tap Wiener filter \(h[0], h[1], h[2]\) to estimate \(X[n]\) from \(Y\).

Correlations.

\[ R_Y[k] = R_X[k] + R_V[k] \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_Y[0] = 5,\ R_Y[\pm 1] = 2,\ R_Y[k] = 0\ (|k| \ge 2). \] \[ R_{XY}[m] = \mathbb E[X[n]Y[n-m]] = R_X[m]. \]

Toeplitz system.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} R_Y[0] & R_Y[1] & R_Y[2] \\ R_Y[1] & R_Y[0] & R_Y[1] \\ R_Y[2] & R_Y[1] & R_Y[0]\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} h_0 \\ h_1 \\ h_2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} R_X[0] \\ R_X[1] \\ R_X[2]\end{bmatrix} \] \[ \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} h_0 \\ h_1 \\ h_2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}. \]

Solve. From row 3: \(2h_1 + 5h_2 = 0 \Rightarrow h_2 = -0.4h_1\). Row 1: \(5h_0 + 2h_1 = 4 \Rightarrow h_0 = 0.8 - 0.4h_1\). Row 2: \(2h_0 + 5h_1 + 2h_2 = 2 \Rightarrow 2(0.8 - 0.4h_1) + 5h_1 + 2(-0.4h_1) = 2\).

\[ 1.6 - 0.8h_1 + 5h_1 - 0.8h_1 = 2 \Rightarrow 1.6 + 3.4h_1 = 2 \Rightarrow h_1 = 0.4/3.4 = 0.1176. \]

Then \(h_0 = 0.8 - 0.4\cdot 0.1176 = 0.7529\), \(h_2 = -0.0471\).

Filter. \(\mathbf h = (0.7529,\ 0.1176,\ -0.0471)\).

Sanity check. The centre tap dominates (as expected for a lightly-smoothed signal), the lags are small, and \(h_0 + h_1 + h_2 = 0.8234\) — the filter's DC gain is less than 1 because it needs to reject noise at DC as well.

Minimum MSE. \(\sigma_X^2 - \mathbf r_{XY}^\top \mathbf h = 4 - (4\cdot 0.7529 + 2\cdot 0.1176 + 0\cdot (-0.0471)) = 4 - 3.2468 = 0.7532\).

Compare with the "pass-through" MSE \(\sigma_V^2 = 1\): the Wiener filter reduces estimation error by ~25%.

docs.title: 3.5.2 Numerical conditioning
docs.text:
The Wiener–Hopf matrix \(\mathbf R_Y\) is Toeplitz and positive-definite (from \(R_Y\) being a valid autocorrelation). Its condition number \(\kappa(\mathbf R_Y)\) depends on the SNR and the autocorrelation length:

  • High SNR, highly coloured (autocorrelation decays slowly): \(\kappa\) large — the filter is effectively ill-conditioned; small errors in \(R_Y\) estimates produce large filter errors.
  • Low SNR, white: \(\kappa\) near 1 — well-conditioned, robust filter.

Practical guidance. Estimate \(R_Y\), \(R_{XY}\) from data using the biased sample autocorrelation (positive-definiteness guaranteed by Chapter 1 §1.4.3); solve with Levinson–Durbin for numerical stability. Avoid naive Gaussian elimination when \(\kappa\) exceeds \(10^4\).

docs.title: 3.6.1 Problem statement
docs.text:
Same as the non-causal case, but with the causality constraint \(h[n] = 0\) for \(n < 0\). This is the real-time filter; it cannot use future observations.

The orthogonality principle still holds, but only for non-negative lags:

\[ \mathbb E\bigl[(X[n] - \hat X[n])Y^*[n-m]\bigr] = 0,\quad m \ge 0. \]

The Wiener–Hopf equations are now one-sided:

\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} h[k]\, R_Y[m-k] = R_{XY}[m],\quad m \ge 0.\;} \]

This is the discrete Wiener–Hopf equation — harder than the two-sided (non-causal) case because a DTFT of both sides introduces unknown terms for \(m < 0\).

docs.title: 3.6.2 Solution via spectral factorization
docs.text:
The classical solution uses spectral factorization (Chapter 1 §1.8) plus a causal-part operation. Step-by-step:

Step 1 — Factor \(S_Y\). Find the causal, monic, minimum-phase \(L(z)\) and \(\sigma_e^2\) such that

\[ S_Y(z) = \sigma_e^2\, L(z)\, L(z^{-1}). \]

Step 2 — Compute the causal part. Form

\[ G(z) = \frac{S_{XY}(z)}{\sigma_e^2\, L(z^{-1})}, \]

and take the causal part \([G(z)]_+\) — the part of the Laurent expansion in non-negative powers of \(z^{-1}\) (i.e. terms \(z^0, z^{-1}, z^{-2}, \dots\)).

Step 3 — Compose the filter.

\[ \boxed{\;H_{\text{causal}}(z) = \frac{[G(z)]_+}{L(z)}\;} \]

The numerator is realisable (causal) and the denominator is causal-minimum-phase, so \(H_{\text{causal}}\) is stable and causal.

docs.title: 3.6.3 The "smoothing" correction
docs.text:
An equivalent statement: the causal Wiener filter is

\[ H_{\text{causal}}(z) = \frac{1}{\sigma_e^2 L(z)}\Bigl[\frac{S_{XY}(z)}{L(z^{-1})}\Bigr]_+. \]

The operation \([\cdot]_+\) is what distinguishes causal from non-causal: without it, \(H = S_{XY}/(\sigma_e^2 L L^{-1}) = S_{XY}/S_Y\) — the non-causal filter of §3.4.

Interpretation. The causal filter is the non-causal filter projected onto the causal subspace in a particular weighted inner product (weighted by the whitening filter \(1/L\)). This projection is what makes the causal filter optimal among causal filters.

docs.title: Worked example 3.6 — causal Wiener filter for AR(1) + white noise
docs.text:
Same setup as Example 3.4: \(X\) AR(1) with \(a = 0.7\), \(\sigma_W = 1\), \(V\) white \(\sigma_V = 0.5\).

Step 1 — Factor \(S_Y\). From Example 3.4:

\[ S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = S_{XX} + S_{VV} = \frac{1 + 0.5(1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2)}{1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2}. \]

Write as \(S_Y(z) = \sigma_e^2 L(z)L(z^{-1})\) with \(L(z) = (1 + bz^{-1})/(1 - az^{-1})\) by factoring the numerator and denominator polynomials in \(z\). Matching coefficients gives \(b \approx 0.2648\) (a small positive root), and \(\sigma_e^2 \approx 0.5\).

Step 2 — Causal part. \(S_{XY}(z) = S_{XX}(z) = \frac{1}{(1-az^{-1})(1-az)}\). Then

\[ G(z) = \frac{S_{XX}(z)}{\sigma_e^2 L(z^{-1})} = \frac{1}{\sigma_e^2(1-az)} \cdot \frac{1-az}{1+bz} \cdot \frac{1}{1-az^{-1}} = \frac{1}{\sigma_e^2}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+bz)(1-az^{-1})}. \]

Partial-fraction expansion with causal-part extraction gives

\[ [G(z)]_+ = \frac{A}{1-az^{-1}},\quad A = \frac{1}{\sigma_e^2(1+ab)}. \]

Step 3 — Compose.

\[ H_{\text{causal}}(z) = \frac{A/(1-az^{-1})}{(1+bz^{-1})/(1-az^{-1})} = \frac{A}{1+bz^{-1}}. \]

Result. The causal Wiener filter is a first-order IIR filter with pole at \(-b \approx -0.2648\) and gain \(A\). Compare with the non-causal filter, which is not rational — a direct consequence of the causality constraint.

MSE penalty. Numerically, the causal MSE is \(\approx 0.42\) versus the non-causal \(\approx 0.31\) — about 35% more error, the price of causality.

docs.title: 3.6.4 Comparison table
docs.text:
Filter Formula Requires Optimal among Non-causal Wiener \(S_{XY}/S_Y\) Full PSDs All linear filters Causal Wiener \([S_{XY}/(\sigma_e^2 L^{-1})]_+ / L\) PSDs + spectral factorization Causal linear filters Kalman (§3.7) Recursive; steady state equals causal Wiener for stationary \(S_Y\) State-space model Causal linear filters (equivalently)

Kalman and causal Wiener give the same filter in steady state when the process is stationary and both are causal. The Kalman formulation has computational advantages (recursive, no large-matrix inversion, handles non-stationarity and multi-channel observations naturally).

docs.title: 3.7.1 State-space model
docs.text:
The Kalman filter solves the LMMSE problem for state-space models:

\[ \boxed{\;x[n] = A x[n-1] + B u[n]\;}\quad\text{(state equation)} \] \[ \boxed{\;y[n] = C x[n] + v[n]\;}\quad\text{(observation equation)} \]

with:

  • \(x[n] \in \mathbb R^d\) — state vector (unknown, to be estimated).
  • \(y[n] \in \mathbb R^m\) — observation vector.
  • \(u[n] \sim \mathcal N(0, Q)\) — process noise (white, independent across \(n\)).
  • \(v[n] \sim \mathcal N(0, R)\) — measurement noise (white, independent of \(u\) and \(x[0]\)).
  • \(x[0] \sim \mathcal N(\hat x_{0|0}, P_{0|0})\) — initial state prior.

The matrices \(A, B, C, Q, R\) are known. The goal is the recursive LMMSE estimate \(\hat x_{n|k} = \mathbb E[x[n] \mid y[1], \dots, y[k]]\).

Two cases: - Filtering (\(k = n\)): estimate the current state. - Prediction (\(k < n\)): forecast future states (used in control and tracking). - Smoothing (\(k > n\)): estimate past states given all future observations (used in offline estimation).

The Kalman filter is the filtering case; it is a predict-update recursion.

docs.title: 3.7.2 The recursion
docs.text:
Initialise \(\hat x_{0|0}\), \(P_{0|0}\). For \(n = 1, 2, \dots\):

Predict step (extrapolate the state and its covariance):

\[ \boxed{\;\hat x_{n|n-1} = A\,\hat x_{n-1|n-1}\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;P_{n|n-1} = A P_{n-1|n-1} A^\top + B Q B^\top\;} \]

Kalman gain (how much to trust the observation):

\[ \boxed{\;K_n = P_{n|n-1} C^\top \bigl(C P_{n|n-1} C^\top + R\bigr)^{-1}\;} \]

Update step (correct the prediction using the observation):

\[ \boxed{\;\hat x_{n|n} = \hat x_{n|n-1} + K_n \bigl(y[n] - C \hat x_{n|n-1}\bigr)\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;P_{n|n} = (I - K_n C) P_{n|n-1}\;} \]

The term \(\nu_n = y[n] - C\hat x_{n|n-1}\) is the innovation (or prediction error) — the part of the observation not predicted by the model. If the model is correct, \(\nu_n\) is white with covariance \(C P_{n|n-1} C^\top + R\).

docs.title: 3.7.3 Interpretation
docs.text:
Quantity Meaning \(\hat x_{n\|n-1}\) Prior mean — belief about \(x[n]\) before seeing \(y[n]\) \(P_{n\|n-1}\) Prior covariance — uncertainty in the prior \(K_n\) Weight on the innovation — the optimal compromise between prior and observation \(y[n] - C\hat x_{n\|n-1}\) Innovation — new information in \(y[n]\) \(\hat x_{n\|n}\) Posterior mean — belief after seeing \(y[n]\) \(P_{n\|n}\) Posterior covariance — reduced uncertainty

Limit cases of the Kalman gain.

  • \(R \to 0\) (noiseless observations): \(K_n \to C^{-1}\), so \(\hat x_{n|n} \to C^{-1}y[n]\) — trust the observation completely.
  • \(R \to \infty\) (useless observations): \(K_n \to 0\), so \(\hat x_{n|n} \to \hat x_{n|n-1}\) — ignore the observation.
  • \(P_{n|n-1} \to 0\) (perfect prior): \(K_n \to 0\) — trust the prior.

The Kalman filter interpolates between these extremes according to the relative uncertainty.

docs.title: Worked example 3.7 — scalar Kalman filter, two steps
docs.text:
Model: \(x[n] = 0.9\, x[n-1] + u[n]\), \(u[n] \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.1)\); \(y[n] = x[n] + v[n]\), \(v[n] \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\). Initial: \(\hat x_{0|0} = 0\), \(P_{0|0} = 1\). Observations: \(y[1] = 2\), \(y[2] = 1.5\).

Step 1 — predict.

\[ \hat x_{1|0} = 0.9 \cdot 0 = 0,\qquad P_{1|0} = 0.9^2 \cdot 1 + 0.1 = 0.91. \]

Kalman gain.

\[ K_1 = P_{1|0}(P_{1|0} + R)^{-1} = 0.91/(0.91 + 1) = 0.4764. \]

Update.

\[ \hat x_{1|1} = 0 + 0.4764\,(2 - 0) = 0.9529,\qquad P_{1|1} = (1 - 0.4764) \cdot 0.91 = 0.4764. \]

Step 2 — predict.

\[ \hat x_{2|1} = 0.9 \cdot 0.9529 = 0.8576,\qquad P_{2|1} = 0.9^2 \cdot 0.4764 + 0.1 = 0.486. \]

Kalman gain.

\[ K_2 = 0.486/(0.486 + 1) = 0.327. \]

Update.

\[ \hat x_{2|2} = 0.8576 + 0.327\,(1.5 - 0.8576) = 1.067,\qquad P_{2|2} = (1 - 0.327)\cdot 0.486 = 0.327. \]

Interpretation. The first observation (\(y[1] = 2\)) pulls the estimate up to \(0.95\), but \(K_1 < 1\) means we don't fully trust it (noise variance = 1, comparable to prior variance = 0.91). The second observation (\(y[2] = 1.5\)) is lower than predicted (\(0.858\)), so it nudges the estimate to \(1.067\). The posterior variance shrinks from \(1 \to 0.476 \to 0.327\) — uncertainty decreases with more data.

docs.title: Worked example 3.8 — steady-state behaviour
docs.text:
Repeat the same scalar model for many steps. The Riccati recursion \(P_{n|n} = f(P_{n-1|n-1})\) converges to a fixed point \(P^\star\) satisfying

\[ P^\star = \frac{(A^2 P^\star + Q) R}{A^2 P^\star + Q + R}. \]

For \(A = 0.9\), \(Q = 0.1\), \(R = 1\):

\[ P^\star = \frac{(0.81 P^\star + 0.1) \cdot 1}{0.81 P^\star + 0.1 + 1} \;\Rightarrow\; P^\star \approx 0.327. \]

The steady-state Kalman gain is \(K^\star = P^\star/(P^\star + 1) \approx 0.246\).

After convergence, the Kalman filter is a linear time-invariant filter:

\[ \hat x_{n|n} = A(1 - K^\star)\hat x_{n-1|n-1} + K^\star y[n] \quad\text{(scalar case)} = 0.9\cdot 0.754\,\hat x_{n-1|n-1} + 0.246\, y[n]. \]

This LTI recursion is exactly what the causal Wiener filter of §3.6 produces for the same process. The Kalman filter is the state-space implementation of the causal Wiener filter, and it converges to it exponentially fast.

docs.title: 3.7.4 The Riccati equation
docs.text:
The discrete algebraic Riccati equation (DARE) for the steady-state covariance is

\[ \boxed{\;P = A P A^\top + B Q B^\top - A P C^\top (C P C^\top + R)^{-1} C P A^\top.\;} \]

Existence and uniqueness. Under stabilisability (unstable modes of \(A\) are affected by the process noise) and detectability (unstable modes are observable through \(C\)), the DARE has a unique positive-definite solution \(P^\star > 0\). Under these conditions, the Kalman filter converges to the steady-state gain \(K^\star\) from any initial \(P_{0|0} \ge 0\).

Solving the DARE in practice. Iterating the Riccati recursion (the Kalman recursion for \(P\) alone) converges in \(O(\log(1/\epsilon))\) iterations — quadratic convergence for small \(Q/R\). For very large \(d\), use the structure-preserving methods (Potter, Joseph form, square-root filters) to avoid numerical loss of positive-definiteness.

docs.title: 3.7.5 Why Kalman is more general than Wiener
docs.text:
The Wiener filter assumes: - Stationarity of all processes involved. - Known second-order statistics. - Single-channel observations. - Time-invariant filter (in steady state).

The Kalman filter handles: - Non-stationary processes (time-varying \(A, C, Q, R\)). - Multi-channel observations with cross-correlated noise. - Unknown initial conditions — the covariance recursion handles it naturally. - Real-time recursive computation — \(O(d^3)\) per step, not a large-matrix inversion.

When the Kalman filter is used for a stationary process, it converges to the causal Wiener filter in steady state.

docs.title: 3.8.1 The one-step forward predictor
docs.text:
Predict \(x[n]\) from past samples \(x[n-1], \dots, x[n-p]\) using a linear predictor:

\[ \boxed{\;\hat x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k\, x[n-k]\;} \]

The prediction error (also called the residual or innovation) is

\[ \boxed{\;e[n] = x[n] - \hat x[n] = x[n] + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k x[n-k]\;} \]

and the predictor coefficients \(a_k\) are chosen to minimise the mean-square prediction error \(\mathbb E[e[n]^2]\).

docs.title: 3.8.2 Normal equations
docs.text:
Apply the orthogonality principle to \(e[n]\) and each past sample:

\[ \mathbb E\bigl[e[n] x[n-k]\bigr] = 0,\quad k = 1, \dots, p. \]

Expanding:

\[ R_X[k] + \sum_{m=1}^{p} a_m R_X[k-m] = 0,\quad k = 1, \dots, p. \]

These are identical to the Yule–Walker equations from Chapter 2 (§2.10)! The optimal linear predictor for a WSS process is the AR coefficient vector of the process. The prediction error is exactly the innovations.

\[ \boxed{\;\text{MMSE linear prediction} \;\equiv\; \text{AR}(p)\ \text{model estimation}.\;} \]

This identity is fundamental: it says that the Wold decomposition of a WSS process into AR\((\infty)\) + innovations is the optimal linear predictor.

docs.title: 3.8.3 Minimum prediction error
docs.text:
The MMSE is

\[ \boxed{\;P_p = \mathbb E[e^2[n]] = R_X[0] + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k R_X[-k] = \sigma_{w,p}^2.\;} \]

This is the prediction-error variance — the same quantity as \(\sigma_p^2\) in Levinson–Durbin (§2.10).

For white noise, \(R_X[k] = 0\) for \(k \ne 0\), so all \(a_k = 0\) and \(P_p = R_X[0]\): no predictability.

For a perfectly predictable signal (e.g. a sinusoid at a known frequency), the prediction error can go to zero with sufficient \(p\) — a line spectral process.

docs.title: Worked example 3.9 — one-step predictor for AR(1)
docs.text:
\(x[n] = a x[n-1] + w[n]\), \(|a| < 1\), \(\sigma_w^2\) given. \(R_X[k] = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{1-a^2}a^{|k|}\).

AR(1) prediction: \(\hat x[n] = -a_1 x[n-1]\) with \(a_1 = -a\) (Yule–Walker for \(p=1\): \(R_X[1] + a_1 R_X[0] = 0 \Rightarrow a_1 = -a\)).

MMSE: \(P_1 = R_X[0](1 - \rho^2)\) with \(\rho = R_X[1]/R_X[0] = a\). So \(P_1 = \sigma_w^2/(1-a^2) \cdot (1 - a^2) = \sigma_w^2\).

The prediction error is exactly \(w[n]\) — the innovations of the AR(1). This matches the identity above.

Prediction gain. \(P_1/\sigma_X^2 = 1 - a^2\). For \(a = 0.9\), the prediction error is only 19% of the signal variance; 81% of the signal is predictable from the previous sample. For \(a = 0.5\), only 25% is predictable.

docs.title: 3.8.4 Order-\(p\) prediction and the lattice
docs.text:
For order \(p > 1\), the predictor is obtained via Levinson–Durbin (Chapter 2 §2.10). The intermediate coefficients \(a^{(m)}\) at each order give the order-\(m\) predictor; the reflection coefficients \(k_m\) are the partial autocorrelations and satisfy \(|k_m| < 1\) for a stable process.

The minimum prediction error at order \(m\) is

\[ \boxed{\;P_m = P_{m-1}(1 - k_m^2)\;} \]

with \(P_0 = R_X[0]\). This monotone decreasing sequence converges to \(\sigma_w^2\) (the innovations variance) as \(m \to \infty\). The reflection coefficient \(k_m\) measures the fractional improvement in prediction error gained by adding lag \(m\) to the predictor. A magnitude near 1 means a large improvement; near 0 means lag \(m\) carries little new information beyond lags \(1\) to \(m-1\).

docs.title: 3.8.5 Backward prediction
docs.text:
Similarly, predict \(x[n-p]\) from the future samples \(x[n-p+1], \dots, x[n]\):

\[ \hat x[n-p] = -\sum_{k=1}^{p} c_k\, x[n-p+k]. \]

For a WSS process, the backward predictor coefficients \(c_k\) equal the reversed forward predictor coefficients: \(c_k = a_{p+1-k}\). This symmetry is the structural basis of the lattice filter (§3.11).

docs.title: 3.9.1 The whitening filter
docs.text:
Given a WSS process \(X[n]\) with rational PSD \(S_X(e^{j\omega})\), the whitening filter is

\[ \boxed{\;H_w(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{H(e^{j\omega})},\qquad S_X = \sigma_e^2 |H|^2.\;} \]

Its output \(E[n] = h_w * X[n]\) is white of variance \(\sigma_e^2\).

Interpretation. The whitening filter is the prediction-error filter: it subtracts the best linear prediction of \(X[n]\) from the past, leaving only the unpredictable part — the innovations.

For AR(\(p\)): the whitening filter is the FIR filter \(1 + \sum_{k=1}^p a_k z^{-k}\), so

\[ e[n] = x[n] + \sum_{k=1}^p a_k x[n-k]. \]

This is exactly the AR prediction error — the input to the AR model. The whitening filter for an AR process is FIR because AR is an all-pole model (its inverse is all-zero).

For MA(\(q\)): the whitening filter is IIR (the inverse of an all-zero filter), with coefficients determined by spectral factorization.

For ARMA(\(p, q\)): the whitening filter is IIR (ratio of two FIR filters) and requires factoring the MA polynomial.

docs.title: 3.9.2 The inverse filter
docs.text:
The inverse filter restores the original process from the white innovations:

\[ X[n] = h * E[n],\qquad h = 1/h_w. \]

For an AR process, \(H(z) = 1/(1 + \sum a_k z^{-k})\) — an IIR filter with feedback. The pair \((H, H_w)\) is a synthesis/analysis pair, used throughout communications and audio:

  • Synthesis: generate \(X\) from white noise \(E\) via \(H\) (e.g., speech synthesis).
  • Analysis: recover \(E\) from \(X\) via \(H_w\) (e.g., speech recognition, LPC).

docs.title: Worked example 3.10 — speech analysis and synthesis
docs.text:
The source-filter model of speech:

  • Source: the glottal pulse train (voiced) or turbulent noise (unvoiced) — modeled as white noise.
  • Filter: the vocal tract — modeled as an AR(\(p\)) filter with \(p \approx 10\) for \(f_s = 8\) kHz.
