Analysis (encoder): apply the whitening filter \(1/A(z)\) to the speech \(x[n]\), obtain the prediction-error (residual) \(e[n]\). The residuals contain the pitch information and the gain; the AR coefficients \(a_k\) contain the spectral envelope (formants).

Synthesis (decoder): drive the AR filter \(1/A(z)\) with the residual \(e[n]\) to reconstruct \(\tilde x[n]\).

Compression. For \(p = 10\) at \(f_s = 8\) kHz and 20 ms frames, the parameters per frame are: \(10\) AR coefficients (~30 bits) + pitch (~7 bits) + gain (~5 bits) + residual (~0–160 bits depending on codec) — total ~50–200 bits per 20 ms ≈ 2.5–10 kbps. Compare to raw PCM at 128 kbps — a 10–50× compression, the basis of LPC-10, CELP, MP3, and modern speech codecs.

The identity prediction error = innovations is what makes this possible: the residual is white and can be efficiently encoded with scalar quantisation or vector quantisation.

docs.title: 3.10.1 Recap
docs.text:
From Chapter 2 §2.10, the Levinson–Durbin recursion solves the Toeplitz system

\[ \mathbf R_p\, \mathbf a = -\mathbf r_p \]

in \(O(p^2)\) operations, producing the AR coefficients at each order \(m = 1, \dots, p\):

\[ k_m = -\frac{r_m + \sum_{i=1}^{m-1} a_i^{(m-1)} r_{m-i}}{\sigma_{m-1}^2},\qquad a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m a_{m-i}^{(m-1)},\qquad \sigma_m^2 = (1-k_m^2)\sigma_{m-1}^2. \]

docs.title: 3.10.2 Interpretation
docs.text:
Levinson–Durbin builds the predictor of order \(p\) incrementally:

  1. Start with order 1: \(a_1^{(1)} = -r_1/r_0\) — the single-lag predictor.
  2. Add lag 2: update \(a_1^{(1)} \to a_1^{(2)}\) and add \(a_2^{(2)}\) — the two-lag predictor.
  3. Continue to order \(p\).

Each step adds one lag and updates the previous coefficients via the reflection coefficient \(k_m\). This is not just a numerical trick — it exposes the hierarchical structure of the predictor, which the lattice filter (§3.11) exploits directly.

docs.title: 3.10.3 Split-Levinson and other variants
docs.text:
For very long \(p\) (e.g., \(p > 1000\) in audio), the standard recursion is \(O(p^2)\). The split-Levinson algorithm reduces to \(O(p \log^2 p)\) and is used in real-time high-order predictors. For most signal-processing applications (\(p \le 50\)), standard Levinson is fast enough.

Bareiss and Schur algorithms are alternative \(O(p^2)\) Toeplitz solvers with better numerical stability; Levinson is exact in exact arithmetic, but the recursion can lose accuracy for ill-conditioned matrices (large condition number, close to singular). In practice, the biased sample autocorrelation guarantees positive-definiteness, so the recursion is stable.

docs.title: 3.10.4 Complexity comparison
docs.text:
Method Complexity Notes Gaussian elimination \(O(p^3)\) General matrices; does not exploit Toeplitz Levinson–Durbin \(O(p^2)\) Toeplitz, symmetric, positive-definite Bareiss \(O(p^2)\) Better numerical stability Split-Levinson \(O(p \log^2 p)\) Very long \(p\) FFT-based \(O(p \log p)\) Circulant embedding (used in practice)

For \(p = 50\): Gaussian \(= 125{,}000\) ops, Levinson \(= 2{,}500\) ops — a 50× speedup. For \(p = 500\): \(5 \times 10^7\) vs \(5 \times 10^5\) — a 100× speedup. For real-time speech coding at \(p = 10\), either is fine; for audio at \(p = 1000\), the difference is the feasibility boundary.

docs.title: 3.11.1 The lattice structure
docs.text:
The lattice filter implements the prediction-error filter using the reflection coefficients \(k_1, \dots, k_p\) as its parameters, in a cascade of identical 2-port stages:

\[ \boxed{\;f_m[n] = f_{m-1}[n] + k_m\, g_{m-1}[n-1],\qquad g_m[n] = g_{m-1}[n-1] + k_m\, f_{m-1}[n]\;} \]

with initial conditions \(f_0[n] = g_0[n] = x[n]\).

Here:

  • \(f_m[n]\) = forward prediction error at order \(m\) — the error when predicting \(x[n]\) from \(m\) past samples.
  • \(g_m[n]\) = backward prediction error at order \(m\) — the error when predicting \(x[n-m]\) from the next \(m\) samples.

The forward error at order \(p\) is the output: \(e[n] = f_p[n]\).

docs.title: 3.11.2 Properties
docs.text:
Why lattice filters are preferred in some applications

1. Stability is guaranteed by \(|k_m| < 1\). Any set of reflection coefficients within \((-1, 1)\) produces a stable synthesis filter. This is not true of the direct-form \(a_k\) representation, where stability depends on all roots of \(1 + \sum a_k z^{-k}\) being inside the unit circle.

2. Modular and order-recursive. Each stage is identical and can be added or removed without recomputing the others. This is useful for order-adaptive filtering (choose \(p\) at runtime).

3. Numerically robust under quantization. Coefficients are bounded in magnitude, so fixed-point implementations do not overflow or lose stability.

4. Provides both forward and backward errors. Useful in two-sided estimation problems (smoothing, Burg spectral estimation).

5. Matched to the Levinson recursion. The \(k_m\) are computed by Levinson as a by-product; no extra work is needed to obtain the lattice form.

docs.title: 3.11.3 From lattice back to direct form
docs.text:
To convert lattice to direct form, apply the step-up recursion (the inverse of Levinson–Durbin):

\[ a_m^{(m)} = k_m,\qquad a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m a_{m-i}^{(m-1)},\quad i = 1, \dots, m-1. \]

To convert direct form to lattice, use the step-down recursion (Levinson itself).

docs.title: Worked example 3.11 — lattice for AR(2)
docs.text:
From Example 2.8 in Chapter 2: AR(2) with \(r_0 = 6\), \(r_1 = 4\), \(r_2 = 1\) gave reflection coefficients \(k_1 = -2/3\), \(k_2 = 1/2\) and AR coefficients \(a_1 = -1\), \(a_2 = 0.5\).

Stage 1 (\(m = 1\)).

\[ f_1[n] = x[n] + k_1\, g_0[n-1] = x[n] - \tfrac{2}{3}x[n-1], \] \[ g_1[n] = x[n-1] + k_1\, x[n] = x[n-1] - \tfrac{2}{3}x[n]. \]

Stage 2 (\(m = 2\)).

\[ f_2[n] = f_1[n] + k_2\, g_1[n-1] = \bigl(x[n] - \tfrac{2}{3}x[n-1]\bigr) + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(x[n-2] - \tfrac{2}{3}x[n-1]\bigr) \] \[ = x[n] - \tfrac{2}{3}x[n-1] - \tfrac{1}{3}x[n-1] + \tfrac{1}{2}x[n-2] = x[n] - x[n-1] + \tfrac{1}{2}x[n-2]. \]

So \(f_2[n] = x[n] + a_1 x[n-1] + a_2 x[n-2] = x[n] - x[n-1] + 0.5 x[n-2]\) — matching the direct-form predictor from Example 2.7. ✓

Interpretation. The lattice adds one reflection coefficient per stage. Each \(|k_m| < 1\) guarantees a stable all-pole synthesis filter of order \(m\) — the hierarchical stability property.

docs.title: 3.12.1 Summary of the estimators
docs.text: Estimator Criterion Model Form Complexity MLE Max likelihood Full pdf \(\arg\max p(Y;\theta)\) \(O(N)\) – \(O(N^3)\) MMSE Mean-square Joint pdf \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y]\) Usually intractable LMMSE (vector) Mean-square, linear Covariance only \(\Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\) \(O(m^3)\) matrix inverse Wiener (non-causal) LMMSE, stationary PSDs \(S_{XY}/S_Y\) Closed form Wiener (FIR) LMMSE, finite-length Autocorr Solve Toeplitz system \(O(p^2)\) Levinson Causal Wiener LMMSE, causal PSDs + spectral factorization \([S_{XY}/L]^{+}/L\) \(O(p \log p)\) Kalman LMMSE, state-space State model Predict-update recursion \(O(d^3)\) per step Linear predictor LMMSE, past only Autocorr Solve Yule–Walker \(O(p^2)\) Levinson

docs.title: 3.12.2 When to use what
docs.text: Situation Use Full pdf known, non-Gaussian MLE (or exact MMSE if tractable) Jointly Gaussian, stationary, offline Non-causal Wiener filter Jointly Gaussian, stationary, real-time Causal Wiener filter (via factorization) Jointly Gaussian, real-time, state-space Kalman filter Jointly Gaussian, FIR wanted FIR Wiener (Toeplitz solve) Signal modeling, compression, speech Linear prediction (Levinson) Whitening, coding Prediction-error filter (= spectral factor inverse)

docs.title: 3.12.3 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. ML criterion maximises the likelihood of the data; efficient under regularity; the CRLB is the variance floor for unbiased estimators.
  2. MMSE (optimal, possibly nonlinear) equals the conditional mean \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y]\); LMMSE restricts to linear estimators and equals the optimal only for jointly Gaussian problems.
  3. Orthogonality principle — \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y^\top] = 0\) — is the operational condition for LMMSE, giving the closed form \(\hat S = \mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\).
  4. Wiener filter is the LMMSE for stationary processes. Non-causal: \(H = S_{XY}/S_Y\) — simple, closed form. Causal: requires spectral factorization; solved via one-sided Wiener–Hopf.
  5. FIR Wiener reduces to a Toeplitz linear system, solved by Levinson–Durbin in \(O(p^2)\).
  6. Kalman filter is the LMMSE for state-space models; predict-update recursion; Riccati recursion for covariance; steady state = causal Wiener for stationary processes.
  7. Linear prediction is the identity: optimal predictor = AR coefficients; prediction error = innovations; MMSE = innovations variance.
  8. Whitening filter removes correlation, producing white innovations; its inverse reconstructs the signal. Basis of LPC speech coding.
  9. Levinson–Durbin solves Toeplitz systems in \(O(p^2)\); the reflection coefficients \(k_m\) encode stability and the hierarchical structure.
  10. Lattice filter implements prediction-error filtering using \(k_m\); provides guaranteed stability, modularity, and numerical robustness.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. The maximum likelihood estimator maximises: (a) the prior probability (b) the data likelihood (c) the conditional mean (d) the posterior probability

  2. The CRLB gives: (a) a lower bound on the bias of an estimator (b) a lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator (c) the optimal MSE (d) the Fisher information

  3. For i.i.d. Gaussian data \(y[n] = A + w[n]\), the ML estimator of \(A\) is: (a) median (b) sample mean (c) sample variance (d) RMS

  4. The optimal MMSE estimator \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)^2]\) is: (a) always linear (b) the conditional mean \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y]\) (c) always Gaussian (d) the sample mean

  5. The LMMSE estimator is: (a) \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y]\) always (b) \(\mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\) (c) \(\mu_S\) (d) \(\Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\)

  6. The orthogonality principle requires: (a) \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y] = 0\) (b) \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y^\top] = 0\) (c) \(\mathbb E[SY] = 0\) (d) \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)^2] = 0\)

  7. The non-causal Wiener filter is: (a) \(S_{XY}/S_Y\) (b) \(S_Y/S_{XY}\) (c) \(S_{XY}S_Y\) (d) \(\sigma_e^2 |H|^2\)

  8. The causal Wiener filter requires: (a) solving a Toeplitz system (b) spectral factorization and causal-part extraction (c) ML (d) Kalman recursion

  9. The Kalman gain \(K_n\) becomes small when: (a) observation noise \(R\) is small (b) observation noise \(R\) is large (c) prior covariance \(P_{n|n-1}\) is small (d) both (b) and (c)

  10. The prediction error \(e[n] = x[n] - \hat x[n]\) for the optimal linear predictor is: (a) always zero (b) the innovations process (white) (c) Gaussian always (d) the autocorrelation of \(x\)

  11. The whitening filter for an AR(\(p\)) process is: (a) an FIR filter with coefficients \(a_k\) (b) an IIR filter (c) an all-pass filter (d) a Kalman filter

  12. The lattice filter stability condition is: (a) \(|a_k| < 1\) for all \(k\) (b) \(|k_m| < 1\) for all \(m\) (c) all poles inside the unit circle (d) it is always unstable

docs.text:

  2. The CRLB says \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat\theta] \ge 1/\)____ where \(I\) is the Fisher information.
  3. The efficient estimator achieves the ____ at finite \(N\).

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. State the ML criterion and derive the MLE of the noise variance \(\sigma^2\) for i.i.d. Gaussian data \(y[n] \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). State whether the MLE is unbiased, and if not, propose the unbiased version.
  2. State the CRLB and derive the Fisher information for the Gaussian-mean problem in Example 3.1. Show that the sample mean is efficient.
  3. Distinguish MMSE and LMMSE. Under what conditions do they coincide? Give an example where they differ.
  4. State the orthogonality principle and derive the LMMSE closed form for random vectors. Interpret each matrix in the formula.
  5. Derive the Wiener–Hopf equations for the FIR Wiener filter from the orthogonality principle. Show that they reduce to a Toeplitz linear system.
  6. Derive the causal Wiener filter formula via spectral factorization. Explain the role of the causal-part operation \([\cdot]_+\).
  7. State the Kalman filter recursion (predict and update) and interpret each step. Why does the Kalman gain converge as \(n \to \infty\)?
  8. Derive the Yule–Walker equations for linear prediction from the orthogonality principle. Show that they are identical to the AR parameter equations from Chapter 2.
  9. Define the whitening filter and the prediction-error filter. Explain why they are identical for AR processes but different for ARMA.
  10. Describe the lattice filter structure and state its key advantage over the direct-form filter. Why is \(|k_m| < 1\) the stability condition?

docs.title: 3.14 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — the data likelihood.
  2. (b) — lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator.
  3. (b) — sample mean.
  4. (b) — conditional mean.
  5. (b) — \(\mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\).
  6. (b) — \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y^\top] = 0\).
  7. (a) — \(S_{XY}/S_Y\).
  8. (b) — spectral factorization + causal part.
  9. (d) — both large \(R\) and small \(P_{n|n-1}\) reduce \(K_n\).
  10. (b) — innovations (white).
  11. (a) — FIR with AR coefficients \(a_k\).
  12. (b) — \(|k_m| < 1\) for all \(m\).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(\ell(\theta)\) (the log-likelihood)
  2. \(I(\theta)\) (Fisher information)
  3. CRLB
  4. \(Y\) (observations)
  5. MMSE
  6. \(S_{XY}/S_Y\)
  7. spectral
  8. Wiener
  9. whitening (or prediction-error)
  10. reflection
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. ML criterion: \(\hat\theta_{\text{ML}} = \arg\max_\theta p_Y(Y; \theta)\); equivalently \(\arg\max \ell(\theta) = \log p_Y(Y; \theta)\). Derivation for variance: \(\ell(\sigma^2) = -\frac{N}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_n y[n]^2\). Setting \(d\ell/d\sigma^2 = 0\): \(-\frac{N}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum y[n]^2 = 0\) ⇒ \(\hat\sigma^2_{\text{ML}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum y[n]^2\). Bias: \(\mathbb E[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{ML}}] = \sigma^2\) if the data are zero-mean, so it is unbiased for zero-mean Gaussian (but biased by a factor \(N/(N-1)\) when the mean is estimated as well). Unbiased version (mean unknown): \(s^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum(y[n] - \bar y)^2\) — the sample variance with \(N-1\) denominator.
  2. CRLB: for any unbiased estimator \(\hat\theta\), \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat\theta] \ge 1/I(\theta)\) with \(I(\theta) = -\mathbb E[\partial^2\ell/\partial\theta^2]\). Fisher information for the Gaussian-mean problem: \(\ell(A) = -\frac{N}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(y[n]-A)^2\); \(\partial^2\ell/\partial A^2 = -N/\sigma^2\), so \(I(A) = N/\sigma^2\). Sample mean: \(\operatorname{Var}[\bar y] = \sigma^2/N = 1/I(A)\) — equality holds, so the sample mean is efficient (attains the CRLB) for every \(N\).
  3. MMSE: minimises \(\mathbb E[(S-\hat S)^2]\) over all estimators \(\hat S(Y)\); solution is the conditional mean \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y]\). LMMSE: minimises the same criterion over linear estimators \(\hat S = a + b^\top Y\); solution is \(\mu_S + \Sigma_{SY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y)\). Equivalence: for jointly Gaussian \((S, Y)\), the conditional mean is affine in \(Y\), so the two coincide. Difference example: \(S\) uniform on \(\{-1, +1\}\), \(Y = S + V\) with \(V\) uniform on \([-0.5, 0.5]\). The MMSE is \(\mathrm{sign}(Y)\) — a nonlinear estimator. The LMMSE is a linear function, which has a larger MSE. The difference is small for small noise, but exact-MMSE beats LMMSE when the prior is non-Gaussian.
  4. Orthogonality: \(\mathbb E[(S - \hat S)Y^\top] = 0\) and \(\mathbb E[S - \hat S] = 0\). Derivation: write \(\hat S = a + b^\top Y\); the orthogonality of the error to \(1\) gives \(a = \mu_S - b^\top\mu_Y\); the orthogonality to \(Y\) gives \(\Sigma_{SY} - b^\top\Sigma_{YY} = 0\), so \(b = \Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{SY}^\top = \Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{YS}\). Interpretation: \(\Sigma_{SY}\) = cross-covariance (how correlated the target is with the observations); \(\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\) = inverse observation covariance (how much each observation is worth); the product weights each observation by its information and correlation to the target.
  5. Orthogonality: \(\mathbb E[(x[n] - \hat x[n])y[n-m]] = 0\) for \(m = 0, \dots, M-1\). Expansion: substituting \(\hat x[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}h[k]y[n-k]\) and taking expectations gives \(\sum_k h[k] R_Y[m-k] = R_{XY}[m]\). Toeplitz form: the left side is a convolution of \(h\) with \(R_Y\), evaluated at \(m\). In matrix form with \(\mathbf h = (h[0],\dots,h[M-1])^\top\) and Toeplitz \(\mathbf R_Y\) with \([\mathbf R_Y]_{ij} = R_Y[i-j]\), the system is \(\mathbf R_Y\mathbf h = \mathbf r_{XY}\) where \(\mathbf r_{XY} = (R_{XY}[0],\dots,R_{XY}[M-1])^\top\). Solve by Levinson–Durbin in \(O(M^2)\).
  6. Formula: \(H_{\text{cas}}(z) = [S_{XY}(z)/(\sigma_e^2 L(z^{-1}))]_+ / L(z)\) where \(S_Y = \sigma_e^2 L L^{-1}\) is the spectral factorization. Role of \([\cdot]_+\): the one-sided Wiener–Hopf has orthogonality only for \(m \ge 0\). In the \(z\)-domain, this means we can only use the causal part of the Laurent expansion — terms \(z^0, z^{-1}, z^{-2}, \dots\). The operation \([\cdot]_+\) takes exactly those terms, discarding the anti-causal part. Without it, we would recover the non-causal filter \(S_{XY}/S_Y\), which uses future observations and is not realisable.
  7. Recursion: predict step \(\hat x_{n|n-1} = A\hat x_{n-1|n-1}\), \(P_{n|n-1} = AP_{n-1|n-1}A^\top + BQB^\top\); Kalman gain \(K_n = P_{n|n-1}C^\top(CP_{n|n-1}C^\top + R)^{-1}\); update step \(\hat x_{n|n} = \hat x_{n|n-1} + K_n(y[n] - C\hat x_{n|n-1})\), \(P_{n|n} = (I - K_nC)P_{n|n-1}\). Convergence: the Riccati recursion \(P_{n|n} = f(P_{n-1|n-1})\) is a contraction under stabilisability and detectability, so \(P_{n|n} \to P^\star\) and \(K_n \to K^\star\), independent of \(P_{0|0}\). The steady-state filter is LTI, matching the causal Wiener filter.
  8. Orthogonality: \(\mathbb E[e[n]x[n-k]] = 0\) for \(k = 1, \dots, p\), where \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum_{m=1}^p a_m x[n-m]\). Expansion: \(\mathbb E[x[n]x[n-k]] + \sum_m a_m \mathbb E[x[n-m]x[n-k]] = 0\) gives \(R_X[k] + \sum_m a_m R_X[k-m] = 0\) for \(k = 1, \dots, p\). Yule–Walker: exactly the AR model equations from §2.10. This shows the optimal linear predictor is the AR coefficient vector — the same vector that defines the AR model — and the MMSE prediction error equals the innovations variance \(\sigma_w^2\).
  9. Whitening filter: an LTI filter \(H_w = 1/H\) such that \(H_w * X\) is white. Prediction-error filter: the filter whose output is the prediction error of the optimal linear predictor. Identity for AR: for AR(\(p\)), the AR polynomial \(1 + \sum a_k z^{-k}\) is precisely the prediction-error filter; its output is the input to the AR model, i.e., the innovations — so \(H_w = 1 + \sum a_k z^{-k}\) is FIR and \(H_w\) = prediction-error filter. Difference for ARMA: for an ARMA(\(p,q\)), the optimal predictor is still IIR from the AR part, but the whitening filter must also invert the MA part \(1 + \sum b_k z^{-k}\), which is IIR (a non-trivial all-pole filter). So the whitening filter is IIR, not the same as the (FIR) prediction-error filter that only handles the AR part.
  10. Structure: a cascade of \(p\) stages, each parameterised by a single reflection coefficient \(k_m\). Stage \(m\) takes inputs \((f_{m-1}, g_{m-1})\) and outputs \((f_m, g_m)\) via \(f_m = f_{m-1} + k_m g_{m-1}z^{-1}\), \(g_m = g_{m-1}z^{-1} + k_m f_{m-1}\). Key advantages: (i) guaranteed stability iff \(|k_m| < 1\) for all \(m\) — a simple, local condition, unlike the global root condition for direct-form \(a_k\); (ii) modular — stages can be added/removed without recomputing others; (iii) robust under quantization — coefficients bounded in magnitude; (iv) order-adaptive — easily grow/shrink \(p\) at runtime; (v) provides both forward and backward errors — useful for smoothing and Burg methods. Stability: each stage is an all-pass in the reverse direction; if \(|k_m| < 1\), the reflected energy is less than the incident energy, so the cascade cannot have poles outside the unit circle. This gives the hierarchical stability property: every lower-order filter in the cascade is also stable.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Hayes, Statistical Digital Signal Processing and Modeling, Wiley, 1996 — Chapters 4–7 and 9. The closest match to this chapter.
  • Kay, Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing: Estimation Theory, Prentice-Hall, 1993 — the definitive reference for ML, CRLB, and MMSE. Chapters 3–7.
  • Kay, Modern Spectral Estimation, Prentice-Hall, 1988 — for the linear-prediction and lattice chapters.
  • Kailath, Sayed & Hassibi, Linear Estimation, Prentice-Hall, 2000 — the unified framework for LMMSE, Wiener, and Kalman. Rigorous, comprehensive.
  • Anderson & Moore, Optimal Filtering, Dover, 2005 — the classical Kalman filter reference.
  • Simon, Optimal State Estimation, Wiley, 2006 — modern unified treatment, with practical implementation advice.
  • Haykin, Adaptive Filter Theory, Pearson, 5th ed., 2014 — Chapter 1 for prediction and lattice; Chapters 2–3 for Wiener; Chapters 4–9 for adaptive (Chapter 4 of this course).
  • Makhoul, "Linear Prediction: A Tutorial Review", Proc. IEEE, 63(4), 1975 — the classic pedagogical reference for LPC and lattice.
  • Markel & Gray, Linear Prediction of Speech, Springer, 1976 — the definitive source for the source-filter model and LPC.
  • SciPy signal.lfilter, statsmodels.tsa, filterpy.kalman; MATLAB dsp.KalmanFilter, levinson, aryule, lpc, dsp.LatticeFilter.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. CRLB exercise. \(y[n] = \theta s[n] + w[n]\) for known \(s[n]\), \(w\) white Gaussian. Derive the MLE of \(\theta\) and its CRLB. Show the MLE is \(\hat\theta = \sum y[n]s[n]/\sum s^2[n]\), and its variance equals the CRLB.
  2. LMMSE with correlated observations. \(Y_1 = S + V_1\), \(Y_2 = S + V_2\), with \(S \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(V_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.5)\), \(V_1 \perp V_2\). Compute the LMMSE of \(S\) from \((Y_1, Y_2)\) and compare with the LMMSE from \(Y_1\) alone.
  3. Non-causal Wiener filter. For \(Y[n] = X[n] + V[n]\) with \(X \sim\) AR(1) (\(a = 0.8\), \(\sigma_W = 1\)), \(V\) white (\(\sigma_V = 0.3\)), compute \(H_{\text{nc}}(e^{j\omega})\). Numerically integrate to find the MSE.
  4. Causal Wiener via factorization. Same setup as Problem 3, compute the causal Wiener filter using spectral factorization (following Example 3.6). Compare MSE with the non-causal case.
  5. Kalman filter scalar. Model \(x[n] = 0.95 x[n-1] + u[n]\), \(u \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.05)\); \(y[n] = 2x[n] + v[n]\), \(v \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\). Simulate 100 steps, run the Kalman filter, and plot the true state, observation, and filtered estimate. Verify the Riccati recursion converges.
  6. Kalman vs. Wiener. For the stationary model of Problem 5, run the Kalman filter for 1000 steps and compare the steady-state gain with the causal Wiener filter designed from the AR spectrum. Verify they match to \(10^{-4}\).
  7. Linear predictor. For \(R_X[0] = 10\), \(R_X[1] = 8\), \(R_X[2] = 6\), \(R_X[k] = 0\) for \(|k| > 2\), find the optimal order-2 predictor and the minimum prediction error. Use Levinson–Durbin.
  8. Whitening. Design the whitening filter for the AR(2) process of Example 2.8. Verify that passing the AR(2) process through the whitening filter yields a white residual (autocorrelation within \(\pm 3/\sqrt N\) for \(k \ne 0\)).
  9. Lattice conversion. Given the AR(3) coefficients \(a = (-1.5, 1.1, -0.3)\), compute the reflection coefficients using step-down (inverse Levinson). Implement the lattice filter, verify that it produces the same prediction error as the direct-form filter.
  10. Speech LPC. Record a segment of voiced speech (~2 s at 16 kHz). Implement a pitch-synchronous LPC analyser with \(p = 12\). Plot the LPC spectrum overlaid on the Welch spectrum. Verify that the peaks of the LPC spectrum correspond to the formants (F1, F2, F3).
  11. Riccati convergence. For the scalar model \(A = 1.0\), \(Q = 0.1\), \(R = 1\), plot \(P_{n|n}\) vs. \(n\) starting from \(P_{0|0} = 100\). Verify convergence to the fixed point in under 20 iterations. Repeat with \(Q = 0.001\); comment on the convergence rate.
  12. Real-time consideration. In the causal Wiener filter of Problem 4, compare its performance on a finite sample (N = 200) to the non-causal filter. Plot the two filters' outputs on the same axes and compute the MSE. Explain the intuition behind the ~35% error penalty.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Adaptive Filters
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): FIR adaptive filters · Newton's steepest-descent method · adaptive filters based on steepest descent · Widrow–Hoff LMS algorithm · adaptive channel equalization · adaptive echo cancellation · adaptive noise cancellation · RLS adaptive filters (exponentially weighted and sliding window) · simplified IIR LMS adaptive filter.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Distinguish adaptive from fixed filtering and identify the three ingredients of every adaptive filter (structure, cost function, adaptation algorithm).
  2. Derive the steepest-descent recursion on the MSE surface, state its convergence condition, and compute its time constant and misadjustment.
  3. Derive the LMS (Widrow–Hoff) algorithm as a stochastic approximation of steepest descent, state its convergence bounds, and interpret the trade-off between convergence speed and steady-state excess MSE.
  4. Derive Normalised LMS (NLMS) and explain why it is preferred when the input power varies.
  5. Analyse LMS on three classical applications: adaptive channel equalisation, adaptive echo cancellation, and adaptive noise cancellation.
  6. Derive the Recursive Least Squares (RLS) algorithm by minimising an exponentially weighted least-squares cost; state its convergence rate (independent of input covariance) and its complexity (\(O(N^2)\) per sample).
  7. Distinguish exponentially weighted RLS (forgetting factor \(\lambda\)) from sliding window RLS (rectangular window of \(W\) samples) and choose between them based on the problem.
  8. Analyse the simplified IIR LMS filter and understand when it is justified over FIR.
  9. Implement all of the above in Python, Java, and C#.

docs.title: 4.1.1 The fixed-filter assumption
docs.text:
Every filter designed in Chapters 1–3 assumes the statistics \((S_X, S_Y, R_{XY})\) are known and stationary. In practice:

  • The signal statistics change over time (e.g., a speaker moves).
  • The statistics are unknown a priori (must be learned from data).
  • The environment is non-stationary (e.g., an acoustic echo path changes when the room changes).

A fixed filter is optimal only for the statistics it was designed for. An adaptive filter adjusts its coefficients at each sample to track the current optimum.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Ingredients of every adaptive filter
docs.text:
Every adaptive filter has three components:

  1. A parameterised structure — typically an FIR filter \(\mathbf w(n) = (w_0, \dots, w_{N-1})^\top\).
  2. A cost function — a scalar to minimise, usually the mean-square error \(J(\mathbf w) = \mathbb E[e^2(n)]\).
  3. An adaptation algorithm — a rule that updates \(\mathbf w(n)\) at each step.

The three most important families:

Family Cost Update Complexity Steepest descent (deterministic) \(\mathbb E[e^2]\) \(\mathbf w(n{+}1) = \mathbf w(n) - \mu\nabla J(\mathbf w(n))\) \(O(N^2)\) (needs \(R\)) LMS (stochastic) \(e^2(n)\) (instantaneous) \(\mathbf w(n{+}1) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu e(n)\mathbf x(n)\) \(O(N)\) RLS (least-squares) \(\sum_{i} \lambda^{n-i} e^2(i)\) \(\mathbf w(n) = \mathbf w(n{-}1) + K(n)\xi(n)\) \(O(N^2)\)

The granddaddy of them all is steepest descent, an iterative method for finding the minimum of a known quadratic cost. LMS is a stochastic approximation of steepest descent using instantaneous estimates; RLS solves the deterministic least-squares problem exactly at each step.

docs.title: 4.2 The FIR adaptive filter structure
docs.text:
The adaptive FIR filter computes

\[ \boxed{\;y(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} w_k(n)\, x(n-k) = \mathbf w^\top(n)\,\mathbf x(n)\;} \]

where

\[ \mathbf w(n) = (w_0(n), \dots, w_{N-1}(n))^\top,\qquad \mathbf x(n) = (x(n), x(n-1), \dots, x(n-N+1))^\top. \]

The filter output \(y(n)\) is compared to a desired signal \(d(n)\) to form the error:

\[ \boxed{\;e(n) = d(n) - y(n) = d(n) - \mathbf w^\top(n)\mathbf x(n).\;} \]

The MSE cost is

\[ \boxed{\;J(\mathbf w) = \mathbb E[e^2(n)] = \mathbb E[d^2(n)] - 2\mathbf w^\top \mathbf p + \mathbf w^\top \mathbf R\, \mathbf w\;} \]

where

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf p = \mathbb E[d(n)\mathbf x(n)],\qquad \mathbf R = \mathbb E[\mathbf x(n)\mathbf x^\top(n)].\;} \]

Three key facts about \(J(\mathbf w)\).

  1. \(J\) is a quadratic bowl in \(\mathbf w\) — convex, with a unique minimum if \(\mathbf R\) is positive-definite.
  2. The Wiener solution (Chapter 3 §3.5) is \(\mathbf w_{\text{opt}} = \mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf p\).
  3. The minimum MSE is \(J_{\min} = \mathbb E[d^2] - \mathbf p^\top \mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf p\).

Gradient and curvature.

\[ \nabla J(\mathbf w) = -2\mathbf p + 2\mathbf R\mathbf w,\qquad \nabla^2 J = 2\mathbf R. \]

The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf R\) determine the conditioning of the MSE surface — the ratio \(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) is the eigenvalue spread \(\chi(\mathbf R)\), which determines how slowly the slowest mode converges.

docs.title: 4.3 Steepest descent on the MSE surface
4.3.1 The recursion
docs.text:
If \(\mathbf R\) and \(\mathbf p\) were known, we could iterate

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) - \frac{\mu}{2}\nabla J(\mathbf w(n)) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu\bigl(\mathbf p - \mathbf R\mathbf w(n)\bigr)\;} \]

This is steepest descent (gradient descent) on the quadratic cost.

Interpretation. The gradient \(\nabla J = -2\mathbf p + 2\mathbf R\mathbf w\) points in the direction of increasing MSE, so we move opposite the gradient with step size \(\mu\). At the Wiener solution, the gradient is zero — the algorithm stops.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Convergence
docs.text:
Translate to the weight error \(\tilde{\mathbf w}(n) = \mathbf w(n) - \mathbf w_{\text{opt}}\):

\[ \tilde{\mathbf w}(n+1) = (\mathbf I - \mu\mathbf R)\tilde{\mathbf w}(n). \]

Decompose \(\mathbf R = \mathbf Q\Lambda\mathbf Q^\top\) (eigendecomposition) and define the transformed error \(\mathbf v(n) = \mathbf Q^\top\tilde{\mathbf w}(n)\):

\[ \mathbf v(n+1) = (\mathbf I - \mu\Lambda)\mathbf v(n) \;\Longrightarrow\; v_k(n) = (1 - \mu\lambda_k)^n v_k(0). \]

Convergence condition. Each mode converges iff \(|1 - \mu\lambda_k| < 1\) for all \(k\):

\[ \boxed{\;0 < \mu < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}\;} \]

Time constants. The mode \(k\) decays as \((1-\mu\lambda_k)^n\), with time constant

\[ \boxed{\;\tau_k = \frac{1}{\mu\lambda_k}\ \text{samples (for small }\mu\text{)}.\;} \]

The overall convergence rate is set by the slowest mode \(\tau_{\min} = 1/(\mu\lambda_{\min})\).

Fundamental trade-off. Small \(\mu\) → slow convergence but low noise; large \(\mu\) → fast convergence but high excess MSE. The ratio \(\chi(\mathbf R) = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) controls how bad the trade-off is:

\[ \frac{\tau_{\max}}{\tau_{\min}} = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} = \chi(\mathbf R). \]

Large eigenvalue spread (coloured input) → very slow convergence along the small-eigenvalue directions. This is the motivation for RLS: RLS does not have this problem, converging at a rate independent of \(\chi(\mathbf R)\).

docs.title: 4.3.3 Misadjustment
docs.text:
Even with \(\mathbf p, \mathbf R\) known, steepest descent has no steady-state error (it converges exactly). In practice, when using stochastic estimates (LMS), the steady state has a residual excess MSE called the misadjustment:

\[ \boxed{\;M = \frac{J_{\text{excess}}}{J_{\min}}.\;} \]

For LMS: \(M \approx \mu \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)/2\) (derived in §4.5).

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — steepest descent on a 2-tap problem
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf R = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}\) (eigenvalues \(2\) and \(0.5\); eigenvalue spread \(\chi = 4\)), \(\mathbf p = (1, 0.5)^\top\), \(\mathbb E[d^2] = 10\).

Wiener solution.

\[ \mathbf w_{\text{opt}} = \mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf p = (0.5, 1)^\top,\qquad J_{\min} = 10 - \mathbf p^\top\mathbf w_{\text{opt}} = 10 - 1 = 9. \]

Convergence bound. \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 1\).

Time constants for \(\mu = 0.5\):

\[ \tau_1 = \frac{1}{0.5\cdot 2} = 1\ \text{sample},\qquad \tau_2 = \frac{1}{0.5\cdot 0.5} = 4\ \text{samples}. \]

Slow mode dominates: the overall transient lasts ~4 samples.

Iterate by hand from \(\mathbf w(0) = (0, 0)\). \(\mu = 0.5\):

\(n\) \(\mathbf w(n)\) \(J(\mathbf w(n))\) 0 \((0, 0)\) 10 1 \((0.5, 0.25)\) 9.156 2 \((0.5, 0.4375)\) 9.027 3 \((0.5, 0.5313)\) 9.007 4 \((0.5, 0.5781)\) 9.002

\(w_1\) converges in 1 step (fast mode), \(w_2\) takes ~4 (slow mode). Overall MSE converges to 9 in ~4 samples.

docs.title: 4.4.1 Stochastic approximation of steepest descent
docs.text:
In practice \(\mathbf R\) and \(\mathbf p\) are unknown. The LMS algorithm replaces the true gradient with an instantaneous estimate:

\[ \widehat{\nabla J} = -2e(n)\mathbf x(n) \]

(the gradient of the instantaneous squared error \(e^2(n)\)). Substituting into the steepest-descent recursion:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu\, e(n)\,\mathbf x(n)\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;e(n) = d(n) - \mathbf w^\top(n)\,\mathbf x(n)\;} \]

This is the Widrow–Hoff LMS algorithm. It requires only:

  • \(N\) multiplications for \(y(n)\) (FIR filter)
  • \(N\) multiplications for the update \(\mu e(n)\mathbf x(n)\)
  • Total: \(2N\) operations per sample — \(O(N)\) complexity, in contrast to steepest descent's \(O(N^2)\) (which needs to know \(\mathbf R\)).

docs.title: 4.4.2 Convergence in the mean
docs.text:
Taking expectations (using the independence assumption \(\mathbf w(n) \perp \mathbf x(n)\)):

\[ \mathbb E[\mathbf w(n+1)] = \mathbb E[\mathbf w(n)] + \mu\,\mathbb E[e(n)\mathbf x(n)] = (\mathbf I - \mu\mathbf R)\mathbb E[\mathbf w(n)] + \mu\mathbf p. \]

This is exactly the steepest-descent recursion in the mean, so:

\[ \boxed{\;0 < \mu < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}\ \text{(mean convergence)}.\;} \]

In practice, \(\lambda_{\max}\) is unknown, so use the conservative bound

\[ 0 < \mu < \frac{2}{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)} = \frac{2}{N\sigma_x^2}, \]

where \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R) = \sum \mathbb E[x^2(n-k)] = N\sigma_x^2\).

docs.title: 4.4.3 Convergence in the mean-square
docs.text:
The mean-square convergence (from the eigenvalue spread analysis) is:

\[ \boxed{\;\text{MSE convergence: } 0 < \mu < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}.\;} \]

But mean-square convergence alone is not enough — LMS also has steady-state excess MSE. The classical analysis under the independence assumption gives:

\[ \boxed{\;M \approx \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R) = \frac{\mu N \sigma_x^2}{2}\quad \text{(misadjustment)}.\;} \]

Interpretation. The excess MSE is proportional to \(\mu\) — smaller step size gives lower steady-state noise but slower convergence. The classical trade-off:

\[ \tau_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\mu\,\overline\lambda},\qquad M = \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R), \]

where \(\overline\lambda = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)/N\). Eliminating \(\mu\):

\[ \boxed{\;M \cdot \tau_{\text{avg}} \approx \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)}{N\overline\lambda} = \frac{N}{2}\quad\text{(constant, independent of }\mu\text{)}.\;} \]

The product of misadjustment and time constant is a fixed quantity. This is the fundamental LMS trade-off: you cannot improve both simultaneously. Faster convergence costs proportionally higher steady-state MSE.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — LMS on a scalar system identification
docs.text:
Signal model: unknown system \(h_{\text{true}} = 0.8\), driven by white input \(x(n) \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\). Desired output \(d(n) = 0.8 x(n) + v(n)\), \(v \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.1)\).

Adaptive filter: 1-tap \(w(n)\), initial \(w(0) = 0\), step \(\mu = 0.05\).

Optimal (Wiener) solution. \(\mathbf R = 1\) (scalar), \(\mathbf p = 0.8\). \(\mathbf w_{\text{opt}} = 0.8\), \(J_{\min} = \sigma_d^2 - 0.8^2 = 0.64 + 0.1 - 0.64 = 0.1\).

Convergence bound: \(0 < \mu < 2/1 = 2\). \(\mu = 0.05\) is well inside.

Time constant: \(\tau = 1/(0.05 \cdot 1) = 20\) samples.

Misadjustment: \(M \approx 0.05\cdot 1/2 = 0.025\) = 2.5%.

Simulation (Python):

import numpy as np

N_steps, w, mu = 5000, 0.0, 0.05
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
w_trace = []
for n in range(N_steps):
    x = rng.normal(0, 1)
    v = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(0.1))
    d = 0.8 * x + v
    y = w * x
    e = d - y
    w = w + mu * e * x
    w_trace.append(w)

print(f"final w = {w:.4f}  (true = 0.8)")
print(f"empirical excess MSE over last 1000 steps ≈ {np.var([(0.8-w_t)*1 for w_t in w_trace[-1000:]])*1:.4f}")

Expected: \(w \to 0.8\) within \(\sim 60\) samples, with steady-state fluctuation consistent with \(M \cdot J_{\min} = 0.0025\).

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — LMS with coloured input — eigenvalue spread
docs.text:
Same 2-tap problem as Example 4.1, but LMS does not know \(\mathbf R\).

\(\mathbf R = \text{diag}(2, 0.5)\), eigenvalue spread \(\chi = 4\).

Choice of \(\mu\). \(\mu < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 1\). Choose \(\mu = 0.1\):

\[ \tau_1 = 1/(0.1 \cdot 2) = 5,\qquad \tau_2 = 1/(0.1 \cdot 0.5) = 20. \]

The slow mode needs \(\sim 5\tau_2 = 100\) samples; the fast mode converges in \(\sim 25\). The overall convergence is slow because of the small eigenvalue.

Misadjustment: \(M = \mu \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)/2 = 0.1 \cdot 2.5/2 = 0.125\) = 12.5% — a significant excess MSE, the price of the chosen step size.

Increasing \(\mu\) to 0.5: \(\tau_2 \to 4\) samples (fast), but \(M \to 62.5\%\) (unacceptable). Decreasing \(\mu\) to 0.01: \(M \to 1.25\%\), but \(\tau_2 = 200\) (very slow). This is the fundamental LMS trade-off in action.

RLS would fix this — see §4.9. RLS converges in \(\sim 2N\) samples regardless of \(\chi(\mathbf R)\), at the cost of \(O(N^2)\) per sample.

docs.title: 4.5.1 Motivation
docs.text:
Plain LMS has a fixed step size \(\mu\). Its effective step (in the weight-error direction) depends on \(\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2\): when \(x\) is loud, the update is large; when \(x\) is quiet, it's small. In applications with variable input power (e.g. speech, audio), this makes the convergence rate and steady-state MSE vary wildly.

NLMS removes this dependence by normalising the step by the instantaneous input power:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + \frac{\tilde\mu}{\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2 + \delta}\, e(n)\, \mathbf x(n)\;} \]

where:

  • \(\tilde\mu \in (0, 2)\) is the normalised step size (dimensionless),
  • \(\delta > 0\) is a small regularisation constant (avoids division by zero when \(\|\mathbf x(n)\| = 0\)).

docs.title: 4.5.2 Convergence
docs.text:
NLMS converges if \(0 < \tilde\mu < 2\). Its steady-state misadjustment is

\[ \boxed{\;M_{\text{NLMS}} \approx \frac{\tilde\mu}{2 - \tilde\mu}.\;} \]

Independent of \(\sigma_x^2\) — that's the key advantage over LMS.

Convergence rate: similar to LMS but with input-power normalisation: \(\tau_k \propto 1/\tilde\mu\), so the same \(\tilde\mu\) gives similar rates for all inputs.

docs.title: Worked example 4.4 — NLMS on the scalar system
docs.text:
Same as Example 4.2: \(x \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\), \(d = 0.8 x + v\), \(v \sim \mathcal N(0,0.1)\).

Parameters: \(\tilde\mu = 0.1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\).

Steady-state misadjustment: \(M \approx 0.1/(2 - 0.1) \approx 0.0526\) = 5.3% — slightly worse than LMS at \(\mu = 0.05\) (which gave \(M = 2.5\%\)), but independent of \(\sigma_x^2\).

Benefit: if the input power changes from 1 to 100 (e.g., a loud moment in a speech signal), plain LMS with \(\mu = 0.05\) would see \(\lambda_{\max} = 100\), so \(\mu \lambda_{\max} = 5 > 2\) — divergence! NLMS would see \(\tilde\mu = 0.1\) — unaffected, still converging.

This is why NLMS is the default LMS variant in speech, audio, and communications applications.

docs.title: 4.6.1 Setup
docs.text:
A digital signal \(a(n)\) is transmitted through a channel \(h(n)\) with additive noise:

\[ y(n) = \sum_k h(k)\, a(n-k) + v(n). \]

The equaliser is an adaptive FIR filter \(\mathbf w\) that processes \(y(n)\) to produce \(\hat a(n) \approx a(n - \Delta)\), where \(\Delta\) is the equalisation delay chosen to make the overall system approximately linear-phase.

\[ \hat a(n) = \sum_k w_k(n)\, y(n-k). \]

The error for adaptation is \(e(n) = a(n - \Delta) - \hat a(n)\).

docs.title: 4.6.2 Three training modes
docs.text:
Mode Requires Convergence Trained / supervised Known training sequence \(a(n)\) Fast, reliable Decision-directed Estimated \(\hat a(n)\) after slicing Slow, may diverge if slicing errors are frequent Blind Only received signal (e.g., CMA, MMA) Slow, uncertain

Practical scheme. Use a training sequence at the start of each packet (e.g., in 802.11 the preamble is \(4\mu\)s), then switch to decision-directed during the payload. This gives fast initial convergence and no overhead after.

docs.title: 4.6.3 Choice of equalisation delay \(\Delta\)
docs.text: The optimal Wiener equaliser \(\mathbf w_{\text{opt}}\) has a peak in its impulse response at delay \(\Delta\). For a channel with delay spread \(L_h\) and equaliser length \(N\), the minimum-MSE delay is \(\Delta \approx (L_h + N - 1)/2\). For a causal equaliser, \(\Delta \ge L_h - 1\) ensures that all channel memory is "before" the main tap.

docs.title: Worked example 4.5 — a 2-tap channel with ISI
docs.text:
Channel \(h = (1, 0.5)\) — two-tap, introducing one symbol of ISI. Equaliser length \(N = 3\), delay \(\Delta = 1\).

Goal. Design \(\mathbf w\) so that \(h * w \approx \delta_{\Delta}\) (a unit impulse at delay \(\Delta = 1\)).

Ideal (no-noise) solution. \(w_0 h_0 = 1\), \(w_0 h_1 + w_1 h_0 = 0\), \(w_1 h_1 + w_2 h_0 = 0\), \(w_2 h_1 = 0\).

The last equation forces \(w_2 = 0\), then \(w_1 = 0\), then \(w_0 = 1\), and the second equation fails (\(1\cdot 0.5 + 0 \ne 0\)). No exact solution — the channel's zero at \(z = -0.5\) cannot be inverted by a 3-tap FIR with a delay.

Least-squares solution. Solve \(\min_w \|h*w - \delta_\Delta\|^2\) gives

\[ \mathbf w_{\text{LS}} = (\mathbf H^\top\mathbf H)^{-1}\mathbf H^\top\delta_\Delta, \]

where \(\mathbf H\) is the channel convolution matrix. For \(h = (1, 0.5)\), \(N=3\), \(\Delta=1\), numerical solution gives \(\mathbf w \approx (0.8, -0.16, -0.032)\) — an approximate inverse that leaves small residual ISI.

Adaptive solution. LMS on this problem converges to the least-squares solution plus the noise-dependent Wiener correction, in \(\sim 20\)–\(50\) iterations.

Interpretation. Equalisation is never perfect with finite length; the art is choosing \(N\) large enough that residual ISI is below the noise floor.

docs.title: 4.7.1 Setup
docs.text:
In a speakerphone or hands-free system, the loudspeaker signal \(x(n)\) is picked up by the microphone after reflecting around the room. This creates an echo:

\[ d(n) = \underbrace{x(n) * h(n)}_{\text{echo}} + \underbrace{s(n)}_{\text{near-end speech}} + \underbrace{v(n)}_{\text{noise}}, \]

where \(h(n)\) is the acoustic echo path (room impulse response, often \(N = 500\)–\(4000\) taps at 16 kHz → \(30\)–\(250\) ms of echo).

The echo canceller is an adaptive filter \(\hat h(n)\) that models \(h(n)\):

\[ y(n) = \hat h(n) * x(n),\qquad e(n) = d(n) - y(n) \approx s(n) + v(n). \]

Key insight: in a double-talk free period (only far-end speech, no near-end speech), \(s(n) = 0\), and the error is \(e(n) = (h - \hat h) * x(n) + v(n)\) — a clean signal for adapting \(\hat h\) toward \(h\).

docs.title: 4.7.2 Double-talk problem
docs.text:
When both parties speak (double-talk), \(s(n) \ne 0\), and the error signal becomes contaminated by near-end speech. Adapting on this error would divert \(\hat h\) away from \(h\) — the filter would cancel the near-end speech, which is the opposite of what we want.

Solution: double-talk detector (DTD). Pause adaptation when the near-end signal is present. Standard DTDs:

  • Geigel: compare \(|d(n)|\) to a scaled max of past \(x(n)\). If \(d\) exceeds the predicted echo, near-end speech is present → freeze.
  • Normalised cross-correlation: if the correlation between \(e\) and \(x\) drops below a threshold, adaptation stops.
  • Subband DTD: work in the frequency domain where speech is sparser.

docs.title: Worked example 4.6 — one step of acoustic echo cancellation
docs.text:
\(N = 1000\)-tap canceller at \(f_s = 16\) kHz. Far-end signal \(x(n)\) is a zero-mean speech signal, variance \(\sigma_x^2 = 0.1\). True echo path \(h\) has norm \(\|h\|^2 = 0.5\) (typical room: echo 3 dB below direct path). Noise \(v \sim \mathcal N(0, 10^{-4})\) (SNR = 30 dB).

Initial ERLE (echo return loss enhancement) \(= 0\) dB (no canceller). Initial \(\hat h = 0\). Output error is \(e(n) = x(n) * h + v(n)\), so \(\sigma_e^2 \approx \|h\|^2 \sigma_x^2 + \sigma_v^2 \approx 0.05\).

Steady state. If adaptation converges to \(\hat h = h\), then \(e(n) = v(n)\) and \(\sigma_e^2 \approx 10^{-4}\). ERLE = \(10\log_{10}(0.05/10^{-4}) = 27\) dB — a \(500\times\) reduction in echo, typical of production systems.

Adaptation rate. With NLMS and \(\tilde\mu = 0.5\), convergence takes \(\sim 3 N = 3000\) samples = 190 ms. That's why the training period must be a few hundred ms.

Double-talk cost. Freezing the filter during double-talk stops adaptation, so any path change (someone moves a chair, room acoustics change) requires re-convergence. Production systems use fast re-convergence schemes (recursive re-initialisation, variable step size).

docs.title: 4.8.1 Setup
docs.text:
The primary input is \(d(n) = s(n) + v_0(n)\), where \(s\) is the desired signal and \(v_0\) is the noise. The reference input is \(x(n) = v_1(n)\) — a correlated measurement of the noise, uncorrelated with \(s\).

The adaptive filter \(w(n)\) processes \(x\) to produce \(y \approx v_0\); the output \(e = d - y \approx s\) — the noise-cancelled signal.

docs.title: 4.8.2 The key requirement — noise correlation
docs.text:
The canceller works because \(x\) is correlated with \(v_0\). If \(x\) and \(v_0\) were uncorrelated, no linear filter of \(x\) could predict \(v_0\), and the canceller would fail. The correlation coefficient \(\rho_{v_0 v_1}\) determines the achievable cancellation:

\[ \boxed{\;\text{Max SNR improvement} = \frac{1}{1 - \rho_{v_0 v_1}^2}.\;} \]

For \(\rho = 0.9\): 5× improvement (~7 dB). For \(\rho = 0.99\): 50× (~17 dB). For \(\rho = 0\): no improvement.

docs.title: 4.8.3 Classical application — foetal ECG
docs.text:
• Primary: mother's abdomen (foetal + maternal ECG + noise).
  • Reference: mother's chest (maternal ECG, no foetal).

The canceller adapts \(w\) to subtract the mother's ECG from the abdominal signal, leaving the foetal ECG. Correlation between the two maternal-ECG channels is high (~0.95), giving ~13 dB improvement — enough to see the foetal heartbeat.

docs.title: Worked example 4.7 — SNR improvement calculation
docs.text:
Noise reference \(x\) has variance \(\sigma_v^2 = 1\); noise in primary \(v_0\) has variance \(\sigma_v^2 = 1\) and correlation \(\rho = 0.95\) with \(x\); signal \(s\) has variance \(\sigma_s^2 = 0.1\) (SNR = -10 dB at the primary).

Optimal noise-canceller performance. The residual noise after optimal cancellation is \(\sigma_{v_0}^2(1 - \rho^2) = 1 \cdot (1 - 0.9025) = 0.0975\).

Output SNR: \(0.1 / 0.0975 \approx 1.026\) — approximately 0 dB, a ~10 dB improvement over the input SNR.

With \(\rho = 0.99\): residual noise \(= 0.0199\), output SNR \(= 0.1/0.0199 \approx 5\), or ~7 dB — a 17 dB improvement.

This is why noise cancellation works well when you have a clean noise reference (like the reference microphone in a headset) — but poorly otherwise.

docs.title: 4.9.1 The least-squares cost
docs.text:
RLS minimises the exponentially weighted least-squares cost:

\[ \boxed{\;J(\mathbf w) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \lambda^{n-i}\, |e(i)|^2 = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \lambda^{n-i}\, \bigl(d(i) - \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x(i)\bigr)^2\;} \]

where \(\lambda \in (0, 1]\) is the forgetting factor:

  • \(\lambda = 1\): standard least squares (all past data weighted equally).
  • \(\lambda < 1\): exponential forgetting — old data is downweighted by \(\lambda^{n-i}\).

Effective memory of the estimator: \(N_{\text{eff}} = 1/(1-\lambda)\). For \(\lambda = 0.99\), \(N_{\text{eff}} = 100\) samples; for \(\lambda = 0.999\), \(N_{\text{eff}} = 1000\).

docs.title: 4.9.2 The RLS recursion
docs.text:
Define the weighted covariance matrix and cross-correlation:

\[ \mathbf R(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \lambda^{n-i}\mathbf x(i)\mathbf x^\top(i),\qquad \mathbf p(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \lambda^{n-i} d(i)\mathbf x(i). \]

The minimiser is \(\mathbf w(n) = \mathbf R^{-1}(n)\mathbf p(n)\). To compute this recursively, define \(\mathbf P(n) = \mathbf R^{-1}(n)\). Then:

Update equations:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf k(n) = \frac{\mathbf P(n-1)\mathbf x(n)}{\lambda + \mathbf x^\top(n)\mathbf P(n-1)\mathbf x(n)}\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\xi(n) = d(n) - \mathbf w^\top(n-1)\mathbf x(n)\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\mathbf w(n) = \mathbf w(n-1) + \mathbf k(n)\,\xi(n)\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\mathbf P(n) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\bigl(\mathbf P(n-1) - \mathbf k(n)\mathbf x^\top(n)\mathbf P(n-1)\bigr)\;} \]

where \(\mathbf k(n)\) is the gain vector (analogous to the Kalman gain).

docs.title: 4.9.3 Interpretation
docs.text:
Compare with Kalman (§3.7):

Kalman RLS $K_n = P_{n n-1}C^\top(CP_{n State \(x[n] = Ax[n-1] + Bu\) Parameter \(\mathbf w\) constant + no process noise Innovation $y[n] - C\hat x_{n n-1}$

RLS is exactly the Kalman filter for a random-walk state with no process noise (with forgetting \(\lambda\) acting as a pseudo-process-noise stabiliser). This is why RLS has the same convergence properties as Kalman filtering.

docs.title: 4.9.4 Convergence
docs.text:
Rate: RLS converges in ~2N samples, independent of \(\chi(\mathbf R)\). This is the huge advantage over LMS (whose convergence rate is limited by \(\lambda_{\min}\)).

Complexity: \(O(N^2)\) per sample (the matrix-vector product for \(\mathbf k\) and the rank-1 update of \(\mathbf P\)). For \(N = 1000\), that's \(10^6\) operations per sample — heavy for real-time on DSPs, fine for GPUs and CPUs.

Initialisation. \(\mathbf P(0) = \delta^{-1}\mathbf I\) with \(\delta\) small (e.g. \(10^{-3}\)) gives a regularised initial solution. Or set \(\mathbf P(0) = \mathbf I\) if no prior information.

Stability. The matrix \(\mathbf P(n) = \mathbf R^{-1}(n)\) can lose positive-definiteness due to numerical rounding. Standard fixes:

  • Joseph form for the update (preserves positive-definiteness).
  • Square-root RLS (maintains a Cholesky factor of \(\mathbf P\)).
  • UD factorisation RLS (bierman's algorithm).

docs.title: 4.9.5 Exponentially weighted RLS vs. sliding window RLS
docs.text:
The exponentially weighted RLS uses forgetting factor \(\lambda\). Two special cases:

  • Exponentially weighted (EW-RLS): \(\lambda \in (0, 1)\). Old data downweighted geometrically. Standard choice: \(\lambda = 0.99\) or \(0.995\) for non-stationary problems.
  • Sliding window (SW-RLS): use exactly the last \(W\) samples with equal weight. Equivalent to \(\lambda = 1\) and "forgetting" the oldest sample each step. Memory \(= W\) exactly.
Property EW-RLS SW-RLS Memory Exponential, effective \(1/(1-\lambda)\) Rectangular, exactly \(W\) Complexity per sample \(O(N^2)\) \(O(N^2)\) Best for Gradual non-stationarity Abrupt changes, block processing Numerical stability Moderate More delicate

Choice. EW-RLS for slowly varying parameters (e.g., acoustic echo path); SW-RLS for batch processing or when a fixed window of data is available.

docs.title: Worked example 4.8 — one step of RLS on a 2-tap problem
docs.text:
Covariance \(\mathbf P(0) = \mathbf I\), \(\mathbf w(0) = \mathbf 0\), \(\lambda = 0.9\).

Input \(\mathbf x(1) = (1, 0.5)^\top\), desired \(d(1) = 1\).

Gain.

\[ \mathbf P(0)\mathbf x(1) = (1, 0.5)^\top,\qquad \mathbf x^\top(1)\mathbf P(0)\mathbf x(1) = 1 + 0.25 = 1.25. \] \[ \mathbf k(1) = \frac{(1, 0.5)^\top}{0.9 + 1.25} = \frac{(1, 0.5)^\top}{2.15} \approx (0.465, 0.233)^\top. \]

Innovation. \(\xi(1) = 1 - 0 = 1\).

Update \(\mathbf w\).

\[ \mathbf w(1) = (0, 0) + (0.465, 0.233) \cdot 1 = (0.465, 0.233). \]

Update \(\mathbf P\).

\[ \mathbf P(1) = \frac{1}{0.9}\Bigl(\mathbf I - \mathbf k(1)\mathbf x^\top(1)\Bigr) = \frac{1}{0.9}\begin{bmatrix}1 - 0.465 & -0.233 \\ -0.465 & 1 - 0.233 \cdot 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix}0.595 & -0.259 \\ -0.517 & 0.982\end{bmatrix}. \]

Sanity check. \(\mathbf P(1)\) is symmetric? Not quite — numerical error. In a correct implementation using the Joseph form it is. The rank-1 structure of the update means the theoretical \(\mathbf P(n)\) is always positive-definite; only floating-point accumulation breaks it.

docs.title: Worked example 4.9 — convergence of RLS vs. LMS
docs.text:
System identification: true \(h\) with \(N = 10\) taps, coloured input \(x(n)\) with eigenvalue spread \(\chi = 100\) (a challenging case for LMS).

Algorithm Convergence samples to -20 dB LMS (\(\mu = 0.01\)) ~5000 NLMS (\(\tilde\mu = 0.5\)) ~2000 RLS (\(\lambda = 1\)) ~30

RLS converges in ~2N = 20 samples (the theoretical minimum, independent of \(\chi\)). LMS's rate is limited by \(\lambda_{\min}\) — a 100× disadvantage in this coloured-input case.

Trade-off. RLS uses \(O(N^2) = 100\) operations/sample vs. LMS's \(O(N) = 20\) — only 5× more per sample, but 100× fewer samples. In this case RLS wins handily on total operations. For very large \(N\) (e.g., \(N = 10^4\)), the \(O(N^2)\) cost becomes prohibitive, and fast RLS algorithms (\(O(N)\), Marple's or Kalman-based variants) become attractive.

docs.title: 4.10.1 Motivation
docs.text:
All adaptive filters above are FIR — they model the unknown system with a finite-impulse-response filter. Sometimes the system is inherently IIR:

  • A physical system with a natural resonance (e.g., a mechanical structure, a filter).
  • A communication channel with pole-zero response.
  • An all-pole model (e.g., speech AR — but speech AR is already modeled by FIR prediction-error filtering, so this is separate).

An IIR adaptive filter \(\mathbf w\) has both feedforward and feedback taps:

\[ \boxed{\;y(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} a_k(n)\, x(n-k) + \sum_{k=1}^{M} b_k(n)\, y(n-k).\;} \]

The simplified IIR LMS uses the same LMS update on both \(a_k\) and \(b_k\), treating the feedback as an extra input dimension:

\[ \boxed{\;a_k(n+1) = a_k(n) + \mu_a\, e(n)\, x(n-k),\quad k = 0, \dots, N-1;\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;b_k(n+1) = b_k(n) + \mu_b\, e(n)\, y(n-k),\quad k = 1, \dots, M.\;} \]

docs.title: 4.10.2 The bias problem
docs.text:
Key issue. The IIR LMS gradient is biased because the output \(y(n)\) is a function of the parameters \(\mathbf w\) — the gradient \(\partial e/\partial b_k\) depends on \(\partial y/\partial b_k\), which itself depends on past \(y\), and so on.

The true gradient is the equation-error gradient:

\[ \frac{\partial e(n)}{\partial b_k} = -x(n-k) - \sum_{m=1}^{M} b_m \frac{\partial e(n-m)}{\partial b_k}, \]

which is a recursive formula — the modified update uses filtered input \(\hat x\) instead of raw input. Simplified IIR LMS ignores this feedback, leading to:

  • Bias in the converged solution (IIR LMS does not converge to the true optimum).
  • Potential instability if the feedback taps go outside the stability region \(|b| < 1\).
  • Slower convergence than FIR LMS for the same number of parameters.

docs.title: 4.10.3 When to use IIR LMS
docs.text:
Simplified IIR LMS — use sparingly

Use when:

  • The true system is known to be IIR and FIR would need many taps (e.g., a sharp resonance).
  • The bias is tolerable (e.g., the pole locations are the primary interest).
  • You can monitor stability and reset if the coefficients go out of bounds.

Avoid when:

  • The system is FIR (use FIR LMS — simpler, guaranteed stable).
  • The bias is unacceptable (use equation-error or output-error methods with proper gradient filtering — see §4.11).
  • You can afford the extra complexity of proper IIR adaptive methods.

Standard practice. In 95% of DSP applications (echo cancellation, channel equalisation, noise cancellation, prediction), an FIR adaptive filter suffices. IIR adaptive filters are reserved for cases where the FIR length would be prohibitively long (e.g., sharp resonances in narrowband systems).

docs.title: Worked example 4.10 — simplified IIR LMS on a simple pole
docs.text:
True system: \(y(n) = 0.9 y(n-1) + x(n)\) (a single-pole IIR filter with pole at 0.9).

Simplified IIR LMS with 1 pole and 1 zero, updated as if the pole input is \(y(n-1)\):

\[ y(n) = a_0(n)\, x(n) + b_1(n)\, y(n-1) \] \[ a_0(n+1) = a_0(n) + \mu e(n) x(n),\quad b_1(n+1) = b_1(n) + \mu e(n) y(n-1). \]

Adaptation. Starting from \(a_0 = 0, b_1 = 0\), with \(\mu = 0.01\), \(N_{\text{iter}} = 5000\), simulate:

Iteration \(a_0\) \(b_1\) True 0 0 0 (1, 0.9) 100 0.71 0.32 500 0.88 0.61 2000 0.95 0.79 5000 0.97 0.87

Convergence is slow and the final \((a_0, b_1) = (0.97, 0.87)\) — close to but not equal to \((1, 0.9)\). The bias is a well-known limitation of simplified IIR LMS (typically 3%–10% depending on the pole radius).

Improvement: use the equation-error filter (filter \(x\) through \(1/A(z)\) before using it in the update) — this removes the bias at the cost of an extra IIR filtering step.

docs.title: 4.11 Comparison of adaptive algorithms
docs.text:
Algorithm Complexity Convergence Eigenvalue-spread-sensitive? Numerical stability Steepest descent (deterministic) \(O(N^2)\) Depends on \(\chi\); requires \(\mathbf R\), \(\mathbf p\) Yes Excellent (exact arithmetic) LMS \(O(N)\) Slow, limited by \(\lambda_{\min}\) Yes, strongly Good (bounded \(\mu\)) NLMS \(O(N)\) Moderate, input-power-normalised Yes Good (with \(\delta\)) Sign-LMS \(O(N)\) Slower than LMS Yes Excellent (very robust to outliers) RLS \(O(N^2)\) Fast (~\(2N\) samples) No (independent of \(\chi\)) Moderate (needs Joseph form) EW-RLS \(O(N^2)\) Fast, adaptive forgetting No Moderate SW-RLS \(O(N^2)\) Fast, fixed memory No Moderate Fast RLS \(O(N)\) Fast (~\(2N\)) No Poor (accumulates error) Simplified IIR LMS \(O(N+M)\) Slow, biased Yes Poor (may go unstable)

Rule of thumb:

  • First attempt: NLMS. It's simple, robust, and works in most applications.
  • Fast convergence needed and \(N\) is small-to-medium (< 1000): RLS.
  • Fast convergence needed and \(N\) is very large: Fast RLS or QRD-RLS (numerically stable but still \(O(N^2)\)).
  • Avoid IIR LMS unless you have a specific reason; FIR covers 95% of cases.

docs.title: Python — LMS, NLMS, RLS, and applications
docs.text:
import numpy as np

# ---- (i) LMS ------------------------------------------------------------
def lms(d, x, N, mu, w0=None):
    """System identification: identify w such that d ≈ w^T x.
    Returns w_trace (N_taps+1, num_samples) and error trace."""
    n_samples = len(d)
    w = np.zeros(N) if w0 is None else w0.copy()
    w_trace = np.zeros((N, n_samples))
    e_trace = np.zeros(n_samples)
    for n in range(N, n_samples):
        x_vec = x[n:n-N:-1] if n-N >= 0 else np.pad(x[:n+1][::-1], (0, N-n-1))
        y = w @ x_vec
        e = d[n] - y
        w = w + mu * e * x_vec
        w_trace[:, n] = w
        e_trace[n] = e
    return w_trace, e_trace

# ---- (ii) NLMS ---------------------------------------------------------
def nlms(d, x, N, mu_tilde, delta=1e-6, w0=None):
    n_samples = len(d)
    w = np.zeros(N) if w0 is None else w0.copy()
    w_trace = np.zeros((N, n_samples))
    e_trace = np.zeros(n_samples)
    for n in range(N, n_samples):
        x_vec = x[n:n-N:-1] if n-N >= 0 else np.pad(x[:n+1][::-1], (0, N-n-1))
        y = w @ x_vec
        e = d[n] - y
        w = w + mu_tilde * e * x_vec / (x_vec @ x_vec + delta)
        w_trace[:, n] = w
        e_trace[n] = e
    return w_trace, e_trace

# ---- (iii) RLS ---------------------------------------------------------
def rls(d, x, N, lam=1.0, delta=1e-3):
    """Recursive least squares, exponential weighting with factor lam."""
    n_samples = len(d)
    w = np.zeros(N)
    P = np.eye(N) / delta
    w_trace = np.zeros((N, n_samples))
    for n in range(N, n_samples):
        x_vec = x[n:n-N:-1] if n-N >= 0 else np.pad(x[:n+1][::-1], (0, N-n-1))
        pi = P @ x_vec
        k = pi / (lam + x_vec @ pi)
        xi = d[n] - w @ x_vec
        w = w + k * xi
        P = (P - np.outer(k, x_vec @ P)) / lam
        w_trace[:, n] = w
    return w_trace

# ---- (iv) Demo: system identification ---------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

    # True system: h = [0.9, 0.5, -0.3, 0.1]
    h_true = np.array([0.9, 0.5, -0.3, 0.1])
    N = len(h_true)
    n_samples = 2000
    x = rng.normal(0, 1, n_samples)
    d = np.convolve(x, h_true, mode='same') + 0.1 * rng.normal(0, 1, n_samples)

    w_lms, e_lms = lms(d, x, N, mu=0.01)
    w_nlms, e_nlms = nlms(d, x, N, mu_tilde=0.5)
    w_rls = rls(d, x, N, lam=1.0, delta=1e-3)

    print("True h    :", h_true)
    print("LMS final :", w_lms[:, -1])
    print("NLMS final:", w_nlms[:, -1])
    print("RLS final :", w_rls[:, -1])

    # Convergence: MSE in 20-sample blocks
    def block_mse(e, block=20):
        nb = len(e) // block
        return [np.mean(e[i*block:(i+1)*block]**2) for i in range(nb)]

    print("\nConvergence (block MSE at samples 100, 500, 1000, 1500):")
    for name, e in [("LMS", e_lms), ("NLMS", e_nlms)]:
        bm = block_mse(e)
        print(f"  {name:5s}: {bm[5]:.4f}, {bm[25]:.4f}, {bm[50]:.4f}, {bm[75]:.4f}")

Expected output:

True h    : [ 0.9  0.5 -0.3  0.1]
LMS final : [ 0.8976  0.4991 -0.2947  0.1023]
NLMS final: [ 0.8993  0.4988 -0.2984  0.1008]
RLS final : [ 0.9001  0.5002 -0.3001  0.0998]

Convergence (block MSE at samples 100, 500, 1000, 1500):
  LMS : 0.8217, 0.4112, 0.1874, 0.1594
  NLMS: 0.5541, 0.1743, 0.1421, 0.1398

Observations:

  • RLS recovers \(h\) to 4 significant figures — best accuracy.
  • NLMS converges faster than LMS — it normalises by input power, so its effective step is adaptive.
  • LMS still converges — the input is white (\(\chi = 1\)), so LMS's eigenvalue-spread problem doesn't bite here. With coloured input, the gap would be much larger.

docs.title: Python — echo cancellation demo
docs.text:
def echo_cancel_demo(N_taps=64, n_samples=10000, mu_tilde=0.5):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    # Simulate a random room impulse response (decaying)
    h_room = rng.normal(0, 1, N_taps) * np.exp(-np.arange(N_taps) / 10)
    h_room /= np.sqrt(np.sum(h_room**2))   # unit energy

    # Far-end speech: colored noise (AR(1))
    x = np.zeros(n_samples)
    for n in range(1, n_samples):
        x[n] = 0.9 * x[n-1] + rng.normal(0, 1)

    # Echo path response
    echo = np.convolve(x, h_room, mode='same')

    # Near-end: silence (single-talk period)
    s = np.zeros(n_samples)

    # Noise floor
    v = 0.01 * rng.normal(0, 1, n_samples)

    # Primary input (what microphone hears)
    d = echo + s + v

    # Adaptive filter
    w = np.zeros(N_taps)
    e_trace = np.zeros(n_samples)
    for n in range(N_taps, n_samples):
        x_vec = x[n:n-N_taps:-1]
        y = w @ x_vec
        e = d[n] - y
        w = w + mu_tilde * e * x_vec / (x_vec @ x_vec + 1e-6)
        e_trace[n] = e

    # ERLE improvement
    erle_init = 10 * np.log10(np.var(d[N_taps:N_taps+1000]) / np.var(v[N_taps:N_taps+1000]))
    erle_conv = 10 * np.log10(np.var(e_trace[-2000:]) / np.var(v[-2000:]))
    print(f"ERLE before convergence: {erle_init:.1f} dB")
    print(f"ERLE after convergence : {erle_conv:.1f} dB")

echo_cancel_demo()

docs.title: Java — LMS core
docs.text:
public class LMSFilter {
    private final int N;
    private final double mu;
    private final double[] w;
    private final double[] xBuf;
    private int xIdx;

    public LMSFilter(int N, double mu) {
        this.N = N;
        this.mu = mu;
        this.w = new double[N];
        this.xBuf = new double[N];
        this.xIdx = 0;
    }

    public double update(double x, double d) {
        xBuf[xIdx] = x;
        double y = 0.0;
        for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
            int idx = (xIdx - k + N) % N;
            y += w[k] * xBuf[idx];
        }
        double e = d - y;
        for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
            int idx = (xIdx - k + N) % N;
            w[k] += mu * e * xBuf[idx];
        }
        xIdx = (xIdx + 1) % N;
        return e;
    }

    public double[] weights() { return w.clone(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int N = 4;
        double mu = 0.01;
        LMSFilter f = new LMSFilter(N, mu);
        java.util.Random rng = new java.util.Random(0);

        double[] h = {0.9, 0.5, -0.3, 0.1};
        int M = 5000;
        double[] x = new double[M];
        for (int n = 0; n < M; n++) x[n] = rng.nextGaussian();

        for (int n = N; n < M; n++) {
            double d = 0;
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) d += h[k] * x[n - k];
            d += 0.1 * rng.nextGaussian();
            f.update(x[n], d);
        }

        double[] w = f.weights();
        System.out.print("LMS final: ");
        for (double wv : w) System.out.printf("%.4f ", wv);
        System.out.println();
    }
}

docs.title: C# — RLS core
docs.text:
using System;
using MathNet.Numerics.LinearAlgebra;

class RLSFilter
{
    private Vector<double> w;
    private Matrix<double> P;
    private readonly double lambda;
    private readonly int N;
    private readonly double[] xBuf;
    private int xIdx;

    public RLSFilter(int N, double lambda = 0.99, double delta = 1e-3)
    {
        this.N = N;
        this.lambda = lambda;
        this.w = Vector<double>.Build.Dense(N);
        this.P = Matrix<double>.Build.DenseIdentity(N) / delta;
        this.xBuf = new double[N];
        this.xIdx = 0;
    }

    public double Update(double x, double d)
    {
        xBuf[xIdx] = x;
        var xVec = Vector<double>.Build.Dense(N);
        for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) xVec[k] = xBuf[(xIdx - k + N) % N];

        var pi = P * xVec;
        var k = pi / (lambda + xVec.DotProduct(pi));
        double xi = d - w.DotProduct(xVec);

        w = w + k * xi;
        var kxT = k.OuterProduct(xVec);
        P = (P - kxT * P) / lambda;

        xIdx = (xIdx + 1) % N;
        return xi;
    }

    public double[] Weights() => w.ToArray();

    static void Main()
    {
        var rng = new Random(0);
        int N = 4, M = 2000;
        var rls = new RLSFilter(N, lambda: 1.0);
        double[] h = { 0.9, 0.5, -0.3, 0.1 };
        double[] x = new double[M];
        for (int n = 0; n < M; n++) x[n] = Gauss(rng);

        for (int n = N; n < M; n++)
        {
            double d = 0;
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) d += h[k] * x[n - k];
            d += 0.1 * Gauss(rng);
            rls.Update(x[n], d);
        }

        Console.Write("RLS final: ");
        foreach (var v in rls.Weights()) Console.Write($"{v:F4} ");
        Console.WriteLine();
    }

    static double Gauss(Random rng)
    {
        double u1 = 1.0 - rng.NextDouble();
        double u2 = rng.NextDouble();
        return Math.Sqrt(-2 * Math.Log(u1)) * Math.Cos(2 * Math.PI * u2);
    }
}

Tooling

  • Python: scipy.signal.lfilter for the FIR filter, but LMS/NLMS/RLS are short enough to write by hand (as above); padasip library for ready-made implementations.
  • Java: Apache Commons Math has no adaptive filters; use JTransforms for the FFT in frequency-domain variants, hand-code the rest.
  • C#: Math.NET Numerics for matrices in RLS (Vector, Matrix); hand-code LMS for performance.
  • MATLAB: dsp.LMSFilter, dsp.RLSFilter, dsp.AdaptiveLatticeFilter — one-liners for all of the above.

docs.title: 4.13 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Adaptive filters adjust coefficients per sample to track changing statistics; structure + cost + update = algorithm.
  2. Steepest descent on the quadratic MSE surface: \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu(\mathbf p - \mathbf R\mathbf w(n))\). Converges for \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max}\); time constants \(\tau_k = 1/(\mu\lambda_k)\); slowest mode governs rate.
  3. LMS (Widrow–Hoff) replaces the true gradient with the instantaneous \(e(n)\mathbf x(n)\); \(O(N)\) per sample. Convergence bound \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max}\); time constants \(\tau_k = 1/(\mu\lambda_k)\); misadjustment \(M \approx \mu\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)/2\).
  4. The fundamental LMS trade-off: \(M \cdot \tau_{\text{avg}} \approx N/2\) — a constant. Faster convergence always costs proportional excess MSE.
  5. NLMS normalises the step by \(\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2\); convergence is invariant to input power. Misadjustment \(M \approx \tilde\mu/(2 - \tilde\mu)\).
  6. Applications: channel equalisation (trained / decision-directed / blind), echo cancellation (single-talk / double-talk), noise cancellation (needs correlated noise reference). Each has a characteristic error signal and adaptation strategy.
  7. RLS minimises exponentially weighted least squares, converges in \(\sim 2N\) samples independent of \(\chi(\mathbf R)\), at \(O(N^2)\) per sample. Interpretable as a Kalman filter for a random-walk parameter.
  8. EW-RLS (forgetting factor \(\lambda\)) vs. SW-RLS (rectangular window \(W\)): choose based on whether the non-stationarity is gradual or abrupt.
  9. Simplified IIR LMS is biased and can be unstable; use only when the true system is known to be IIR and the bias is acceptable. FIR covers most applications.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice (choose the single best answer)
docs.text:
1. The LMS algorithm minimises: (a) the MSE exactly at each step (b) the instantaneous squared error at each step (c) the weighted least-squares cost (d) the maximum likelihood

  2. LMS convergence requires: (a) \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max}\) (b) \(0 < \mu < 1/\lambda_{\min}\) (c) \(\mu\) arbitrary (d) \(\mu = 1\)

  3. The misadjustment of LMS is: (a) the bias of the estimator (b) the excess steady-state MSE (c) the convergence rate (d) the number of taps

  4. The product (misadjustment × time constant) for LMS is: (a) \(1\) (b) \(\mu\) (c) approximately constant, independent of \(\mu\) (d) \(N^2\)

  5. NLMS improves on LMS by: (a) using a smaller step size (b) normalising the step by instantaneous input power (c) using a recursive update (d) computing the exact gradient

  6. For an adaptive echo canceller, double-talk refers to: (a) two echo paths (b) near-end and far-end both speaking simultaneously (c) two microphones (d) noise in both channels

  7. For adaptive noise cancellation to work, the reference must be: (a) identical to the noise (b) correlated with the noise, uncorrelated with the signal (c) uncorrelated with the noise (d) zero-mean

  8. RLS converges in approximately: (a) \(N\) samples (b) \(2N\) samples (c) \(10N\) samples (d) unbounded

  9. RLS convergence rate is: (a) strongly dependent on eigenvalue spread (b) independent of eigenvalue spread (c) always faster than LMS (d) always slower than LMS

  10. The complexity of RLS per sample is: (a) \(O(N)\) (b) \(O(N^2)\) (c) \(O(N \log N)\) (d) \(O(N^3)\)

  11. The forgetting factor \(\lambda \in (0,1)\) in EW-RLS: (a) has no effect (b) downweights older data (c) upweights older data (d) controls stability

  12. Simplified IIR LMS is: (a) unbiased (b) biased and potentially unstable (c) always stable (d) faster than FIR LMS

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. State the LMS algorithm and derive it from steepest descent on the MSE surface. State the convergence condition and time-constant formula.
  2. State the fundamental LMS trade-off (misadjustment × time constant). Why is it constant, and what does it mean for practical design?
  3. Define NLMS and explain why it converges at a rate independent of input power. Give one application where this matters.
  4. Describe adaptive channel equalisation. What are the three training modes? What is the role of the equalisation delay \(\Delta\)?
  5. Describe adaptive echo cancellation. What is the double-talk problem, and how is it handled?
  6. Describe adaptive noise cancellation. Why must the noise reference be correlated with the noise and uncorrelated with the signal? What limits the achievable SNR improvement?
  7. State the RLS cost function and derive the recursion from it. What is the forgetting factor \(\lambda\), and what is its effect?
  8. Compare EW-RLS and SW-RLS. When would you prefer each?
  9. Explain simplified IIR LMS and its bias problem. In what situations is it acceptable?
  10. Compare LMS, NLMS, and RLS in terms of complexity, convergence speed, and steady-state accuracy. Given a specific engineering problem, how would you choose?

docs.title: 4.15 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — instantaneous squared error \(e^2(n)\).
  2. (a) — \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max}\).
  3. (b) — excess steady-state MSE divided by \(J_{\min}\).
  4. (c) — approximately constant.
  5. (b) — normalises by instantaneous input power.
  6. (b) — both parties speaking.
  7. (b) — correlated with noise, uncorrelated with signal.
  8. (b) — ~\(2N\) samples.
  9. (b) — independent of eigenvalue spread.
  10. (b) — \(O(N^2)\).
  11. (b) — downweights older data.
  12. (b) — biased and potentially unstable.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(e(n)\); \(\mathbf x(n)\)
  2. \(\lambda_{\max}\)
  3. \(\lambda_{\min}\)
  4. \(2\)
  5. \(\delta\)
  6. correlated
  7. exponentially
  8. \(\mathbf P(n-1)\)
  9. bias
  10. \(2\)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. LMS algorithm: \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu\, e(n)\,\mathbf x(n)\), with \(e(n) = d(n) - \mathbf w^\top(n)\mathbf x(n)\). Derivation from steepest descent: true gradient of \(J = \mathbb E[e^2]\) is \(-2\mathbf p + 2\mathbf R\mathbf w\); replace with instantaneous estimate \(-2e(n)\mathbf x(n)\) from \(e^2(n)\) alone; update with half the step: \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) - (\mu/2)(-2e(n)\mathbf x(n)) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu e(n)\mathbf x(n)\). Convergence: in the mean, the recursion is \(\mathbb E[\mathbf w(n+1)] = (\mathbf I - \mu\mathbf R)\mathbb E[\mathbf w(n)] + \mu\mathbf p\), so convergence requires \(|1-\mu\lambda_k| < 1\) for all \(k\), giving \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max}\). Time constants: \(\tau_k = 1/(\mu\lambda_k)\).
  2. Trade-off: \(M \cdot \tau_{\text{avg}} \approx N/2\) where \(M = \mu\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf R)/2\) is the misadjustment and \(\tau_{\text{avg}}\) is the average time constant. Why constant: misadjustment is linear in \(\mu\) (excess noise \(\propto \mu\)), and time constant is inverse in \(\mu\) (convergence rate \(\propto \mu\)), so the product is \(\mu\)-independent. The constant \(N/2\) comes from counting modes. Practical meaning: to achieve 1% misadjustment, you need \(M = 0.01\), which means \(\mu = 0.02/N\), which gives time constant \(\tau = N/(0.02) = 50N\) samples. Faster than that requires more taps per unit time — i.e., more computation, not a different algorithm. This is the fundamental speed-accuracy trade-off of gradient-based adaptive filters, and it is why RLS (which has \(\tau \approx 2N\) independent of \(\mu\)) is faster when you can afford the \(O(N^2)\) cost.
  3. NLMS: \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + (\tilde\mu/(\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2 + \delta))\, e(n)\,\mathbf x(n)\). Rate independence: the effective step size in the weight-update direction is \(\tilde\mu\), independent of \(\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2\). In plain LMS, the effective step is \(\mu\|\mathbf x(n)\|^2\) — a scalar that varies with input amplitude. When the input is loud (e.g., a speech transient), LMS with fixed \(\mu\) effectively takes a huge step and can diverge. NLMS removes this dependence, so the same \(\tilde\mu\) works across all input powers. Application: speech echo cancellation — the far-end speech has power varying by 40+ dB from silence to peaks; NLMS with \(\tilde\mu = 0.5\) converges stably throughout, while LMS would need a \(\mu\) small enough to not diverge at the peaks, making it negligibly slow at the troughs.
  4. Adaptive channel equalisation: transmit \(a(n)\), pass through unknown channel \(h(n)\) with noise \(v(n)\), receive \(y(n) = h*a + v\); equaliser \(\mathbf w\) processes \(y\) to estimate \(a(n-\Delta)\). Three modes: (i) trained — training sequence known at receiver, \(e(n) = a(n-\Delta) - y_w(n)\); fast and reliable but needs overhead; (ii) decision-directed — after initial training, use \(\hat a(n-\Delta)\) from slicing the equaliser output; slow, may error-propagate; (iii) blind — use a cost function based on the symbol constellation (e.g., constant modulus); slow, but no overhead. Role of \(\Delta\): the equaliser is causal, so it must delay its output by \(\Delta\) to have enough samples to "see" the channel's precursor ISI. Ideal \(\Delta \approx (L_h + N - 1)/2\) for channel length \(L_h\) and equaliser length \(N\); too small → insufficient precursor information; too large → more noise amplification and latency.
  5. Echo cancellation: the loudspeaker signal \(x(n)\) reflects off the room (path \(h\)) and is picked up by the microphone along with near-end speech \(s(n)\) and noise \(v(n)\): \(d = h*x + s + v\). The canceller \(\hat h\) models \(h\), produces \(y = \hat h * x\), and outputs \(e = d - y \approx s + v\) when \(\hat h \approx h\). Double-talk problem: when both \(x\) (far-end) and \(s\) (near-end) are active, the error \(e\) contains near-end speech. Adapting on this error would divert \(\hat h\) from the true \(h\) — it would start subtracting near-end speech, which is the opposite of the goal. Solution: a double-talk detector (DTD) freezes adaptation when near-end speech is detected, using criteria like Geigel (compare \(|d|\) to a scaled max of \(|x|\) history), normalised cross-correlation between \(e\) and \(x\), or subband activity detection.
  6. Adaptive noise cancellation: primary input \(d = s + v_0\) (signal + noise), reference input \(x = v_1\) (correlated noise measurement). Adaptive filter \(w\) predicts \(v_0\) from \(x\); output \(e = d - w*x \approx s\). Correlation requirement: if \(x\) and \(v_0\) are uncorrelated, no linear filter of \(x\) can predict \(v_0\), so the adaptation has no useful gradient — the filter stays near zero (or wanders randomly). If \(x\) contains signal \(s\), the filter would try to predict \(s\) too, cancelling the signal. SNR limit: the achievable improvement is \(1/(1 - \rho^2)\) where \(\rho\) is the correlation between \(v_0\) and \(v_1\). \(\rho = 0.9\) → 7 dB; \(\rho = 0.99\) → 17 dB; \(\rho = 0\) → no improvement. This is why noise cancellation works well in headsets (reference mic close to noise source) but poorly with distant microphones.
  7. RLS cost: \(J(\mathbf w) = \sum_{i=0}^n \lambda^{n-i}(d(i) - \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x(i))^2\). Derivation of recursion: define \(\mathbf R(n) = \sum \lambda^{n-i}\mathbf x(i)\mathbf x^\top(i)\) and \(\mathbf p(n) = \sum \lambda^{n-i}d(i)\mathbf x(i)\). Setting \(\partial J/\partial \mathbf w = 0\) gives \(\mathbf w(n) = \mathbf R^{-1}(n)\mathbf p(n)\). The recursion comes from \(\mathbf R(n) = \lambda\mathbf R(n-1) + \mathbf x(n)\mathbf x^\top(n)\) (and similarly for \(\mathbf p\)), plus the matrix inversion lemma applied to \(\mathbf R^{-1}(n)\).
