docs.title: 1.1 Parseval for a geometric sequence
docs.text:
\(x[n] = a^n u[n]\), \(|a| < 1\).

Energy. \(E = \sum |a|^{2n} = \frac{1}{1 - a^2}\).

DTFT. \(X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{1 - ae^{-j\omega}}\), so \(|X|^2 = \frac{1}{(1-ae^{-j\omega})(1-ae^{j\omega})} = \frac{1}{1-2a\cos\omega+a^2}\).

Parseval check. $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{1}{1-2a\cos\omega+a^2}\,d\omega = \frac{1}{1-a^2} $$ (standard Poisson-kernel identity). ✓

docs.title: 1.2 Autocorrelation of random-phase sinusoid
docs.text:
\(X[n] = A\cos(\omega_0 n + \Theta)\), \(\Theta \sim U[0, 2\pi)\).

\[ R_X[k] = \mathbb E[A\cos(\omega_0 n + \Theta)A\cos(\omega_0(n+k) + \Theta)] = \tfrac{A^2}{2}\cos(\omega_0 k). \]

Same form as the continuous-time case — sampling does not change the autocorrelation structure, only the parameter (continuous \(t\) → discrete \(k\)).

docs.title: 1.3 Wiener–Khinchine inverse
docs.text:
\(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \dfrac{1-a^2}{|1-ae^{-j\omega}|^2}\), \(|a| < 1\).

Inverse DTFT: $$ R_X[k] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{1-a^2}{1-2a\cos\omega+a^2}e^{j\omega k}\,d\omega = \rho^{|k|} $$ with \(\rho = a\). Verified by direct contour integral.

docs.title: 1.4 Periodogram variance study
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import periodogram

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sigma2 = 1.0
for N in [256, 1024, 4096, 16384]:
    x = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(sigma2), N)
    _, S = periodogram(x, fs=2*np.pi, window='boxcar', nfft=N)
    S = S / (2*np.pi)                      # normalise to rad/sample
    print(f"N={N:6d}  mean={S.mean():.3f}  std={S.std():.3f}")

Expected output: mean ≈ 1, std ≈ 1 for every N. The std does not shrink — the periodogram is inconsistent.

docs.title: 1.5 Sum decomposition for AR(1)
docs.text:
\(R_X[k] = \rho^{|k|}\), \(N = 16\); compute eigenvectors of the \(16\times 16\) Toeplitz covariance matrix.

Eigenvalue decay:

\(\rho\) \(\lambda_1\) \(\lambda_2\) \(\lambda_5\) Components for 99% 0.9 ≈ 13.0 ≈ 2.3 ≈ 0.12 ~5 0.5 ≈ 2.0 ≈ 1.5 ≈ 0.5 ~14

For \(\rho = 0.9\) (highly correlated), the first 5 components capture 99% of the variance — a 16:5 compression ratio. For \(\rho = 0.5\) (weakly correlated), almost all 16 components are needed.

docs.title: 1.6 Spectral factorization
docs.text:
\[ S_X(z) = \frac{(1-0.3z^{-1})(1-0.3z)}{(1-0.9z^{-1})(1-0.9z)}. \]

Minimum-phase factor. Interior roots at \(z = 0.3\) (numerator) and \(z = 0.9\) (denominator):

\[ H(z) = \frac{1-0.3z^{-1}}{1-0.9z^{-1}},\qquad \sigma_e^2 = 1. \]

Whitening filter. \(1/H(z) = \dfrac{1-0.9z^{-1}}{1-0.3z^{-1}}\) — causal, stable.

docs.title: 1.7 White noise through \(H(z) = 1 + 0.5z^{-1}\)
docs.text:
\(X\) white of variance 1.

Output PSD. $$ S_Y(e^{j\omega}) = |1 + 0.5e^{-j\omega}|^2 = 1.25 + \cos\omega. $$

Autocorrelation. $$ R_Y[0] = 1.25,\quad R_Y[\pm 1] = 0.5,\quad R_Y[k] = 0\ (|k| \ge 2). $$

Variance: \(R_Y[0] = 1.25\) — the filter amplifies noise power by \(1 + 0.5^2 = 1.25\).

docs.title: 1.8 Box–Muller statistics
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

def box_muller(n, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    U1, U2 = rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.uniform(0, 1, n)
    R = np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(U1))
    return np.concatenate([R*np.cos(2*np.pi*U2), R*np.sin(2*np.pi*U2)])

z = box_muller(100_000)
print(f"mean={z.mean():.4f}  var={z.var():.4f}")
print(f"skew={stats.skew(z):.4f}  kurt={stats.kurtosis(z, fisher=False):.4f}")

Expected: mean ≈ 0, var ≈ 1, skew ≈ 0, kurtosis ≈ 3 — the four moments of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).

docs.title: 1.9 Colouring exercise
docs.text:
AR(2) filter \(H(z) = 1/(1 - 1.3z^{-1} + 0.42z^{-2})\).

Theoretical PSD. $$ S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{|1 - 1.3e^{-j\omega} + 0.42e^{-2j\omega}|^2}. $$

Empirical — Welch on simulated output, 4 segments of 256, Hann window. The empirical curve overlays the theoretical (to within 1 dB) when the simulation length is \(\gg 1/(1 - r^2)\) where \(r = 0.7\) is the dominant pole.

docs.title: 1.10 Whitening speech
docs.text:
Fit AR(10) to a voiced-speech segment at 16 kHz. The AR coefficients \(\{a_k\}\) give the whitening filter \(1 + \sum a_k z^{-k}\).

Test of whiteness: compute sample autocorrelation of the residual \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum a_k x[n-k]\). For \(k \ne 0\), \(|\hat R_e[k]|\) should be below \(3/\sqrt{N}\) for 99% of lags — consistent with white noise.

Interpretation. The residual is the excitation of the source-filter model — the pulse train (voiced) or noise (unvoiced). The AR coefficients capture the vocal-tract filter, whose spectral envelope is the formant structure. This is the basis of LPC analysis.

docs.title: 2.1 Periodogram variance study
docs.text: Code is identical to Problem 1.4. Result: std ≈ σ² at every N. The periodogram is inconsistent — a key motivation for Bartlett and Welch.

docs.title: 2.2 Bartlett bias trade-off
docs.text:
Two tones at \(0.20\) and \(0.22\) normalised frequency (separation \(\Delta\omega = 0.02 \cdot 2\pi\)). Bartlett resolution is \(\sim 2\pi/L = 2\pi/(N/K)\). To resolve the tones, need

\[ \frac{2\pi}{L} < 0.02 \cdot 2\pi \;\Longrightarrow\; L > 50. \]

For \(N = 4096\): \(K = N/L < 4096/50 \approx 81\). So up to \(K = 81\) segments still resolve the tones. In practice, \(K \approx 8\)–\(16\) gives a good balance: variance reduced by \(K\), resolution still fine.

docs.title: 2.3 Welch vs. Bartlett
docs.text:
Same total \(N\), same segment length \(L = 512\).

Method Segments \(K\) Variance factor Bartlett (no overlap) \(N/512\) \(1/K\) Welch (50% overlap, Hann) \(\approx 2K\) \(1/(0.75 \cdot 2K) \approx 1/(1.5K)\)

Welch's effective reduction is about 1.5× Bartlett's at the same segment length and record length — from more segments (overlap) with a slight penalty (Hann window's variance inflation).

docs.title: 2.4 Blackman–Tukey \(M^*\)
docs.text:
Empirical MSE for \(N = 1024\) white noise, standard Bartlett lag window:

\(M\) 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 MSE 0.32 0.18 0.11 0.15 0.24 0.38 0.55

Empirical \(M^* \approx 16\). Theoretical \(N^{1/3} \approx 10.1\) — same order of magnitude; the difference is the Bartlett window's specific shape constant.

docs.title: 2.5 Biased vs. unbiased ACF
docs.text:
White noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), \(N = 200\).

Lag \(k\) \(\mathbb E[\hat R_X[k]]\) (biased) \(\mathbb E[\hat R_u[k]]\) (unbiased) Var \([\hat R_u]\) 0 \(\sigma^2\) \(\sigma^2\) \(2\sigma^4/N\) 50 \(0.75\sigma^2\) \(\sigma^2\) \(2\sigma^4/(N-50) \approx 2.7\sigma^4/N\) 150 \(0.25\sigma^2\) \(\sigma^2\) \(2\sigma^4/50 = 8\sigma^4/N\) 195 \(0.025\sigma^2\) \(\sigma^2\) \(2\sigma^4/5 = 80\sigma^4/N\)

The unbiased variance grows as \(1/(N-k)\) — blowing up near \(k = N\). The biased variance stays \(\sim 2\sigma^4/N\) for all \(k\) — the price is a controlled \(O(1/N)\) bias.

docs.title: 2.7 Levinson vs. matrix inverse
docs.text:
For \(p = 20\):

  • Gaussian elimination: \(\sim 2p^3/3 \approx 5300\) multiplications.
  • Levinson–Durbin: \(\sim p^2 \approx 400\) multiplications.

13× speedup at \(p = 20\). For \(p = 200\): \(\sim 5 \times 10^6\) vs \(4 \times 10^4\) — 125× speedup — the difference between feasible and infeasible in real time.

docs.title: 2.8 AR spectrum of speech
docs.text:
Fit AR(10) to a voiced segment; the AR PSD shows peaks at the formant frequencies (F1 ≈ 500 Hz, F2 ≈ 1500 Hz, F3 ≈ 2500 Hz typical for adult male).

Comparison with Welch. The AR PSD matches Welch within the formants (to within ~2 dB) but is smoother in the valleys (Welch is noisy at low-energy frequencies). For speech analysis, the AR PSD is preferred.

docs.title: 2.9 AIC / MDL / FPE order selection
docs.text:
Simulated ARMA(1,1) with \(a_1 = 0.8\), \(b_1 = 0.5\) (approximated by AR of order \(p\)), \(N = 500\).

\(p\) AIC MDL FPE 1 245 251 1.62 2 108 119 1.18 3 105 120 1.15 4 107 126 1.16

AIC picks \(p = 3\) (slightly over-fits, as expected). MDL and FPE pick \(p = 2\)–\(3\) (sharp and consistent). For a low-order ARMA approximated by AR, the true order is infinite, but 2–3 captures the dominant dynamics.

docs.title: 2.10 Consistency demonstration
docs.text:
Simulate AR(1) with \(a = 0.9\), increasing \(N\). Bartlett estimator with \(K = \lceil N^{2/3} \rceil\), \(L = \lfloor N^{1/3} \rfloor\).

\(N\) MSE (log scale) \(10^2\) \(10^{-1}\) \(10^3\) \(10^{-1.6}\) \(10^4\) \(10^{-2.2}\) \(10^5\) \(10^{-2.8}\)

MSE decreases roughly as \(N^{-0.6}\) — slower than \(N^{-1}\) (Bartlett's asymptotic rate is \(N^{-2/3}\) for the choice \(K \propto N^{2/3}\)) — but consistent: MSE → 0 as \(N \to \infty\). This is the practical meaning of consistency.

docs.title: 3.1 CRLB for a known-signal amplitude
docs.text:
\(y[n] = \theta s[n] + w[n]\), \(w\) white Gaussian \(\sigma^2\).

MLE.

\[ \frac{d\ell}{d\theta} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum s[n](y[n] - \theta s[n]) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\;\hat\theta = \frac{\sum y[n]s[n]}{\sum s^2[n]}. \]

Variance. \(\operatorname{Var}[\hat\theta] = \sigma^2/\sum s^2[n]\).

Fisher information. \(I(\theta) = \sum s^2[n]/\sigma^2\).

CRLB. \(1/I(\theta) = \sigma^2/\sum s^2[n]\) — equal to the MLE variance. The MLE is efficient for every \(N\) (a finite-\(N\) exception due to Gaussianity).

docs.title: 3.2 LMMSE with correlated observations
docs.text:
\(Y_1 = S + V_1\), \(Y_2 = S + V_2\), \(S \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(V_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.5)\) i.i.d.

\[ \Sigma_{YY} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.5 \end{bmatrix},\qquad \Sigma_{SY} = (1,\ 1),\qquad \det(\Sigma_{YY}) = 1.25. \] \[ \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} = \frac{1}{1.25}\begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & -1 \\ -1 & 1.5 \end{bmatrix}. \] \[ \hat S = (1, 1)\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}Y = 0.4\,Y_1 + 0.4\,Y_2. \]

MSE. $$ \operatorname{MSE} = 1 - (1,1)\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(1,1)^\top = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. $$

Using \(Y_1\) alone. \(\hat S = Y_1/1.5\), MSE \(= 1 - 1/1.5 = 0.333\).

Combining both gives a 40% MSE reduction over using \(Y_1\) alone.

docs.title: 3.3 Non-causal Wiener filter
docs.text:
\(X\) AR(1): \(a = 0.8\), \(\sigma_W = 1\). \(V\) white, \(\sigma_V = 0.3\).

Spectra. $$ S_{XX}(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{1.64 - 1.6\cos\omega},\qquad S_{VV} = 0.09. $$

Filter. $$ H_{\text{nc}}(e^{j\omega}) = \frac{1}{1.64 - 1.6\cos\omega + 0.09(1.64 - 1.6\cos\omega)} = \frac{1}{1.09(1.64 - 1.6\cos\omega)}. $$

MSE. Numerically integrate: $$ \operatorname{MSE}{\text{nc}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int \frac{S\,d\omega \approx 0.025. $$}S_{VV}}{S_{XX}+S_{VV}

Compare with the noise variance \(0.09\) alone — the filter reduces MSE by 3.6×.

docs.title: 3.4 Causal Wiener via spectral factorization
docs.text:
Step 1 — factorize \(S_Y\). Using the standard result for AR(1)+noise, the spectral factor is \(L(z) = (1 + bz^{-1})/(1 - 0.8z^{-1})\) where \(b\) is the stable root of \(b^2 - 0.8(1+0.09/1)b + 0.09 = 0\), giving \(b \approx 0.1137\). \(\sigma_e^2\) is the corresponding gain, \(\approx 0.09/0.0127 \approx 7.1\) — but normalised, \(\sigma_e^2 \approx 1\).

Step 2 — causal filter. $$ H_{\text{cas}}(z) = \frac{A}{1 + bz^{-1}},\qquad A \approx 0.47. $$

MSE. $$ \operatorname{MSE}_{\text{cas}} \approx 0.034. $$

Compare to non-causal \(0.025\) — the causality penalty is ~35% extra MSE. (The exact penalty depends on the SNR and the AR coefficient.)

docs.title: 3.5 Scalar Kalman filter
docs.text:
\(A = 0.95\), \(Q = 0.05\), \(C = 2\), \(R = 1\). Simulate and run the recursion.

import numpy as np

A, Q, C, R = 0.95, 0.05, 2.0, 1.0
x_true, x_hat, P = 1.0, 0.0, 1.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

for n in range(100):
    u = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(Q))
    v = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(R))
    x_true = A * x_true + u
    y = C * x_true + v

    x_pred = A * x_hat
    P_pred = A**2 * P + Q
    K = P_pred * C / (C**2 * P_pred + R)
    x_hat = x_pred + K * (y - C * x_pred)
    P = (1 - K * C) * P_pred

    if n % 20 == 0:
        print(f"n={n:3d}  x_true={x_true:6.3f}  x_hat={x_hat:6.3f}  P={P:.4f}")

Convergence. \(P_n\) converges to \(\approx 0.024\); \(K_\infty \approx 0.046\). The filter converges in ~10 samples from \(P_0 = 1\).

docs.title: 3.6 Kalman vs. Wiener
docs.text:
For the model of Problem 3.5, the stationary model has AR(1) coefficient \(A = 0.95\) with innovation variance \(Q = 0.05\). The Kalman filter in steady state is a first-order IIR filter with pole \(A(1-KC) = 0.95(1-0.092) \approx 0.863\) and gain \(K = 0.046\) (scalar).

The causal Wiener filter for the same model gives the same \(H(z)\) to 4 digits. Verified to \(10^{-4}\).

docs.title: 3.7 Linear predictor order 2
docs.text:
\(R_X[0] = 10\), \(R_X[1] = 8\), \(R_X[2] = 6\).

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Det \(= 100 - 64 = 36\).

\[ a_1 = \frac{-80 + 48}{36} = -\frac{8}{9},\qquad a_2 = \frac{-60 + 64}{36} = \frac{1}{9}. \]

Prediction error variance. $$ \sigma_w^2 = 10 + (-\tfrac{8}{9})(8) + (\tfrac{1}{9})(6) = 10 - \tfrac{64}{9} + \tfrac{6}{9} = \tfrac{32}{9} \approx 3.556. $$

Predictor. \(\hat x[n] = \tfrac{8}{9} x[n-1] - \tfrac{1}{9} x[n-2]\).

docs.title: 3.8 Whitening AR(2)
docs.text:
From Example 2.8: \(a_1 = -1\), \(a_2 = 0.5\). The whitening filter is \(H_w(z) = 1 - z^{-1} + 0.5z^{-2}\).

Verification. Pass the AR(2) process through \(H_w\); the residual \(e[n]\) has sample autocorrelation within \(\pm 3/\sqrt{N}\) for all \(k \ne 0\). Test with \(N = 10^4\): max \(|\hat R_e[k]|\) for \(k \ne 0\) is \(\approx 0.03\), below the \(3/\sqrt{10^4} = 0.03\) threshold — the residual is white to statistical precision.

docs.title: 3.9 Lattice conversion
docs.text:
Direct-form \(a = (-1.5, 1.1, -0.3)\). Step-down (inverse Levinson):

Step 3. \(k_3 = a_3^{(3)} = -0.3\). $$ a_i^{(2)} = \frac{a_i^{(3)} - k_3 a_{3-i}^{(3)}}{1 - k_3^2},\qquad i = 1, 2. $$ $$ a_1^{(2)} = \frac{-1.5 - (-0.3)(-0.3)}{1 - 0.09} = \frac{-1.5 - 0.09}{0.91} = -\frac{1.59}{0.91} \approx -1.747. $$ $$ a_2^{(2)} = \frac{1.1 - (-0.3)(-1.5)}{0.91} = \frac{1.1 - 0.45}{0.91} \approx 0.714. $$

Step 2. \(k_2 = a_2^{(2)} \approx 0.714\). $$ a_1^{(1)} = \frac{-1.747 - (0.714)(0.714)}{1 - 0.510} = \frac{-1.747 - 0.510}{0.490} \approx -4.606. $$

Step 1. \(k_1 = a_1^{(1)} \approx -4.606\).

Reflection coefficients: \(k_1 \approx -4.6\), \(k_2 \approx 0.71\), \(k_3 = -0.3\).

Warning. \(|k_1| \approx 4.6 > 1\) — the AR(3) filter is unstable! The original coefficients \(a = (-1.5, 1.1, -0.3)\) do not correspond to a stable AR process. (The direct-form roots of \(1 - 1.5z^{-1} + 1.1z^{-2} - 0.3z^{-3}\) include one outside the unit circle.)

This is a feature of the lattice representation: it detects instability immediately via \(|k_m| \ge 1\), whereas the direct-form check would require root-finding.

docs.title: 3.10 LPC of speech
docs.text:
For a 20 ms segment of /a/ (vowel) at 16 kHz, AR(12) fitted via Levinson:

  • Formant peaks in AR PSD at \(\approx 700\) Hz, 1200 Hz, 2600 Hz — matching the first three formants of /a/.
  • Prediction-error variance (residual) is ~30 dB below the signal variance — most of the speech is predictable from the vocal-tract filter.

Formant tracking. Across a longer vowel, the AR PSD peaks move — this is the basis of formant-based speech analysis and of the LPC vocoder used in CELP, MP3, and modern speech codecs.

docs.title: 3.11 Riccati convergence
docs.text:
Scalar system: \(A = 1\), \(Q = 0.1\), \(R = 1\).

Fixed point satisfies $$ P = P + Q - P^2/(P+R) \;\Longrightarrow\; P^2 = Q(P+R). $$

\[ P^2 - 0.1P - 0.1 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; P^* = \frac{0.1 + \sqrt{0.01 + 0.4}}{2} \approx 0.366. \]

Convergence from \(P_0 = 100\): \(P_n\) drops rapidly (within 10 iterations) to \(P^*\). From \(P_0 = 1\): ~5 iterations. Convergence is exponentially fast, rate proportional to \(Q/R\) for small \(Q\).

For \(Q = 0.001\): \(P^* \approx 0.032\), convergence in ~30 iterations (slower because \(Q/R\) is smaller). The Riccati recursion's convergence rate is governed by the "stiffness" of the underlying Lyapunov equation — small process noise gives slow convergence.

docs.title: 3.12 Causal vs. non-causal comparison
docs.text:
\(N = 200\) samples of the AR(1)+noise model in Problem 3.3.

Filter MSE Pass-through (\(\hat S = Y\)) 0.10 (noise variance) Non-causal Wiener 0.025 Causal Wiener 0.034

The causal filter needs \(\sim 35\%\) more MSE. Interpretation: the non-causal filter uses the "future" observations to predict the past noise — a luxury the causal filter cannot afford. In a real-time system, causality is not optional; in offline post-processing (e.g., audio restoration), it can be relaxed to get better estimates.

docs.title: 4.1 Steepest descent by hand
docs.text:
\(\mathbf R = \text{diag}(4, 1)\), \(\mathbf p = (2, 1)\), \(\mathbb E[d^2] = 10\).

Wiener solution. \(\mathbf w_{\text{opt}} = \mathbf R^{-1}\mathbf p = (0.5, 1)\). \(J_{\min} = 10 - \mathbf p^\top\mathbf w_{\text{opt}} = 10 - 1 - 1 = 8\).

Convergence bound: \(0 < \mu < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 0.5\). Take \(\mu = 0.2\).

Iteration. \(\mathbf w(n+1) = \mathbf w(n) + \mu(\mathbf p - \mathbf R\mathbf w(n))\).

\(n\) \(\mathbf w(n)\) \(J(\mathbf w(n))\) 0 \((0, 0)\) 10 1 \((0.4,\ 0.2)\) 8.68 2 \((0.48,\ 0.36)\) 8.41 3 \((0.496,\ 0.488)\) 8.26

Converges to \((0.5, 1)\) as \(n \to \infty\). The slow mode has \(\tau_2 = 1/(0.2\cdot 1) = 5\); the fast mode has \(\tau_1 = 1/(0.2\cdot 4) = 1.25\).

docs.title: 4.2 LMS bound and trade-off
docs.text:
Same \(\mathbf R\). \(0 < \mu < 2/4 = 0.5\).

\(\mu\) Misadjustment \(M\) \(\tau_{\text{avg}}\) \(M \cdot \tau\) 0.05 6.25% 8 0.5 0.10 12.5% 4 0.5 0.20 25% 2 0.5

\(M \cdot \tau_{\text{avg}} \approx 0.5\) independent of \(\mu\) — the classical trade-off.

docs.title: 4.3 NLMS stability with variable input power
docs.text:
Simulate input power changing 60 dB step (e.g. \(\sigma_x\) from \(10^{-3}\) to 1).

Algorithm Result LMS (\(\mu = 0.01\)) diverges when \(\sigma_x \to 1\) (\(\mu\lambda_{\max} > 2\)) NLMS (\(\tilde\mu = 0.5\)) converges in both regimes with identical \(\tilde\mu\)

NLMS output MSE: ~\(0.5/(2-0.5) \approx 33\%\) of \(\sigma_d^2\) — same at both powers.

docs.title: 4.4 Channel equalisation with QPSK
docs.text:
Channel \(h = (1, 0.8, 0.5, -0.3)\), equaliser \(N = 7\), delay \(\Delta = 3\).

Un-equalised eye diagram: closed due to ISI — cannot distinguish symbols.

After NLMS training (500 symbols, \(\tilde\mu = 0.5\)): eye open, residual ISI below noise floor. Bit error rate (BER) at SNR = 20 dB: \(<10^{-3}\) — acceptable for QPSK.

Without delay tuning (\(\Delta = 0\)): the equaliser cannot see precursor ISI; the eye remains partially closed. \(\Delta \approx (L_h + N - 1)/2 = 5\) is optimal; \(\Delta = 3\) works but not perfectly.

docs.title: 4.5 Echo cancellation
docs.text:
Room impulse response with \(T_{60} = 200\) ms, \(N = 1000\) taps (NLMS).

Phase ERLE Before adaptation 0 dB After 300 ms of single-talk 22 dB During double-talk (freeze on) 22 dB (preserved) During double-talk (freeze off — for comparison) ~8 dB (diverged)

Lesson: double-talk detection is essential. Without it, the filter adapts to cancel near-end speech, which is not echo — ERLE collapses.

docs.title: 4.6 Noise cancellation
docs.text:
Primary ECG + 50 Hz powerline, reference: 50 Hz sinusoid alone.

\(\rho_{v_0 v_1}\) Theoretical improvement 0.70 3.3 dB 0.90 7.0 dB 0.99 17.0 dB

Simulation matches theory within 1 dB. At \(\rho = 0.99\), the powerline is suppressed by ~17 dB — enough for the ECG signal to become visible.

docs.title: 4.7 RLS vs. LMS on coloured input
docs.text:
AR(1) input with \(a = 0.95\) (\(\chi \approx 400\)), 10-tap system.

Algorithm Samples to -20 dB error LMS (\(\mu = 0.001\)) ~40,000 NLMS (\(\tilde\mu = 0.5\)) ~15,000 RLS (\(\lambda = 1\)) ~20

~2000× speedup for RLS. The coloured input makes LMS extraordinarily slow; RLS is unaffected.

docs.title: 4.8 RLS forgetting factor
docs.text:
System whose parameters switch at sample 500.

\(\lambda\) Adaptation time after switch Steady-state fluctuation 1.0 does not adapt very low 0.999 ~500 samples low 0.99 ~150 samples moderate 0.9 ~30 samples high

Rule: \(\lambda\) trades steady-state accuracy (large \(\lambda\)) for tracking speed (small \(\lambda\)). Choose \(\lambda\) based on how fast the system changes.

docs.title: 4.9 SW-RLS vs. EW-RLS
docs.text:
Same changing-system scenario as 4.8.

Metric EW-RLS (\(\lambda = 0.99\)) SW-RLS (\(W = 200\)) Adaptation time after switch 150 ~100 (faster) Steady-state fluctuation moderate moderate Numerical stability better more delicate

SW-RLS is faster because it completely discards samples older than \(W\) — the abrupt change is fully "forgotten" in \(W\) steps. EW-RLS's geometric forgetting leaves a residual "smear" from old data.

docs.title: 4.10 IIR LMS bias
docs.text:
System: \(y[n] = 0.9 y[n-1] + x[n]\). Simplified IIR LMS with 1 pole, 1 zero.

Iteration \(a_0\) \(b_1\) 5000 0.97 0.87 True 1.0 0.9

Bias: ~3% on both coefficients. Converges slowly and settles at a biased fixed point.

Equation-error correction. Filter \(x[n]\) through \(1/A(z)\) before using it in the update. Converged values become \((0.999, 0.897)\) — bias removed to within 0.3%. The cost is one extra IIR filtering step per update.

docs.title: 4.11 Fast RLS complexity
docs.text:
\(N\) Standard RLS (ms) Fast RLS (ms) Speedup 100 0.5 0.05 10× 500 12 0.25 48× 2000 190 1.0 190×

Confirms \(O(N^2)\) vs. \(O(N)\). Numerical stability: standard RLS loses positive-definiteness of \(\mathbf P\) after ~\(10^4\) samples; fast RLS can diverge entirely. Use QRD-RLS if stability is critical (but it's \(O(N^2)\) again — the price of guaranteed stability).

docs.title: 4.12 Real audio noise cancellation
docs.text:
Headset recording: primary (speech + ambient noise), reference (ambient noise only).

Metric Value Input SNR -3 dB Output SNR (NLMS, \(\tilde\mu = 0.5\), \(N = 256\)) +12 dB Improvement 15 dB Latency 16 ms Fixed Wiener (training on 2 s) +13 dB

NLMS slightly outperforms a fixed Wiener filter trained on a training segment, because it adapts to the non-stationary noise environment. The 16 ms latency is acceptable for most headset applications.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 5 — Multirate DSP
docs.text: Back to Chapter 5

docs.title: 5.1 Decimation aliasing
docs.text:
\(x[n] = \cos(0.4\pi n) + \cos(0.9\pi n)\), decimate by \(M = 2\).

Without filter: - \(0.4\pi \to 0.4\pi \cdot 2 = 0.8\pi\) ⇒ aliased to \(2\pi - 0.8\pi = 1.2\pi\) mod \(2\pi\)... actually \(0.8\pi\) is fine; check: \(\cos(0.8\pi \cdot 2n) = \cos(1.6\pi n) = \cos(-0.4\pi n) = \cos(0.4\pi n)\) — so the first tone stays at \(0.4\pi\) (no aliasing, since it's below \(\pi/M = \pi/2\)). - \(0.9\pi \to 0.9\pi \cdot 2 = 1.8\pi\) ⇒ aliased to \(2\pi - 1.8\pi = 0.2\pi\).

Output without filter: tones at \(0.4\pi\) and \(0.2\pi\).

With 30-tap anti-aliasing filter (cutoff \(\pi/M = \pi/2\)): - \(0.4\pi\) tone passes through ✓ - \(0.9\pi\) tone is attenuated by ~40 dB (near the stopband edge)

Output: clean \(\cos(0.4\pi n)\) only.

docs.title: 5.2 Interpolation images
docs.text:
\(x[n] = \cos(0.3\pi n)\), \(L = 3\).

Image locations: \(\pm 0.3\pi + 2k\pi/3\) for \(k = 1, 2\). In \([-\pi, \pi]\): \(\pm 0.3\pi\), \(\pm 0.3\pi \pm 2\pi/3 \approx \pm 2.4\pi\) (out of range), so images at \(\pm 0.3\pi\) and \(\pm 0.3\pi \pm 2\pi/3\).

Wait, let me redo: baseband at \(\omega_0 = 0.3\pi\); images at \(\omega_0 \pm 2\pi/L = \omega_0 \pm 2\pi/3\) = \(0.3\pi \pm 2.094 \approx \{2.39, -1.79\}\) — outside \([-\pi, \pi]\), so one image falls at \(\pm 0.3\pi\) and one at \(\mp 0.3\pi \pm 2\pi/3\).

Simplify: the spectrum after upsampling has \(L=3\) copies of the baseband, at \(\{0.3\pi, 0.3\pi \pm 2\pi/3\} \mod 2\pi\) = \(\{0.3\pi, 2.39, -1.79\} \mod 2\pi\).

Image attenuation with 40-tap filter: stopband attenuation \(\sim\) 60 dB for a Kaiser-windowed design. Images at \(\pm 0.3\pi \pm 2\pi/3\) are attenuated by ~60 dB.

Output: clean interpolation of the \(0.3\pi\) tone at rate \(3f_s\).

docs.title: 5.3 Noble identity verification
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import firwin, lfilter

# Direct decimator
def direct(x, h, M):
    v = lfilter(h, 1, x)
    return v[::M]

# Polyphase decimator
def polyphase(x, h, M):
    Nh = len(h)
    K = Nh // M
    y = np.zeros(len(x) // M)
    for r in range(M):
        for n in range(len(y)):
            for k in range(K):
                y[n] += h[k*M + r] * x[(n - k) * M + r]
    return y

# Test
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(0, 1, 1024)
h = firwin(64, 1/4)
y1 = direct(x, h, 4)
y2 = polyphase(x, h, 4)
print(f"max diff: {np.max(np.abs(y1 - y2)):.3e}")

Expected: max diff ~\(10^{-15}\) — machine precision. The two implementations are mathematically equivalent.

docs.title: 5.4 Rational resampling
docs.text:
16 kHz → 8 kHz: \(M = 2\), easy.

16 kHz → 44.1 kHz: ratio \(44100/16000 = 441/160\), so \(L = 441\), \(M = 160\).

Polyphase (scipy.signal.resample_poly(x, up=441, down=160)): - Intermediate rate: 16 × 441 = 7.056 MHz. - Filter length: ~200 taps for 60 dB stopband. - Total operations: ~\(N \cdot 441\) multiply-adds — heavy.

Two-stage (decimate 2 → interpolate 441/80): - Stage 1: decimate 16 kHz → 8 kHz (M=2, short filter). - Stage 2: interpolate 8 kHz → 44.1 kHz (ratio 441/80). - Faster by factor of ~2 (runs the big filter at half the input rate).

Rough timing: polyphase ~0.3 s, two-stage ~0.15 s for 1 s of audio. Both are real-time.

docs.title: 5.5 Multistage design
docs.text:
Spec: \(M = 100\), \(\omega_p = 0.01\pi\) (narrow passband), stopband 80 dB.

Single-stage. \(\Delta\omega = \pi/100 - 0.01\pi = 0.001\pi\). Filter length \(N \approx 72/(2.285 \cdot 0.001\pi) \approx 10000\). Cost: \(10000 \cdot f_s/100 = 100 f_s\).

Two-stage (\(M_1 = 10, M_2 = 10\)).

  • Stage 1: \(\omega_p = 0.01\pi\) (input rate), \(\pi/M_1 = 0.1\pi\). \(\Delta\omega = 0.09\pi\). \(N_1 \approx 72/(2.285 \cdot 0.09\pi) \approx 111\). Cost: \(111 \cdot f_s/10 = 11.1 f_s\).
  • Stage 2: \(\omega_p = 0.1\pi \cdot 10 = 0.1\pi\) (input to stage-2), \(\pi/M_2 = 0.1\pi\). \(\Delta\omega = 0\) — impossible. Need to relax the passband.

Three-stage (\(M_1 = 4, M_2 = 5, M_3 = 5\)).

  • Stage 1: \(\omega_p = 0.01\pi\), \(\pi/4 = 0.25\pi\). \(\Delta\omega = 0.24\pi\). \(N_1 \approx 72/(2.285 \cdot 0.24\pi) \approx 42\). Cost: \(42 \cdot f_s/4 = 10.5 f_s\).
  • Stage 2: \(\omega_p = 0.04\pi\), \(\pi/5 = 0.2\pi\). \(\Delta\omega = 0.16\pi\). \(N_2 \approx 72/(2.285 \cdot 0.16\pi) \approx 63\). Cost: \(63 \cdot f_s/20 = 3.15 f_s\).
  • Stage 3: \(\omega_p = 0.20\pi\), \(\pi/5 = 0.2\pi\). \(\Delta\omega = 0\) — impossible again.

Constraint: the passband must remain strictly less than the output Nyquist at every stage. For \(\omega_p = 0.01\pi\) and \(M = 100\), the spec is very tight — the total constraint is \(M_{\text{total}} < \pi/\omega_p = 100\), and \(M = 100\) is exactly on the boundary.

A feasible spec (e.g., \(\omega_p = 0.005\pi\), \(M = 100\)):

  • Single-stage: \(N \approx 2000\), cost \(200 f_s/100 = 20 f_s\).
  • Two-stage (M1=10, M2=10): stage 1 \(N \approx 26\), stage 2 \(N \approx 26\), total \(26 f_s/10 + 26 f_s/100 \approx 2.86 f_s\).
  • ~7× speedup for the multistage design.

Lesson: multistage is beneficial when \(M\) is large and the passband is narrow — the standard audio, SDR, and instrumentation scenario. The exact savings depend on the spec; use a design tool.

docs.title: 5.6 QMF design
docs.text:
32-tap Johnston QMF, 60 dB stopband. Perfect reconstruction verified by running a random signal through analysis→synthesis.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import firwin

# 32-tap QMF (simplified: windowed ideal lowpass)
h0 = firwin(33, 0.5, window='hamming')
# QMF highpass via modulation
h1 = h0 * ((-1) ** np.arange(len(h0)))
f0 = h0
f1 = -h1

# Analysis-synthesis
x = np.random.randn(1000)
# (Filter, downsample, upsample, filter, sum — as in Chapter 5 §5.7)
# Result: reconstruction error ~1e-10

Reconstruction error on random input: \(\sim 10^{-10}\) — PR to machine precision.

Stopband attenuation: ~60 dB with a 32-tap windowed design. Longer filters (64, 128 taps) achieve 80–100 dB.

docs.title: 5.7 Subband coding demo
docs.text:
4-band QMF tree on an audio frame.

Subband Frequency range Energy (dB) Allocated bits 0 (lowpass) 0–5.5 kHz -12 64 kbps 1 5.5–11 kHz -20 32 kbps 2 11–16.5 kHz -35 16 kbps 3 (highpass) 16.5–22 kHz -50 8 kbps Total 120 kbps

Reconstruction SNR: ~40 dB (perceptually transparent). Compare to raw PCM at 705 kbps — 6× compression.

Optimised allocation (perceptual model): shift more bits to band 0–1, zero out band 3. Target: 96 kbps, still ~35 dB SNR — 7× compression.

docs.title: 5.8 Haar DWT on test signal
docs.text:
Signal: 1024-sample sequence \(x[n] = \sin(2\pi \cdot 0.1 \cdot n) + 0.5 \cdot u[n - 512]\) (step at \(n = 512\)).

Level 1 approximation: captures the smooth part — a downsampled version of the signal (step still present, sinusoid averaged).

Level 1 detail: nearly zero in smooth regions, spike at \(n = 256\) (where the step falls in the level-1 scale) — the details localise the transient.

Level 5 decomposition:

  • Level 5 approximation: 32 samples — captures the slow trend.
  • Levels 1–5 details: isolate features at 5 scales. The step appears in level 1 detail as a single spike; the sinusoid contributes small coefficients spread over levels.

Compression. Keeping only the top 50 coefficients (out of 1024) and zeroing the rest gives SNR ~30 dB — the signal is 20× compressible in the Haar basis.

docs.title: 5.9 Vanishing moments
docs.text:
db4 (4 vanishing moments): DWT of \(x[n] = n^2\) for \(n = 0, \dots, N-1\).

Detail coefficients: all \(\approx 0\) (up to numerical precision). The quadratic signal is captured entirely by the approximation coefficients — because db4 has 4 vanishing moments, hence zero inner product with polynomials of degree < 4.

db2 (2 vanishing moments): DWT of \(n^2\) gives nonzero details — db2 only annihilates linear signals, not quadratics.

Implication. Choose the wavelet's vanishing moments to match the smoothness of your signal. For piecewise-linear signals, db2 suffices; for quadratic, db4; for cubic, db6.

docs.title: 5.10 Wavelet denoising
docs.text:
Signal: smooth chirp + white noise (SNR = 5 dB).

Method SNR improvement Noisy input 5 dB Lowpass filter (order 30) 8 dB Haar DWT + hard threshold (\(3\sigma\)) 12 dB db4 DWT + hard threshold (\(3\sigma\)) 18 dB

db4 is much better because it captures the smooth structure of the chirp with few coefficients, so the thresholded reconstruction is cleaner. The lowpass filter attenuates the chirp's high-frequency portion along with the noise — the wavelet preserves it (the chirp is smooth in every scale).

Rule of thumb. For denoising signals with localised features (edges, transients), wavelets beat Fourier. For stationary signals, both work but wavelets are usually simpler to tune.

docs.title: 5.11 JPEG 2000 preview
docs.text:
Cameraman image (512×512), 2-D DWT (Haar vs. db4), uniform quantisation.

Compression ratio Haar PSNR db4 PSNR 5:1 38 dB 40 dB 10:1 32 dB 36 dB 20:1 27 dB 33 dB 50:1 22 dB 28 dB

db4 gives 5–6 dB better PSNR at high compression ratios — the vanishing moments give a sparser representation of natural images (which are piecewise-smooth).

JPEG (block DCT) at same ratios: typically 2–4 dB worse than JPEG 2000 (db4), plus block artifacts at high compression. The DWT avoids blocking by spreading the transform across the whole image.

docs.title: 5.12 Real-world 44.1 → 48 kHz conversion
docs.text:
File: 10 s of music at 44.1 kHz.

Method Time (Python) Quality (listen) Linear interpolation 0.1 s Audible artifacts scipy.signal.resample_poly 2.5 s Transparent Polyphase + 200-tap filter 2.2 s Transparent Multistage (2 stages) 1.4 s Transparent

Multistage is 1.8× faster than single-stage polyphase at the same quality. The linear interpolation fails at high frequencies — audible "ghosting" and high-frequency distortion.

For production: use libsamplerate, SoX, or a hardware ASRC chip — all implement multistage polyphase with Kaiser-windowed sinc filters.

docs.title: ECEG-6423 — Multimedia Signal Processing

MSc in Communication Engineering · Year 1, Semester II · Elective II

This is the course website for Multimedia Signal Processing — the second course in the DSP track. It extends the statistical and multirate tools of ECEG-6303 into the three pillars of multimedia: images, speech, and video.

📖 Part of the MSc DSP track

Companion course: ECEG-6303 — Advanced DSP. Both share the DSP Primer and software setup.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this course you should be able to:

  1. Digitize images, speech, and video — model the human visual and auditory systems, apply sampling and quantization, understand colour spaces.
  2. Carry out image transforms — DFT, DCT, DST, Walsh–Hadamard, Haar, Slant, Karhunen–Loève, and SVD — and choose between them for compression, enhancement, and analysis.
  3. Enhance and restore images — point operations, histogram equalization, spatial filtering, edge enhancement, inverse and Wiener restoration, constrained least-squares.
  4. Compress images — predictive coding, transform coding, vector quantization, block truncation, wavelet coding, colour coding; understand JPEG and JPEG 2000.
  5. Process speech — time-domain and frequency-domain short-time analysis, pitch estimation, formant extraction, cepstral analysis, LPC.
  6. Recognize and synthesize speech — dynamic time warping, hidden Markov models, text-to-speech, speaker verification.
  7. Process video — sampling and rate conversion, 2D and 3D motion estimation, video coding, compression standards (H.264, HEVC), error control, streaming.

docs.title: Section A — Image Fundamentals
docs.text:
A1. (b) 0.83 — \(C_M = (120-20)/(120+20) = 100/140 \approx 0.714\), wait: 100/140 = 0.714. Hmm, let me recompute: (120-20)/(120+20) = 100/140 = 0.714. Option (a) is 0.71. So A1 = (a) 0.71.

A2. (b) 4–8 cycles/degree.

A3. (c) \(1/(2\Delta x)\).

A4. 2-D sampling theorem: a band-limited image with spectrum zero outside \([-F_x, F_x] \times [-F_y, F_y]\) can be exactly reconstructed from samples on a lattice with spacing \(\Delta x, \Delta y\) iff \(1/\Delta x > 2F_x\) and \(1/\Delta y > 2F_y\). Equivalently, sampling frequencies exceed twice the highest spatial frequencies in both directions.

A5. Two reasons: (i) YCbCr separates luminance (perceptually important, high spatial resolution) from chroma (perceptually less important, can be subsampled); (ii) human vision has much lower spatial resolution for chroma than for luminance, so 4:2:0 subsampling (halving chroma resolution in both directions) reduces data by 50% with almost no perceptual loss.

A6. For uniform quantizer with step \(\Delta = 2A/L\), the error \(e = Q(f) - f\) is approximately uniform on \([-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]\) if the signal is dense within each bin. Variance: \(\sigma_e^2 = \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2\, de = \Delta^2/12\). If signal has variance \(\sigma_f^2\) and peak-to-RMS ratio \(A/\sigma_f\), then \(L = A/(\sqrt{12}\sigma_e)\), so \(\text{SNR} = \sigma_f^2/\sigma_e^2 = 12 \sigma_f^2/\Delta^2 = \frac{L^2\sigma_f^2}{A^2} \cdot 3 = 3\cdot L^2/(A^2/\sigma_f^2)\). In dB: \(\text{SNR}_{dB} \approx 6 b + 4.77 - 20\log_{10}(A/\sigma_f)\) where \(b\) = bit depth.

A7. Kronecker product \(A \otimes B\) is the block matrix with blocks \(a_{ij} B\); result size \(mp \times nq\) for \(A\) \(m \times n\) and \(B\) \(p \times q\). Vec identity: \(\text{vec}(AXB) = (B^\top \otimes A)\text{vec}(X)\). Useful because it converts 2-D operations into 1-D matrix-vector products, enabling fast algorithms (separable filtering, 2-D FFT) and analysis (eigenvalues of \(A \otimes B\) are products).

A8. Without dither: false contours (visible stair-step bands) at quantization boundaries. Adding dither converts the structured quantization error into random noise that the eye averages out — perceptually smoother even though numerical MSE is higher.

docs.title: Section B — Image Processing Techniques
docs.text:
B1. (b) Real coefficients and better energy compaction.

B2. (b) Data-dependent (basis depends on the covariance, must be transmitted).

B3. Median filtering: an isolated outlier (salt or pepper pixel) is not the median of its neighborhood, so it is removed. Mean filtering: the outlier contaminates all pixels in the neighborhood (spreads the noise). Median preserves edges (median of a step neighborhood lies on the step); mean blurs edges. Median is preferred for salt-and-pepper; mean is preferred for Gaussian noise.

B4. Continuous: input \(r\) has PDF \(p_r(r)\) and CDF \(C(r) = \int_0^r p_r(s)ds\). Output \(s = (L-1)C(r)\). Then \(p_s(s) = p_r(r)/|ds/dr| = p_r(r)/((L-1)p_r(r)) = 1/(L-1)\) on \([0, L-1]\) — uniform. Discrete version uses empirical CDF, giving approximate uniformity.

B5. Wiener derivation: minimize \(\mathbb E[|F - W G|^2]\) over linear filters \(W\) where \(G = HF + N\). Optimal \(W = \mathbb E[FG^*]/\mathbb E[|G|^2] = H^* S_f/(|H|^2 S_f + S_ u)\). Assumptions: (i) \(f, u\) zero-mean, uncorrelated; (ii) \(S_f, S_ u\) known; (iii) LSI filter; (iv) linear minimum-MSE criterion.

B6. JPEG pipeline: (1) split into 8×8 blocks; (2) RGB→YCbCr, subsample chroma 4:2:0; (3) 8×8 DCT per block; (4) quantize with a table scaled by quality factor; (5) zigzag scan; (6) Huffman entropy coding; (7) (decoder side) inverse steps. Three redundancies exploited: coding (Huffman), interpixel (DCT), psychovisual (quantization table).

B7. Radon transform: \(R( ho, heta) = \int\int f(x,y)\delta(x\cos heta + y\sin heta - ho)dxdy\) — line integrals at angle \( heta\). Fourier slice theorem: \(\widehat R(\omega, heta) = F(\omega\cos heta, \omega\sin heta)\) — 1-D FT of projection = 2-D FT of \(f\) along the slice. FBP: (i) FT each projection; (ii) multiply by ramp \(|\omega|\); (iii) IFT; (iv) back-project over all angles. The ramp corrects the \(1/r\) blur of plain back-projection.

docs.title: Section C — Speech Fundamentals
docs.text:
C1. (c) 150–250 Hz.

C2. Four subsystems: lungs (power source — airflow), larynx / vocal folds (source — quasi-periodic pulse train for voiced, noise for unvoiced), vocal tract (filter — formants from acoustic resonances), articulators (tongue, lips, velum — configure the tract shape). Together they produce a source-filter cascade that generates the speech waveform.

C3. The speech spectrum is \(|X(f)| = |G(f)| \cdot |H(f)|\) — glottal source times vocal-tract filter. Whispered speech: the source is non-periodic (vocal folds open), so pitch is absent. But the vocal tract is unchanged, so the formants are identical to normal speech — the filter alone carries the linguistic information. This is why whispered speech is fully intelligible.

docs.title: Section D — Speech Methods
docs.text:
D1. (b) Lower than 0.15.

D2. Trade-off: longer window → better frequency resolution, worse time resolution (Heisenberg: \(\Delta t \cdot \Delta f \ge 1/(4\pi)\)). Narrowband (40 ms): resolves pitch harmonics and shows them as fine horizontal bands; good for pitch/formant analysis. Wideband (10 ms): resolves pitch pulses as vertical stripes; good for voicing and timing analysis.

D3. LPC model: \(x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^p a_k x[n-k] + e[n]\). Minimize \(\mathbb E[e[n]^2]\): \(\partial/\partial a_k = 2\sum e[n]x[n-k] = 0\). Substituting \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum_l a_l x[n-l]\): \(\sum_l a_l R[k-l] = -R[k]\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, p\). Matrix: \(\mathbf R\mathbf a = -\mathbf r\) with \(\mathbf R\) Toeplitz.

D4. Cepstrum: \(c[n] = \text{IFFT}\{\log|X[k]|\}\). In log-spectrum, source (pitch) and filter (formants) are additive. In cepstral domain, they occupy different quefrency ranges — filter (smooth envelope) at low quefrency near 0; pitch (harmonic comb) at high quefrency at \(n = T_0\) (pitch period in samples). Pitch at high quefrency because the IFFT of a comb with spacing \(F_0\) is a peak at period \(T_0\).

D5. Levinson–Durbin: recursion from order \(m-1\) to \(m\): \(k_m = -(R[m] + \sum_{i=1}^{m-1}a_i^{(m-1)}R[m-i])/\sigma_{m-1}^2\); \(a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m a_{m-i}^{(m-1)}\); \(\sigma_m^2 = (1 - k_m^2)\sigma_{m-1}^2\). Reflection coefficients: \(k_m\) = partial autocorrelation at lag \(m\) — correlation between \(x[n]\) and \(x[n-m]\) after removing intermediate lags. \(|k_m| < 1\) is the necessary and sufficient condition for AR stability.

D6. Autocorrelation: cheap, works for most; prone to octave errors. Cepstrum: robust to formants, handles weak fundamentals; requires long frames. LPC residual (SIFT): best accuracy — the LPC filter whitens residual, leaving a sharp pitch peak. SIFT for coding; cepstrum for analysis; ACF for embedded/cheap.

docs.title: Section E — Speech Applications
docs.text:
E1. (a) Evaluation, decoding, training.

E2. \(\hat W = \arg\max_W \Pr(W \mid X) \propto \arg\max_W \Pr(X \mid W)\Pr(W)\). Acoustic model: \(\Pr(X \mid W)\) — likelihood of audio given word sequence. Language model: \(\Pr(W)\) — prior probability of word sequence. Useful: enables independent training on different data (acoustic on transcribed speech, language on large text corpora), and lets context resolve acoustic ambiguity.

E3. DTW: optimal monotone path aligning two sequences. Recursion: \(C(i,j) = d(x_i, y_j) + \min(C(i-1,j), C(i,j-1), C(i-1,j-1))\). Sakoe–Chiba band restricts path to within \(r\) of the diagonal — reduces cost from \(O(MN)\) to \(O(Mr)\), regularizes to prevent pathological warping.

E4. Verification: 1:1 — "Is this the claimed speaker?" (authentication). Identification: 1:N — "Which enrolled speaker is this?" (forensics, personalization). Features: MFCCs, x-vectors, pitch statistics, speaking rate, idiolect.

docs.title: Section F — Video Processing
docs.text:
F1. (b) \(f_s\) below 2× the wheel's rotation frequency.

F2. \(I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0\) from brightness constancy + first-order Taylor. Aperture: one equation, two unknowns — motion underdetermined. LK solution: assume constant \(u, v\) over a window, giving \(N\) equations, then least-squares: \(\mathbf u = (A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\mathbf b\). Aperture resolved by having enough independent constraints in the window; fails at flat regions (both \(I_x, I_y\) small).

F3. Pipeline: I/P/B classification → motion estimation → motion-compensated prediction → residual → DCT → quantize → entropy-code. Motion-compensated prediction: removes temporal redundancy — the residual (aligned difference between current and predicted frame) is much sparser than the frame itself, and the DCT compacts it further. This is the main source of compression in inter-frame coding.

F4. Efficiency (typical 1080p at PSNR 35 dB): H.264 = 6 Mbps, HEVC = 3.8 Mbps (−38%), AV1 = 3.4 Mbps (−43%). For 4K streaming: HEVC if HEVC hardware decode is universal on the target devices (most modern TVs, phones, browsers); AV1 if compression is more important than decode compatibility (Netflix, YouTube use AV1; older devices need fallback). Recommendation: AV1 with H.264 fallback for maximum efficiency; HEVC only if you need universal hardware decode without fallback.

docs.title: Grading rubric (for instructors)
docs.text:
Band Mark Criteria A 90–100 All questions correct or with minor arithmetic slips; derivations rigorous; interpretation insightful B 75–89 Most questions correct; occasional conceptual gaps; derivations mostly sound C 60–74 Basic understanding demonstrated; some errors in derivations or interpretation F < 60 Significant conceptual gaps; major derivations missing or wrong

Point allocations:

  • MCQs: all-or-nothing.
  • Short answers: partial credit for correct key steps.
  • Derivations: partial credit per correct line.

Common errors to watch for (and their marks):

  • Confusing necessary and sufficient conditions (deduct 1–2).
  • Wrong sign in a Lagrange/KKT multiplier (deduct 1).
  • Missing or incorrect assumption in a derivation (deduct 1–2).
  • Numerical error in a final answer without correct method (deduct 2–3).
  • Correct answer with no working (deduct full marks).
  • Copying a formula without stating when it applies (deduct 1–2).

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
On successful completion, students will be able to:

  • Digitize images, speech, and video signals.
  • Carry out image transforms.
  • Restore images.
  • Compress and reconstruct images.
  • Process and apply speech signals using different analysis techniques and algorithms.
  • Process and apply video signals using various analysis techniques.

docs.title: Competences
docs.text: The student will understand and apply how images are processed and reconstructed, how speech signals are analyzed and processed, and how video signals are analyzed and processed.

docs.title: Chapter summaries
docs.text:
Ch 1 — Continuous and Discrete Images and Systems. Light, luminance, brightness, contrast; the eye and monochrome vision model; image processing problems and applications; the vision camera and digital processing system; 2-D sampling theory and aliasing; image quantization (Lloyd–Max, dither); color images; linear systems and shift invariance; Fourier transform, Z-transform; matrix theory results; block matrices and Kronecker products.

Ch 2 — Image Processing Techniques. Image transforms (2-D orthogonal and unitary, DFT, DCT, DST, Walsh–Hadamard, Haar, Slant, KL, SVD). Image enhancement (point ops, histogram, spatial filtering, edge enhancement, colour enhancement). Image restoration (observation models, sources of degradation, inverse and Wiener, geometric mean filter, nonlinear filters, smoothing splines, constrained least squares). Image compression and reconstruction from projections (image data rates, pixel coding, predictive and transform coding, BTC, wavelet coding, colour image coding, Radon transform, back-projection, algebraic restoration).

Ch 3 — Introduction to Digital Speech Processing. Digital speech processing, transmission and storage, synthesis, speaker verification, speech recognition, production mechanism, classification of sounds, models of production.

Ch 4 — Time and Frequency Domain Speech Processing. Short-time analysis; time-domain parameters (energy, magnitude, ZCR, ACF, pitch by parallel processing); frequency-domain (STFT, filter bank, spectrogram, formant extraction, pitch extraction, analysis–synthesis); homomorphic analysis and LPC of speech.

Ch 5 — Applications of Speech Processing. Speech recognition — specification of a typical application, voice response systems, spectral estimation, dynamic time warping, HMM. Speech synthesis — text-to-speech, VoIP. Speaker verification and identification.

Ch 6 — Digital Video Processing. Video representation and modelling; video sampling and rate conversion; 2-D and 3-D motion estimation; video coding; compression standards; error control; streaming video.
