docs.text:
• Jain, Fundamentals of Digital Image Processing, PHI, 1995 — Chapters 5–7 cover enhancement, restoration, and compression.
  • Gonzalez & Woods, Digital Image Processing, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018 — Chapters 3–6 and 10 for the full classical treatment.
  • Pratt, Digital Image Processing, 4th ed., Wiley, 2007 — the encyclopedic reference.
  • Rao & Yip, The Transform and Data Compression Handbook, CRC Press, 2001 — DCT, KLT, and other transforms in depth.
  • Ahmed, Natarajan & Rao, "Discrete Cosine Transform", IEEE Trans. Computers, 1974 — the original DCT paper.
  • Oppenheim & Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, PHI — for the transform theory.
  • Lim, Two-Dimensional Signal and Image Processing, Prentice-Hall, 1990 — comprehensive 2-D transform and filter theory.
  • Jain, "Image data compression: A review", Proc. IEEE, 1981 — the classical survey.
  • Clarke, Transform Coding of Images, Academic Press, 1985 — detailed DCT analysis.
  • Wallace, "The JPEG Still Picture Compression Standard", Commun. ACM, 1991 — the definitive JPEG reference.
  • Taubman & Marcellin, JPEG 2000: Image Compression Fundamentals, Standards and Practice, Springer, 2002 — the definitive JPEG 2000 book.
  • Tour of Filtered Back-Projection: Kak & Slaney, Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging, IEEE Press, 1988 (available free online).
  • Natterer, The Mathematics of Computerized Tomography, Wiley, 2001 — rigorous FBP theory.
  • Buades, Coll & Morel, "A Non-Local Algorithm for Image Denoising", CVPR 2005 — the non-local means paper.
  • Dabov et al., "Image Denoising by Sparse 3D Transform-Domain Collaborative Filtering", IEEE TIP, 2007 — the BM3D paper.
  • SciPy, scikit-image, OpenCV, PyWavelets documentation.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. DCT energy compaction. Apply the 2-D DCT to a natural image (or Lena). Sort the coefficients by magnitude. What fraction of the total energy is in the top 1%, 5%, 10% of coefficients? Repeat for the DFT — quantify the difference.

  2. JPEG simulation. Implement the JPEG pipeline (DCT, quantization, entropy coding) for a single grayscale image. Compare compression ratios and PSNR at quality levels 10, 50, 90. Visualise the blocking artifacts at low quality.

  3. KL vs. DCT. Compute the KLT of a small correlated image block, truncate to \(M\) components, and reconstruct. Do the same with the DCT. At what \(M\) does each reach 30 dB PSNR?

  4. Histogram equalization. Implement histogram equalization and histogram specification from scratch. Apply to a dark image and to an overexposed image. Compare with cv2.equalizeHist.

  5. Median vs. bilateral denoising. Add salt-and-pepper and Gaussian noise to a natural image. Compare median, bilateral, and non-local means for both noise types. Which is best for which?

  6. Wiener filter with unknown noise. Blur a clean image with a Gaussian PSF (σ = 2). Add white Gaussian noise. Apply inverse filtering, Wiener filtering, and CLS. Compare PSNR. Tune the regularisation parameter.

  7. Predictive coding. Implement DPCM with 1-D, 2-D, and 3-tap predictors on a grayscale image. Compute the entropy of the residuals for each. Plot the rate-distortion curve.

  8. BTC implementation. Implement BTC with block sizes 4×4 and 8×8, with quantized mean/std to 4/6/8 bits. Compare compression ratio and PSNR to JPEG at the same rate.

  9. Wavelet denoising. Take a noisy image, apply a 5-level DWT (db4), hard- or soft-threshold the detail coefficients at \(3\sigma\), and reconstruct. Compare PSNR to the Wiener filter.

  10. Radon transform. Implement the Radon transform of a small binary shape (e.g., a disc, a rectangle). Visualise the sinogram. Reconstruct via unfiltered back-projection and filtered back-projection. Compare the two reconstructions — the blur of unfiltered BP should be visible.

  11. FBP on a Shepp–Logan phantom. Reconstruct the Shepp–Logan phantom (standard test image for CT) from projections at 90°, 180°, and 360°. Compare quality at each. Demonstrate the failure of FBP with too few angles.

  12. Art with noisy projections. Add 1% Gaussian noise to the projections of a Shepp–Logan phantom. Compare FBP reconstruction vs. iterative reconstruction (ART or SIRT, 50 iterations). Report PSNR and visual quality.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Introduction to Digital Speech Processing and Recognition
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 2 tutorial + 1 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): digital speech processing · digital transmission and storage of speech · speech synthesis · speaker verification and identification · speech recognition and aids to the handicapped · speech production mechanism · classification of speech sounds · nature of the speech signal · models of speech production.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Describe the speech production mechanism: lungs, larynx, vocal tract, nasal cavity, articulators, and the acoustic consequences of each.
  2. Classify speech sounds as vowels, diphthongs, and consonants; distinguish voiced from unvoiced sounds; place consonants by place and manner of articulation.
  3. Analyse the speech waveform, spectrum, and spectrogram. Identify formants, pitch, and the voiced/unvoiced distinction.
  4. State the source-filter model of speech production and explain how it underlies LPC (linear predictive coding) and formant synthesis.
  5. Compute key speech parameters: fundamental frequency, pitch period, formant frequencies, short-time energy, zero-crossing rate, and speech bandwidth.
  6. Describe the data rates of raw and compressed speech, and compute storage and transmission requirements.
  7. State the four main applications: transmission/storage, synthesis, recognition, speaker verification/ID — and the technology behind each.
  8. Describe aids to the handicapped based on speech processing (reading machines, prostheses, hearing aids).
  9. Implement basic speech analysis in Python, Java, and C#.

docs.title: 3.1 What is speech?
docs.text:
Speech is the acoustic signal produced by the human vocal apparatus to communicate linguistic information. It is:

  • Acoustic — a pressure wave in air, measurable with a microphone.
  • Time-varying — the signal changes continuously as the speaker articulates.
  • Non-stationary — its statistical properties change over tens of milliseconds.
  • Quasi-stationary — over short intervals (~10–30 ms), it can be approximated as stationary, which is the foundation of short-time analysis.

Speech vs. audio. Speech is human-produced, has linguistic structure (phonemes, words, sentences), and occupies a specific bandwidth (50 Hz – 8 kHz for most of its energy). Audio is a broader category (music, environmental sounds) that shares signal-processing tools but differs in statistics and perception.

Language vs. speaker. A speech signal carries two layers of information:

  • Linguistic — what is being said (words, phonemes). Speaker-independent.
  • Paralinguistic / speaker-specific — who is saying it (identity, emotion, age, gender, health). Speaker-specific.

This two-layer structure is why the same signal supports both speech recognition (extract the words) and speaker recognition (extract the identity) — the two tasks are theoretically separate even though they operate on the same waveform.

docs.title: 3.2 The speech production mechanism
docs.text: Speech is produced by the coordinated action of four subsystems, from the bottom up:

docs.title: 3.2.1 The lungs (power source)
docs.text:
The lungs provide the airflow that drives speech. During speech, we exhale steadily for several seconds; the airflow is regulated by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. The result is a quasi-steady volume velocity of air through the vocal tract — typically 100–300 cm³/s during normal phonation.

Without airflow, no speech. Whispering produces speech with airflow but without vocal-fold vibration; normal speech uses both.

docs.title: 3.2.2 The larynx and vocal folds (sound source)
docs.text:
The larynx houses the vocal folds (formerly "vocal cords"), two elastic membranes that can be:

  • Open (abducted) — air flows freely → unvoiced sounds (/s/, /f/, /p/, /t/, /k/).
  • Vibrating (adducted, with tension) — air flows through in puffs → voiced sounds (/a/, /z/, /b/, /d/, /g/, and all vowels).

The phonation mechanism. When the vocal folds are closed and pressure builds up beneath them, they are pushed open; the airflow then reduces the pressure (Bernoulli effect), pulling them back together; the cycle repeats. The result is a quasi-periodic pulse train of air puffs at the fundamental frequency \(F_0\).

Fundamental frequency. The rate of vocal-fold vibration:

Speaker Typical \(F_0\) Pitch period \(T_0 = 1/F_0\) Adult male 80–150 Hz 6.7–12.5 ms Adult female 150–250 Hz 4–6.7 ms Child 200–400 Hz 2.5–5 ms

\(F_0\) is what we perceive as pitch. The harmonics at \(k F_0\) (\(k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)) are what give voiced speech its rich spectral structure.

The glottal pulse. Each cycle of vocal-fold vibration produces a glottal pulse — a brief, asymmetric wave with a fundamental period \(T_0\) and a broadband harmonic spectrum. The glottal pulse is the excitation of the speech signal.

docs.title: 3.2.3 The vocal tract (filter)
docs.text:
Above the larynx, the vocal tract — the pharynx (throat), oral cavity (mouth), and nasal cavity (nose) — acts as an acoustic filter that shapes the glottal pulse into recognizable speech sounds.

The vocal tract as an acoustic tube. Approximate dimensions of an adult male:

  • Length: ~17 cm (a quarter-wavelength resonator → first resonance at \(c/(4L) \approx 340/(4 \cdot 0.17) \approx 500\) Hz).
  • Cross-section: varies from 0 to ~5 cm² along its length, controlled by the tongue, jaw, lips, and velum.
  • Speed of sound in warm, humid air: \(c \approx 350\) m/s.

Formants. The resonances of the vocal-tract tube are called formants \(F_1, F_2, F_3, \ldots\). They appear as peaks in the spectrum of voiced speech.

Vowel \(F_1\) (Hz) \(F_2\) (Hz) \(F_3\) (Hz) /i/ (beat) 270 2290 3010 /ɪ/ (bit) 390 1990 2550 /ɛ/ (bet) 530 1840 2480 /æ/ (bat) 660 1720 2410 /a/ (father) 730 1090 2440 /ɔ/ (bought) 570 840 2410 /ʊ/ (book) 440 1020 2240 /u/ (boot) 300 870 2240

(Typical adult male values, varies by speaker and dialect.)

The first two formants carry most vowel identity. In the \((F_1, F_2)\) plane, vowels form a "vowel quadrilateral" — the classic vowel chart (IPA) is directly the image of the vowel space in the \((F_1, F_2)\) coordinates.

docs.title: 3.2.4 The articulators
docs.text:
The articulators shape the vocal tract:

  • Tongue — the most important articulator. Its body (front/back) controls the low formants; its tip/blade controls high formants and constrictions for consonants.
  • Lips — opening (rounded) or closing.
  • Velum (soft palate) — closes the nasal cavity (oral sounds) or opens it (nasal sounds like /m/, /n/).
  • Jaw — gross up/down movement affecting the vocal-tract length.
  • Pharynx — constriction affects the higher formants.
  • Epiglottis — protects the airway during swallowing.

The configuration of the articulators at any instant determines the shape of the vocal tract, which determines the formants, which determines the sound. Speech is the continuous trajectory of that configuration over time.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — acoustic tube resonances
docs.text:
Model the vocal tract as a uniform tube of length \(L = 17\) cm, closed at the glottis and open at the lips.

Boundary conditions. Closed at one end, open at the other — the quarter-wave resonator.

Resonant frequencies.

\[ f_n = \frac{(2n - 1)\, c}{4 L},\qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \]

With \(c = 350\) m/s, \(L = 0.17\) m:

\[ f_1 = \frac{350}{4 \cdot 0.17} \approx 515\ \text{Hz}, $$ $$ f_2 = \frac{3 \cdot 350}{4 \cdot 0.17} \approx 1544\ \text{Hz}, $$ $$ f_3 = \frac{5 \cdot 350}{4 \cdot 0.17} \approx 2574\ \text{Hz}. \]

These are in the right range for a neutral vowel (schwa, /ə/), which is produced with a uniform tract — the vowels /i/, /u/, /a/ all deviate from this by articulator movement.

Speaker variation. A female with \(L = 14\) cm has formants ~20% higher; a child with \(L = 10\) cm has formants ~70% higher. This is why men's and women's vowel spectra look "shifted" — the same articulatory configuration gives different formant frequencies. Recognizing vowels speaker-independently is one of the hard problems of speech recognition (solved by vocal-tract-length normalization).

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — pitch period from a waveform
docs.text:
A voiced speech signal has an obvious periodic structure. Count the cycles in a 100 ms window: if there are 12 cycles, then

\[ F_0 = \frac{12}{0.1\ \text{s}} = 120\ \text{Hz},\qquad T_0 = \frac{1}{F_0} = 8.33\ \text{ms}. \]

The pitch period \(T_0\) is visible as the spacing between successive large peaks in the waveform; \(F_0\) is its reciprocal.

At a sampling rate \(f_s = 16\) kHz, the pitch period is

\[ T_0 \cdot f_s = \frac{8.33\ \text{ms}}{62.5\ \mu\text{s}} \approx 133\ \text{samples}. \]

So pitch detection in the digital domain looks for peaks separated by ~130 samples in this case. This is the time-domain pitch estimation covered in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 3.3 Classification of speech sounds
docs.text: Speech is a sequence of phones — minimal sound units. Each phone belongs to one of three broad classes:

docs.title: 3.3.1 Vowels
docs.text:
Vowels are the "open" sounds: the vocal tract is unobstructed, airflow is laminar, and the sound is always voiced. The vowel's identity is determined by the articulatory configuration, which determines the formants \(F_1, F_2, F_3\).

Classical articulatory description.

  • Tongue height (high / mid / low) ↔ \(F_1\) (low \(F_1\) = high vowel).
  • Tongue backness (front / central / back) ↔ \(F_2\) (high \(F_2\) = front vowel).
  • Rounding (rounded / unrounded) ↔ \(F_3\) (lowers \(F_3\) for rounded).

In English, the ~12 monophthongs occupy the vowel quadrilateral: /i, ɪ, ɛ, æ, a, ɔ, ʊ, u, ʌ, ə, ɜ, ɑ/.

Diphthongs are vowels whose formants glide from one vowel target to another within a syllable: /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /ɔɪ/, /eɪ/, /oʊ/. Their spectral trajectory is what distinguishes them from the monophthongs.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Consonants
docs.text:
Consonants involve a constriction or closure of the vocal tract. They are classified by three attributes:

1. Voicing. Voiced (vocal folds vibrate) vs. unvoiced (no vibration).

2. Place of articulation. Where the constriction occurs:

Place Articulators Examples Bilabial Upper and lower lips /p/, /b/, /m/ Labiodental Lower lip + upper teeth /f/, /v/ Dental Tongue tip + teeth /θ/, /ð/ Alveolar Tongue tip + alveolar ridge /t/, /d/, /n/, /s/, /z/, /l/, /r/ Postalveolar Tongue blade + hard palate /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/ Palatal Tongue body + hard palate /j/ Velar Tongue back + soft palate /k/, /g/, /ŋ/ Glottal Vocal folds /h/, /ʔ/

3. Manner of articulation. How the airflow is modified:

Manner Description Examples Plosives (stops) Complete closure → sudden release (burst) /p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /k/, /g/ Fricatives Narrow constriction → turbulent noise /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/ Affricates Closure + slow release /tʃ/, /dʒ/ Nasals Full oral closure + open nasal cavity /m/, /n/, /ŋ/ Liquids (approximants) Partial closure, resonant /l/, /r/ Glides (semivowels) Transitional, like vowels /w/, /j/

docs.title: 3.3.3 Summary table
docs.text: Sound class Voiced? Constriction? Pitch present? Waveform look Vowels Yes No (open) Yes Periodic, high energy Diphthongs Yes Transitional Yes Periodic, gliding Liquids, glides Yes Partial Yes Periodic, formant-like Nasals Yes Full oral + open nasal Yes Periodic, damped Voiced fricatives Yes Narrow Yes + turbulent noise Periodic + noise Unvoiced fricatives No Narrow No Noise Voiced plosives Yes (closure + burst) Full → burst Brief Silent closure, then burst, then periodic Unvoiced plosives No Full → burst No Silent closure, then burst

docs.title: Worked example 3.3 — voiced/unvoiced decision from the signal
docs.text:
We observe two 20 ms speech frames:

Frame A: periodic peaks every ~8 ms, high amplitude, smooth spectral envelope with peaks around 700 Hz and 1200 Hz.

Frame B: noisy, no periodic structure, low amplitude, broadband spectrum with energy concentrated at 4–8 kHz.

Classification:

  • Frame A: voiced — periodic (vocal-fold vibration), low formants (vowel or liquid), high energy. Likely a vowel.
  • Frame B: unvoiced — aperiodic (turbulent noise), high frequencies (fricative). Likely a fricative like /s/ or /ʃ/.

Quantitative features (Chapter 4):

  • Short-time energy — high for voiced, low for unvoiced fricatives.
  • Zero-crossing rate (ZCR) — low for voiced (smooth), high for unvoiced (rapid sign changes).
  • Autocorrelation peak — high at \(k = T_0\) for voiced, near zero for unvoiced.

These three features together give reliable voiced/unvoiced decisions — the front end of every speech recognition system.

docs.title: 3.4 The nature of the speech signal
3.4.1 Time-domain view
docs.text:
The speech waveform \(x(t)\) (or \(x[n]\)) has very different characteristics depending on the phone:

  • Voiced speech: quasi-periodic, with period \(T_0 = 1/F_0\); slow envelope modulation (vocal-tract filter shaping the harmonics).
  • Unvoiced speech: noise-like, aperiodic, low energy (except for fricatives, which are moderate).
  • Silence: near zero (with background noise).
  • Plosives: brief silence followed by a burst (impulse-like).

The waveform is not directly interpretable for linguists — this is why the spectrum and spectrogram are more useful.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Frequency domain
docs.text:
The spectrum of a short-time speech frame (typically 10–30 ms) shows:

  • Harmonics at \(k F_0\) (from the glottal pulse) — visible as a comb of peaks.
  • Formants — the envelope of the harmonic peaks, with resonances at \(F_1, F_2, F_3\), etc.
  • High-frequency roll-off — the glottal spectrum falls at ~-12 dB/octave.

A typical vowel spectrum shows the harmonics (spaced \(F_0\) apart) modulated by the formant envelope (broad peaks at \(F_1, F_2, F_3\)). The formants determine the vowel identity; the harmonic spacing determines the pitch.

docs.title: 3.4.3 The spectrogram
docs.text:
The spectrogram is the time-frequency representation of speech — the most important visualization in speech processing. It is computed by short-time Fourier analysis (Chapter 4 §4.4) — window the signal into short frames, compute the spectrum of each, display as an image (time on x-axis, frequency on y-axis, magnitude as colour).

Reading a spectrogram:

Visible feature Interpretation Horizontal bands (dark) Formants — vowel identity Vertical striations Pitch periods — voiced speech Broad diffuse energy at high frequency Fricatives (/s/, /ʃ/) Short vertical spike Plosive burst Dark region near 500 Hz + harmonics Nasal (extra formant at low frequency) Blank regions Silence or very low energy

The spectrogram is the phonetician's primary tool — trained phoneticians can read the phoneme sequence from a spectrogram, though not perfectly.

docs.title: 3.4.4 Speech bandwidth and sampling
docs.text:
Where is speech's energy?

Band Content Contribution 50–300 Hz Fundamental frequency, low harmonics Pitch, voicing 300–1000 Hz First formant \(F_1\) Vowel height 1000–3000 Hz Second formant \(F_2\), most consonant info Vowel backness, consonant place 3000–8000 Hz Third formant \(F_3\), fricatives, plosive bursts Fine consonant detail 8000–20000 Hz Airborne noise, negligible speech info Sparsely used

Speech bandwidths:

  • Narrowband telephony: 300–3400 Hz (8 kHz sampling). Intelligible but "telephone-like" — sounds like a phone call. What the PSTN uses.
  • Wideband / HD voice: 50–7000 Hz (16 kHz sampling). Noticeably clearer; standard in VoLTE, VoIP, and modern codecs.
  • Super-wideband: 50–14000 Hz (32 kHz sampling). Used in some conferencing systems.
  • Full-band: 20–20000 Hz (44.1 or 48 kHz sampling). Studio quality.

Nyquist sampling. To capture up to \(W\) Hz of speech, we need \(f_s > 2W\):

Speech bandwidth Required sampling rate 3.4 kHz (narrowband) 8 kHz (standard telephony) 7 kHz (wideband) 16 kHz 14 kHz (super-wideband) 32 kHz 20 kHz (full-band) 44.1 or 48 kHz

The 8 kHz rate for telephony is the historical legacy: 4 kHz is about the bandwidth needed for intelligible speech; 8 kHz satisfies Nyquist; it's been the standard since the 1960s and is still used in every mobile phone call.

docs.title: Worked example 3.4 — speech data rates
docs.text:
Raw PCM, narrowband telephony.

  • Sampling rate: 8 kHz
  • Bit depth: 8 bits (μ-law compressed) or 16 bits (linear)
  • Bitrate: \(8000 \times 8 = 64\) kbps (μ-law), \(8000 \times 16 = 128\) kbps (linear PCM).

Raw PCM, wideband.

  • Sampling: 16 kHz
  • Bit depth: 16 bits
  • Bitrate: \(16000 \times 16 = 256\) kbps.

CD-quality audio.

  • Sampling: 44.1 kHz, 16 bits, stereo
  • Bitrate: \(44100 \times 16 \times 2 = 1411\) kbps.

Compressed speech codecs:

Codec Rate Speech quality G.711 (μ-law PCM) 64 kbps Toll quality G.726 (ADPCM) 32 kbps Toll quality G.729 (CS-ACELP) 8 kbps Toll quality AMR-NB 4.75–12.2 kbps Mobile quality AMR-WB 6.6–23.85 kbps HD voice Opus 6–510 kbps Adjustable LPC-10 2.4 kbps Military / very low rate MELPe 600 bps Military / very low rate

Storage example. One hour of speech:

Codec Bitrate Storage for 1 hour G.711 64 kbps 28.8 MB G.729 8 kbps 3.6 MB AMR-WB 12.2 kbps 5.5 MB LPC-10 2.4 kbps 1.08 MB

The compression from G.711 (28.8 MB) to LPC-10 (1.08 MB) is ~27:1 — and the speech is still intelligible (though somewhat robotic). This is the headline of speech coding.

docs.title: 3.5.1 The source-filter model
docs.text:
The most influential model of speech production, introduced by Fant (1960):

Source-filter model

Speech is modelled as a glottal source filtered by the vocal tract:

\[ X(f) = G(f)\, H(f), \]

where:

  • \(G(f)\) = spectrum of the glottal pulse (source) — broadband, with harmonic structure at \(F_0\).
  • \(H(f)\) = transfer function of the vocal tract (filter) — all-pole, with resonances at the formants.

Consequences.

  • The source determines pitch (harmonics at \(F_0\)) and voicing (periodic vs. noise).
  • The filter determines the formants — the vowel identity, consonant place of articulation.
  • Source and filter are independent — you can whisper at the same pitch (source off, filter on) or speak the same vowel at different pitches (source changes, filter stable). This is why whispering is intelligible.

docs.title: 3.5.2 The LPC model
docs.text:
The linear predictive coding (LPC) model is a parametric realization of the source-filter model. It assumes:

  • Filter: an all-pole (AR) filter of order \(p\) (typically \(p = 10\) for 8 kHz speech, \(p = 16\)–\(20\) for 16 kHz). $$ H(z) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k z^{-k}} $$
  • Source: either a pulse train at pitch \(F_0\) (voiced) or a white noise generator (unvoiced).

The LPC coefficients \(a_k\) are estimated by Levinson–Durbin (Chapter 2 of ECEG-6303) from the autocorrelation of short-time frames. The prediction error \(e[n]\) is the residual — the driving source, which is close to the glottal pulse train (voiced) or white noise (unvoiced).

Why LPC matters.

  • Compact: \(p = 10\) coefficients + \(F_0\) + gain + voicing ≈ 40–50 bits per 20 ms frame, giving 2.4 kbps.
  • Fast: Levinson–Durbin is \(O(p^2)\).
  • Interpretable: the LPC coefficients are the AR parameters of the vocal tract; the LPC spectrum approximates the spectral envelope (formants).
  • The basis of every modern speech codec — CELP, AMR, Opus, G.729.

docs.title: Worked example 3.5 — LPC spectrum
docs.text:
An LPC model of order \(p = 2\) for a vowel has coefficients \(a_1 = -1.5\), \(a_2 = 0.7\), gain \(G = 1\).

Filter. \(H(z) = 1/(1 - 1.5z^{-1} + 0.7z^{-2})\).

Frequency response. The denominator roots:

\[ 1 - 1.5 z^{-1} + 0.7 z^{-2} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; z^2 - 1.5 z + 0.7 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; z = 0.75 \pm j 0.37. \]

\(|z| = \sqrt{0.75^2 + 0.37^2} \approx 0.837\), angle \(\theta = \arctan(0.37/0.75) \approx 0.457\) rad.

Resonant frequency. \(f = \theta/(2\pi) \cdot f_s\). At \(f_s = 8\) kHz:

\[ f \approx \frac{0.457}{2\pi} \cdot 8000 \approx 582\ \text{Hz}. \]

Bandwidth. Related to the pole radius: \(\text{BW} \approx (-\ln|z|) \cdot f_s/\pi \approx 0.178 \cdot 8000/\pi \approx 453\) Hz.

So this 2-pole model has a resonance at ~580 Hz with ~450 Hz bandwidth — a single formant. A real vowel needs \(p = 10\) (5 formants × 2 poles each), giving peaks at \(F_1, F_2, F_3, F_4, F_5\).

LPC spectrum. \(|H(e^{j\omega})|^2\) peaks at the resonance frequencies — so plotting \(1/|A(e^{j\omega})|^2\) gives the spectral envelope, from which the formants can be read directly.

docs.title: 3.5.3 The articulatory model
docs.text:
A more detailed model that simulates the physical vocal tract: a cascade of acoustic tubes whose cross-sectional areas vary along the tract. The Kelly–Lochbaum model (1962) is the classic digital-tube model.

Structure. The tract is divided into \(N\) short sections, each a two-way delay line (forward and backward acoustic waves). The vocal-tract shape is parameterized by the areas \(A_1, \ldots, A_N\); changing these parameters changes the formants — exactly like moving the articulators.

Advantages. Physically meaningful — the parameters are articulatory (tongue position, lip rounding) rather than acoustic (LPC coefficients).

Disadvantages. More parameters (one per section), harder to estimate from speech, computationally more expensive.

Modern use. Articulatory synthesis is used in research on speech production, speech therapy (visual feedback of tongue position), and animation (talking heads). Production TTS uses LPC or unit selection, not articulatory synthesis.

docs.title: 3.5.4 Comparison of models
docs.text:
Model Parameters Complexity Estimation Use Source-filter \(F_0\) + formants Low Manual or from spectrum Speech analysis, synthesis LPC \(p\) AR coefficients + \(F_0\) + gain + voicing Medium Levinson–Durbin Standard in codecs and recognition Articulatory Section areas (5–20) + source High Not typically estimated Research, animation

The LPC model is the sweet spot: compact enough for low-bit-rate coding, physical enough to interpret, and mathematically tractable (Yule–Walker / Levinson).

docs.title: 3.6.1 From analogue to digital
docs.text:
Speech is a continuous-time analogue signal; digital processing requires:

  1. Anti-alias filter — analog lowpass at \(f_s/2\) (e.g., 4 kHz for 8 kHz sampling) to prevent aliasing.
  2. Sampling at \(f_s\) (e.g., 8 kHz narrowband, 16 kHz wideband).
  3. Quantization to \(b\) bits per sample (16-bit linear is standard for processing; 8-bit μ-law is standard for telephony).
  4. Encoding (μ-law, A-law, or linear PCM) for storage / transmission.

μ-law and A-law compression. Human hearing is logarithmic — the perceptual difference between quiet sounds is much smaller than the perceptual difference between loud sounds. μ-law / A-law compress the dynamic range by 8-bit logarithmic quantization, giving quality comparable to 12-bit linear — at half the bit rate of 16-bit linear.

The standard telephone bitstream is 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kbps μ-law PCM, known as G.711. It is the foundation of the entire PSTN.

docs.title: 3.6.2 The processing pipeline
docs.text:
Typical digital speech processing pipeline:

  1. Pre-emphasis — a first-order highpass \(H(z) = 1 - \alpha z^{-1}\) with \(\alpha \approx 0.95\), compensating the glottal roll-off (-6 dB/octave) and flattening the spectrum for analysis.
  2. Framing — divide the signal into short overlapping frames (20–30 ms, 50% overlap).
  3. Windowing — apply Hamming or Hann window to each frame.
  4. Feature extraction — compute the features for the task (LPC, MFCC, pitch, energy, ZCR).
  5. Decision / modelling — classification, coding, synthesis.

docs.title: 3.6.3 Pre-emphasis and framing
docs.text:
Why pre-emphasis? The glottal spectrum falls at ~-12 dB/octave. Without compensation, the analysis emphasises low frequencies where the energy is concentrated, and high-frequency formants (like \(F_3\) and \(F_4\)) become hard to resolve. The pre-emphasis filter \(1 - 0.95z^{-1}\) inverts the slope, flattening the spectrum.

Why framing? Speech is quasi-stationary: over ~20 ms, the vocal-tract configuration is approximately constant, so the signal's statistical properties are stationary. Framing lets us apply stationary tools (Fourier, autocorrelation, LPC) to each frame independently.

Why windowing? A rectangular window has a poor sidelobe response (~-13 dB first sidelobe), causing spectral leakage — energy from one frequency bin "leaks" into neighbours. The Hamming window has -43 dB sidelobes, the Hann window -31 dB — better for analysis.

docs.title: Worked example 3.6 — framing and overlap
docs.text:
Speech sampled at \(f_s = 16\) kHz. Frame size \(N = 400\) samples (25 ms); overlap \(= 50\%\) (200 samples).

  • Number of frames per second: \(16000 / (400 - 200) = 80\) frames/s.
  • Frame rate: 80 Hz.
  • For a 3-second utterance: 240 frames.
  • Number of features per second (if each frame has 12 LPC coefficients): \(80 \times 12 = 960\) LPC coefficients/s.

This is the standard feature rate for speech analysis — the "resolution" of any time-varying speech model.

docs.title: 3.6.4 Speech coding (compression)
docs.text:
The problem. Raw speech at 64 kbps (G.711) is too much for mobile networks, satellite links, and archival storage. Compression trades fidelity for bits.

Classification of codecs.

Type Approach Bit rate Quality Waveform Direct time-domain quantization (PCM, DPCM, ADPCM) 64–32 kbps Excellent Parametric Model-based (LPC, vocoder) 2.4–4.8 kbps Fair-robotic Hybrid Waveform + model (CELP family) 4.8–24 kbps Toll quality

The waveform / parametric trade-off. Waveform codecs preserve the exact waveform → high fidelity but high bit rate. Parametric codecs preserve only the perceptual properties (formants, pitch) → low bit rate but lose individual voice details (the famous "vocoder" sound). Hybrid codecs combine both — a linear prediction model (LPC) for the formants, plus a codebook-excited residual for detail (CELP).

Standard codecs:

Standard Technique Rate G.711 (μ-law PCM) Waveform 64 kbps G.726 (ADPCM) Waveform 32 kbps G.728 (LD-CELP) Hybrid 16 kbps G.729 (CS-ACELP) Hybrid 8 kbps AMR-NB ACELP 4.75–12.2 kbps AMR-WB ACELP 6.6–23.85 kbps Opus CELP + LPC (hybrid) 6–510 kbps LPC-10 Parametric (US DoD) 2.4 kbps

Modern mobile phone calls use AMR-NB or AMR-WB (or EVS for the newest VoLTE systems), typically at 12.2–24 kbps. The PSTN at the other end uses G.711 at 64 kbps — the two are transcoded at the network boundary.

docs.title: 3.7 Applications of speech processing
docs.text: Speech processing has four major application families:

docs.title: 3.7.1 Digital transmission and storage
docs.text:
Transmission. Every phone call, VoIP session, and video conference carries compressed speech. The main challenges:

  • Bandwidth efficiency — compress to fit the channel (typically 4.8–24 kbps for mobile).
  • Robustness to errors — channel errors must not destroy the speech (error concealment, FEC, retransmission).
  • Latency — real-time constraints (typically < 200 ms end-to-end).
  • Jitter — variable network delay must be buffered (de-jitter buffer).

Storage. Voicemail, podcasts, call archives, audiobooks, digital assistants (Siri, Alexa) — all store compressed speech.

docs.title: 3.7.2 Speech synthesis (text-to-speech)
docs.text:
Speech synthesis converts text to spoken audio. Three generations:

Concatenative synthesis — splice pre-recorded speech units (phones, diphones, syllables) from a recorded corpus. High naturalness but large storage.

Parametric synthesis — generate speech from a model (LPC or vocoder) with text-derived parameters. Low storage but "robotic". The famous DECtalk used this approach.

Neural synthesis (modern) — TTS systems based on deep neural networks (WaveNet, Tacotron, Transformer-TTS). Naturalness nearly indistinguishable from human speech. Current systems include Google's WaveNet / Tacotron, Amazon Polly, Microsoft Azure TTS, OpenAI's Voice Engine.

TTS pipeline.

  1. Text normalization — expand abbreviations, numbers, symbols.
  2. Text-to-phoneme conversion — grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) rules or dictionaries.
  3. Prosody prediction — pitch, duration, stress from syntactic and semantic analysis.
  4. Waveform generation — concatenative or neural.
  5. Post-processing — smoothing, normalisation.

docs.title: 3.7.3 Speech recognition
docs.text:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) converts audio to text. Three generations:

Template matching (1950s–1980s) — store spectral templates of words, match the input to the closest template via dynamic time warping (DTW).

Statistical (1980s–2010s) — model speech units with hidden Markov models (HMM) and Gaussian mixtures. Train on large corpora; use Viterbi decoding. The dominant paradigm for 30 years (Chapter 5 covers HMM in detail).

Neural (2010s–present) — end-to-end deep learning. DeepSpeech, wav2vec, Whisper, and modern commercial systems achieve ~5% word error rate on clean read speech. Modern ASR needs far less handcrafted feature engineering — the neural network learns the features and the acoustic model jointly.

ASR challenges.

  • Speaker variability — pitch, accent, vocal-tract length.
  • Environmental noise — background noise, reverberation.
  • Speaking style — casual, fast, disfluent speech.
  • Vocabulary size — large-vocabulary continuous speech recognition (LVCSR) with 100k+ words.
  • Language model — grammar, semantics, context.

docs.title: 3.7.4 Speaker verification and identification
docs.text:
Speaker recognition identifies the speaker from their voice.

  • Speaker identification — "Which of the enrolled speakers is this?" (1:N classification).
  • Speaker verification — "Is this speaker who they claim to be?" (1:1 verification).
  • Speaker diarization — "Who spoke when?" in a multi-speaker recording.

Features. Speaker identity is encoded in:

  • Spectral envelope (vocal-tract length → formant spacing).
  • Pitch statistics (mean \(F_0\), pitch dynamics).
  • Speaking rate, rhythm, prosody.
  • Pronunciation and idiolect (words chosen, accents).

Classical approach. Gaussian mixture models (GMM) on MFCC features, with universal background models (UBM) for normalisation.

Modern approach. Deep neural networks (d-vectors, x-vectors, ECAPA-TDNN). Very low error rates on standard benchmarks (NIST SRE).

Application. Authentication (banking by phone), forensic identification, access control, personalised assistants (Alexa voice profiles).

docs.title: 3.7.5 Aids to the handicapped
docs.text:
Speech processing supports the disabled through:

Reading machines for the blind — OCR + TTS: scan text, synthesize speech. Classic systems: Kurzweil Reading Machine (1976), modern apps: Voice Dream Reader, Microsoft's Seeing AI.

Hearing aids and cochlear implants — real-time speech enhancement, noise reduction, frequency shaping, binaural processing. Modern hearing aids use machine-learning-based speech enhancement.

Speech-to-text for the deaf — ASR + display; automated captioning (YouTube, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet).

Text-to-speech for the mute — "voice banking" for ALS patients (record phrases while still able, then synthesize); Stephen Hawking's voice (DECtalk).

Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) — apps that let users select words/pictures and synthesize speech, used by non-verbal individuals.

Speech therapy tools — visualization of formants, pitch, loudness for feedback; automated scoring of pronunciation.

Parkinson's / dysarthria aids — speech enhancement, slowed playback, intelligibility-boosting processing.

Speech processing is one of the most impactful areas of DSP for human-centred technology — the technology's value to a blind reader or a hearing-aid user is immediate and dramatic.

docs.title: Worked example 3.7 — reading machine data rate
docs.text:
A blind user wants to listen to a book. The book has 400 pages, ~500 words per page, ~5 characters per word + spaces ≈ 6 chars/word → 2400 chars/page → 960 000 characters total.

TTS output rate: typical English speech is ~150 words/min = 900 chars/min.

Total playback time: \(960000 / 900 \approx 1067\) min ≈ 18 hours.

Storage at different rates:

Codec Bitrate Storage G.711 64 kbps 8.5 MB G.729 8 kbps 1.1 MB LPC-10 2.4 kbps 320 KB Modern neural TTS (on-device) typically 24–48 kbps 3.2–6.4 MB

For real-time playback the storage requirement is modest; the bigger challenge is the TTS model itself (neural TTS models are 20–100 MB, downloaded once).

docs.title: 3.8 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Speech is a non-stationary but quasi-stationary acoustic signal, carrying linguistic and speaker-specific information.
  2. Production mechanism: lungs (power) → larynx/vocal folds (source) → vocal tract (filter) → articulators (shape).
  3. Vocal-fold vibration at \(F_0\) (80–400 Hz) produces voiced speech; vocal-fold opening produces unvoiced speech; the two are the fundamental axis of classification.
  4. Vocal-tract resonances are the formants \(F_1, F_2, F_3, \ldots\) — the primary determinant of vowel identity.
  5. Speech sounds are vowels (open, voiced), diphthongs (gliding vowels), and consonants (constricted; classified by voicing, place, manner).
  6. Spectrogram is the time-frequency representation, the most important visualization of speech; formants, pitch, fricatives, and plosives are all visible.
  7. Speech bandwidth: 300–3400 Hz for telephony (8 kHz sampling); 50–7000 Hz for wideband (16 kHz); 20–20 kHz for full-band.
  8. Source-filter model: speech = glottal source × vocal-tract filter. Explains the independence of pitch (source) and vowel identity (filter).
  9. LPC model: all-pole vocal tract, driven by a pulse train (voiced) or noise (unvoiced); \(p \approx 10\) coefficients capture the spectral envelope; estimated via Levinson–Durbin.
  10. Data rates: raw PCM 64–256 kbps; compressed 2.4–24 kbps. Speech coding is what makes mobile telephony and VoIP possible.
  11. Four applications: transmission/storage, synthesis (TTS), recognition (ASR), speaker ID. Modern systems use neural networks for all four.
  12. Aids to the handicapped — reading machines, hearing aids, cochlear implants, captioning, augmentative communication, voice banking.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. Voiced speech is produced by: (a) turbulence at a constriction (b) vocal-fold vibration (c) plosive release (d) nasal resonance

  2. The fundamental frequency \(F_0\) for an adult male is typically: (a) 20–50 Hz (b) 80–150 Hz (c) 300–800 Hz (d) 2–5 kHz

  3. Formants are: (a) harmonics of \(F_0\) (b) vocal-tract resonances (c) glottal pulses (d) consonant bursts

  4. The first formant \(F_1\) of a high vowel like /i/ is: (a) high (b) low (c) zero (d) equal to \(F_2\)

  5. Which consonant type is always unvoiced? (a) vowel (b) nasal (c) voiceless fricative (d) liquid

  6. The source-filter model states that: (a) speech = source + filter (b) speech = source × filter (c) speech = source - filter (d) speech = filter / source

  7. In the LPC model, the vocal tract is modelled as: (a) an FIR filter (b) an all-pole filter (c) a comb filter (d) a linear-phase filter

  8. Narrowband telephony uses a sampling rate of: (a) 4 kHz (b) 8 kHz (c) 16 kHz (d) 44.1 kHz

  9. G.711 compresses speech at: (a) 2.4 kbps (b) 8 kbps (c) 64 kbps (d) 128 kbps

  10. The spectrogram shows: (a) time only (b) frequency only (c) time-frequency magnitude (d) phase only

  11. Speaker verification is a: (a) 1:N classification (b) 1:1 verification (c) N:N comparison (d) N:1 synthesis

  12. The source-filter model implies that pitch and vowel identity are: (a) the same thing (b) independent (c) inversely proportional (d) uncorrelated with the signal

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. The four subsystems of speech production are lungs, larynx, vocal tract, and ____.
  2. The vocal-fold vibration rate is the ____ frequency \(F_0\).
  3. The vocal-tract resonances are called ____.
  4. The first two formants \(F_1, F_2\) determine vowel ____.
  5. Consonants are classified by voicing, place, and ____ of articulation.
  6. The spectrogram shows ____, ____, and ____ of the speech.
  7. Speech telephony uses sampling at ____ kHz to cover 300–3400 Hz.
  8. The source-filter model expresses the speech spectrum as $G(f) \cdot $____.
  9. LPC stands for ________ coding.
  10. G.729 compresses speech to ____ kbps.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Describe the speech production mechanism in one paragraph. Name the four subsystems and their acoustic roles.
  2. Classify vowels and consonants. For consonants, name the three articulatory dimensions and give two examples of each.
  3. Draw (or describe) the spectrogram of a spoken word. What features correspond to formants, pitch, fricatives, plosives?
  4. Explain the source-filter model. Why does it explain the intelligibility of whispered speech?
  5. Derive the acoustic tube resonances for a uniform vocal tract of length \(L = 17\) cm closed at the glottis and open at the lips. What are the first three resonances?
  6. Define LPC and explain its relation to the source-filter model. What does "prediction error" correspond to physically?
  7. Compute the data rate of raw 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz sampling. Compare with G.711, G.729, and Opus at 12 kbps. Discuss the trade-off.
  8. List the four main applications of speech processing and give one concrete example of each.
  9. Describe aids to the handicapped based on speech processing. Name three specific technologies and their users.
  10. Compare speaker verification and speaker identification. What are the main features used for each?

docs.title: 3.10 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — vocal-fold vibration.
  2. (b) — 80–150 Hz.
  3. (b) — vocal-tract resonances.
  4. (b) — low (high vowel = low \(F_1\)).
  5. (c) — voiceless fricative (and voiceless plosives).
  6. (b) — speech = source × filter (multiplicative).
  7. (b) — all-pole (AR) filter.
  8. (b) — 8 kHz.
  9. (c) — 64 kbps.
  10. (c) — time-frequency magnitude.
  11. (b) — 1:1 verification.
  12. (b) — independent.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. articulators (or nasal cavity)
  2. fundamental
  3. formants
  4. identity
  5. manner
  6. time; frequency; magnitude
  7. 8
  8. \(H(f)\)
  9. linear predictive
  10. 8
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Production mechanism: air from the lungs drives the larynx, where the vocal folds either vibrate (voiced) or remain open (unvoiced). The airflow is filtered by the vocal tract — the pharynx, oral cavity, and nasal cavity — which resonantly shapes the spectrum according to the configuration of the articulators (tongue, lips, velum, jaw). The result is a speech waveform whose harmonic structure (source) is modulated by formant resonances (filter). The four subsystems: lungs (power), larynx (source), vocal tract (filter), articulators (shape control).
  2. Vowels: open, voiced, no constriction; identity determined by the formants \(F_1, F_2\) (related to tongue height and backness). Consonants: constricted or closed vocal tract. Three dimensions: (i) voicing — voiced vs. unvoiced (e.g., /b/ vs. /p/); (ii) place — bilabial, alveolar, velar, etc. (e.g., /p/ bilabial, /t/ alveolar, /k/ velar); (iii) manner — plosive, fricative, nasal, liquid, glide (e.g., /p/ plosive, /s/ fricative, /m/ nasal).
  3. Spectrogram of "banana" /bəˈnænə/: (i) silent closure for /b/ — blank; (ii) burst and short silence; (iii) formant bands for /ə/ — horizontal dark bands around 500 and 1500 Hz; (iv) /n/ — formant bands shifted slightly, with a nasal murmur in the low frequency; (v) /æ/ — formants at ~660 and ~1720 Hz; (vi) /n/ again; (vii) /ə/ again. Formants: horizontal dark bands. Pitch: vertical striations within voiced segments. Fricatives: diffuse broadband energy at high frequency. Plosives: brief vertical spike at release.
  4. Source-filter model: the speech spectrum is the product of the glottal source spectrum (harmonic at \(F_0\), with -12 dB/octave roll-off) and the vocal-tract filter spectrum (all-pole, with formant resonances). Whispered speech: the source is not periodic (vocal folds open) so no pitch, but the filter (vocal tract shape) is unchanged — the formants are the same, so vowel identity is preserved. The speech is intelligible because the filter carries the linguistic information; the source only carries pitch and voicing, which are prosodic not lexical.
  5. Tube resonances: for a tube of length \(L\), closed at one end and open at the other, the resonant wavelengths are \(\lambda_n = 4L/(2n-1)\) → frequencies \(f_n = (2n-1) c/(4L)\). With \(c = 350\) m/s, \(L = 0.17\) m: \(f_1 \approx 515\) Hz, \(f_2 \approx 1544\) Hz, \(f_3 \approx 2574\) Hz. Interpretation: these are the formants of a neutral vowel (schwa, /ə/) — the uniform tract produces equally spaced formants. Vowels like /i/ and /u/ arise from deviating the tract from this uniform shape.
  6. LPC: linear predictive coding models each speech sample as a linear combination of \(p\) previous samples plus a prediction error: \(x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^p a_k x[n-k] + e[n]\). The coefficients \(a_k\) are estimated to minimise the prediction-error energy (Yule–Walker equations, Levinson–Durbin). Source-filter relation: the AR filter \(1/A(z)\) models the vocal tract; the prediction error \(e[n]\) models the glottal source — it is close to a pulse train for voiced speech, or white noise for unvoiced. So LPC decomposes the speech into filter (vocal tract) and source (glottal pulse train) — a parametric realization of the source-filter model.
  7. Raw PCM: 16 kHz × 16 bit = 256 kbps. G.711: 8 kHz × 8 bit (μ-law) = 64 kbps — a 4:1 reduction with minor quality loss. G.729: 8 kbps — a 32:1 reduction from 256 kbps; toll quality (fine for voice but loses some nuance). Opus at 12 kbps: similar quality to G.729 with more modern features (variable rate, FEC, stereo). Trade-off: lower bit rate → more compression → more modelling assumptions → more fragile to non-speech sounds, accents, noise. Below ~2.4 kbps, only parametric vocoders work, and they sound robotic. Above ~16 kbps, waveform codecs give near-transparent quality. The "knee" of the trade-off is ~8–12 kbps.
  8. Applications: (i) Transmission / storage — compressed speech in every phone call, VoIP, audiobook, and podcast. (ii) Speech synthesis (TTS) — text-to-speech for virtual assistants (Siri, Alexa), screen readers, audiobook generation. (iii) Speech recognition (ASR) — dictation, automated captioning, voice search, virtual assistants. (iv) Speaker recognition — voice authentication in banking, forensic identification, personalised experiences. (Also: aids to the handicapped, which are applications of (ii) and (iii) with a social focus.)
  9. Aids: (i) Reading machines (OCR + TTS) — blind users; Kurzweil Reading Machine and modern apps (Seeing AI, Voice Dream Reader). (ii) Hearing aids and cochlear implants — hard-of-hearing users; real-time speech enhancement, noise reduction, frequency shaping. (iii) Captioning / speech-to-text — deaf users; automated captioning on YouTube, Teams, Zoom. (Additional: augmentative and alternative communication for non-verbal users; speech therapy visualisation tools; voice banking for ALS patients — Stephen Hawking's DECtalk voice.)
  10. Verification vs. identification: (i) Verification — "Is this speaker who they claim to be?" 1:1 comparison with a claimed identity. Used for authentication (banking by phone, access control). (ii) Identification — "Which enrolled speaker is this?" 1:N classification. Used for forensics, personalised assistants, speaker diarization. Features: for both, the key features are MFCC (mel-frequency cepstral coefficients) or x-vectors — short-time spectral envelopes that capture speaker-specific vocal-tract characteristics. Additional: \(F_0\) statistics (mean and range of pitch), speaking rate, prosody, pronunciation idiosyncrasies. Modern systems use deep networks trained on speaker classification (x-vectors, ECAPA-TDNN) for state-of-the-art accuracy.

docs.text:
• Rabiner & Schafer, Digital Processing of Speech Signals, Prentice Hall, 1978 — the classical textbook; Chapters 1–3 cover everything in this chapter in more depth.
  • O'Shaughnessy, Speech Communications: Human and Machine, 2nd ed., IEEE Press, 2000 — excellent on speech production and perception.
  • Deller, Proakis & Hansen, Discrete-Time Processing of Speech Signals, IEEE Press, 2000 — the standard graduate reference.
  • Quatieri, Discrete-Time Speech Signal Processing, Prentice Hall, 2001 — exceptional on source-filter and homomorphic methods.
  • Flanagan, Speech Analysis Synthesis and Perception, 2nd ed., Springer, 1972 — the classic physical-acoustics reference.
  • Fant, Acoustic Theory of Speech Production, Mouton, 1960 — the original source-filter model paper.
  • Stevens, Acoustic Phonetics, MIT Press, 1998 — the definitive reference on the acoustic phonetics of English.
  • Ladefoged, A Course in Phonetics, 7th ed., Cengage, 2014 — the standard introduction to phonetics.
  • Huang, Acero & Hon, Spoken Language Processing, Prentice Hall, 2001 — modern comprehensive reference, covers all four applications.
  • Rabiner & Juang, Fundamentals of Speech Recognition, Prentice Hall, 1993 — the HMM reference (Chapter 5).
  • Taylor, Text-to-Speech Synthesis, Cambridge University Press, 2009 — the standard TTS reference.
