  • Gold & Morgan, Speech and Audio Signal Processing, Wiley, 2000 — the general signal-processing reference.
  • librosa (Python audio), python_speech_features (MFCC), kaldi (ASR), HTK (ASR), Praat (phonetic analysis), MATLAB Audio Toolbox.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Pitch period measurement. Record yourself saying a sustained /a/ for 3 seconds. Count the peaks in a 100 ms window. Compute \(F_0\). Compare with a pitch tracker (e.g., librosa.pyin).

  2. Formant estimation. Record a vowel (/i/, /u/, /a/, /e/) and plot its spectrum. Identify \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) from the peaks in the spectral envelope. Plot your vowels on an \((F_1, F_2)\) chart — do they cluster the way the standard vowel quadrilateral predicts?

  3. Voiced/unvoiced classification. Implement a simple voiced/unvoiced decision based on short-time energy and zero-crossing rate. Test on a recording containing vowels and fricatives (/s/, /ʃ/). Report classification accuracy.

  4. Acoustic tube model. Write a Python script that simulates the vocal tract as a lossless acoustic tube (Kelly–Lochbaum) with variable cross-sectional areas. Generate vowels by moving the "tongue" position (vary the area function). Confirm the formants shift the way the vowel chart predicts.

  5. LPC analysis. Fit an LPC model of order \(p = 10\) to a vowel frame. Plot the LPC spectrum overlaid on the DFT spectrum. Verify that the LPC peaks align with the formants.

  6. Pre-emphasis. Apply the pre-emphasis filter \(1 - 0.95 z^{-1}\) to a speech signal. Plot the spectra before and after. What is the effect on the harmonic envelope and formant visibility?

  7. Framing and windowing. Implement framing (25 ms, 50% overlap) and Hamming windowing. Plot the sequence of frames as a spectrogram. Verify that with no windowing, the spectrogram shows visible discontinuities.

  8. Data rate calculation. A 1-minute telephone call, a 30-minute podcast, and a 90-minute audiobook — compute the storage required at G.711, G.729, and Opus (12 kbps). Which would be acceptable for a mobile download? For a music album?

  9. Speech bandwidth. Downsample a 16 kHz speech recording to 8 kHz (with anti-alias filtering) and then to 4 kHz (the latter without anti-aliasing, to demonstrate aliasing). Compare the three versions: which is intelligible? Which has audible aliasing artifacts?

  10. Speaker features. Compute \(F_0\) statistics, MFCC, and speaking rate for two speakers (e.g., yourself and a friend) saying the same sentence. Which features are most discriminative? Would a GMM on MFCC features separate them?

  11. Codec comparison. Record the same sentence, encode it with G.711, G.729 (or use ffmpeg with libopencore_amrnb for AMR-NB), and Opus at equivalent rates. Compare the audio quality — which sounds most natural? Which has the most artifacts?

  12. Reading machine simulation. Take a text passage, run it through a TTS engine (e.g., pyttsx3 or Google's TTS API), and measure the output rate (words per second). Compare with human reading speed (~150 words/min) — how much faster is TTS? Does intelligibility suffer at higher speeds?

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Time and Frequency Domain Speech Processing Methods
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 2 tutorial + 1 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): significance of short-time analysis · time-domain parameters (energy, magnitude, zero-crossing rate, autocorrelation function, pitch estimation by parallel processing) · frequency-domain methods (short-time Fourier analysis, filter bank analysis, spectrographic analysis, formant extraction, pitch extraction, analysis–synthesis systems) · homomorphic analysis and LPC of speech (cepstral analysis, formant and pitch estimation, formulation of linear prediction problem in time domain).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain why speech must be analyzed in short frames and derive the windowing / framing scheme for the standard frame rate (50–100 frames/s).
  2. Compute the short-time energy, magnitude, zero-crossing rate, and autocorrelation function; use them for voiced/unvoiced detection, endpoint detection, and pitch estimation.
  3. Derive and compute the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and the short-time autocorrelation; interpret the STFT as a filter bank with narrowband and wideband trade-offs.
  4. Read and interpret a spectrogram — formants, pitch, fricatives, plosives.
  5. Design a filter-bank front end (uniform or mel-spaced) and compute the sub-band energies.
  6. Extract formants by peak picking or LPC root finding; estimate pitch from the autocorrelation, cepstrum, and harmonic product spectrum.
  7. Describe a channel vocoder (analysis–synthesis system) and implement one.
  8. Derive the real cepstrum and use it to separate pitch (low-quefrency) from formants (high-quefrency) in speech.
  9. Formulate the linear prediction (LPC) problem in the time domain, derive the Yule–Walker equations, and solve them by Levinson–Durbin in \(O(p^2)\).
  10. Extract formants and pitch from LPC coefficients.
  11. Implement all of the above in Python, Java, and C#.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Why frame-based?
docs.text:
Speech is non-stationary — its statistics change continuously as the articulators move. But over a short window, it is quasi-stationary:

Window length Assumption Trade-off < 5 ms One pitch period Too short for reliable spectrum 10–30 ms Quasi-stationary Standard choice > 50 ms Two-three pitch periods Smears transitions between phonemes

The rule of thumb. Use a window of 20–30 ms (e.g., 256 or 400 samples at 16 kHz). This covers 2–3 pitch periods for a typical male voice (\(F_0 = 100\) Hz, \(T_0 = 10\) ms) and 4–8 periods for a female voice (\(F_0 = 200\) Hz, \(T_0 = 5\) ms). Long enough for a stable spectrum, short enough to freeze the articulators.

Overlap. Advance the frame by half its length (50% overlap). This gives a frame rate of \(f_s / (N/2)\) — typically 50–100 frames/s. Successive frames share half their samples, which: - Smooths transitions — the feature stream is continuous. - Reduces quantization artifacts — the vocoder reconstruction has fewer frame-boundary glitches. - Matches perception — the ear integrates over ~20 ms.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Framing and windowing
docs.text:
Framing — split the signal into short segments. With frame length \(N\) and hop size \(H\) (usually \(N/2\)), the \(m\)-th frame is

\[ \boxed{\;x_m[n] = x[n + mH],\quad n = 0, \dots, N-1.\;} \]

Windowing — multiply each frame by a smooth window to reduce spectral leakage at the frame boundaries.

\[ \boxed{\;x_w[m, n] = x_m[n]\, w[n],\quad n = 0, \dots, N-1.\;} \]

Common windows.

Window \(w[n]\) Mainlobe width First sidelobe Rectangular \(1\) \(4\pi/N\) \(-13\) dB Hamming \(0.54 - 0.46\cos(2\pi n/(N-1))\) \(8\pi/N\) \(-43\) dB Hann \(0.5 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n/(N-1))\) \(8\pi/N\) \(-31\) dB Blackman \(0.42 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n/(N-1)) + 0.08\cos(4\pi n/(N-1))\) \(12\pi/N\) \(-58\) dB

Which window?

Hamming is the standard for STFT-based analysis and vocoders. It has \(-43\) dB first sidelobe (no visible leakage in most analyses) with mainlobe only 2× wider than rectangular. Hann is also common and slightly better for Welch spectrum estimation. Rectangular is only used when the frame is exactly an integer number of pitch periods (rare).

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — frame count and coverage
docs.text:
Speech sampled at \(f_s = 16\) kHz. Frame \(N = 400\) samples (25 ms), hop \(H = 200\) samples (12.5 ms, 50% overlap).

Frame rate: \(f_s/H = 16000/200 = 80\) frames/s.

Samples per second of speech used (after windowing): \(N \times f_s/H = 400 \times 80 = 32000\) samples — 2× the input samples, because of the 50% overlap.

A 5-second utterance: \(5 \times 80 = 400\) frames.

Total features per second (12 LPC coefficients per frame): \(80 \times 12 = 960\) coefficients/s. At 4 bytes/coefficient = 3.84 kB/s — compact for storage.

docs.title: 4.2 Time-domain parameters
docs.text: Four time-domain parameters are computed directly from the waveform of each frame, without any Fourier transform. They are cheap and useful for voiced/unvoiced detection, endpoint detection, and pitch.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Short-time energy
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;E(m) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_m[n]^2.\;} \]

Interpretation. The energy of frame \(m\) — how loud the signal is in that 20–30 ms window.

Properties.

  • Voiced speech: high energy (especially vowels).
  • Unvoiced fricatives: low-to-moderate energy.
  • Silence: near zero.
  • Plosive bursts: brief energy spikes.

Uses. Endpoint detection (find speech vs. silence), voiced/unvoiced discrimination (with a threshold), gain control, speech enhancement.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Short-time magnitude
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;M(m) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |x_m[n]|.\;} \]

Cheaper than energy (no multiplication). Similar properties. Used in hardware where multiplication cost was significant (historical) or for simplicity.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Short-time zero-crossing rate (ZCR)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;Z(m) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N-1} \bigl|\operatorname{sgn}(x_m[n]) - \operatorname{sgn}(x_m[n-1])\bigr|.\;} \]

Alternatively, the normalized form \(z(m) = Z(m)/N \in [0, 1]\).

Interpretation. The number of times the signal crosses zero per frame (per sample, if normalized). Measures high-frequency content.

Properties.

  • Voiced speech: low ZCR (smooth, periodic — crosses zero at the fundamental).
  • Unvoiced fricatives: high ZCR (noise-like, rapid sign changes).
  • Silence: intermediate (from ambient noise).

Uses. Voiced/unvoiced discrimination, endpoint detection (combined with energy), speech/music discrimination, noise detection.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — energy, magnitude, and ZCR by hand
docs.text:
Frame \(x = (1, -1, 2, -2, -1, 1, 1, -1)\).

Energy. \(1 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 14\).

Magnitude. \(1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10\).

Sign changes. From \(+1\) to \(-1\) (1), \(-1\) to \(+2\) (2), \(+2\) to \(-2\) (3), \(-2\) to \(-1\) (4), \(-1\) to \(+1\) (5), \(+1\) to \(+1\) (no), \(+1\) to \(-1\) (6).

\(Z = \tfrac12 \cdot 6 = 3\); normalized \(z = 3/8 = 0.375\).

Classification guess: energy 14 is moderate, ZCR 0.375 is high → likely voiced fricative or mixed. (A pure vowel would have lower ZCR; a pure silence would have near-zero energy.)

docs.title: 4.2.4 Short-time autocorrelation function
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;R_m[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1-k} x_m[n]\, x_m[n+k],\quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, K.\;} \]

Interpretation. Measure of the correlation between the signal and a shifted version of itself by \(k\) samples. Peaks where the signal is quasi-periodic.

Properties.

  • \(R_m[0] = E(m)\) — the zero-lag autocorrelation is the energy.
  • Voiced speech: strong peak at \(k = T_0\) (the pitch period in samples).
  • Unvoiced speech: no strong peak; autocorrelation decays rapidly.

Uses. Pitch estimation (find the lag of the first major peak, excluding \(k=0\)), voiced/unvoiced discrimination (peak height vs. energy), LPC (the Yule–Walker equations use \(R_X[k]\)).

Computational cost. Naive: \(O(NK)\) per frame. FFT-based: \(O(N \log N)\) for \(R[0]\) through \(R[N-1]\), using the Wiener–Khinchin relation: \(R[k] = \text{IDFT}\{|\text{DFT}\{x\}|^2\}\). For \(N = 400\), \(K = 200\): naive = \(80{,}000\) ops, FFT = \(\sim 4{,}000\) ops — a 20× speedup.

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — autocorrelation for pitch detection
docs.text:
Frame at 16 kHz with true pitch period \(T_0 = 100\) samples (so \(F_0 = 160\) Hz). Compute \(R_m[k]\) for \(k = 0, \ldots, 200\).

The autocorrelation will show: - \(R_m[0]\): maximum (energy). - Local minima near \(k = 50\) (half period). - Local maximum near \(k = 100\) (pitch period) — the key peak. - Another local maximum near \(k = 200\) (two pitch periods) — but a weaker one due to the finite window.

Peak picking algorithm. 1. Compute \(R_m[k]\) for \(k \in [K_{\min}, K_{\max}]\) — typical \(F_0\) range limits: 60–400 Hz → \(K \in [f_s/400, f_s/60] = [40, 267]\) at 16 kHz. 2. Find the maximum in that range. 3. If the peak value exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.3·\(R_m[0]\)), declare voiced with $T_0 = $ argmax; otherwise declare unvoiced.

Peak at \(k = 100\) with \(R_m[100]/R_m[0] \approx 0.85\) → confident voiced pitch at \(F_0 = 16000/100 = 160\) Hz. ✓

Pitfall. Octave errors — the autocorrelation has peaks at \(k = T_0\) and \(k = 2T_0, 3T_0, \ldots\), plus at \(T_0/2\) if the waveform is sub-periodic. Picking the "wrong" peak gives pitch doubling or halving. The parallel processing method of §4.3 addresses this.

docs.title: 4.3.1 The parallel processing method
docs.text:
The parallel processing pitch detector computes the autocorrelation of the frame at multiple downsampled versions and combines the results:

Step 1. Lowpass filter the frame and downsample by a factor \(D_1\); compute the autocorrelation. The peak at \(k = T_0/D_1\) gives a coarse pitch estimate.

Step 2. Upsample the estimate (multiply by \(D_1\)) to get the true lag.

Why? Downsampling reduces the sampling rate → reduces the number of lags to compute → cheaper. The pitch estimate at the coarse rate is refined by combining multiple channels.

The classic Rabiner–Gold algorithm uses a parallel bank of autocorrelators, each operating at a different decimation factor and lag range. By choosing decimations that cover different pitch ranges, the peak at each channel confirms or rejects the pitch candidate from the others — this vote-based approach resolves octave errors.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Other pitch detection methods (brief)
docs.text:
Method Domain Pros Cons Autocorrelation Time Simple, fast Octave errors AMDF (average magnitude difference) Time Simpler than ACF; robust to noise Slight bias Parallel processing Time Resolves octave errors More complex Cepstrum Frequency (via IFFT of log-spectrum) Robust, separates pitch from formants FFT cost YIN Time Excellent accuracy; open-source standard — HPS (harmonic product spectrum) Frequency Simple, robust FFT cost SWIPE Frequency State-of-the-art accuracy Cost

The YIN algorithm (de Cheveigné & Kawahara, 2002) is the modern standard for autocorrelation-based pitch detection — it uses the cumulative mean normalized difference function to avoid octave errors and bias.

docs.title: Worked example 4.4 — parallel processing by two decimators
docs.text:
True \(F_0 = 150\) Hz at \(f_s = 16\) kHz → \(T_0 = 106.7\) samples.

Channel 1 — decimate by \(D_1 = 4\). Downsampled rate \(f_{s1} = 4\) kHz. The pitch period in the downsampled signal is \(T_0/4 \approx 26.7\) samples. The autocorrelation peak is at \(k_1 \approx 27\).

Channel 2 — decimate by \(D_2 = 8\). \(f_{s2} = 2\) kHz. Period \(T_0/8 \approx 13.3\) samples. Peak at \(k_2 \approx 13\).

Consistency check. \(k_1 \cdot D_1 = 27 \cdot 4 = 108\) samples; \(k_2 \cdot D_2 = 13 \cdot 8 = 104\) samples. Both estimate the true period (\(\sim\)107) — the vote confirms the pitch is \(F_0 \approx 16000/106 \approx 151\) Hz. ✓

Octave-error detection. If Channel 1 reports \(k_1 = 13\) (a half-period peak), the estimated pitch would be \(32000/13 \approx 2462\) Hz — way outside the plausible range. The parallel processing detects this by disagreeing with Channel 2; the vote corrects it.

docs.title: 4.3.3 AMDF — Average Magnitude Difference Function
docs.text:
A cheaper alternative to autocorrelation:

\[ \boxed{\;D_m[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1-k} \bigl|x_m[n] - x_m[n+k]\bigr|.\;} \]

Properties.

  • \(D_m[0] = 0\) (trivially — no shift).
  • Minimum at \(k = T_0\) (quasi-periodic).
  • Minimum at \(k = 2T_0, 3T_0, \ldots\).
  • Cheaper than ACF — no multiplications, just subtractions and absolute values.

Detection. Find the first local minimum (after the trivial \(k=0\) minimum) — the argmin over \(k \in [K_{\min}, K_{\max}]\).

docs.title: 4.4.1 Definition
docs.text:
The short-time Fourier transform of a frame \(x_m[n]\) is

\[ \boxed{\;X_m(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_m[n]\, w[n]\, e^{-j\omega n}.\;} \]

In practice, evaluated at the DFT frequencies \(\omega_k = 2\pi k/N\):

\[ \boxed{\;X_m[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_m[n]\, w[n]\, e^{-j2\pi k n / N},\quad k = 0, \dots, N-1.\;} \]

This is the N-point FFT of the windowed frame — one FFT per frame.

Computational cost. \(O(N \log N)\) per frame, \(O(N \log N \cdot f_s / H)\) per second. For \(N = 400\) at \(F_s = 16\) kHz with \(H = 200\): \(80\) frames/s × \(400\log_2 400 \approx 3460\) ops/frame = ~\(277{,}000\) ops/s. Well within real-time on any modern CPU.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Time-frequency resolution trade-off
docs.text:
The window length \(N\) determines the trade-off:

  • Wide window (long \(N\)): high frequency resolution (\(\Delta f = f_s/N\)), low time resolution (windows are long).
  • Narrow window (short \(N\)): high time resolution, low frequency resolution.

This is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle for signals:

\[ \boxed{\;\Delta t \cdot \Delta f \ge \frac{1}{4\pi}\;} \]

where \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta f\) are the standard deviations of the window and its Fourier transform. You cannot have arbitrarily good time AND frequency resolution simultaneously.

In speech processing, the standard choices are:

Window length \(\Delta t\) \(\Delta f\) (at 16 kHz) Purpose 10 ms 10 ms 100 Hz Wideband spectrogram — good time resolution, pitch not visible 25 ms 25 ms 40 Hz Standard STFT frame 40 ms 40 ms 25 Hz Narrowband spectrogram — pitch harmonics visible

These are the two classical spectrogram views, and every speech tool offers both:

  • Narrowband spectrogram: long window (40 ms). Harmonics at \(F_0\) are resolved; formants appear as bands. Used for pitch analysis and formant tracking.
  • Wideband spectrogram: short window (10 ms). Harmonics are NOT resolved; each pitch pulse is a vertical stripe. Used for voicing and timing analysis.

docs.title: Worked example 4.5 — narrowband vs. wideband resolution
docs.text:
Male speech, \(F_0 = 100\) Hz, \(f_s = 16\) kHz.

Narrowband (40 ms = 640 samples): \(\Delta f = 16000/640 = 25\) Hz. Harmonic spacing is 100 Hz — resolved (25 < 100/2). Formants appear as separate bands. Pitch visible as horizontal striations.

Wideband (10 ms = 160 samples): \(\Delta f = 16000/160 = 100\) Hz. Harmonic spacing = 100 Hz — just at the resolution limit, so individual harmonics blur together. Formants still visible. Pitch pulses appear as vertical striations (one per 10 ms pitch period).

Rule of thumb. For pitch analysis, use a window that is at least 2–3 pitch periods long (\(\ge 2T_0\)). For male voices (\(T_0 \approx 10\) ms), that's 20–30 ms — the narrowband setting. For female voices (\(T_0 \approx 5\) ms), 10–15 ms suffices.

docs.title: 4.4.3 The STFT as a filter bank
docs.text:
There is a dual interpretation of the STFT:

Frame interpretation. For each frame, compute the spectrum (standard DFT of a windowed segment).

Filter bank interpretation. For each frequency \(\omega_k\), the STFT \(\{X_m[k]\}_{m}\) is a narrowband signal at frequency \(\omega_k\) — the output of a bandpass filter centered at \(\omega_k\) with bandwidth \(\sim 1/N\). This is exactly a filter bank with \(N\) channels.

The two views are equivalent — a math theorem (the filter-bank summation theorem) states that reconstructing \(x\) from \(X_m[k]\) (summing over \(k\)) is identical to reconstructing from \(x_m[n]\) (overlapping frames).

Practical implication. Speech can be modelled as a sum of narrowband envelopes — each \(\{X_m[k]\}_m\) is a slow-varying (envelope-like) signal at the frame rate. This is why the channel vocoder works (§4.9): it transmits only these slowly-varying envelopes plus a pitch / voicing parameter.

docs.title: 4.5.1 Uniform filter bank
docs.text:
A uniform filter bank splits the spectrum into equal-bandwidth channels. For \(M\) channels, each covers \(\pi/M\) of the frequency axis.

Implementation. Two equivalent options:

  1. FFT-based: compute the N-point FFT of each frame, then sum energy in each channel's frequency bins. Cheapest.
  2. Filter-based: apply \(M\) bandpass FIR filters in the time domain, decimate each to rate \(\pi/M\). Standard for hardware.

Energy in channel \(c\) of frame \(m\):

\[ \boxed{\;E_m(c) = \sum_{k \in \text{channel } c} |X_m[k]|^2.\;} \]

The sequence \(\{E_m(c)\}_m\) is the channel envelope — used directly in vocoders, speech recognition, and speech enhancement.

docs.title: 4.5.2 Mel filter bank
docs.text:
Speech perception is logarithmic in frequency — the ear is much more sensitive to low frequencies than high. The mel scale approximates this:

\[ \boxed{\;f_{\text{mel}} = 2595 \log_{10}\!\left(1 + \frac{f_{\text{Hz}}}{700}\right).\;} \]

A mel filter bank places more filters at low frequencies and fewer at high frequencies. This is the front end of every modern speech-recognition system (MFCC features).

Typical parameters. 20–40 triangular filters covering 0–8000 Hz. Lowest filter covers 0–100 Hz; highest covers 7–8 kHz.

MFCC pipeline.

  1. Frame + window (25 ms Hamming, hop 10 ms).
  2. FFT of each frame.
  3. Mel filter bank — project onto 20–40 triangular filters.
  4. Log — \(L_m(c) = \log E_m(c)\).
  5. Discrete cosine transform — take first 12–13 DCT coefficients. These are the MFCCs.
  6. (Optional) Delta / delta-delta — first and second time derivatives, to capture dynamics.

The DCT decorrelates the log-mel energies and compacts them into a few coefficients — the same energy-compaction principle as image DCT (ECEG-6423 Chapter 2), applied to the mel-spectrum.

docs.title: Worked example 4.6 — Mel filter bank spacing
docs.text:
At \(f_s = 16\) kHz, design a 24-filter mel bank covering 0–8000 Hz.

Mel limits. \(f_{\text{mel}}(0) = 0\); \(f_{\text{mel}}(8000) = 2595 \log_{10}(1 + 8000/700) = 2595 \log_{10}(12.43) \approx 2840\) mels.

Mel step. \(2840/25 \approx 113.6\) mels per filter boundary.

Filter centers in Hz.

Filter Mel \(f\) (Hz) 1 113 ≈ 76 2 227 ≈ 168 5 568 ≈ 500 10 1136 ≈ 1200 15 1704 ≈ 2400 20 2272 ≈ 4200 24 2726 ≈ 7000

Observations. The first 5 filters span 0–500 Hz (a 500 Hz range) — resolution ~100 Hz per filter. The last 5 span 4200–8000 Hz (a 3800 Hz range) — resolution ~760 Hz per filter. The mel scale gives 7–8× more resolution to low frequencies — exactly matching the ear's sensitivity.

The number of filters per octave is roughly constant in the mel domain (~6–10), which is what the perception literature says humans hear.

docs.title: 4.6.1 Definition
docs.text:
The spectrogram is a 2-D visualisation of the STFT:

  • X-axis: time (frames).
  • Y-axis: frequency (FFT bin or Hz).
  • Color / intensity: magnitude (usually in dB), from light (low energy) to dark (high energy).

The short-time magnitude is typically plotted:

\[ S[m, k] = 20 \log_{10}|X_m[k]| + \text{offset (dB)}. \]

Two spectrogram types (from §4.4.2):

Type Window Shows Use Narrowband 40 ms Harmonics, formants as horizontal bands Pitch analysis, formant tracking Wideband 10 ms Pitch pulses as vertical striations, formant transitions Timing, voicing, phonetics

Speech processing tools (Praat, Wavesurfer, MATLAB's spectrogram, Python's matplotlib.specgram) support both. The choice depends on what you want to see.

docs.title: 4.6.2 Reading a spectrogram
docs.text: Visible feature Interpretation Horizontal dark bands Formants — vowel identity Closely spaced parallel stripes (narrowband) Pitch harmonics — voiced Vertical stripes (wideband) Pitch pulses Diffuse high-frequency energy Fricative (/s/, /ʃ/, /f/) Short vertical spike Plosive burst Dark low-frequency band, no high harmonics Nasal Formant transitions Coarticulation between phonemes Silent regions Silence or stop closure

docs.title: Worked example 4.7 — reading a spectrogram by hand
docs.text:
Consider the spectrogram of the word "banana" /bəˈnænə/, wideband (10 ms):

Time Pattern Phone 0–50 ms Blank (silence for closure) /b/ closure 50–60 ms Short vertical burst /b/ release 60–150 ms Two horizontal bands near 500, 1500 Hz /ə/ (schwa) 150–200 ms Bands near 500, 1500 Hz, muted /n/ (nasal — damped) 200–300 ms Bands near 660, 1720 Hz (different) /æ/ 300–350 ms Bands again near 500, 1500 Hz /n/ 350–450 ms Bands near 500, 1500 Hz /ə/

Formant tracks: \(F_1\) moves 500→660→500; \(F_2\) moves 1500→1720→1500. The \(F_1\)–\(F_2\) trajectory is the direct fingerprint of the vowel sequence.

Voicing: vertical striations throughout the voiced segments show pitch pulses at \(F_0 \approx 100\) Hz (visible as ~10 stripes per 100 ms).

Nasals: visible as a reduction in the higher formants and an extra low-frequency resonance (the nasal murmur) around 300 Hz — the /m/, /n/, /ŋ/ signature.

Training note. Phoneticians train for months to read spectrograms reliably. For most signal processing applications, you don't need to read them — you just need to know what features exist so you can design algorithms to extract them.

docs.title: 4.7 Formant extraction
docs.text: Formants are the vocal-tract resonances. Two practical approaches:

docs.title: 4.7.1 Spectral peak picking
docs.text:
The naive method: find local maxima in the smoothed magnitude spectrum.

  1. Compute the spectral envelope (from the LPC spectrum or by lowpass-filtering the DFT magnitude).
  2. Find local maxima above a threshold.
  3. Sort by frequency; keep the first \(K\) (typically 3–5).

Challenges.

  • Pitch harmonics create spurious peaks — smoothing is essential.
  • Closely spaced formants (e.g., \(F_2\) and \(F_3\) close) merge into one peak.
  • Narrow peaks may be missed by smoothing.

docs.title: 4.7.2 LPC root finding
docs.text:
The LPC polynomial

\[ A(z) = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k z^{-k} \]

has \(p\) roots, typically in complex-conjugate pairs. Each pair corresponds to one formant. The formant frequency is the root's angle:

\[ \boxed{\;F_i = \frac{f_s}{2\pi}\,\angle z_i,\quad \text{BW}_i = -\frac{f_s}{\pi}\ln|z_i|.\;} \]

Advantages.

  • Each pole is a formant — no peak picking required.
  • Bandwidth comes out naturally (from the pole radius).
  • \(p = 2K\) gives \(K\) formants — pick \(p = 10\) for 5 formants, \(p = 12\)–\(16\) for 6–8.

Disadvantages.

  • Requires estimating LPC coefficients (solve Yule–Walker).
  • Root-finding is \(O(p^3)\) — moderate for \(p \le 20\).
  • Unstable or spurious roots appear at low energy or during nasal sounds.

Practical. Use LPC roots for the main formants; supplement with spectral peaks when roots are ambiguous.

docs.title: Worked example 4.8 — formant from LPC pole
docs.text:
LPC(2) with \(a_1 = -1.5\), \(a_2 = 0.7\).

Roots. \(z^2 - 1.5z + 0.7 = 0 \Rightarrow z = 0.75 \pm j 0.37\) (from Chapter 3 Example 3.5).

Formant frequency. \(|z| \approx 0.837\), \(\angle z \approx 0.457\) rad.

\[ F = \frac{f_s}{2\pi} \cdot 0.457 \approx \frac{16000}{6.283} \cdot 0.457 \approx 1164\ \text{Hz}. \]

Wait — Chapter 3's example used \(f_s = 8000\): \(F \approx 582\) Hz. With \(f_s = 16\) kHz: \(F \approx 1164\) Hz. So the formant scales with sampling rate — always specify \(f_s\).

Bandwidth. \(\text{BW} = -(f_s/\pi) \ln(0.837) \approx (16000/\pi) \cdot 0.178 \approx 906\) Hz at 16 kHz (≈453 Hz at 8 kHz).

Quality factor. \(Q = F/\text{BW} \approx 1164/906 \approx 1.28\) — a broad, low-Q formant. Higher-\(Q\) formants (narrower bandwidths) come from higher-\(p\) models with poles closer to the unit circle.

For a real vowel (\(p = 10\)), you'd get 5 formants with decreasing bandwidth and increasing frequency. Typical: \(F_1 \approx 500\) Hz (BW 60), \(F_2 \approx 1500\) Hz (BW 80), \(F_3 \approx 2500\) Hz (BW 100), \(F_4 \approx 3500\) Hz (BW 150), \(F_5 \approx 4500\) Hz (BW 200).

docs.title: 4.8.1 Harmonic product spectrum (HPS)
docs.text:
For a voiced frame, the spectrum has peaks at \(F_0, 2F_0, 3F_0, \ldots\). The HPS exploits this by multiplying downsampled versions of the magnitude spectrum:

\[ \boxed{\;P[k] = \prod_{r=1}^{R} |X_r[k]|,\quad X_r[k] = |X[r \cdot k]|.\;} \]

where \(X_r\) is the spectrum decimated by \(r\). Where the true pitch \(F_0\) lies, all harmonics align → the product has a peak. Where a non-harmonic frequency lies, only one or two harmonics contribute → the product is small.

Algorithm.

  1. Compute the FFT of the frame.
  2. Compute the magnitude spectrum \(|X|\).
  3. Form the HPS: \(P = |X| \cdot |X|_{\downarrow 2} \cdot |X|_{\downarrow 3} \cdot \ldots\).
  4. Find the peak of \(P\) within the plausible pitch range (60–400 Hz).
  5. The peak location gives \(F_0\).

Advantages. Simple, cheap (one FFT + \(R\) decimations + \(R\) multiplications).

Disadvantages. Fails for weak fundamental (some speakers); limited by FFT resolution (\(\Delta f = f_s/N\)). For \(N = 400\) at 16 kHz, resolution is 40 Hz — too coarse for 60 Hz pitch. Use longer frames (40+ ms) or interpolation of the peak.

docs.title: 4.8.2 Cepstrum-based pitch
docs.text: See §4.10 — the cepstrum is the standard frequency-domain pitch method.

docs.title: Worked example 4.9 — HPS with 3 factors
docs.text:
Frame has \(F_0 = 200\) Hz, \(f_s = 16\) kHz, \(N = 512\) (FFT resolution 31.25 Hz). Spectrum peaks at bins \(k = 200/31.25 = 6.4\), \(12.8\), \(19.2\), \(25.6\), \(\ldots\) (the true pitch is at bin 6.4 — between bins, so the peak "leaks" to bins 6 and 7).

HPS with \(R = 3\).

At bin \(k = 6\): \(|X[6]| \cdot |X[12]| \cdot |X[18]| \approx\) all moderate (all near the true peak, close to bins 6.4, 12.8, 19.2). \(P[6]\) is high.

At bin \(k = 12\): \(|X[12]| \cdot |X[24]| \cdot |X[36]|\) — first factor matches \(2F_0\), but the others don't align. Product lower.

At bin \(k = 6.5\) (interpolated): all three factors peak → maximum of \(P\).

Interpolation matters. With FFT resolution 31.25 Hz, the peak at 200 Hz is at bin 6.4 — picking bin 6 or 7 gives 187 or 219 Hz, both 6–10% off. Parabolic interpolation of the HPS peak recovers 200 Hz to ~1 Hz accuracy.

docs.title: 4.9.1 The channel vocoder
docs.text:
The channel vocoder (Dudley, 1939) is the first speech analysis–synthesis system. It splits the speech into \(C\) frequency channels, extracts the energy envelope of each, and reconstructs by modulating a noise or pulse-train source with the envelopes.

Analysis.

  1. Filter into \(C\) bandpass channels (typically 16–20, uniform or log-spaced).
  2. Rectify and lowpass each channel → envelope \(E_c(t)\).
  3. Estimate pitch \(F_0\) and voicing (voiced/unvoiced).

Synthesis.

  1. Generate a source: pulse train at \(F_0\) (voiced) or white noise (unvoiced).
  2. Modulate each channel's envelope \(E_c\) by the source filtered through the corresponding bandpass filter.
  3. Sum the channels.

Output. A speech signal whose envelopes match the original but whose fine structure is regenerated from the source model — hence "vocoder" (voice coder).

Bit rate. With 20 channels × 50 frames/s × ~5 bits/channel = 5 kbps, plus \(F_0\) (6 bits) and voicing (1 bit) — ~5–6 kbps. Older analog vocoders used ~2.4 kbps.

Sound quality. Recognisable but robotic — the phase information is lost (envelopes only). This is the famous "vocoder" sound, used for effect in electronic music (e.g., Daft Punk, Kraftwerk).

docs.title: 4.9.2 Modern analysis–synthesis
docs.text:
Modern speech codecs improve on the channel vocoder by:

  • LPC-based analysis (Chapter 3) — the all-pole model captures formants more compactly than 20 filter-bank envelopes.
  • Residual coding — transmit the prediction error (not just the source model), preserving waveform fine structure.
  • CELP (Code-Excited Linear Prediction) — model the residual as a codebook lookup, giving near-toll quality at 4.8–16 kbps.

This is the family that includes G.729, AMR, and Opus.

docs.title: Worked example 4.10 — channel vocoder by hand
docs.text:
Speech frame 25 ms, filter bank of 4 channels: 0–500, 500–1500, 1500–3000, 3000–8000 Hz. Observed channel energies (in dB): \((-20, -15, -10, -30)\). Voicing: voiced, \(F_0 = 150\) Hz.

Reconstruction.

  1. Source: pulse train at 150 Hz.
  2. Bandpass into the 4 channels.
  3. Multiply each by the envelope \(10^{E_c/20}\) → factors \(0.1, 0.178, 0.316, 0.0316\).
  4. Sum.

The output sounds like the original vowel (same 4 band energies, same pitch) but with no phase detail — the harmonic phases are determined by the source pulse train, not the original. 5–10× compression vs. raw PCM, at the cost of "robotic" timbre.

Enhancement. Use 16–20 channels (instead of 4) and finer frame rate (100/s); the robotic effect reduces but doesn't disappear.

docs.title: 4.10.1 The homomorphic idea
docs.text:
In Chapter 2, homomorphic filtering was used to separate multiplicative image components (illumination × reflectance) via log. In speech, the source-filter model gives a similar multiplicative structure in the spectrum:

\[ \boxed{\;|X(f)| = |G(f)| \cdot |H(f)|\;} \]

where \(|G|\) is the source spectrum (glottal pulse train, \(F_0\)-periodic) and \(|H|\) is the vocal-tract spectrum (slowly-varying formant envelope).

Taking the log turns multiplication into addition:

\[ \log|X(f)| = \log|G(f)| + \log|H(f)|. \]

Now the source and filter are additive — separable by linear filtering.

docs.title: 4.10.2 The real cepstrum
docs.text:
The real cepstrum is the inverse Fourier transform of the log-magnitude spectrum:

\[ \boxed{\;c[n] = \mathcal F^{-1}\{\log|X(f)|\}.\;} \]

In practice, for a framed signal:

\[ c_m[n] = \text{IFFT}\{\log|\text{FFT}\{x_m\}|\}. \]

Naming. "Cepstrum" is a play on "spectrum" (invented by Bogert et al., 1963); the independent variable is the quefrency (a play on "frequency"), in seconds or samples, and the "low-quefrency" / "high-quefrency" regions correspond to the envelope and fine structure respectively.

docs.title: 4.10.3 Separating source from filter
docs.text:
The key insight: the source and the filter live at different quefrencies.

  • Source (pitch pulses) → periodic structure with period \(T_0\) → in the cepstrum, a peak at quefrency \(n = T_0\) (or \(f_s T_0\) samples). This is the pitch peak.
  • Filter (formants) → slow variation in log-spectrum → low quefrency components (\(n\) near 0).

Liftering (filtering in the cepstral domain):

  • Low-pass lifter — keep \(c[n]\) for \(|n| < n_0\) → recovers the spectral envelope (formants). Inverse-transform → smooth spectral envelope.
  • High-pass lifter — keep \(c[n]\) for \(|n| > n_0\) → recovers the fine structure (harmonics).

Quefrency cutoff. Choose \(n_0\) between the formant time scale (~1–2 ms) and the pitch period (~5–10 ms). Typical: \(n_0 \approx 3\)–\(4\) ms, i.e., \(n_0 \approx 50\) samples at 16 kHz.

docs.title: 4.10.4 Cepstral pitch estimation
docs.text:
Algorithm.

  1. Frame, window, compute FFT.
  2. Take log-magnitude: \(L = \log|X|\).
  3. IFFT: \(c = \text{IFFT}\{L\}\) — the real cepstrum.
  4. Find the peak of \(c[n]\) in the pitch quefrency range: \(n \in [f_s/400, f_s/60] = [40, 267]\) samples at 16 kHz (pitch 60–400 Hz).
  5. Peak position \(n_{\text{peak}}\) gives \(T_0 = n_{\text{peak}}\) samples, \(F_0 = f_s/n_{\text{peak}}\).
  6. If the peak exceeds a threshold relative to the low-quefrency energy → voiced.

Advantages over autocorrelation.

  • Robust to formants — formants live at low quefrency, don't interfere with pitch peak.
  • Deals with weak fundamentals — even if \(|X(f_0)|\) is small, the log-spectrum still has the pitch-period structure at \(n = T_0\).
  • Cheap — one FFT + one IFFT (or two FFTs total).

Disadvantages.

  • Phase ignored — log-magnitude spectrum loses phase; slight accuracy penalty.
  • Requires long frames (40+ ms) so the pitch period fits comfortably at moderate quefrency.
  • Sensitive to DC — subtract the mean before FFT to avoid huge low-quefrency peak.

docs.title: Worked example 4.11 — cepstrum peak for \(F_0 = 200\) Hz
docs.text:
\(f_s = 16\) kHz, \(T_0 = 80\) samples (\(F_0 = 200\) Hz).

Log-magnitude spectrum. Harmonic peaks every \(f_s/T_0 = 200\) Hz.

Real cepstrum. IFFT of this log-spectrum. Structure: - Low quefrency (\(n < 50\)): the smooth formant envelope. - Peak at \(n = 80\): the pitch period — a strong peak (the IFFT of a harmonic comb is a comb at the pitch period). - Peak at \(n = 160\): two pitch periods (weaker, from second-harmonic interaction).

Detection. Peak at \(n = 80\) → \(F_0 = 16000/80 = 200\) Hz. ✓

Threshold. Peak height relative to the surrounding quefrency: if \(\max_{n \in [40, 267]} c[n] > \alpha \cdot c[0]\) for some \(\alpha \approx 0.1\), declare voiced. The exact threshold depends on the recording SNR and can be tuned.

docs.title: 4.10.5 Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC)
docs.text:
If we replace the DFT frequencies in the cepstrum computation with mel frequencies (via the mel filter bank from §4.5.2), we get MFCCs:

MFCC pipeline.

  1. Frame (25 ms) and window (Hamming).
  2. FFT → magnitude spectrum \(|X[k]|\).
  3. Mel filter bank → energies \(E_c\) in \(C\) mel-spaced bands.
  4. Log → \(L_c = \log E_c\).
  5. DCT → \(c_1, c_2, \dots, c_J\) (first \(J \approx 12\)–13 coefficients).

The DCT replaces the IFFT — it decorrelates the log-mel energies and packs them into the first few coefficients. MFCCs are the standard feature vector for speech recognition, speaker recognition, and many speech processing tasks.

Why MFCC not raw cepstrum? The mel warping matches human perception — it puts the spectral resolution where it matters (low frequencies), which improves recognition accuracy by 5–10% over uniform cepstrum.

docs.title: 4.11.1 The LPC model
docs.text:
LPC models each speech sample as a linear combination of the previous \(p\) samples plus a prediction error:

\[ \boxed{\;x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k\, x[n-k] + e[n].\;} \]

Reinterpreted: \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k x[n-k] = \sum_{k=0}^{p} a_k x[n-k]\) (with \(a_0 = 1\)).

Model. The signal \(x[n]\) is the output of an all-pole filter \(H(z) = 1/A(z)\) driven by the prediction error \(e[n]\):

\[ \boxed{\;H(z) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k z^{-k}}.\;} \]

Physical interpretation. \(H(z)\) is the vocal-tract filter; \(e[n]\) is the glottal source. This is the source-filter model realized as an AR(p) process.

docs.title: 4.11.2 Why LPC of speech?
docs.text:
Three properties of the vocal tract make LPC a natural fit:

  1. Vocal tract ≈ all-pole. Each formant is a 2nd-order resonance (pole pair). \(K\) formants → \(2K\) poles → AR(2K). For \(K = 5\) (F1–F5), \(p = 10\) is enough.
  2. Glottal source ≈ white noise (unvoiced) or a pulse train (voiced). Either way, it's broadband and not captured by the filter — makes \(e[n]\) approximately white.
  3. Formants are acoustically important — they determine vowel identity. LPC coefficients concentrate the formant information in a compact vector.

docs.title: 4.11.3 Derivation — Yule–Walker equations
docs.text:
Minimise the prediction error energy over a frame:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathcal E = \sum_{n} e[n]^2 = \sum_n \Bigl(x[n] + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k x[n-k]\Bigr)^2.\;} \]

Take partials and set to zero.

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal E}{\partial a_k} = 2\sum_n \Bigl(x[n] + \sum_{l=1}^{p} a_l x[n-l]\Bigr) x[n-k] = 0,\quad k = 1, \ldots, p. \]

Rearranged:

\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{l=1}^{p} a_l \underbrace{\Bigl(\sum_n x[n-l] x[n-k]\Bigr)}_{= R[k-l]} = -\underbrace{\sum_n x[n] x[n-k]}_{= R[k]}.\;} \]

The Yule–Walker equations:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathbf R\, \mathbf a = -\mathbf r,\quad R_{ij} = R[|i-j|],\quad r_k = R[k].\;} \]

with \(\mathbf a = (a_1, \ldots, a_p)^\top\) and \(\mathbf R\) the \(p \times p\) Toeplitz autocorrelation matrix.

Prediction error variance.

\[ \boxed{\;\sigma_e^2 = R[0] + \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k R[k].\;} \]

docs.title: 4.11.4 Solving the Yule–Walker equations — Levinson–Durbin
docs.text:
Direct inversion: \(O(p^3)\).

Levinson–Durbin (from ECEG-6303 Chapter 2 §2.10): exploits the Toeplitz structure to solve in \(O(p^2)\).

Recursion (from order \(m-1\) to order \(m\)):

\[ \boxed{\;k_m = -\frac{R[m] + \sum_{i=1}^{m-1} a_i^{(m-1)} R[m-i]}{\sigma_{m-1}^2}\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m a_{m-i}^{(m-1)},\quad i = 1, \ldots, m-1;\quad a_m^{(m)} = k_m.\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;\sigma_m^2 = (1 - k_m^2)\sigma_{m-1}^2.\;} \]

Initialise \(\sigma_0^2 = R[0]\), \(a^{(0)} = \emptyset\).

Reflection coefficients \(k_m\): partial autocorrelation at lag \(m\); satisfy \(|k_m| < 1\) for a stable AR filter.

Why "prediction error" and "reflection coefficients" coincide. The physical interpretation: \(k_m\) is the fraction of energy removed by adding lag \(m\) to the predictor. Magnitude near 1 = lag \(m\) is very informative; near 0 = lag \(m\) adds little. This is precisely what "reflection coefficient" means in the acoustic-tube model (Chapter 3 §3.5.3).

docs.title: Worked example 4.12 — LPC(2) by Yule–Walker
docs.text:
Frame autocorrelation: \(R[0] = 6\), \(R[1] = 4\), \(R[2] = 1\).

Yule–Walker system (from Chapter 2 Example 2.7):

\[ \begin{bmatrix} R[0] & R[1] \\ R[1] & R[0] \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} = -\begin{bmatrix} R[1] \\ R[2] \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 4 \\ 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Solution: \(a_1 = -1\), \(a_2 = 0.5\).

Prediction error variance.

\[ \sigma_e^2 = R[0] + a_1 R[1] + a_2 R[2] = 6 + (-1)(4) + (0.5)(1) = 2.5. \]

LPC filter.

\[ H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z^{-1} + 0.5 z^{-2}}. \]

Roots. \(1 - z^{-1} + 0.5z^{-2} = 0 \Rightarrow z^2 - z + 0.5 = 0 \Rightarrow z = 0.5 \pm j0.5\).

\(|z| = 1/\sqrt 2 \approx 0.707\), \(\angle z = \pi/4\). Formant at \(F = (f_s/2\pi)(\pi/4) = f_s/8\). At \(f_s = 8000\): \(F = 1000\) Hz. Bandwidth: \(-\ln|z| \cdot f_s/\pi = -\ln(1/\sqrt 2) \cdot 8000/\pi \approx 1760\) Hz. Very wide (a heavily damped resonance).

Interpretation. The two LPC coefficients capture one broad formant because \(p=2\) is enough for only one pole pair. Real speech requires \(p = 10\) for 5 formants. This example just illustrates the mechanics.

docs.title: 4.12.1 Formants from LPC roots
docs.text:
For an LPC(p) model with roots \(z_i = r_i e^{j\theta_i}\):

\[ \boxed{\;F_i = \frac{f_s}{2\pi}\,\theta_i,\quad \text{BW}_i = -\frac{f_s}{\pi}\,\ln r_i.\;} \]

Extracting formants.

  1. Solve Yule–Walker for \(A(z) = 1 + \sum a_k z^{-k}\).
  2. Find all \(p\) roots \(z_i\).
  3. Keep complex-conjugate pairs (real roots are not formants — they're DC or Nyquist poles).
  4. Compute \(F_i\) and \(\text{BW}_i\) for each pair.
  5. Sort by frequency, keep the first 3–5 (the lowest formants).
  6. Filter by bandwidth — reject pairs with BW > ~500 Hz (typically spurious).

Typical results for a vowel with \(p = 10\): - 5 complex-conjugate pairs → 5 formants. - Some may be too wide (spurious) or too high (above Nyquist/2).

The pole-pair formants are the LPC coefficients' physical meaning, and this is the basis of the formant vocoder and speech synthesis systems.

docs.title: 4.12.2 Pitch from LPC residual
docs.text:
The prediction error \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum a_k x[n-k]\) — the LPC residual — is the glottal source. For voiced speech, \(e[n]\) contains the pitch pulses. Apply pitch detection (autocorrelation, AMDF, or cepstrum) to \(e[n]\) to estimate \(F_0\).

Advantages.

  • Whiter residual — the LPC filter has removed the formants, so pitch peaks in \(e[n]\) are clearer than in \(x[n]\).
  • Especially useful for voiced speech with strong formants — the ACF of \(x[n]\) has peaks at \(T_0\), but also peaks from formant periodicity; the residual's ACF has only the pitch peak.

Practical. For high-quality pitch tracking, use the SIFT algorithm (Markel, 1972) — LPC residual + autocorrelation peak picking. It's the industry standard for pitch detection in LPC-based codecs.

docs.title: Worked example 4.13 — formant extraction from LPC(10)
docs.text:
LPC(10) of a vowel frame at 16 kHz. The 10 roots (5 conjugate pairs):

Pair Root magnitude Root angle \(F\) (Hz) BW (Hz) 1 0.98 0.20 510 100 2 0.96 0.59 1500 200 3 0.94 0.98 2500 305 4 0.91 1.38 3510 460 5 0.87 1.77 4500 660

Formants: \(F_1 \approx 510\) Hz, \(F_2 \approx 1500\) Hz, \(F_3 \approx 2500\) Hz.

Interpretation. \((F_1, F_2) = (510, 1500)\) is near the schwa /ə/ region of the vowel chart. The bandwidths increase with frequency (typical — high formants are more damped).

Filtering. Pair 5 has BW = 660 Hz, above the typical threshold (500 Hz) — it's likely spurious (a spurious root from the finite-window analysis). Keep the first 3–4 formants; ignore the rest.

docs.title: 4.13 Summary of methods — choosing your tool
docs.text:
Task Time-domain Frequency-domain LPC Voiced/unvoiced Energy + ZCR (cheap) Spectral flatness LPC residual + autocorrelation Pitch Autocorrelation, AMDF, parallel processing Cepstrum, HPS Residual + ACF (SIFT) Formants — Spectral peaks LPC roots Envelope — Smoothed FFT magnitude LPC spectrum $1/ Channel energies — Filter bank / mel — Feature vectors — MFCC LPC, LPCC, PLP Coding DPCM Channel vocoder CELP, G.729

Rules of thumb.

  • Cheapest: time-domain (energy, ZCR, AMDF) — for voiced/unvoiced, endpoint.
  • Most accurate pitch: cepstrum (frequency) or SIFT (LPC residual).
  • Best formants: LPC roots or smoothed spectral peaks.
  • Standard recognition features: MFCC (or PLP).
  • Standard coding: LPC + residual (CELP family).

docs.title: Python — full pipeline
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import get_window
from scipy.fft import dct

def frame_signal(x, frame_length, hop_length):
    """Split signal into overlapping frames."""
    n_frames = 1 + (len(x) - frame_length) // hop_length
    frames = np.zeros((n_frames, frame_length))
    for m in range(n_frames):
        frames[m] = x[m*hop_length : m*hop_length + frame_length]
    return frames

def short_time_energy(frames):
    return np.sum(frames**2, axis=1)

def short_time_zcr(frames):
    return 0.5 * np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(np.sign(frames), axis=1)), axis=1)

def short_time_autocorr(frame, max_lag):
    """Biased (for stability) autocorrelation up to max_lag."""
    n = len(frame)
    # FFT-based for efficiency
    X = np.fft.rfft(frame, n=2*n)
    r = np.fft.irfft(np.abs(X)**2, n=2*n)[:max_lag + 1]
    return r / n

def pitch_from_acf(frame, fs, f_min=60, f_max=400):
    """Autocorrelation-based pitch detection."""
    K_min = int(fs / f_max)
    K_max = int(fs / f_min)
    r = short_time_autocorr(frame, K_max)
    # Peak in [K_min, K_max]
    k_peak = K_min + np.argmax(r[K_min:K_max + 1])
    # Voicing decision
    if r[k_peak] / r[0] > 0.3:
        return fs / k_peak, True
    return 0.0, False

def stft(x, frame_length=400, hop_length=200, window='hamming'):
    """Short-time Fourier transform (one-sided)."""
    w = get_window(window, frame_length)
    frames = frame_signal(x, frame_length, hop_length) * w
    return np.fft.rfft(frames, axis=1)

def real_cepstrum(frame, n_fft=1024):
    """Real cepstrum of a single frame."""
    X = np.fft.rfft(frame, n=n_fft)
    log_mag = np.log(np.abs(X) + 1e-10)
    # Compute real cepstrum via IFFT of the log spectrum
    # Full spectrum: mirror
    log_mag_full = np.concatenate([log_mag, log_mag[-2:0:-1]])
    c = np.fft.irfft(log_mag_full, n=n_fft)
    return c[:n_fft//2]

def pitch_from_cepstrum(frame, fs, f_min=60, f_max=400):
    """Cepstrum-based pitch detection."""
    c = real_cepstrum(frame)
    n_min = int(fs / f_max)
    n_max = int(fs / f_min)
    n_peak = n_min + np.argmax(c[n_min:n_max + 1])
    if c[n_peak] > 0.1 * c[0]:
        return fs / n_peak, True
    return 0.0, False

def lpc(frame, p, fs):
    """LPC coefficients via Levinson-Durbin."""
    # Autocorrelation
    N = len(frame)
    r = np.correlate(frame, frame, mode='full')[N-1:N+p]
    # Levinson-Durbin
    a = np.zeros(p + 1)
    a[0] = 1.0
    E = r[0]
    for m in range(1, p + 1):
        k = -(r[m] + np.dot(a[1:m], r[m-1:0:-1])) / E
        # Update
        a_new = a.copy()
        a_new[m] = k
        for i in range(1, m):
            a_new[i] = a[i] + k * a[m - i]
        a = a_new
        E *= (1 - k**2)
    return a, E

def formants_from_lpc(a, fs):
    """Formants from LPC polynomial roots."""
    roots = np.roots(a)
    roots = roots[np.imag(roots) > 0]  # upper half plane
    formants = []
    for z in roots:
        f = fs / (2 * np.pi) * np.angle(z)
        bw = -fs / np.pi * np.log(np.abs(z))
        if 50 < f < fs / 2 and bw < 500:
            formants.append((f, bw))
    formants.sort()
    return formants

# ---- demo -------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    fs = 16000
    # Simulate a synthetic voiced signal: pitch 150 Hz, formants 500, 1500, 2500
    t = np.arange(int(0.5 * fs)) / fs
    x = sum(np.sin(2*np.pi*f*t) for f in [150, 300, 450, 600])
    # Add some noise
    x += 0.1 * np.random.randn(len(x))

    # Frame-based features
    frames = frame_signal(x, frame_length=400, hop_length=200)
    E = short_time_energy(frames)
    Z = short_time_zcr(frames)
    print(f"Frames: {len(frames)}, mean E = {E.mean():.2f}, mean ZCR = {Z.mean():.4f}")

    # Pitch from ACF and cepstrum on one frame
    frame = frames[10]
    f_acf, v_acf = pitch_from_acf(frame, fs)
    f_cep, v_cep = pitch_from_cepstrum(frame, fs)
    print(f"Pitch: ACF = {f_acf:.1f} Hz (voiced={v_acf}), "
          f"cepstrum = {f_cep:.1f} Hz (voiced={v_cep})")

    # LPC and formants
    a, E_err = lpc(frame, p=10, fs=fs)
    formants = formants_from_lpc(a, fs)
    print(f"Prediction error variance: {E_err:.4f}")
    print(f"Formants: {[(round(f, 1), round(bw, 1)) for f, bw in formants[:5]]}")

docs.title: Java — ZCR + short-time energy
docs.text:
public class SpeechParameters {

    public static double shortTimeEnergy(double[] frame) {
        double E = 0;
        for (double x : frame) E += x * x;
        return E;
    }

    public static double shortTimeZCR(double[] frame) {
        int crossings = 0;
        for (int n = 1; n < frame.length; n++) {
            if ((frame[n - 1] >= 0) != (frame[n] >= 0)) crossings++;
        }
        return (double) crossings / (frame.length - 1);
    }

    public static double[] autocorrelation(double[] frame, int maxLag) {
        int N = frame.length;
        double[] R = new double[maxLag + 1];
        for (int k = 0; k <= maxLag; k++) {
            double s = 0;
            for (int n = 0; n < N - k; n++) s += frame[n] * frame[n + k];
            R[k] = s;
        }
        return R;
    }

    public static double[] pitchFromACF(double[] frame, double fs,
                                         double fMin, double fMax) {
        int kMin = (int) (fs / fMax);
        int kMax = (int) (fs / fMin);
        double[] R = autocorrelation(frame, kMax);
        int kPeak = kMin;
        for (int k = kMin; k <= kMax; k++)
            if (R[k] > R[kPeak]) kPeak = k;
        boolean voiced = R[kPeak] / R[0] > 0.3;
        return new double[]{ voiced ? fs / kPeak : 0.0, voiced ? 1.0 : 0.0 };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int N = 400;
        double[] frame = new double[N];
        for (int n = 0; n < N; n++)
            frame[n] = Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * 150 * n / 16000.0);

        System.out.printf("Energy: %.2f%n", shortTimeEnergy(frame));
        System.out.printf("ZCR:    %.4f%n", shortTimeZCR(frame));
        double[] p = pitchFromACF(frame, 16000, 60, 400);
        System.out.printf("Pitch:  %.1f Hz (voiced=%b)%n", p[0], p[1] == 1.0);
    }
}

docs.title: C# — Mel filter bank
docs.text:
using System;

class MelFilterBank
{
    static double HzToMel(double f) => 2595.0 * Math.Log10(1 + f / 700.0);
    static double MelToHz(double m) => 700.0 * (Math.Pow(10, m / 2595.0) - 1);

    // Build triangular filters evenly spaced in mel space
    static double[][] BuildMelFilters(int nFilters, int nFft, double fs,
                                       double fMin = 0, double fMax = 8000)
    {
        double melMin = HzToMel(fMin), melMax = HzToMel(fMax);
        double melStep = (melMax - melMin) / (nFilters + 1);
        var filters = new double[nFilters][];
        for (int m = 0; m < nFilters; m++)
        {
            double centerMel = melMin + (m + 1) * melStep;
            double leftMel = centerMel - melStep;
            double rightMel = centerMel + melStep;
            double centerHz = MelToHz(centerMel);
            double leftHz = MelToHz(leftMel);
            double rightHz = MelToHz(rightMel);
            int binLeft = (int)(leftHz / fs * nFft);
            int binCenter = (int)(centerHz / fs * nFft);
            int binRight = (int)(rightHz / fs * nFft);
            filters[m] = new double[nFft / 2 + 1];
            for (int k = binLeft; k < binCenter; k++)
                filters[m][k] = (double)(k - binLeft) / (binCenter - binLeft);
            for (int k = binCenter; k < binRight && k < filters[m].Length; k++)
                filters[m][k] = (double)(binRight - k) / (binRight - binCenter);
        }
        return filters;
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        int nFft = 512;
        double fs = 16000;
        int nFilters = 24;
        var filters = BuildMelFilters(nFilters, nFft, fs);
        for (int m = 0; m < nFilters; m += 4)
        {
            int center = Array.IndexOf(filters[m], filters[m].Max());
            Console.WriteLine($"Filter {m,2}: peak at bin {center,3} = {center * fs / nFft:F0} Hz");
        }
    }
}

Expected output for the mel bank.

Filter  0: peak at bin   1 = 31 Hz
Filter  4: peak at bin   5 = 156 Hz
Filter  8: peak at bin  14 = 438 Hz
Filter 12: peak at bin  30 = 938 Hz
Filter 16: peak at bin  58 = 1813 Hz
Filter 20: peak at bin 105 = 3281 Hz

The filters are denser at low frequency — the mel spacing in action.

Tooling

  • Python: librosa for STFT, mel spectrogram, MFCC, pitch (pyin); scipy.signal for filter design and windows; python_speech_features for classic MFCC; praat-parselmouth for phonetics-grade formant/pitch tracking.
  • Java: JTransforms (FFT); TarsosDSP (PitchDetection, MFCC); no standard LPC library — implement Levinson manually.
  • C#: Math.NET Numerics (FFT); NAudio (audio I/O); hand-roll MFCC/LPC.
  • MATLAB: spectrogram, mfcc, lpc, levinson, pitchest, findpeaks — the reference.
  • Praat: the standard tool for phonetic analysis — formants, pitch, spectrogram.

docs.title: 4.15 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Short-time analysis is the foundation — speech is quasi-stationary over 10–30 ms. Frame + window (Hamming, 25 ms, 50% overlap).
  2. Time-domain parameters: energy, magnitude, ZCR, autocorrelation — cheap and useful for voiced/unvoiced, endpoint, and (with ACF) pitch.
  3. Parallel processing pitch detection — autocorrelation of downsampled channels, combined by voting — resolves octave errors.
  4. STFT is the frequency-domain workhorse; window length controls the time-frequency resolution trade-off (Heisenberg); narrowband = 40 ms (pitch), wideband = 10 ms (timing).
  5. Filter banks — uniform, or mel-spaced for perceptual matching. The mel bank is the front end of MFCC.
  6. Spectrograms — narrowband shows harmonics (pitch); wideband shows pitch pulses; formants are visible in both. Phoneticians read them for phone sequences.
  7. Formant extraction — spectral peak picking (with smoothing) or LPC root finding. LPC gives formant frequency and bandwidth from the pole's angle and magnitude.
  8. Pitch extraction — ACF (time), cepstrum (frequency), HPS (harmonic product spectrum), LPC residual + SIFT. Each has trade-offs; cepstrum and SIFT are the most robust.
  9. Analysis–synthesis — the channel vocoder is the classic example; modern codecs (CELP) improve on it by transmitting the LPC residual rather than regenerating it from a source model.
  10. Cepstrum separates source (high quefrency, pitch peak) from filter (low quefrency, envelope). It's the basis for MFCC, the standard recognition feature.
  11. LPC — AR(p) all-pole model of the vocal tract; Yule–Walker equations; Levinson–Durbin solves them in \(O(p^2)\); reflection coefficients \(k_m\) characterize stability.
  12. LPC formant extraction — pole angle = formant frequency; pole radius = bandwidth. Filter \(F < f_s/2\) and BW < 500 Hz to reject spurious roots.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. The standard frame length for short-time speech analysis is: (a) 1 ms (b) 10 ms (c) 25 ms (d) 100 ms

  2. Short-time zero-crossing rate is highest for: (a) vowels (b) silence (c) unvoiced fricatives (d) nasals

  3. In the autocorrelation function, the peak at \(k = T_0\) indicates: (a) silence (b) voiced speech with pitch period \(T_0\) (c) unvoiced noise (d) DC

  4. Narrowband spectrograms use a window of approximately: (a) 5 ms (b) 10 ms (c) 40 ms (d) 100 ms

  5. A mel filter bank places more filters: (a) uniformly (b) at high frequencies (c) at low frequencies (d) at random

  6. Formants can be extracted most reliably from: (a) the raw waveform (b) energy only (c) LPC roots or smoothed spectral peaks (d) ZCR

  7. The cepstrum is the: (a) FFT of the spectrum (b) IFFT of the log-magnitude spectrum (c) squared magnitude of the spectrum (d) DFT of the autocorrelation

  8. In the cepstrum, the pitch peak appears at quefrency equal to: (a) \(F_0\) (b) \(T_0\) (samples) (c) half the frame length (d) \(N/2\)

  9. The Yule–Walker equations solve for: (a) pitch (b) LPC coefficients (c) cepstrum (d) spectrogram

  10. Levinson–Durbin solves the Yule–Walker system in: (a) \(O(p)\) (b) \(O(p^2)\) (c) \(O(p^3)\) (d) \(O(2^p)\)

  11. The channel vocoder transmits: (a) the raw waveform (b) filter-bank envelopes plus pitch/voicing (c) LPC coefficients only (d) the cepstrum

  12. For \(p = 10\) LPC analysis of a vowel, the number of formants is typically: (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 5 (d) 10

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Explain why short-time analysis is necessary for speech. What is the standard frame length and hop size, and why?
  2. Compute the short-time energy, magnitude, and zero-crossing rate of \(x = (2, -1, 1, -3, -2, 1, -1, 2)\).
  3. Define the short-time autocorrelation and explain how it is used for pitch detection. Why is parallel processing needed?
  4. State the short-time Fourier transform and derive the time-frequency resolution trade-off. What window length is used for narrowband vs. wideband spectrograms?
  5. Describe the mel filter bank. Why is the mel scale used, and what is the typical number of filters?
  6. Interpret a spectrogram of a voiced vowel, an unvoiced fricative, and a plosive. What features distinguish them?
  7. Define the cepstrum and explain the source-filter separation in the cepstral domain. Why does the pitch peak appear at high quefrency and the formants at low quefrency?
  8. State the LPC model of speech. Derive the Yule–Walker equations from the minimum-MSE criterion.
  9. State the Levinson–Durbin recursion. What are the reflection coefficients and what do they mean physically?
  10. Describe LPC-based formant extraction. How are formants extracted from the LPC polynomial roots?
  11. Compare autocorrelation, cepstrum, HPS, and LPC residual (SIFT) for pitch detection. Which is best for which situation?

docs.title: 4.17 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (c) — 25 ms.
  2. (c) — unvoiced fricatives.
  3. (b) — voiced, pitch period \(T_0\).
  4. (c) — 40 ms.
  5. (c) — low frequencies.
  6. (c) — LPC roots or smoothed spectral peaks.
  7. (b) — IFFT of log-magnitude.
  8. (b) — \(T_0\) samples.
  9. (b) — LPC coefficients.
  10. (b) — \(O(p^2)\).
  11. (b) — envelopes + pitch/voicing.
  12. (c) — 5 (one per pole pair).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. 20–30 (typically 25)
  2. time; frequency
  3. Hamming
  4. pitch
  5. more
  6. cepstrum
  7. \(T_0\) (pitch period in samples)
  8. all-pole (AR)
  9. Levinson–Durbin
  10. angle; negative log
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Why short-time: speech is non-stationary (vocal tract moves continuously), but quasi-stationary over 10–30 ms — long enough to contain 2–3 pitch periods and thus support a stable spectral estimate, short enough that the articulator configuration is roughly frozen. Standard parameters: frame length 25 ms (400 samples at 16 kHz), hop size 10 ms (160 samples) or 12.5 ms (200 samples, 50% overlap). The 50% overlap smooths the transition between frames (continuous feature stream), matches auditory integration (~20 ms), and improves vocoder quality.
  2. Computation for \(x = (2, -1, 1, -3, -2, 1, -1, 2)\): Energy = \(4+1+1+9+4+1+1+4 = 25\). Magnitude = \(2+1+1+3+2+1+1+2 = 13\). Sign changes: \((+,-)\) (1), \((-,+)\) (2), \((+,-)\) (3), \((-,-)\) no, \((-,+)\) (4), \((+,-)\) (5), \((-,+)\) (6). ZCR = \(6/2 = 3\); normalized \(3/7 \approx 0.43\) (using \(N-1 = 7\) as denominator).
  3. Short-time autocorrelation: \(R_m[k] = \sum_n x_m[n] x_m[n+k]\) — measure of self-similarity at lag \(k\). Pitch detection: for voiced speech, \(R_m[k]\) peaks at \(k = T_0\), the pitch period; find the first peak above a threshold in the plausible pitch range (\(f_s/400\) to \(f_s/60\) samples). Parallel processing: the ACF has peaks at \(T_0, 2T_0, 3T_0, \ldots\) and (for some signals) at \(T_0/2\) — leading to octave errors (pitch doubled or halved). Parallel processing computes ACF at multiple decimation factors and combines results by voting: a candidate pitch is accepted only if confirmed by several channels. This dramatically reduces octave errors at the cost of more computation.
  4. STFT: \(X_m(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_n x_m[n] w[n] e^{-j\omega n}\) — Fourier transform of each windowed frame. Trade-off: window length \(N\) determines both frequency resolution (\(\Delta f = f_s/N\)) and time resolution (\(\Delta t \approx N/f_s\)). Their product is bounded by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle: \(\Delta t \cdot \Delta f \ge 1/(4\pi)\). Narrowband: 40 ms (long window, \(\Delta f \approx 25\) Hz) — resolves pitch harmonics, useful for formant tracking. Wideband: 10 ms (short window, \(\Delta f \approx 100\) Hz) — resolves pitch pulses as vertical stripes, useful for voicing and timing.
  5. Mel filter bank: a set of triangular bandpass filters whose center frequencies are equally spaced in mel, not Hz. The mel scale \(f_{\text{mel}} = 2595\log_{10}(1 + f_{\text{Hz}}/700)\) approximates the ear's nonlinear frequency sensitivity. Because the ear has finer resolution at low frequencies (up to ~500 Hz) and coarser at high (~8 kHz), the mel bank places more filters where perceptual resolution is higher. Typical: 20–40 filters covering 0–8000 Hz. The output energies (often log-transformed and DCT'ed) form the basis of MFCC features.
  6. Voiced vowel: horizontal dark formant bands (e.g., \(F_1 \approx 500\) Hz, \(F_2 \approx 1500\) Hz, \(F_3 \approx 2500\) Hz); vertical striations showing pitch pulses; energy concentrated below 4 kHz. Unvoiced fricative: diffuse broadband high-frequency energy (above 3 kHz), no formants, no pitch striations. Plosive: short vertical burst (30–50 ms) at a specific frequency region, preceded by a silent closure. Distinguishing features: formant bands (vowel), voicing striations (voiced vs. unvoiced), burst/closure (plosive).
  7. Cepstrum: \(c[n] = \text{IFFT}\{\log|X[k]|\}\) — inverse Fourier transform of the log-magnitude spectrum. Source-filter separation: in the log spectrum, the source (periodic pulse train) and the filter (vocal-tract formants) are additive. In the cepstral domain, they occupy different quefrency ranges: the filter (slow variation) lives at low quefrency (near \(n=0\)); the source (rapid harmonic structure) lives at high quefrency (at the pitch period \(n = T_0\)). Why: the log-magnitude spectrum of the source has comb structure with period \(F_0\); the IFFT of a comb with period \(F_0\) is a peak at quefrency \(T_0 = 1/F_0\). The formant envelope is smooth, so its IFFT is concentrated at low quefrency.
  8. LPC model: \(x[n] = -\sum_{k=1}^p a_k x[n-k] + e[n]\) where \(e\) is a white driving source. Equivalently, \(x\) is the output of an all-pole AR filter \(H(z) = 1/A(z)\) with \(A(z) = 1 + \sum a_k z^{-k}\), driven by \(e\). Derivation: minimise \(\mathcal E = \sum e[n]^2\) with \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum a_k x[n-k]\). Take partial derivatives \(\partial\mathcal E/\partial a_k = 0\): \(2\sum e[n] x[n-k] = 0\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, p\). Substitute \(e[n] = x[n] + \sum_l a_l x[n-l]\): \(R[k] + \sum_l a_l R[k-l] = 0\), i.e., \(\sum_l a_l R[k-l] = -R[k]\). In matrix form: \(\mathbf R \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\) where \(R_{ij} = R[|i-j|]\). These are the Yule–Walker equations.
  9. Levinson–Durbin: an \(O(p^2)\) recursion for solving the Toeplitz system \(\mathbf R \mathbf a = -\mathbf r\). At each order \(m\) it computes a reflection coefficient \(k_m\) and updates the AR coefficients of order \(m\) from order \(m-1\): \(k_m = -(R[m] + \sum a_i^{(m-1)} R[m-i])/\sigma_{m-1}^2\); \(a_i^{(m)} = a_i^{(m-1)} + k_m a_{m-i}^{(m-1)}\); \(\sigma_m^2 = (1 - k_m^2)\sigma_{m-1}^2\). Reflection coefficients: \(k_m\) is the partial autocorrelation at lag \(m\) — the correlation between \(x[n]\) and \(x[n-m]\) after removing the linear effect of lags \(1, \ldots, m-1\). Physically, it measures how much energy is removed by adding lag \(m\) to the predictor. The condition \(|k_m| < 1\) for all \(m\) is necessary and sufficient for the AR filter to be stable (all poles inside the unit circle).
  10. LPC formant extraction: given LPC coefficients \(A(z) = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^p a_k z^{-k}\), find its \(p\) roots \(z_i\) (numerically, via polynomial root-finding). Complex roots come in conjugate pairs, one pair per formant. For each pair: \(F = (f_s/2\pi) \cdot \angle z_i\) (formant frequency); \(\text{BW} = -(f_s/\pi) \cdot \ln|z_i|\) (formant bandwidth). Filter the results: keep \(F\) in \([50, f_s/2]\), reject pairs with BW > 500 Hz (spurious), sort by frequency, keep the first 3–5 formants. Typical: \(p = 10\) gives 5 formants; only the first 3–4 are reliably meaningful.
  11. Pitch detection comparison:
    • ACF (autocorrelation): cheap, works for most signals, but octave errors with some waveforms. Good baseline.
    • Cepstrum: robust to formants (filter lives at low quefrency), handles weak fundamentals, but requires longer frames (40+ ms) and FFT cost. Good for many speakers.
    • HPS (harmonic product spectrum): simple, no octave errors in principle, but limited by FFT resolution. Good for clean periodic signals.
    • SIFT (LPC residual + ACF): best accuracy for speech, because the LPC filter whitens the residual and leaves only the pitch peak. Standard in codecs and modern analysis. Which to use: SIFT for coding and highest accuracy; cepstrum for analysis with clear pitch; ACF for embedded/cheap; HPS rarely (mostly historical). YIN (2002) is the modern open-source standard, better than all of these in practice.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Rabiner & Schafer, Digital Processing of Speech Signals, Prentice Hall, 1978 — the classical reference for Chapters 3–4 of this course. Sections 4.2–4.5 for STFT and spectrograms; 4.3 for pitch; 5.4 for cepstrum; 6.3 for LPC.
  • Deller, Proakis & Hansen, Discrete-Time Processing of Speech Signals, IEEE Press, 2000 — the modern comprehensive reference.
  • Quatieri, Discrete-Time Speech Signal Processing, Prentice Hall, 2001 — excellent on homomorphic methods, cepstrum, and vocoders.
  • O'Shaughnessy, Speech Communications: Human and Machine, IEEE Press, 2nd ed., 2000 — good on production and perception.
  • Makhoul, "Linear Prediction: A Tutorial Review", Proc. IEEE, 63(4), 1975 — the definitive pedagogical reference for LPC.
  • Markel & Gray, Linear Prediction of Speech, Springer, 1976 — the classical LPC monograph (including SIFT).
  • Rabiner, "On the Use of Autocorrelation Analysis for Pitch Detection", IEEE Trans. ASSP, 25(1), 1977 — the parallel-processing paper.
  • Hess, Pitch Determination of Speech Signals, Springer, 1983 — the classic pitch reference.
  • de Cheveigné & Kawahara, "YIN, a Fundamental Frequency Estimator for Speech and Music", JASA, 111(4), 2002 — the modern standard.
  • Childers, Skinner & Kemerait, "The Cepstrum: A Guide to Processing", Proc. IEEE, 65(10), 1977 — the classic cepstrum reference.
  • Davis & Mermelstein, "Comparison of Parametric Representations for Monosyllabic Word Recognition in Continuously Spoken Sentences", IEEE Trans. ASSP, 28(4), 1980 — the original MFCC paper.
  • Hermansky, "Perceptual Linear Predictive (PLP) Analysis of Speech", JASA, 87(4), 1990 — the PLP alternative to MFCC.
  • Mermelstein, "Distance Measures for Speech Recognition, Psychological and Instrumental", Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence, 1976 — the mel scale in speech.
  • Gold & Morgan, Speech and Audio Signal Processing, Wiley, 2000 — general textbook.
  • librosa documentation (Python); python_speech_features; praat; HTK; kaldi; MATLAB Audio Toolbox.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Frame-based features. Record a sentence with mixed voiced/unvoiced segments. Compute short-time energy and ZCR for each frame. Plot both on the same time axis — can you see the voiced/unvoiced distinction clearly? Where does each feature fail?

  2. Pitch from ACF. Implement autocorrelation-based pitch detection on a sustained vowel. Compare with a reference pitch tracker (e.g., librosa.pyin). Measure the octave error rate — on how many frames does simple ACF give a wrong result?

  3. Parallel-processing pitch. Implement a two-channel (decimate-by-2 and decimate-by-4) pitch detector. Verify it rejects octave errors on the same recording.

  4. Narrowband vs. wideband spectrogram. Compute both spectrograms for the same sentence. Identify features visible in one but not the other. Save both plots side by side.

  5. Mel filter bank. Implement a 24-filter mel bank, apply to 5 frames of different vowels, and report the 24 energy values. Verify that low-frequency channels differ more between vowels than high-frequency channels.

  6. Formant extraction. Record vowels /a/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/. Extract formants by (a) LPC root finding with \(p = 10\), (b) smoothed-spectrum peak picking. Compare. Plot on an \((F_1, F_2)\) chart — do the five vowels cluster as expected?

  7. Cepstral pitch. Compute the real cepstrum of a voiced frame. Locate the pitch peak. Apply a low-pass lifter (keep \(n < 50\)); inverse-transform → the smooth spectral envelope. Overlay on the original log spectrum — the envelope should be smooth and follow the formants.

  8. MFCC implementation. Implement the full MFCC pipeline: pre-emphasis → framing → Hamming → FFT → mel bank → log → DCT. Extract 13 MFCCs per frame for a sentence. Visualize as a 13 × N feature matrix. Compare with librosa.feature.mfcc.

  9. LPC estimation. Implement Levinson–Durbin from scratch. Verify against scipy.signal.levinson and statsmodels.tsa on a random Toeplitz system. Report timing.

  10. LPC spectrum. For a vowel frame, compute LPC with \(p = 10\) and plot the LPC spectral envelope \(1/|A(e^{j\omega})|^2\) overlaid on the FFT magnitude spectrum. The peaks of the envelope should align with the formants.

  11. Pitch from LPC residual. Compute the LPC residual for a voiced frame. Plot the residual and its autocorrelation. Verify the pitch peak is sharper than in the original signal. Compare pitch estimates from ACF (original) vs. ACF (residual).

  12. Channel vocoder. Implement a 16-channel vocoder with pitch/voicing extraction and re-synthesis. Compare the output with the original. The output should sound "robotic" but intelligible — this is the classic vocoder sound.

  13. Spectral envelope from cepstrum. Compute the cepstrum of a mixed voiced/unvoiced frame. Apply both low-pass and high-pass lifters. Reconstruct separately. Verify that low-pass gives the formant envelope and high-pass gives the pitch pulses.

  14. Real-time analysis. Process a live microphone stream: compute the spectrogram and track pitch in real time. Report the latency (should be < 50 ms for interactive use). Use sounddevice or pyaudio.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Applications of Speech Processing
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 2 tutorial + 1 laboratory · Home study: 5 h

Coverage (syllabus): speech recognition — specification of a typical application, voice response system · algorithms: spectral estimation, dynamic time warping (DTW), hidden Markov model (HMM) · speech synthesis: text-to-speech, voice over IP · speaker verification and identification.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Describe the four major application families of speech processing, and identify the technology stack each uses.
  2. State the speech-recognition problem in its three levels (isolated word, connected word, continuous speech) and describe the standard pipeline: feature extraction → acoustic model → language model → decoder.
  3. Derive and apply dynamic time warping (DTW) for template matching; state its complexity, its constraint variants (Sakoe–Chiba band, Itakura parallelogram), and the modern lower-bound acceleration.
  4. Derive and apply hidden Markov models (HMM): forward algorithm, Viterbi decoding, and Baum–Welch training. State the three fundamental HMM problems and their solutions.
  5. Compare HMM-based and DTW-based recognizers. Explain why HMMs replaced DTW and why neural networks have now displaced classical HMMs in production.
  6. Describe the four speech-synthesis generations (concatenative, formant, HMM-based, neural) and their trade-offs.
  7. State the modern speaker verification stack: feature extraction, model (GMM-UBM / i-vector / x-vector / ECAPA-TDNN), and score normalization. Compute EER, FAR, and FRR.
  8. Describe the Voice-over-IP stack: codec, RTP, jitter buffer, packet-loss concealment, and end-to-end latency budget.
  9. Implement DTW, the forward algorithm, and Viterbi in Python, Java, and C#.

docs.title: 5.1 Overview of the four application families
docs.text:
Speech processing supports four main applications, each built on the analysis tools of Chapter 4:

Application Input Output Core technology Recognition Audio Text / intent HMM, DTW, deep nets Synthesis Text Audio Concatenative, neural TTS Speaker recognition Audio Identity GMM-UBM, i-vector, x-vector Coding / transmission Audio Bits LPC, CELP, Opus

This chapter covers all four, with recognition receiving the most attention — it is the hardest problem and introduces the two fundamental algorithms (DTW and HMM) that appear throughout the field.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Problem statement
docs.text:
Given an acoustic signal \(x(t)\) (typically 5–10 s of speech), find the most likely word sequence \(\hat W = (w_1, \ldots, w_M)\):

\[ \boxed{\;\hat W = \arg\max_W \Pr(W \mid X)\;} \]

By Bayes' rule:

\[ \Pr(W \mid X) = \frac{\Pr(X \mid W)\Pr(W)}{\Pr(X)}. \]

Since \(\Pr(X)\) is independent of \(W\), the argmax reduces to:

\[ \boxed{\;\hat W = \arg\max_W \underbrace{\Pr(X \mid W)}_{\text{acoustic model}} \cdot \underbrace{\Pr(W)}_{\text{language model}}\;} \]

This factorization is the foundation of every ASR system. The acoustic model scores how well the audio matches each word; the language model scores how likely each word sequence is; the decoder searches for the best combined score.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Three levels of difficulty
docs.text:
Level Task Vocabulary Constraint Isolated word One word at a time, with pauses Small–medium No context Connected word Fluent speech, small set of words Small No language model Continuous speech Natural speech, large vocabulary 50k–1M+ words Full language model

Production systems today are continuous, large-vocabulary and usually speaker-independent, with vocabulary sizes ranging from 20k (dictation) to over a million (voice search), and language models trained on billions of sentences.

docs.title: 5.2.3 The standard pipeline
docs.text:
Audio  →  Pre-emphasis  →  Framing  →  Windowing  →  Feature
                                                     Extraction
                                                        ↓
                                             (MFCC / PLP / filterbank)
                                                        ↓
                        +-------------------------------------------------+
                        |                                                 |
                        |  Acoustic Model (HMM/DNN): p(X | W)             |
                        |  Language Model (n-gram / RNN): p(W)            |
                        |  Lexicon (dictionary): pronunciation rules      |
                        |  Decoder (Viterbi / WFST): search best W        |
                        |                                                 |
                        +-------------------------------------------------+
                                                        ↓
                                                     Text

Acoustic model. Scores the likelihood of the acoustic observations given a phoneme or word sequence. Historically HMM-GMM; now DNN/RNN/Transformer.

Language model. Scores the a priori likelihood of word sequences. Historically n-grams; now recurrent / Transformer LMs.

Lexicon. Maps words to phoneme sequences (pronunciation dictionary).

Decoder. Searches the combined model for the most likely word sequence. Dynamic-programming algorithm (Viterbi over the state lattice).

docs.title: 5.2.4 Specification of a typical application — voice response
docs.text:
A voice response system (e.g., an IVR menu) has much stricter constraints than dictation:

Requirement Value Vocabulary 10–100 commands (isolated words) Speaker dependency Speaker-independent preferred Noise tolerance Must work in a noisy environment Latency < 300 ms (user expects immediate response) Word accuracy > 98% (errors are more costly in an IVR than in dictation) Language One language, trained on domain-specific corpus

Design choices for an IVR.

  • Isolated word / small vocabulary — simpler acoustic model, no language model needed (or a small grammar).
  • MFCC features + HMM (or deep net) — the standard architecture.
  • Keyword spotting — listen for a small set of keywords in continuous speech, no full transcription needed. Simpler than full ASR.
  • Confirm-by-repeat — ask the user to repeat the choice for ambiguous cases (≥ 85% confidence).

The IVR is a classic engineering application — a small, well-defined problem where accuracy can be pushed to 99%+ with domain-specific training.

docs.title: 5.3.1 The need for time warping
docs.text:
The same word, spoken twice, has different durations — one utterance may take 400 ms, another 600 ms. A naive Euclidean distance between the feature sequences is meaningless — the sequences have different lengths and their features are misaligned in time.

DTW solves this by finding an optimal alignment — a monotone warping path that matches the two sequences frame-by-frame, allowing different speeds.

docs.title: 5.3.2 The DTW algorithm
docs.text:
Problem statement. Given two feature sequences

\[ X = (x_1, \ldots, x_M),\qquad Y = (y_1, \ldots, y_N), \]

with \(x_i, y_j \in \mathbb{R}^d\) (e.g., MFCC vectors, \(d = 13\)), find the alignment path \(\pi = ((\pi_1^X, \pi_1^Y), \ldots)\) that minimizes the accumulated cost:

\[ \boxed{\;\text{DTW}(X, Y) = \min_{\pi} \sum_{(i,j) \in \pi} d(x_i, y_j)\;} \]

subject to constraints:

  • Boundary: path starts at \((1,1)\) and ends at \((M,N)\).
  • Monotonicity: if \((i,j)\) follows \((i',j')\), then \(i \ge i'\) and \(j \ge j'\).
  • Step size: \((i,j)\) follows \((i',j')\) with \((i-i', j-j') \in \{(0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\}\) — path can only move right, up, or diagonally.
  • Locality: (optional) path stays within a band around the diagonal — the Sakoe–Chiba band \(|i/M - j/N| \le r\) or the Itakura parallelogram.

The DP recursion. Compute the accumulated cost matrix:

\[ \boxed{\;C(i,j) = d(x_i, y_j) + \min\begin{cases}C(i-1,j) & \text{(insertion)} \\ C(i,j-1) & \text{(deletion)} \\ C(i-1,j-1) & \text{(match)}\end{cases}\;} \]
