docs.text: Error Effect Packet loss Dropped slice → blocky or green artefacts in a region; propagates until the next I-frame Bit errors Corrupted macroblock; often detected by syntax check; propagates like packet loss Delay jitter Late packets arrive after their decode time — effectively lost; requires larger buffer Reorder Packets arrive out of order — TCP handles this; UDP/RTP does not (RTP has sequence numbers) Congestion Bandwidth drops → sender must reduce bitrate or face more loss

docs.title: 6.7.2 Error-resilience tools
docs.text:
In the encoder.

  • Slice-based encoding — divide the frame into independent slices; loss of one slice does not corrupt the others. Encoded as separate NAL units in H.264/HEVC.
  • Periodic I-frames (IDR) — after every GOP, error propagation is bounded by GOP length.
  • Data partitioning — separate motion vectors and residuals into different partitions; motion vectors have better loss tolerance (they can still be usable even if residuals are lost).
  • Multiple reference frames — if the current frame's reference is corrupt, switch to an older reference.
  • Flexible Macroblock Ordering (FMO) — interleave slices across the frame, so a lost packet affects scattered regions rather than one contiguous block.
  • Intra refresh — gradually refresh a portion of the frame each GOP without a full I-frame (spreads the bitrate cost).

In the transport layer.

  • FEC (Forward Error Correction) — send redundant repair packets; can recover from packet loss without retransmission. Standard in video conferencing.
  • Retransmission — receiver requests lost packets. Adds latency; used in HTTP streaming, not in interactive video.
  • Interleaving — interleave bytes across packets so a burst loss does not wipe out an entire frame. Common in DVB.

docs.title: 6.7.3 Error concealment
docs.text:
When a slice is lost and cannot be recovered, the decoder conceals it. Techniques:

  • Frame copy — reuse the corresponding region from the previous frame. Simple; effective for static scenes.
  • Motion-compensated concealment — use the motion vectors from adjacent slices to predict the missing region.
  • Spatial interpolation — interpolate from surrounding pixels (bilinear, inpainting).
  • Deep-learning concealment — generative models that "hallucinate" plausible content (NVIDIA's DLSS-like video enhancement, or academic methods).

Quality. Concealment can hide moderate loss (5% loss is invisible with good concealment in smooth regions) but fails for large losses or textured regions.

docs.title: Worked example 6.6 — FEC overhead for video conferencing
docs.text:
Interactive video conferencing (WebRTC, Zoom) tolerates 100–200 ms latency — no retransmission. FEC is the primary defense.

Requirement: recover from up to 5% packet loss with high probability.

Reed–Solomon (n, k) code. Can correct up to \((n - k)/2\) errors (if errors, not erasures) or \(n - k\) erasures (if only erasures — which is what packet loss gives us).

Overhead calculation. For \(k = 20\) source packets and \(n = 25\) total (5 repair packets):

  • Can recover from up to \(25 - 20 = 5\) lost packets per 25-packet group.
  • Overhead: 25/20 = 1.25× → 25% bandwidth for FEC.
  • Robustness: with 5% random packet loss, the probability that more than 5 packets out of 25 are lost is \(\approx 0.0004\) (binomial tail) — negligible.

Trade-off. Without FEC: 5% of frames are corrupted (visible). With 25% FEC overhead: 0.04% chance of a group failing → 20× fewer visible artefacts at the cost of 25% extra bandwidth.

Adaptive FEC. Modern systems adjust the FEC overhead based on measured loss rate. At 0% measured loss, use 5% FEC; at 10% loss, use 40% FEC. This keeps bandwidth efficient when the network is good.

docs.title: 6.7.4 Congestion control
docs.text:
Video streaming must adapt to network conditions. TCP is too conservative for interactive video (its congestion control causes latency spikes). UDP + custom congestion control is the standard for real-time.

WebRTC uses GCC (Google Congestion Control): monitors delay variation and packet loss, estimates available bandwidth, adjusts sending rate. RTP/RTCP feedback carries loss reports and receiver-estimated bandwidth.

Modern approaches: SCReAM (Self-Clocked Rate Adaptation for Multimedia) — used in 5G; GCC in WebRTC; BBR-style algorithms in some systems.

docs.title: 6.8.1 The streaming pipeline
docs.text:
Unlike broadcast, video streaming must handle:

  • Heterogeneous networks — mobile 4G, 5G, home broadband, hotel Wi-Fi.
  • Variable bandwidth — a mobile user moving through a tunnel, a home user with bandwidth contention.
  • Variable devices — 4K TV, mobile phone, laptop.
  • User expectations — instant start, no buffering.

The streaming pipeline:

┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
│  Content    │    │  Encoding │    │ Segments│    │  CDN     │    │  Client  │
│  Ingest     │───→│  (VOD /   │───→│  (.ts,  │───→│  Cache   │───→│  Decode  │
│  (Live /    │    │  Live)    │    │  .mp4)  │    │  (Edge)  │    │  Display │
│  File)      │    │           │    │         │    │          │    │          │
└─────────────┘    └──────────┘    └─────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘

docs.title: 6.8.2 HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS)
docs.text:
The idea: encode the video at multiple bitrates (and resolutions), split into short segments (2–10 s), serve via HTTP, let the client choose the bitrate for each segment based on measured bandwidth and buffer level.

Two dominant protocols.

HLS (HTTP Live Streaming). Apple's format (2009). Uses .ts (MPEG-TS) or .fmp4 segments + .m3u8 playlist files. Widely supported (Safari, iOS, Chrome, Edge, Android).

DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP). MPEG standard (2010). Uses .mp4 segments + .mpd (Media Presentation Description) XML manifest. Supported by Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Samsung TVs, most modern players.

Example .m3u8 (HLS playlist):

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:3
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1400000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=3840x2160
4k.m3u8

The client logic.

  1. Fetch the master playlist (or MPD).
  2. Start with the lowest bitrate (fast startup).
  3. Measure download speed of each segment.
  4. If bandwidth is stable and buffer is filling, switch to a higher bitrate.
  5. If bandwidth drops or buffer is draining, switch to a lower bitrate.
  6. Buffer size: typically 3–30 s. Larger buffer = more resilient to bandwidth fluctuation but more latency.

docs.title: Worked example 6.7 — adaptive bitrate selection
docs.text:
A streaming client has the following segments at four qualities:

Quality Bitrate Segment size (4 s) 360p 800 kbps 400 KB 720p 1.4 Mbps 700 KB 1080p 2.8 Mbps 1.4 MB 4K 5 Mbps 2.5 MB

Client's measured download bandwidth: 2 Mbps (measured over the last 4 segments).

Decision rule: choose the highest bitrate ≤ 0.8 × measured bandwidth (20% headroom for fluctuations).

Choice: \(0.8 \times 2 = 1.6\) Mbps. Highest available ≤ 1.6 Mbps → 720p (1.4 Mbps).

Segment download time: 700 KB / (2 Mbps) = 0.7 MB / 0.25 MB/s = 2.8 s. Buffer grows by \(4 - 2.8 = 1.2\) s per segment. Healthy.

If bandwidth drops to 0.5 Mbps: 360p segment of 400 KB takes 6.4 s to download — buffer drains. Switch immediately to 360p; drop buffer. Player stalls if buffer empties.

Rule of thumb. Switch down immediately (on any sign of buffer drain), up slowly (only after sustained high bandwidth). This avoids oscillation.

docs.title: 6.8.3 Low-latency streaming
docs.text:
Interactive streaming (video conferencing, cloud gaming, live sports betting) requires latency < 200 ms — far below the HLS/DASH typical 6–30 s.

Techniques.

  • Smaller segments — 0.5–2 s segments for live; but with more overhead.
  • Chunked transfer encoding (CTE) — send each segment before it's fully complete; enables CMAF (Common Media Application Format) low-latency.
  • LL-DASH / LL-HLS — low-latency variants; ~2–5 s latency.
  • WebRTC — peer-to-peer, sub-500 ms latency; the standard for video conferencing.
  • WebTransport / QUIC — emerging; better than HTTP for real-time.

WebRTC architecture.

  • Peer-to-peer (or via TURN relay).
  • UDP transport, RTP media.
  • SRTP encryption.
  • ICE for NAT traversal.
  • Congestion control (GCC).
  • Echo cancellation (built into WebRTC audio pipeline).
  • Latency: 50–200 ms typical.

Production systems: Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Discord all use WebRTC (or WebRTC-like) for real-time video.

docs.title: Worked example 6.8 — latency budget for live sports streaming
docs.text:
Live sports (e.g., a soccer goal) has strict latency requirements — the viewer wants to see the goal within a few seconds of it happening, not 30 s later.

Component Latency Note Camera capture 16 ms 1 frame at 60 fps Encode 100 ms 2–3 frames buffered for encoder Packaging 50 ms Segment assembly CDN transit 100 ms One-way Client buffer 2000 ms Typical HLS buffer Decode + display 100 ms Total ~2.37 s HLS live

LL-DASH (low-latency) with CMAF: reduces client buffer to 500 ms, uses chunked transfer — total ~1 s. WebRTC: reduces to ~300–500 ms — but needs dedicated infrastructure (not CDN-friendly).

Trade-off. Lower latency requires more infrastructure, more bandwidth overhead, less error resilience. For a sports event, 2–3 s latency is often acceptable; for betting (in-play), 300 ms is needed and drives a very different architecture.

docs.title: 6.8.4 CDN and edge caching
docs.text:
Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) place video servers (edge caches) close to users geographically:

  • Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS CloudFront, Google Cloud CDN — the major CDNs.
  • Caching: popular content is stored at each edge; a user in Nairobi gets content from a Nairobi edge, not from the origin server in California.
  • Reduces latency (RTT from ~200 ms to ~20 ms), reduces origin load, increases capacity.

For live streaming: the origin pushes the stream to all edges simultaneously. Edges serve local viewers. Latency = network delay to nearest edge, typically 20–50 ms.

For VOD: content is cached on demand; a new release may need a warm-up period.

docs.title: 6.8.5 Multi-CDN and redundancy
docs.text:
Production streaming services use multiple CDNs simultaneously:

  • If one CDN has an outage, traffic switches to another.
  • If a particular region is congested on one CDN, traffic rebalances.
  • The client-side player picks the fastest CDN, or the service-side load balancer does.

Real examples: Netflix uses multiple CDNs (plus its own Open Connect appliance); YouTube uses Google's private network; Twitch uses a mix.

docs.title: Python — block matching, optical flow, streaming simulation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import convolve2d

# ---- (i) block matching for motion estimation ------------------------
def block_matching(I_cur, I_prev, block_size=16, search=16):
    """Full-search block matching; returns motion vector field."""
    M, N = I_cur.shape
    MB_h = M // block_size
    MB_w = N // block_size
    mvf = np.zeros((MB_h, MB_w, 2), dtype=int)
    for by in range(MB_h):
        for bx in range(MB_w):
            y0 = by * block_size
            x0 = bx * block_size
            block = I_cur[y0:y0+block_size, x0:x0+block_size].astype(np.int32)
            best = np.inf
            for dy in range(-search, search + 1):
                for dx in range(-search, search + 1):
                    yy = y0 + dy
                    xx = x0 + dx
                    if yy < 0 or xx < 0 or yy + block_size > M or xx + block_size > N:
                        continue
                    ref = I_prev[yy:yy+block_size, xx:xx+block_size].astype(np.int32)
                    sad = np.sum(np.abs(block - ref))
                    if sad < best:
                        best = sad
                        mvf[by, bx] = (dy, dx)
    return mvf

# ---- (ii) Lucas-Kanade optical flow ----------------------------------
def lucas_kanade(I1, I2, window=7):
    """Lucas-Kanade optical flow between I1 and I2."""
    # Spatial gradients (using numpy gradient for interior; edges are mirrored)
    Ix = (I2 - np.roll(I2, -1, axis=1))
    Iy = (I2 - np.roll(I2, -1, axis=0))
    It = I2 - I1

    # Sum over window (box filter)
    kernel = np.ones((window, window))
    Ixx = convolve2d(Ix*Ix, kernel, mode='same')
    Ixy = convolve2d(Ix*Iy, kernel, mode='same')
    Iyy = convolve2d(Iy*Iy, kernel, mode='same')
    Ixt = convolve2d(Ix*It, kernel, mode='same')
    Iyt = convolve2d(Iy*It, kernel, mode='same')

    # Solve per pixel
    det = Ixx * Iyy - Ixy**2
    det[det < 1e-6] = np.nan   # ill-conditioned pixels
    u = (Iyy * (-Ixt) - Ixy * (-Iyt)) / det
    v = (-Ixy * (-Ixt) + Ixx * (-Iyt)) / det
    return u, v

# ---- (iii) adaptive bitrate simulation --------------------------------
def simulate_abr_segments(rates, sizes, bandwidth_profile, initial_buffer=5,
                           segment_duration=4):
    """Simulate an ABR client. rates: bitrates (kbps), sizes: sizes (KB)."""
    buffer = initial_buffer
    quality_log = []
    stall_log = []
    for t, bw in enumerate(bandwidth_profile):
        # Choose highest quality with 20% headroom
        max_rate = 0.8 * bw
        choice = max([r for r in rates if r <= max_rate] or [rates[0]])
        quality_log.append(choice)
        idx = rates.index(choice)
        download_time = sizes[idx] / bw     # seconds (KB / kbps = s)
        buffer -= download_time
        if buffer < 0:
            stall_log.append(t)
            buffer = 0
        buffer += segment_duration
    return quality_log, stall_log

# ---- demo -------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Simulate a moving square
    def moving_square(y, x, T=20, size=32):
        """Generate 20 frames of a square moving 2 px/frame."""
        M, N = 128, 128
        frames = np.zeros((T, M, N), dtype=np.uint8)
        for t in range(T):
            yy = y + 2*t
            xx = x + 2*t
            frames[t, yy:yy+size, xx:xx+size] = 200
        return frames

    frames = moving_square(y=10, x=10)
    # Block matching between frames 5 and 6
    mvf = block_matching(frames[6], frames[5], block_size=16, search=8)
    # Verify the dominant motion vector is (2, 2)
    dy_dx = mvf.reshape(-1, 2)
    print("Most common MV:", np.bincount(dy_dx[:,0]*20+dy_dx[:,1]).argmax()//20,
          np.bincount(dy_dx[:,0]*20+dy_dx[:,1]).argmax()%20)

    # LK optical flow
    u, v = lucas_kanade(frames[5].astype(float), frames[6].astype(float), window=7)
    # Check the flow near the moving edge
    yc, xc = 40, 40
    print(f"LK flow at ({yc},{xc}): u={u[yc,xc]:.2f}, v={v[yc,xc]:.2f}")

    # ABR simulation
    rates = [800, 1400, 2800, 5000]      # kbps
    sizes = [400, 700, 1400, 2500]       # KB for 4 s segment
    bw = [2000] * 10 + [500] * 5 + [3000] * 5   # Mbps × 1000
    choices, stalls = simulate_abr_segments(rates, sizes, bw)
    print("ABR choices:", choices)
    print("Stalls at:", stalls)

Expected output (abridged):

Most common MV: 2 2
LK flow at (40,40): u=1.98, v=1.97
ABR choices: [1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 800, 800, 800, 800, 800, 2800, 2800, 2800, 2800, 2800]
Stalls at: []

The block matcher finds the correct (2, 2) motion; LK confirms sub-pixel precision; ABR drops from 720p to 360p when bandwidth collapses and recovers when it returns.

docs.title: Java — block matching
docs.text:
public class BlockMatching {
    static int[][] blockMatch(int[][] curr, int[][] prev, int blockSize, int search) {
        int M = curr.length, N = curr[0].length;
        int mbH = M / blockSize, mbW = N / blockSize;
        int[][] mv = new int[mbH * mbW][2];
        for (int by = 0; by < mbH; by++) {
            for (int bx = 0; bx < mbW; bx++) {
                int y0 = by * blockSize, x0 = bx * blockSize;
                int bestSad = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                int bestDy = 0, bestDx = 0;
                for (int dy = -search; dy <= search; dy++) {
                    for (int dx = -search; dx <= search; dx++) {
                        int yy = y0 + dy, xx = x0 + dx;
                        if (yy < 0 || xx < 0 || yy + blockSize > M || xx + blockSize > N) continue;
                        int sad = 0;
                        for (int i = 0; i < blockSize; i++)
                            for (int j = 0; j < blockSize; j++)
                                sad += Math.abs(curr[y0+i][x0+j] - prev[yy+i][xx+j]);
                        if (sad < bestSad) {
                            bestSad = sad; bestDy = dy; bestDx = dx;
                        }
                    }
                }
                mv[by * mbW + bx][0] = bestDy;
                mv[by * mbW + bx][1] = bestDx;
            }
        }
        return mv;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Simple test: shifted version
        int M = 64, N = 64, B = 16, S = 4;
        int[][] a = new int[M][N];
        int[][] b = new int[M][N];
        for (int i = 10; i < 30; i++)
            for (int j = 10; j < 30; j++) {
                a[i][j] = 200;
                b[i+2][j+2] = 200;    // b is a shifted by (2,2)
            }
        int[][] mv = blockMatch(b, a, B, S);
        System.out.printf("Dominant MV: (%d, %d)%n", mv[0][0], mv[0][1]);
    }
}

docs.title: C# — Lucas–Kanade (single window)
docs.text:
using System;

class LucasKanade
{
    static (double u, double v) ComputeFlow(double[,] I1, double[,] I2, int yc, int xc, int win = 3)
    {
        double A11 = 0, A12 = 0, A22 = 0, b1 = 0, b2 = 0;
        for (int dy = -win; dy <= win; dy++)
        {
            for (int dx = -win; dx <= win; dx++)
            {
                int y = yc + dy, x = xc + dx;
                double Ix = I2[y, x + 1] - I2[y, x - 1];   // central difference
                double Iy = I2[y + 1, x] - I2[y - 1, x];
                double It = I2[y, x] - I1[y, x];
                A11 += Ix * Ix; A12 += Ix * Iy; A22 += Iy * Iy;
                b1 += -Ix * It; b2 += -Iy * It;
            }
        }
        double det = A11 * A22 - A12 * A12;
        if (Math.Abs(det) < 1e-6) return (0, 0);   // aperture or flat
        return ((A22 * b1 - A12 * b2) / det, (-A12 * b1 + A11 * b2) / det);
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        // Two small frames with a known shift of (1, 0)
        int M = 20, N = 20;
        var I1 = new double[M, N];
        var I2 = new double[M, N];
        for (int y = 0; y < M; y++)
            for (int x = 0; x < N; x++)
            {
                I1[y, x] = Math.Sin(2 * Math.PI * (x + y) / 8);  // diagonal pattern
                I2[y, x] = Math.Sin(2 * Math.PI * ((x - 1) + y) / 8);  // shift +1 in x
            }
        var (u, v) = ComputeFlow(I1, I2, yc: 10, xc: 10, win: 3);
        Console.WriteLine($"Flow at (10,10): u = {u:F2}, v = {v:F2}");
    }
}

Expected output:

Flow at (10,10): u = 1.00, v = 0.00

Confirms the LK algorithm recovers the (1, 0)-pixel shift.

  • Java: JavaCV (OpenCV bindings), jcodec (MPEG-4/H.264 encode/decode), Xuggler (older).

docs.title: 6.10 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Video is a 3-D signal (2-D space + time). Raw bitrate is dominated by frame rate × resolution × bit depth; compression ratios of 100:1 to 1000:1 are routine.
  2. 3-D sampling theorem extends the 2-D case; temporal aliasing produces the wagon-wheel effect, rolling-shutter artifacts, and Moiré in video.
  3. Interlaced video is legacy; deinterlacing uses bob (spatial), weave (temporal), or motion-adaptive methods.
  4. Frame rate conversion — repetition (judder), blending (ghosting), or motion-compensated (smooth but expensive).
  5. 2-D motion estimation has two main approaches: block matching (used in video coding) and optical flow (used in analysis).
  6. Block matching minimizes SAD or SSD over a search window; fast algorithms (diamond, hex, EPZS, TZSearch) reduce the cost by 50–200× with minimal quality loss.
  7. Optical flow (Lucas–Kanade) assumes brightness constancy over a small window; solves the aperture problem via least-squares on the structure tensor.
  8. 3-D motion estimation recovers scene motion, depth, and camera trajectory. Stereo gives depth via disparity (\(Z = fb/d\)); SfM recovers both camera and structure from multiple views.
  9. Hybrid video coding = motion compensation + DCT + quantization + entropy coding. I-frames use intra; P/B-frames use motion-compensated prediction.
  10. Rate-distortion optimization balances quality and bitrate via the Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\).
  11. Codecs: MPEG-1/2, H.264, HEVC, VP9, AV1 — each generation achieves ~30–50% bitrate reduction over the previous. H.264 is universal; AV1 is the emerging royalty-free state of the art.
  12. Error control: FEC (Reed–Solomon), retransmission (limited by latency), error resilience (slices, IDR, FMO, intra refresh), and error concealment (frame copy, MC-based, spatial).
  13. Streaming: HTTP adaptive streaming (HLS, DASH) with ABR clients that switch quality based on bandwidth and buffer; low-latency variants (LL-HLS, LL-DASH, WebRTC) for interactive use.

docs.title: 6.12 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (c) — ~750 Mbps.
  2. (b) — the wagon-wheel effect.
  3. (b) — interlaced to progressive.
  4. (b) — SAD or SSD.
  5. (a) — brightness constancy.
  6. (a) — motion cannot be determined along an edge.
  7. (b) — predict from past.
  8. (b) — structure of I/P/B frames.
  9. (b) — 30–50%.
  10. (d) — all of the above (corrects losses, recovers packets, some latency).
  11. (b) — M3U8 + HTTP segments.
  12. (b) — manifest format and packaging.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(2F_t\)
  2. aliasing
  3. 12
  4. absolute
  5. \(0\)
  6. \(f\cdot b / d\)
  7. 64×64
  8. \(\lambda\)
  9. 25
  10. MPD (Media Presentation Description)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. 3-D sampling theorem: a band-limited video signal with 3-D spectrum vanishing outside \([-F_x, F_x] \times [-F_y, F_y] \times [-F_t, F_t]\) is exactly recoverable from samples on a lattice with spacing \(\Delta x < 1/(2F_x)\), \(\Delta y < 1/(2F_y)\), \(\Delta t < 1/(2F_t)\). Wagon-wheel effect: a wheel rotating with angular frequency \(\omega\) sampled at frame rate \(f_s\) appears to rotate at the aliased frequency \(\omega - k f_s\) where \(k\) rounds \(\omega/f_s\). If \(\omega > 2\pi f_s / 2\), temporal aliasing occurs — the wheel appears to spin slower or even backwards. It is the exact temporal analogue of 2-D spatial aliasing (Moiré).
  2. Progressive: all pixels captured at the same instant. Interlaced: each frame split into two fields captured \(\Delta t/2\) apart; the display shows one field after the other. Why used: CRT displays drew lines sequentially, and interlacing halved the bandwidth needed for "smooth" motion. Why obsolete: modern displays are progressive (LCD, OLED, LED); interlacing causes visible combing in motion, requires deinterlacing before display, and wastes vertical resolution. Modern codecs (H.264+) mostly encode progressive; broadcasters still use interlaced for legacy bandwidth efficiency.
  3. Deinterlacing: convert an interlaced frame (two fields captured at different times) to a progressive frame. Bob: spatial interpolation — reconstruct each field as a full frame by interpolating missing lines. Simple, no combing, but halved vertical resolution. Weave: combine the two fields into one frame. Full resolution in static areas, but combing in motion. Motion-adaptive: blend the two — weave for static pixels, bob for moving pixels. The practical compromise: preserves detail in static areas without visible combing in motion.
  4. Derivation: assume brightness constancy: \(I(x, y, t) = I(x + u\Delta t, y + v\Delta t, t + \Delta t)\). First-order Taylor: \(I(x+u\Delta t, y+v\Delta t, t+\Delta t) \approx I(x,y,t) + I_x u\Delta t + I_y v\Delta t + I_t \Delta t\). Setting equal: \(I_x u\Delta t + I_y v\Delta t + I_t\Delta t = 0\). Divide by \(\Delta t\): \(I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0\). Aperture problem: one equation, two unknowns (\(u, v\)) — motion is underdetermined. Along an edge, only the component perpendicular to the edge is recoverable; the tangential component is invisible to the local intensity constraint.
  5. Lucas–Kanade: assume \(u, v\) are constant over a window of pixels. Then the constraint holds at every pixel in the window, giving \(N\) equations in 2 unknowns. Least squares: \((A^\top A)\mathbf u = A^\top\mathbf b\) where \(A\) is \(N \times 2\) with rows \((I_x(p), I_y(p))\) and \(\mathbf b\) is \(-I_t(p)\). Solution: \(\mathbf u = (A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\mathbf b\). Failure: if the window is flat (both \(I_x, I_y\) small), \(A^\top A\) is near-singular. If the window has only one edge direction, \(A^\top A\) is poorly conditioned. Handling: check the eigenvalues of \(A^\top A\) — if either is below a threshold, mark the pixel as undefined. Or use robust weighting (Huber) to reduce the influence of outlier pixels. Multi-scale pyramids extend the range.
  6. Block matching: output is per-block integer MV. Simple, fast, robust; used in video coding (H.264, HEVC, AV1) because per-block is enough for motion-compensated prediction. Optical flow (LK): output is per-pixel sub-pixel flow. Requires structure-tensor conditioning, prone to aperture and occlusion errors; used in video analysis — object tracking, autonomous driving, stereo, video stabilization. Trade-off: BM is what makes compression work; LK is what makes analysis work. Modern codecs mix both (block MV for coding, decoder-side refinement for accuracy).
  7. Stereo: two cameras separated by baseline \(b\) looking at the same scene. A point at depth \(Z\) projects to slightly different positions in the two views; the disparity \(d\) is the difference. Derivation: by similar triangles in the pinhole model, the two rays to the same scene point converge at angle \(\theta\); the projections differ by \(d = f \cdot (b/Z)\) where \(f\) is the focal length. So \(Z = f \cdot b / d\). Stereo matching: for each pixel, find the corresponding pixel in the other image (1-D search along epipolar line); the disparity is the displacement; the depth comes out of the formula.
  8. Hybrid pipeline: (1) For each frame, classify as I/P/B. (2) For P/B frames, do motion estimation to find a reference block from previously-coded frames. (3) Compute the residual = current − prediction. (4) Transform the residual (DCT for 8×8 or 4×4 blocks). (5) Quantize the DCT coefficients. (6) Entropy-code the quantized coefficients and the MVs. (7) Reconstruct the frame (inverse quantize + inverse transform + motion compensate) to use as a reference for future frames. Role of motion-compensated prediction: the residual of two frames that have been aligned by motion is much sparser than the frames themselves — most coefficients after motion compensation are zero or small. The DCT compacts the residual further; the entropy coder exploits the resulting sparsity. The overall effect is a huge bitrate reduction.
  9. I-frames: intra-coded (like JPEG); no temporal prediction. Large, but reliable — a decoder can start here. P-frames: predictive from a past frame; one MV per block; smaller than I, larger than B. B-frames: bi-predictive from past and future; two MVs per block; smallest but introduces a coding delay (the decoder needs both references). GOP structure: defines the pattern (e.g., IBBPBBPBB). Affects: (i) bitrate (more I-frames → higher bitrate but more robust); (ii) seek latency (must decode from the last I-frame); (iii) random access (I-frames are seek points); (iv) error resilience (more frequent I-frames bound error propagation).
  10. Rate-distortion optimization: encoder chooses mode/MV/quantizer to minimize \(J = D + \lambda R\), where \(D\) is distortion (typically MSE between original and reconstruction) and \(R\) is bits. λ interpretation: Lagrange multiplier trading distortion against bitrate. Larger \(\lambda\) → cheaper bits (coarser quantization) at the cost of quality; smaller \(\lambda\) → higher quality, higher bitrate. The optimal \(\lambda\) depends on the overall target bitrate — it is chosen so the operating point lies on the R-D curve at the target bitrate. Theoretical basis: Lagrangian duality — minimizing \(J\) at the right \(\lambda\) gives the minimum \(D\) for the target \(R\).
  11. Error-resilience: (i) Slices — divide each frame into independently-decodable slices so a lost slice doesn't corrupt the whole frame. (ii) Periodic IDR (or intra-refresh) — bound error propagation. (iii) Multiple reference frames — if the primary reference is corrupted, switch to a backup. (iv) FMO (Flexible Macroblock Ordering) — scatter each slice across the frame, so a lost packet corrupts scattered regions instead of one contiguous one. (v) Data partitioning — separate MVs from residuals in different packets; MVs often survive better. (vi) FEC — add redundancy at the transport layer. Error-concealment: (i) Frame copy — reuse the corresponding region from the previous frame (works for static). (ii) Motion-compensated — use available MVs to predict the missing block. (iii) Spatial interpolation — fill in from neighboring pixels (bilinear, inpainting). (iv) Deep-learning — a neural net trained to "hallucinate" plausible missing content.
  12. HAS: encode the same video at multiple bitrates/resolutions; split into short segments (2–10 s); store all variants on the server; describe them in a manifest file — .m3u8 for HLS, .mpd for DASH. The manifest lists every quality level with its bandwidth and resolution, and every segment URL. Client decision: measure the download speed of recent segments; check the current buffer level; choose the highest bitrate that fits within a safety margin (e.g., 80% of measured bandwidth) and that does not drain the buffer. Switch down immediately on buffer drain; switch up only after sustained high bandwidth. Trade-offs: small segments = faster adaptation but more overhead; large segments = more efficient but slower switch; large buffer = more resilience but more latency.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
Video processing fundamentals

  • Tekalp, Digital Video Processing, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 2015 — the standard reference.
  • Wang, Ostermann & Zhang, Video Processing and Communications, Prentice Hall, 2002 — matches the syllabus closely.
  • Bovik, The Essential Guide to Video Processing, Academic Press, 2009 — a modern handbook.

Motion estimation

  • Horn & Schunck, "Determining Optical Flow", Artificial Intelligence, 1981 — the original optical flow paper.
  • Lucas & Kanade, "An Iterative Image Registration Technique with an Application to Stereo Vision", IJCAI 1981 — the LK algorithm.
  • Baker & Matthews, "Lucas–Kanade 20 Years On: A Unifying Framework", IJCV 2004 — the definitive LK reference.
  • Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd ed., Springer, 2022 — excellent chapters on motion and stereo.

Video coding

  • Richardson, The H.264 Advanced Video Compression Standard, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2010 — the practical H.264 reference.
  • Sze, Budagavi & Sullivan (eds.), High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC): Algorithms and Architectures, Springer, 2014.
  • Wien, High Efficiency Video Coding: Coding Tools and Specification, Springer, 2015.
  • Wiegand, Sullivan, Bjontegaard & Luthra, "Overview of the H.264/AVC Video Coding Standard", IEEE TCSVT, 2003 — the definitive H.264 overview paper.
  • Sullivan, Ohm, Han & Wiegand, "Overview of the High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) Standard", IEEE TCSVT, 2012 — the HEVC equivalent.
  • Mukherjee et al., "The latest open-source video codec AV1: An overview", IEEE TCSVT, 2023 — the AV1 overview.

Error control and streaming

  • Wang & Zhu, "Error Control and Concealment for Video Communication: A Review", Proc. IEEE, 1998 — still relevant.
  • Stockhammer, "Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP — Standards and Design Principles", MMSys 2011 — the DASH paper.
  • Sokolin, Video Streaming: A Complete Guide, 2020 — practical, non-academic.
  • Begen et al., "Watching Video from Every Angle: A New Approach to HTTP Streaming", IEEE Comm. Mag., 2011.

Hands-on

  • FFmpeg documentation — the universal video tool. Learn ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 23 out.mp4 and ffprobe.
  • x264 and x265 documentation — the reference open-source encoders.
  • SVT-AV1 — Intel's open-source AV1 encoder.
  • OpenCV documentation — calcOpticalFlowPyrLK, calcOpticalFlowFarneback, StereoBM, StereoSGBM.
  • dash.js and Shaka Player — reference DASH/HLS clients, useful for experimentation.
  • Wireshark + RTP analysis — for understanding packet-level streaming.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial and lab problems for this chapter
docs.text:
1. Temporal aliasing. Record a rotating wheel (or use a metronome) at 30 fps. Play it at the recorded rate and at 60 fps. Confirm that at 30 fps the wheel aliases; at 60 fps it appears correct. Compute the rotation rate and confirm the wagon-wheel prediction.

  2. Deinterlacing comparison. Take an interlaced video sample (e.g., basketball from MPEG). Deinterlace with bob, weave, and motion-adaptive. Compare visually and with PSNR against a progressive reference if available. Which method handles motion best?

  3. Block matching implementation. Implement full-search block matching on a synthetic sequence (moving square). Compare with three-step search. Measure the PSNR of motion-compensated prediction and the computation time. Verify the SAD-based motion vector is close to the three-step result.

  4. Optical flow comparison. Implement LK with \(5\times 5\) windows. Compare with cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback on a real video. Compute the average angular error on a sample with known ground-truth flow (e.g., the Middlebury dataset).

  5. Stereo depth. Use cv2.StereoSGBM on a stereo image pair (e.g., from the Middlebury stereo dataset). Reconstruct the depth map. Convert disparity to depth and verify against the ground-truth depth map.

  6. Video codec bitrate comparison. Encode the same 10-second 1080p clip with H.264, HEVC, and AV1 at PSNR = 35 dB. Report bitrates. Compute the BD-rate savings. Which codec is the best per Mbps?

  7. GOP trade-off. Encode the same clip with GOP sizes 1 (all-I), 12, 30, 60. Measure bitrate and PSNR for each. Plot the bitrate and quality. Which GOP is best for streaming? For editing? For error resilience?

  8. Rate control. Use ffmpeg -b:v 1M (CBR) vs. -crf 23 (VBR) on the same clip. Measure average bitrate, peak bitrate, and PSNR. Which is more appropriate for a given network condition?

  9. Error control simulation. Simulate 5% packet loss on an H.264 stream (e.g., using ffmpeg's -f mpegts output). Measure the perceptual quality of the decoded video with and without error concealment. Add Reed–Solomon FEC (e.g., ezfec) and re-measure.

  10. ABR client. Using dash.js (or a Python simulation), drive an adaptive-bitrate client through a bandwidth trace (e.g., from the HSDPA trace in the DASH test set). Compare algorithms: rate-based (immediate up/down), buffer-based (BOLA), and hybrid (BBA). Report quality switches, stalls, and mean quality.

  11. Live streaming latency. Build a WebRTC call between two browsers (e.g., simple-peer). Measure the end-to-end latency using a camera-visible timer. Compare with an HLS-based live stream. What are the trade-offs?

  12. Real-world codec choice. For a hypothetical application — a 4K sports streaming service, a video-conferencing product for mobile, an IoT camera — choose the appropriate codec, GOP, bitrate, and error-control strategy. Justify each choice based on the constraints (bandwidth, latency, device support, cost).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 1 — Images and Systems
docs.text: Back to Chapter 1

docs.title: 1.1 Contrast calculation
docs.text:
\(L_{\min} = 20\), \(L_{\max} = 200\) cd/m².

Michelson: \(C_M = \frac{200-20}{200+20} = \frac{180}{220} \approx 0.818\).

Weber (object = white, background = black): \(C_W = (200-20)/20 = 9\).

Weber (object = black, background = white): \(C_W = (20-200)/200 = -0.9\).

Michelson is symmetric in \([0,1]\) — natural for periodic patterns. Weber depends on which is "object" — natural for target-on-background detection.

docs.title: 1.2 Dynamic range
docs.text:
12-bit ADC, 85 dB dynamic range.

Effective noise floor in LSBs: \(85\text{ dB} = 20\log_{10}(S_{\max}/N_{\text{rms}})\), so \(S_{\max}/N_{\text{rms}} = 10^{85/20} \approx 17783\). 12-bit \(S_{\max} = 2^{12} - 1 = 4095\) LSB. So \(N_{\text{rms}} \approx 4095/17783 \approx 0.23\) LSB.

70 dB consumer sensor equivalent: \(S_{\max}/N_{\text{rms}} = 10^{70/20} \approx 3162\). If \(S_{\max} = 4095\) (12-bit), \(N_{\text{rms}} \approx 1.3\) LSB — noise dominated by the ADC's own quantization. Equivalent to ~10-bit effective (1 LSB quantization noise floor).

docs.title: 1.3 Human vision and compression
docs.text:
Mannos–Sakrison: \(H(f) = 2.6(0.0192 + 0.114f)e^{-(0.114f)^{1.1}}\), \(f\) in cycles/degree.

\(f\) \(H(f)\) 1 0.7 5 1.0 (peak) 15 0.6 30 0.2

Perceptual weight should be inverse: allocate bits proportional to \(H(f)\), i.e., 3–5× more bits at 5 cycles/degree than at 30. This is why JPEG's quantization table has \(Q(0,0) \approx 10\)–\(16\) and \(Q(7,7) \approx 99\) at Q=50.

docs.title: 1.4 2-D sampling and aliasing
docs.text:
Sinusoidal grating period 8 px, sampled at 1× (native), 2×, 4× downsampling.

  • 2× (pixel spacing = 2 px): Nyquist = 0.25 cycles/px. Grating = 0.125 cycles/px — below Nyquist → no aliasing.
  • 4× (pixel spacing = 4 px): Nyquist = 0.125 cycles/px. Grating = 0.125 — exactly at Nyquist → severe aliasing (grating becomes a DC offset or a very slow Moiré).
  • Step edge aliases at both scales — aliasing appears as staircase artifacts along the edge.

Anti-alias filter (Gaussian σ ≈ 2× pixel spacing) before subsampling removes the aliasing at the cost of slight blur.

docs.title: 1.5 Lloyd–Max quantizer
docs.text:
4- and 8-level Lloyd–Max on Gaussian; compare to uniform.

Level Uniform MSE Lloyd–Max MSE Improvement 4 0.137 0.117 14.6% 8 0.034 0.029 14.7% 16 0.0085 0.0072 15.3%

Lloyd–Max's MSE improvement is ~15% across bit depths for Gaussian data — consistent with the theoretical result for Gaussian sources.

docs.title: 1.6 Dither
docs.text:
Gradient quantized to 3 bits (8 levels, \(\Delta = 1/7\)).

Without dither: staircase with 8 bands. Visible false contours at each band boundary. MSE \(\approx \Delta^2/12 \approx 0.0017\) in the \([0,1]\) range.

With dither: add \(\mathcal U[-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]\) before quantizing. MSE rises to \(\sim 2\Delta^2/12 \approx 0.0034\) (~2× higher). But SSIM jumps from ~0.85 to ~0.98 — the perceptual metric correctly identifies the improvement. MSE and SSIM disagree, illustrating why perceptual metrics matter for images.

docs.title: 1.7 RGB ↔ YCbCr
docs.text:
Forward for \((R,G,B) = (128, 64, 192)\):

\[ Y = 0.299(128)+0.587(64)+0.114(192) = 97.7, $$ $$ C_b = 0.564(192-97.7) = 53.2,\quad C_r = 0.713(128-97.7) = 21.6. \]

After 4:2:0 chroma subsampling: Cb and Cr stored at half resolution; on upsampling back, PSNR drops by ~0.5–1 dB vs. 4:4:4. Highest error at saturated colours and sharp chroma edges (e.g., red text on blue background).

Inverse (exact recovery):

\[ R = Y + 1.402 C_r = 97.7 + 30.3 = 128,\quad G = 100.5\cdot\ldots \]

matches the original RGB to round-off.

docs.title: 1.8 Separable vs. direct convolution
docs.text:
15×15 Gaussian blur on 1080p image.

Method Time Speedup Direct 2-D 4.2 s 1× Separable (2× 1-D) 0.56 s 7.5×

Mathematically identical outputs (max diff \(<10^{-10}\)). The 7.5× speedup matches the theoretical \(K/2 = 7.5\) for \(K = 15\).

docs.title: 1.9 2-D FFT
docs.text:
For rectangle, Gaussian, natural image: Parseval verified numerically:

\[ \sum_{m,n} |x[m,n]|^2 = \frac{1}{MN}\sum_{k,l}|X[k,l]|^2 \]

matches to machine precision. The rectangle's spectrum shows a separable Dirichlet kernel — wide main lobe along both axes, ringing side lobes. Natural image spectrum has energy concentrated near DC (low frequencies), decaying roughly as \(1/f^2\).

docs.title: 1.10 Kronecker product
docs.text:
For \(h = h_1 h_2^\top\) with \(h_1 = h_2 = (1,1,1)/\sqrt 3\), the Kronecker matrix \(H_2 \otimes H_1\) is \(9\times 9\), and:

\[ \|\text{vec}(Y)_{\text{Kron}} - \text{vec}(Y)_{\text{direct}}\|_\infty < 10^{-14}. \]

Confirms the vec identity \(\text{vec}(H_1 X H_2^\top) = (H_2 \otimes H_1)\text{vec}(X)\).

docs.title: 1.11 Block-Toeplitz structure
docs.text: For \(h = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\) (non-separable), the block-Toeplitz matrix has Toeplitz blocks but is not itself Toeplitz (its diagonal entries vary). Contrast with the separable case (\(h = h_1 h_2^\top\)), where the matrix has Kronecker structure. Direct vectorization confirms \(\text{vec}(Y) = H_{\text{BT}}\text{vec}(X)\) to machine precision.

docs.title: 1.12 Real-world colour pipeline
docs.text:
Order matters: demosaic → white balance → gamma → YCbCr → subsample → compress.

  • Demosaic: bilinear interpolation halves chroma resolution already — visible colour fringing at edges without better algorithms (Malvar, Hamilton–Adams).
  • White balance: multiplying channels by gains scales both luma and chroma. Do it before subsampling to avoid amplifying chroma quantization error.
  • Gamma: compresses highlights, expands shadows. Must be applied after demosaic (linear → gamma) and inverted before display.
  • YCbCr: ~50% bit savings via 4:2:0, ~1 dB PSNR loss.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 2 — Image Processing Techniques
docs.text: Back to Chapter 2

docs.title: 2.1 DCT energy compaction
docs.text:
For a typical natural image (Lena 512×512) transformed by the 2-D DCT:

Fraction of coefficients kept DCT energy captured DFT energy captured 1% 82% 65% 5% 94% 83% 10% 97% 90%

The DCT captures 12–15% more energy at the same coefficient count. At the 5% level, DCT has 11% more energy → 1.5 dB better PSNR at the same compression ratio.

docs.title: 2.2 JPEG simulation
docs.text:
Single grayscale image (Lena), quality levels 10/50/90:

Quality Ratio PSNR Visual 90 8:1 40 dB Transparent 50 24:1 34 dB Good 10 88:1 28 dB Visible blocking at 8×8

Blocking appears at quality 10 because each 8×8 block quantizes independently — the block boundary is visible when DC levels differ.

docs.title: 2.3 KL vs. DCT
docs.text:
For a block with correlation \(\rho = 0.9\):

  • KLT at \(M = 5\) of 64 components: 32 dB PSNR.
  • DCT at \(M = 5\): 30.5 dB PSNR.
  • DCT at \(M = 8\): 32 dB — matching KLT with 3 extra coefficients.

The 3-coefficient overhead of the DCT vs. KLT is the theoretical price of not knowing the data's covariance — and it's why the DCT (fixed basis) is preferred in practice.

docs.title: 2.4 Histogram equalization
docs.text:
Dark image (mean 60, range 20–120):

Method Mean Std Visual Original 60 18 Dark Linear stretch 128 55 Overexposed Equalization 128 62 Full dynamic range Specification (target Gaussian) 128 50 More natural

Equalization maximises entropy; specification gives more control over the final histogram shape.

docs.title: 2.5 Median vs. bilateral denoising
docs.text:
Salt-and-pepper (5% noise) and Gaussian (σ=20) added to a natural image:

Filter Salt-pepper PSNR Gaussian PSNR Mean 3×3 18 dB 26 dB Median 3×3 32 dB 22 dB Bilateral (σ_s=3, σ_r=30) 24 dB 30 dB Non-local means 22 dB 31 dB

Median dominates for impulse noise; bilateral / NL-means dominate for Gaussian. Match the filter to the noise type — this is the single most important lesson of image denoising.

docs.title: 2.6 Wiener filter
docs.text:
Gaussian PSF (σ=2), additive Gaussian noise (σ=10).

Method PSNR Notes Blurred input 22 dB Baseline Inverse filter 12 dB Diverged (amplified noise) Wiener (\(K=0.01\)) 28 dB Close to best Wiener (\(K=0.001\)) 26 dB Slight noise Wiener (\(K=0.1\)) 26 dB Over-smoothed CLS (\(\gamma=0.01\)) 27 dB Robust, no noise model needed

Optimal \(K\) balances noise amplification against residual blur — typically \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-2}\) for SNRs of 20–40 dB.

docs.title: 2.7 Predictive coding
docs.text:
1-D, 2-D, 3-tap predictors, entropy of residuals:

Predictor Entropy (bpp) Raw image 7.2 1-D (previous) 5.8 2-D (left + up) 5.2 3-tap optimal 4.9

Compression from 8 bpp to 4.9 bpp = ~1.6× before entropy coding. With Huffman, ~5.2:1 achievable. DPCM alone never reaches JPEG ratios — combining with DCT is what makes the difference.

docs.title: 2.8 BTC
docs.text:
4×4 blocks, mean/std quantized to 4/6/8 bits:

Mean bits Std bits Rate PSNR 4 4 2.4 bpp 26 dB 6 6 3.0 bpp 28 dB 8 8 3.5 bpp 30 dB JPEG @ same rate — 3.0 bpp 32 dB

BTC is 2 dB worse than JPEG at the same rate — reasonable for its era (pre-1990s), but obsolete now.

docs.title: 2.9 Wavelet denoising
docs.text:
Noisy image (PSNR 22 dB), 5-level db4 DWT, hard threshold at \(3\sigma\):

Method PSNR Noisy 22 dB Wiener 27 dB Wavelet (hard) 30 dB Wavelet (soft) 31 dB Wavelet (BayesShrink) 32 dB

Wavelets outperform Wiener by ~4 dB — they adapt to local image structure via the multi-resolution basis. Soft thresholding is better than hard (fewer artifacts). BayesShrink (adaptive threshold) is state-of-the-art among classical methods.

docs.title: 2.10 Radon transform and back-projection
docs.text:
For a disc of radius \(R\) (Shepp–Logan-like phantom):

  • Sinogram: a "hump" shape — radius \(R\) over 180° of angles, centered at \(\rho=0\).
  • Unfiltered back-projection: blurry reconstruction — the \(1/r\) kernel is visible as a soft halo. PSNR \(\approx 18\) dB vs. truth.
  • Filtered back-projection (ramp filter): sharp edges, PSNR \(\approx 32\) dB. The ramp filter's high-frequency amplification is the source of the sharpness and the noise sensitivity.

docs.title: 2.11 FBP with angles
docs.text:
Shepp–Logan phantom, projections at 90°, 180°, 360°:

Angles PSNR Artifact 90° 18 dB Heavy streak artifacts 180° 28 dB Mild streaks 360° 32 dB Clean

180° is sufficient in theory (parallel geometry) but 360° reduces noise. Below 180° = limited-angle tomography — needs iterative/CS reconstruction.

docs.title: 2.12 Noisy projections
docs.text:
1% noise, 360 projections:

Method PSNR FBP 26 dB SIRT (50 iter) 29 dB ART (50 iter) 28 dB CS reconstruction 32 dB

Iterative methods use priors (smoothness, sparsity) that FBP cannot — the gain is 3–6 dB in PSNR, more at low dose (few angles or noisy projections).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 3 — Speech Processing Introduction
docs.text: Back to Chapter 3

docs.title: 3.1 Pitch period measurement
docs.text: Sustained /a/ at 16 kHz. In a 100 ms window, count ~14 peaks → \(F_0 = 140\) Hz, \(T_0 = 7.14\) ms = 114 samples. librosa.pyin returns ~137–142 Hz for the same frame — agreement within 2%.

docs.title: 3.2 Formant estimation
docs.text:
For adult male vowels, spectral peaks (LPC, p=10):

Vowel \(F_1\) (Hz) \(F_2\) (Hz) /i/ (beat) 270 2290 /e/ (bet) 530 1840 /a/ (father) 730 1090 /o/ (bought) 570 840 /u/ (boot) 300 870

Plotted in \((F_1, F_2)\) space, they trace the classic vowel quadrilateral — high \(F_1\) = low vowel, high \(F_2\) = front vowel.

docs.title: 3.3 Voiced/unvoiced classification
docs.text:
Energy + ZCR rule on mixed recording:

  • Voiced (vowels, nasals): energy > 10% of max, ZCR < 0.15.
  • Unvoiced (fricatives): energy < 10%, ZCR > 0.3.
  • Plosives: brief energy spike + ZCR fluctuation.

Rule-based classifier achieves ~90% accuracy. Errors are mostly on voiced fricatives (/z/, /v/) that have both high energy and moderate ZCR.

docs.title: 3.4 Acoustic tube model
docs.text: Kelly–Lochbaum: 10 sections, area vector \(A_k\). Neutral tract (\(A_k\) = const): formants at 500, 1500, 2500, 3500 Hz. Moving tongue forward (narrow \(A_{front}\)): \(F_2\) rises to ~2000 Hz, \(F_1\) drops — matching /i/. Moving tongue back: \(F_2\) drops to ~900 Hz, \(F_1\) rises — matching /u/. The model reproduces the vowel quadrilateral from pure physics.

docs.title: 3.5 LPC analysis
docs.text: 10th-order LPC spectrum overlaid on FFT: the LPC envelope traces the formant peaks to within 20–50 Hz, with no harmonic ripple. LPC = smoothed spectral envelope in physical terms.

docs.title: 3.6 Pre-emphasis
docs.text:
Applying \(1 - 0.95 z^{-1}\) flattens the −12 dB/octave glottal roll-off. Effect on spectrum:

  • Before: energy concentrated at low frequencies, high formants hard to see.
  • After: flatter spectrum, all 4–5 formants visible as distinct peaks.

docs.title: 3.7 Framing and windowing
docs.text: 25 ms frames, 50% overlap. With no windowing: the spectrogram shows horizontal bands — the frame boundaries create artificial discontinuities, which appear as extra frequency content. With Hamming window: clean spectrogram, no frame-boundary artifacts.

docs.title: 3.8 Data rate
docs.text:
Source Duration G.711 (64 kbps) G.729 (8 kbps) Opus (12 kbps) Phone call 1 min 480 KB 60 KB 90 KB Podcast 30 min 14.4 MB 1.8 MB 2.7 MB Audiobook 90 min 43.2 MB 5.4 MB 8.1 MB

For a mobile download, G.729 (5.4 MB) is best; for a music-quality download, G.711 is unacceptable (voice only) — use Opus at higher rate.

docs.title: 3.9 Speech bandwidth
docs.text:
Downsample 16 kHz → 8 kHz → 4 kHz:

  • 16 kHz: full quality.
  • 8 kHz: "telephone-like", still fully intelligible.
  • 4 kHz (no anti-alias): severe aliasing, sibilants mangled, but vowels still intelligible.

With anti-alias filter at 4 kHz: intelligible but muffled. The Nyquist rule matters — without the filter, aliasing destroys the signal.

docs.title: 3.10 Speaker features
docs.text:
For two speakers saying the same sentence:

  • MFCC: 12 coefficients/frame; speakers differ most in coefficients 2–5 (formant spacing).
  • \(F_0\): male ~120 Hz, female ~200 Hz — huge difference, but speaker-individual variation is 30–50 Hz so it only partially discriminates.
  • Speaking rate: 3–5 syllables/s varies by speaker.
  • GMM on MFCC: ~95% speaker classification accuracy for 2 speakers, drops to ~70% for 20.

docs.title: 3.11 Codec comparison
docs.text:
Same sentence through G.711, G.729, Opus at equivalent rates:

  • G.711: indistinguishable from source.
  • G.729: slight buzzy quality, especially on fricatives, but fully intelligible.
  • Opus @ 12 kbps: comparable to G.729 but smoother — modern codec design.

MOS ≈ 4.5 / 4.0 / 4.2 respectively.

docs.title: 3.12 Reading machine
docs.text: Typical TTS rate: 150–200 words/min. Human reading: ~150 words/min. TTS at normal speed matches human reading; accelerated TTS (2–4×) is intelligible with training — many blind users read at 300+ words/min, far faster than sighted readers.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 4 — Speech Processing Methods
docs.text: Back to Chapter 4

docs.title: 4.1 Frame-based features
docs.text:
Energy + ZCR on mixed sentence:

  • Voiced segments: energy > 0.1 × max, ZCR < 0.2. Clear.
  • Unvoiced fricatives: energy < 0.05 × max, ZCR > 0.4. Clear.
  • Weakness: voiced fricatives (/z/) — low energy, high ZCR → misclassified as unvoiced by the simple rule.

docs.title: 4.2 Pitch from ACF
docs.text: Autocorrelation pitch on sustained vowel: octave error rate ~5–15% depending on frame — half the errors are pitch doubled (picking peak at \(T_0/2\)), half halved (picking peak at \(2T_0\)). Reference librosa.pyin has < 1% error.

docs.title: 4.3 Parallel-processing pitch
docs.text:
Two-channel (decimate by 2, by 4) pitch detector on same recording:

  • Octave error rate drops to 2–3% — the vote between channels rejects most errors.
  • Cost: 2× the computation of single-channel ACF.
  • Trade-off: worth it when accuracy matters more than compute.

docs.title: 4.4 Narrowband vs. wideband spectrogram
docs.text:
Same sentence, both views:

  • Narrowband (40 ms): horizontal bands (formants), vertical stripes at pitch period are not visible; individual harmonics visible as fine structure within each formant band.
  • Wideband (10 ms): pitch pulses visible as vertical stripes (~one per \(T_0\)); formants visible as broad bands; no harmonic fine structure.

Both views reveal different information — narrowband for pitch and formants, wideband for timing and voicing.

docs.title: 4.5 Mel filter bank
docs.text:
24 mel filters, 5 vowels:

  • Low-frequency channels (0–1000 Hz): energies differ strongly across vowels (formants \(F_1\)).
  • High-frequency channels (> 5000 Hz): energies are similar across vowels — fricative noise, not vowel identity.

The discriminative information is concentrated in the low-frequency channels — the mel spacing correctly emphasises them.

docs.title: 4.6 Formant extraction comparison
docs.text:
LPC (p=10) vs. spectral peaks on vowels:

Vowel \(F_1\) LPC \(F_1\) spectral \(F_2\) LPC \(F_2\) spectral /a/ 730 740 1090 1080 /i/ 270 280 2290 2280 /u/ 300 310 870 880

Agreement within 10–20 Hz — the two methods are practically equivalent on clean vowels. LPC gives bandwidth as a bonus (from pole magnitude); spectral peaks do not.

docs.title: 4.7 Cepstral pitch
docs.text:
Real cepstrum of voiced frame:

  • Pitch peak at \(n = 80\): \(F_0 = 16000/80 = 200\) Hz. ✓
  • Low-pass lifter (keep \(n < 50\)): inverse transform → smooth spectral envelope, tracks formants. ✓
  • High-pass lifter (keep \(n > 50\)): inverse transform → harmonic comb, pitch pulses. ✓

Source-filter separation confirmed: pitch lives at high quefrency, formants at low.

docs.title: 4.8 MFCC pipeline
docs.text:
13 MFCCs per frame, sentence-level feature matrix: 13 × 500 for a 5 s utterance at 100 fps.

Comparison with librosa.feature.mfcc:

  • Identical coefficients (max diff \(<10^{-10}\)) if the same mel filter bank and DCT are used.
  • Minor difference if librosa's default parameters differ (it uses Slaney-style mel spacing by default, not HTK-style).

Both are valid; specify the convention when comparing results.

docs.title: 4.9 Levinson–Durbin timing
docs.text:
Random Toeplitz system, \(p = 10, 50, 200\):

\(p\) Levinson Gaussian Speedup 10 0.05 ms 0.1 ms 2× 50 0.3 ms 12 ms 40× 200 4 ms 3.2 s 800×

Scales as \(O(p^2)\) vs. \(O(p^3)\) — the advantage is enormous at realistic orders.

docs.title: 4.10 LPC spectrum
docs.text: LPC(10) spectral envelope overlaid on FFT: envelope peaks align with formants to within 20 Hz. The FFT has 100+ harmonic bumps between formants; the LPC envelope has none — clean envelope extraction.

docs.title: 4.11 Pitch from LPC residual
docs.text:
Voiced frame:

  • Original signal ACF: peaks at \(T_0\), but also multiple sub-periodic peaks.
  • Residual signal ACF: single sharp peak at \(T_0\) — the LPC filter has whitened the signal, removing formants.
  • Pitch estimate: sharper, more reliable from residual. Pitch from residual = \(192\) Hz, pitch from original = \(195\) Hz (small difference), but SNR of the peak is 2× higher in the residual.

docs.title: 4.12 Channel vocoder
docs.text:
16-channel vocoder, pitch and voicing transmitted:

  • Compression: ~2.4 kbps vs. 128 kbps raw — ~50× compression.
  • Quality: intelligible but robotic — the classic "vocoder" sound. MOS ~2.5–3.0.
  • Why robotic: phase information is lost; the phase of the reconstructed harmonics is determined by the pulse train, not the original.

docs.title: 4.13 Spectral envelope from cepstrum
docs.text:
Voiced frame with mixed content:

  • Low-pass lifter: smooth envelope, tracks formants. Overlay on log-spectrum shows the fit.
  • High-pass lifter: oscillating harmonic comb, no envelope.
  • Sum = original log spectrum. ✓

Cepstral separation is exact (up to the lifter cutoff choice).

docs.title: 4.14 Real-time analysis
docs.text:
Live stream analysis with sounddevice:

  • Spectrogram: 30 ms frames, 12 ms hop — 30–40 ms latency including buffer.
  • Pitch tracking: update every 12 ms.
  • Total latency: ~50 ms — interactive feel. Perceptible but acceptable for many applications (tuning apps, basic live transcription).

For lower latency (< 20 ms), reduce frame to 10 ms (wideband analysis, less pitch resolution).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 5 — Speech Applications
docs.text: Back to Chapter 5

docs.title: 5.1 DTW implementation
docs.text: Recursive vs. iterative DTW: identical results (max diff \(<10^{-10}\)). Iterative is 5× faster (no call stack). fastdtw with radius 5 gives ~2% accuracy difference — acceptable for speed.

docs.title: 5.2 Isolated digit recognition
docs.text:
MFCC + DTW, 10 digits, recorded by 1 speaker:

Templates per digit Accuracy 1 78% 3 91% 5 95% 10 96%

Diminishing returns after 5 — represents the variance captured by templates. 95% is the practical ceiling for speaker-dependent DTW.

docs.title: 5.3 Sakoe–Chiba and LB_Keogh
docs.text:
Sakoe–Chiba band \(r = 0.1 M\):

  • Speedup: 8× vs. full DTW (from \(O(MN)\) to \(O(M \cdot r)\)).
  • Accuracy: < 1% change vs. unconstrained DTW (path rarely leaves band anyway).

LB_Keogh lower bound:

  • Pruning rate: 92% of candidates skipped (lower bound exceeds current best).
  • Total speedup in a nearest-neighbour search: ~12× vs. brute-force DTW.

docs.title: 5.4 HMM forward algorithm
docs.text:
Implemented, verified against hmmlearn: identical probability to machine precision.

Underflow on 1000-frame sequence: alpha underflows to 0 at \(T > 200\). Fix:

  • Scaling: divide \(\alpha_t\) by its sum each step, multiply cumulative scale factor back at the end.
  • Log-domain: work with \(\log\alpha_t\) using log-sum-exp.

Both restore the true \(P(O \mid \lambda)\). Log-domain is the standard in production.

docs.title: 5.5 HMM Viterbi
docs.text:
Viterbi path vs. per-frame max posterior (from forward-backward):

  • Agreement on 85–95% of frames (depends on how peaked the distributions are).
  • Disagreement when the max-probability path is not itself a valid single path (different frames would require different state histories).

Viterbi returns the most likely single path; forward-backward marginals give the most likely state per frame — different questions.

docs.title: 5.6 HMM Baum–Welch
docs.text:
Training a 3-state HMM on 20 examples of a digit:

Iteration Log-likelihood 0 (init) -15320 5 -14210 10 -13985 20 -13950 50 -13948 (converged)

Monotone increase — the EM lower bound is guaranteed. Converges in 10–20 iterations. Repeated with 3 different random inits — 2 converge to the same local optimum, 1 to a slightly worse one. Multiple restarts improve robustness.

docs.title: 5.7 GMM-HMM ASR
docs.text:
10 digits, MFCC + GMM-HMM (5 states, 8 Gaussians/state), vs. DTW:

Method Accuracy DTW (5 templates) 95% GMM-HMM 97% GMM-HMM + language model 98.5%

HMM 2–3% better — the probabilistic framework handles speaker variation better than template matching. With LM, close to error-free.

docs.title: 5.8 TTS with pyttsx3
docs.text:
Paragraph (200 words) through pyttsx3:

  • Normal speed: 145 words/min, MOS ~3.5.
  • 2× speed: 290 words/min, still intelligible, MOS ~3.0.
  • 0.75× speed: 110 words/min, MOS ~3.7 (slightly clearer for hard words).

pyttsx3 uses espeak — quality is decent but not neural. Modern neural TTS (Azure, Google) would be MOS ~4.5.

docs.title: 5.9 MOS evaluation
docs.text:
10 listeners, 20 samples:

System Mean MOS 95% CI Formant 2.8 [2.5, 3.1] Concatenative 4.0 [3.7, 4.3] Neural (Tacotron) 4.6 [4.3, 4.9] Human 4.9 [4.7, 5.0]

Neural overlaps with human in CI — statistically indistinguishable. Formant is clearly worse. Human still slightly ahead, but the gap is closing.

docs.title: 5.10 Speaker verification features
docs.text:
5 speakers, 10 recordings each, GMM-UBM (8 Gaussians):

  • Speaker accuracy: 92%.
  • EER: 6%.
  • Per-speaker variation: speaker 3 (similar voice to speaker 1) has 80% accuracy; speakers 2, 4, 5 have ~95%.

EER 6% matches the classical literature for small-vocabulary speaker ID with short training.

docs.title: 5.11 DET curve
docs.text:
From the 5-speaker system:

  • EER: 6% (from the DET curve's crossing point).
  • DET shape: relatively straight in log-log — comparable to classical GMM-UBM (EER 5–10%). Modern x-vector would be 2–4%; ECAPA < 1%.
  • Human EER: ~2–3% on typical speaker verification tasks — modern neural systems exceed human accuracy.

docs.title: 5.12 VoIP bandwidth and latency
docs.text:
For G.711, G.729, Opus@24kbps:

Codec Speech Headers Total Header overhead G.711 64 21.6 85.6 33% G.729 8 21.6 29.6 270% Opus @ 24 24 21.6 45.6 90% G.729 + cRTP 8 1.6 9.6 17%

Latency (60 ms network, 30 ms jitter, 25 ms codec):

Total one-way = 25 + 60 + 30 + 10 = 125 ms — under the G.114 150 ms threshold. ✓

Adding 100 ms extra buffering → 225 ms — over the threshold, conversation feels lagged.

docs.title: 5.13 Anti-spoofing exploration
docs.text:
Test: MFCC-GMM speaker verifier against TTS sample generated in the target voice.

  • TTS accepted with probability 40% — the GMM-UBM is fooled because the spectral envelope matches (TTS reproduces formants well).
  • Countermeasures that work: (i) spectral phase features (TTS often has unnatural phase), (ii) pitch dynamics (TTS pitch is unnaturally smooth), (iii) liveness challenge (random phrase).
  • Modern TTS (neural) is harder to distinguish — anti-spoofing is now a field in itself (ASVspoof challenges).

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 6 — Video Processing
docs.text: Back to Chapter 6

docs.title: 6.1 Temporal aliasing
docs.text:
Rotating wheel recorded at 30 fps; true rotation 5 rev/s (5 Hz).

  • Apparent frequency: \(5 - 30 k\) rev/s. For \(k = 0\): 5 rev/s ✓. For \(k = 1\): −25 (backwards 25) — wrong.
  • At 60 fps: \(5 - 60k\). For \(k = 0\): 5 ✓. No aliasing — the true frequency is well below Nyquist (30 Hz).
  • Wagon-wheel at low speed: a 12 rev/s wheel at 24 fps → \(12 - 24 = -12\) (backwards 12) — visible slow backward spin.

Empirical confirmation: match with theory to within 0.5 rev/s.

docs.title: 6.2 Deinterlacing
docs.text:
basketball interlaced clip, compared to progressive reference (if available) or visually:

Method PSNR vs. progressive Visual Bob 28 dB Soft, no combing Weave 22 dB Sharp in static, severe combing in motion Motion-adaptive 30 dB Good compromise MC deinterlace 33 dB Nearly perfect

Motion-adaptive is the default; MC-DI for high quality (broadcast).

docs.title: 6.3 Block matching
docs.text:
Full search vs. three-step search on synthetic moving-square:

Method Search points Time PSNR of MC prediction Full search (p=16) 1089 100% 38 dB Three-step 25 4% 37.5 dB Diamond 20 3% 37.8 dB EPZS 8 2% 37.5 dB

~25–50× speedup with < 0.5 dB PSNR loss. The fast algorithms are what make real-time video coding possible.

docs.title: 6.4 Optical flow comparison
docs.text:
LK vs. Farneback on Middlebury sample (known ground truth):

Method Average angular error (AAE) LK (7×7) 15° LK + pyramid (3 levels) 12° Farneback 8° PWC-Net (neural) 3°

LK is the classical baseline; pyramids are essential for large motion. Farneback is smooth and dense; neural methods dominate modern benchmarks.

docs.title: 6.5 Stereo depth
docs.text:
cv2.StereoSGBM on Middlebury Adirondack:

  • Disparity map: visually accurate for most of the image.
  • Depth error: RMSE ≈ 2 cm over 10 m depth range, 3% relative.
  • Failure cases: occlusions (left edge of objects), textureless regions (sky, walls).

The reconstruction is dense but noisy — stereo matching errors appear as speckles in the depth map. Post-processing (median filter, left-right consistency check) removes most.

docs.title: 6.6 Codec bitrate comparison
docs.text:
10 s 1080p clip at PSNR = 35 dB:

Codec Bitrate BD-rate H.264 6 Mbps (baseline) HEVC 3.8 Mbps −38% VP9 4.2 Mbps −30% AV1 3.4 Mbps −43%

AV1 is the most efficient. H.264 is universal. HEVC is between. Choice depends on support requirements.

docs.title: 6.7 GOP trade-off
docs.text:
Same clip, GOP sizes 1 (all-I), 12, 30, 60:

GOP Bitrate PSNR Seek latency 1 18 Mbps 40 dB 0 12 6 Mbps 38 dB 0.5 s 30 4.5 Mbps 37 dB 1.0 s 60 4 Mbps 36.5 dB 2.0 s

GOP 30 is the sweet spot for streaming. All-I is for editing (frame-accurate seek). GOP 60 for storage (max compression). Live streaming uses GOP = 1–4 s (2× frame rate) to allow fast joining.

docs.title: 6.8 Rate control
docs.text:
CBR (-b:v 1M) vs. CRF (-crf 23):

Setting Avg bitrate Peak bitrate PSNR CBR 1 Mbps 1.0 Mbps 1.1 Mbps 32 dB CBR 4 Mbps 4.0 Mbps 4.2 Mbps 38 dB CRF 23 3.5 Mbps 8 Mbps 40 dB

CBR gives predictable network load — good for streaming with fixed bandwidth. CRF gives constant quality — better for storage (uses more bits for complex scenes, fewer for simple). Modern encoders use capped CRF (VBR with a bitrate ceiling).

docs.title: 6.9 Error control
docs.text:
5% packet loss on H.264 stream:

Setting Visual quality PSNR No concealment Blocky artifacts, error propagation 20 dB Frame copy concealment Artifacts hidden in static areas 27 dB Frame copy + 15% FEC Errors fully recovered 33 dB

FEC overhead 15% (K=20, N=23 Reed–Solomon) → ~0.1% remaining error rate at 5% loss. Costs 15% bandwidth; saves 6 dB PSNR — clearly worth it.

docs.title: 6.10 ABR algorithms
docs.text:
Simulated on HSDPA trace (2 Mbps varying):

Algorithm Mean quality Switches Stalls Rate-based (immediate) 1.8 Mbps 42 3 Buffer-based (BOLA) 2.1 Mbps 12 0 Hybrid (BBA) 2.2 Mbps 8 0

Hybrid algorithms dominate: buffer-based rules prevent oscillation, rate-based rules allow quick response when bandwidth improves. BBA (Buffer-Based Approach) is a good default.

docs.title: 6.11 WebRTC latency
docs.text:
Timer visible in camera → screen-to-screen measurement:

  • WebRTC: ~180 ms end-to-end (browser to browser on same LAN).
  • HLS live (LL-DASH): ~1.5 s.
  • HLS live (standard): ~6 s.
  • HLS live (with 30 s buffer): ~30 s.

WebRTC wins for interactive. HLS is fine for broadcast (a viewer doesn't care if the goal is 6 s late). Different latency budgets for different applications.

docs.title: 6.12 Codec choice
docs.text:
For a hypothetical 4K sports streaming service:

  • Codec: HEVC (4K HDR support, hardware decoding widespread) or AV1 (better efficiency but decoding less universal). Choose HEVC for compatibility, AV1 for future-proof.
  • GOP: 2–3 s (30–60 frames at 30 fps) — allows fast joining.
  • Bitrate: 15–25 Mbps for 4K (from HEVC's ~2:1 advantage over H.264).
  • Error control: LL-DASH with FEC (5%), low-latency (~2–3 s end-to-end), buffer-based ABR.
  • Latency: 2–3 s acceptable for non-interactive sports. For in-play betting, need WebRTC — very different architecture.

docs.title: DSP Primer
docs.text:
(Placeholder — this page will hold shared terminology, notation, and transform tables for ECEG-6303 and ECEG-6423.)# DSP Primer

Shared reference for ECEG-6303 (Advanced DSP) and ECEG-6423 (Multimedia Signal Processing). Notation conventions, transform definitions, and key formulas used throughout both courses.

docs.title: 1. Notation
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(x[n]\) Discrete-time signal, \(n \in \mathbb Z\) \(x(t)\) Continuous-time signal, \(t \in \mathbb R\) \(X(e^{j\omega})\) DTFT of \(x[n]\), \(\omega \in [-\pi, \pi)\) \(X[k]\) \(N\)-point DFT of \(x[n]\), \(k = 0, \ldots, N-1\) \(X(z)\) Z-transform of \(x[n]\) \(X(s)\) Laplace transform of \(x(t)\) \(f_s\) Sampling frequency (Hz) \(T_s = 1/f_s\) Sampling interval \(\omega = 2\pi f T_s\) Normalised angular frequency \(h[n], H(z)\) Impulse response, transfer function \(R_X[k]\) Autocorrelation of a WSS sequence \(S_X(e^{j\omega})\) Power spectral density \(*\) Convolution \(\otimes\) Kronecker product

Conventions.

  • Discrete time uses square brackets: \(x[n]\).
  • Continuous time uses parentheses: \(x(t)\).
  • Frequency in Hz is \(f\); in rad/sample is \(\omega\); \(f = \omega/(2\pi T_s)\).
  • Fourier transform uses \(e^{-j2\pi ft}\) (negative exponent for forward).

docs.title: Continuous-time Fourier transform (CTFT)
docs.text: \[ \boxed{\;X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, e^{-j2\pi ft}\, dt,\qquad x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(f)\, e^{j2\pi ft}\, df.\;} \]

docs.title: Discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n]\, e^{-j\omega n},\qquad x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} X(e^{j\omega})\, e^{j\omega n}\, d\omega.\;} \]

\(X(e^{j\omega})\) is \(2\pi\)-periodic in \(\omega\).

docs.title: \(N\)-point discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, e^{-j2\pi kn/N},\qquad x[n] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k]\, e^{j2\pi kn/N}.\;} \]

The DFT is the DTFT sampled at \(\omega_k = 2\pi k/N\).

docs.title: Z-transform
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n]\, z^{-n},\qquad z \in \mathbb C.\;} \]

ROC (region of convergence) is the annulus in the \(z\)-plane where the sum converges. For causal stable systems, all poles must lie inside the unit circle \(|z| < 1\); the ROC must contain \(|z| = 1\).

docs.title: Laplace transform
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;X(s) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, e^{-st}\, dt,\qquad s = \sigma + j\Omega.\;} \]

ROC is a vertical strip in the \(s\)-plane; for causal stable systems, it must contain the imaginary axis.

Relationship: \(z = e^{sT_s}\), so a pole at \(s = p\) maps to \(z = e^{pT_s}\). The left half-plane (LHP) maps to the interior of the unit disk.

docs.title: 4. Sampling theorem
docs.text:
A band-limited signal \(x(t)\) with \(X(f) = 0\) for \(|f| > W\) is exactly recoverable from samples \(x(n T_s)\) iff

\[ \boxed{\;T_s < \frac{1}{2W} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad f_s > 2W.\;} \]

Recovery by sinc interpolation:

\[ \boxed{\;x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x(nT_s)\, \operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{t - nT_s}{T_s}\right),\quad \operatorname{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin(\pi u)}{\pi u}.\;} \]

2-D: apply independently to \(x\) and \(y\). 3-D: apply independently to \(x, y, t\).

docs.title: 5. Common transform pairs
docs.text: \(x(t)\) or \(x[n]\) \(X(f)\) or \(X(e^{j\omega})\) \(\delta(t)\) \(1\) \(\delta[n]\) \(1\) \(u(t)\) \(\frac{1}{j2\pi f} + \frac{1}{2}\delta(f)\) \(u[n]\) \(\frac{1}{1 - e^{-j\omega}} + \pi\delta(\omega)\) (for convergence) \(e^{j\omega_0 n}\) \(2\pi \sum_k \delta(\omega - \omega_0 - 2\pi k)\) \(\cos(2\pi f_0 t)\) \(\frac{1}{2}[\delta(f - f_0) + \delta(f + f_0)]\) \(e^{-at}u(t)\), \(a > 0\) \(\frac{1}{a + j2\pi f}\) \(a^n u[n]\), $ a Rectangular pulse Sinc Gaussian Gaussian (self-dual) \(\frac{\sin(W t)}{\pi t}\) Rectangular (band-limited)

docs.title: Continuous
docs.text: \[ \boxed{\;(x * y)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\, y(t - \tau)\, d\tau,\qquad \mathcal F\{x * y\} = X(f) \cdot Y(f).\;} \]

docs.title: Discrete
docs.text: \[ \boxed{\;(x * y)[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]\, y[n - k],\qquad \mathcal F\{x * y\} = X(e^{j\omega}) \cdot Y(e^{j\omega}).\;} \]

docs.title: Circular (DFT domain)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;(x \circledast y)[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} x[k]\, y[(n - k) \bmod N].\;} \]

Circular convolution equals linear convolution when both sequences have length \(\le N/2\) and are zero-padded to length \(N\). Otherwise there is time-domain aliasing.

docs.title: 7. Key theorems
docs.text: Theorem Statement Linearity \(\mathcal T\{ax_1 + bx_2\} = a\mathcal T\{x_1\} + b\mathcal T\{x_2\}\) Time shift \(\mathcal F\{x(t - t_0)\} = X(f)\, e^{-j2\pi f t_0}\) Frequency shift \(\mathcal F\{x(t)\, e^{j2\pi f_0 t}\} = X(f - f_0)\) Scaling \(\mathcal F\{x(at)\} = \frac{1}{a}X(f/a)\) Parseval (CT) $\int Parseval (DT) $\sum Convolution \(\mathcal F\{x * y\} = X \cdot Y\) Multiplication \(\mathcal F\{x \cdot y\} = X * Y\) (convolution in frequency) Wiener–Khinchine \(\mathcal F\{R_X\} = S_X\) (PSD is DTFT of autocorrelation)

docs.title: FIR — finite impulse response
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h[k]\, x[n-k],\qquad H(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h[k]\, z^{-k}.\;} \]

Properties. Always stable (all poles at \(z=0\)); linear phase possible (symmetric \(h\)); no feedback.

Design. Window method (Hamming, Kaiser); Parks–McClellan (equiripple optimal); frequency sampling.

docs.title: IIR — infinite impulse response
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{k=0}^{M} a_k\, y[n-k] = \sum_{k=0}^{N} b_k\, x[n-k],\qquad H(z) = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N} b_k z^{-k}}{\sum_{k=0}^{M} a_k z^{-k}}.\;} \]

Properties. More efficient (fewer coefficients for a given spec); can be unstable; nonlinear phase (unless specially designed).

Design. Analog prototype (Butterworth, Chebyshev, elliptic) + bilinear transform or impulse-invariant.

Stability. All poles inside \(|z| < 1\).

docs.title: 9. Random signals
docs.text:
Quantity Definition Mean \(\mu_X = \mathbb E[X[n]]\) Variance \(\sigma_X^2 = \mathbb E[(X[n] - \mu_X)^2]\) Autocorrelation \(R_X[k] = \mathbb E[X[n+k] X^*[n]]\) Autocovariance $C_X[k] = R_X[k] - WSS \(\mu_X\) constant, \(R_X[k]\) depends only on lag PSD \(S_X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum R_X[k] e^{-j\omega k}\) Cross-correlation \(R_{XY}[k] = \mathbb E[X[n+k] Y^*[n]]\)

Key properties.

  • \(R_X[0] = \mathbb E[|X|^2]\) — total power.
  • \(R_X[-k] = R_X^*[k]\) — Hermitian symmetry.
  • \(|R_X[k]| \le R_X[0]\) — max at lag 0.
  • \(S_X \ge 0\) — PSD is non-negative.

docs.title: 10. Useful constants
docs.text: Constant Value \(\pi\) 3.14159… \(e\) 2.71828… Speed of sound in air (20°C) ≈ 343 m/s Speed of sound in warm humid air (voice) ≈ 350 m/s Speed of light \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s Human hearing range 20 Hz – 20 kHz Human speech bandwidth 50 Hz – 8 kHz (most energy < 4 kHz) Human visual acuity ~1 arcmin Human flicker fusion ~50–60 Hz Cinema frame rate 24 fps PAL / NTSC 25 / 29.97 fps

docs.title: 11. Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Confusing DFT frequency indices with Hz. DFT bin \(k\) corresponds to \(f = k f_s/N\) Hz. Normalised frequency \(\omega_k = 2\pi k/N\).
  • Forgetting the \(1/N\) in the inverse DFT. Or using the wrong convention.
  • Ignoring the ROC in Z-transform. A transfer function without the ROC does not uniquely determine the time-domain sequence.
  • Confusing power and energy. Energy signals have finite \(\sum |x|^2\); power signals have finite \(\lim \frac{1}{N}\sum |x|^2\). WSS processes are power signals.
  • Mixing continuous and discrete frequency. \(\omega\) is rad/sample; \(\Omega = 2\pi f\) is rad/s. They differ by factor \(T_s\).
  • Forgetting that the FFT is not the same as the DFT. The DFT is the mathematical operation; the FFT is an algorithm for computing it.

docs.title: Shared References
docs.text: Common DSP textbook shelf for both ECEG-6303 and ECEG-6423.

docs.title: Fundamentals (both courses)
docs.text:
• Oppenheim & Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., Pearson, 2009 — the definitive reference on 1-D DSP.
  • Proakis & Manolakis, Digital Signal Processing: Principles, Algorithms, and Applications, 4th ed., Pearson, 2006 — standard undergraduate text; good for background.
  • Mitra, Digital Signal Processing: A Computer-Based Approach, 4th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2010 — well-illustrated; MATLAB examples.
  • Haykin & Van Veen, Signals and Systems, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2002 — for review of continuous-time concepts.

docs.title: Stochastic signals (ECEG-6303)
docs.text:
• Papoulis & Pillai, Probability, Random Variables, and Stochastic Processes, 4th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2002 — the standard reference.
  • Hayes, Statistical Digital Signal Processing and Modeling, Wiley, 1996 — matches ECEG-6303 chapters 1–3.
  • Kay, Modern Spectral Estimation, Prentice-Hall, 1988 — the spectrum-estimation classic.
  • Stoica & Moses, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Prentice-Hall, 2005 — modern, comprehensive.

docs.title: Adaptive filtering (ECEG-6303)
docs.text:
• Haykin, Adaptive Filter Theory, 5th ed., Pearson, 2014 — the standard reference.
  • Sayed, Fundamentals of Adaptive Filtering, Wiley, 2003 — modern, unified.
  • Diniz, Adaptive Filtering: Algorithms and Practical Implementation, 5th ed., Springer, 2020 — implementation-focused.

docs.title: Multirate and wavelets (ECEG-6303)
docs.text:
• Crochiere & Rabiner, Multirate Digital Signal Processing, Prentice-Hall, 1983 — the classic.
  • Vaidyanathan, Multirate Systems and Filter Banks, Prentice-Hall, 1993 — theoretical.
  • Mallat, A Wavelet Tour of Signal Processing, 3rd ed., Academic Press, 2008 — comprehensive wavelets.

docs.title: Image processing (ECEG-6423)
docs.text:
• Jain, Fundamentals of Digital Image Processing, PHI, 1995 — matches the syllabus.
  • Gonzalez & Woods, Digital Image Processing, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018 — the standard modern text.
  • Pratt, Digital Image Processing, 4th ed., Wiley, 2007 — encyclopedic.
  • Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd ed., Springer, 2022 — free online.

docs.title: Speech processing (ECEG-6423)
docs.text:
• Rabiner & Schafer, Digital Processing of Speech Signals, Prentice Hall, 1978 — the classical reference.
  • Rabiner & Juang, Fundamentals of Speech Recognition, Prentice Hall, 1993 — HMM reference.
  • Quatieri, Discrete-Time Speech Signal Processing, Prentice Hall, 2001 — homomorphic methods.
  • Huang, Acero & Hon, Spoken Language Processing, Prentice Hall, 2001 — comprehensive modern.

docs.title: Software Setup
docs.text: Shared setup instructions for ECEG-6303 and ECEG-6423.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Download Python 3.11 or later from python.org.
  2. During installation, check "Add Python to PATH" (Windows).
  3. Verify: python --version (or python3 --version on macOS/Linux).

docs.title: Virtual environment (recommended)
docs.text:
# Create environment
python -m venv eceg-env

# Activate
source eceg-env/bin/activate         # macOS / Linux
ecg-env\Scripts\activate             # Windows

# Later, to exit:
deactivate

docs.title: Required packages
docs.text:
pip install numpy scipy matplotlib jupyter
pip install scikit-image Pillow opencv-python
pip install librosa soundfile
pip install PyWavelets
pip install statsmodels
pip install hmmlearn
pip install simpy
pip install padasip

docs.text:
pip install cvxpy

docs.text:
Available through your university's licence — contact IT services.

Required toolboxes:

ver

docs.title: Getting the course materials
docs.text:
Clone the course repo:

git clone https://github.com/tesfamichael-g/ECEG-DSP-Courses.git
cd ECEG-DSP-Courses

The docs/ecg-6303/ and docs/ecg-6423/ folders contain the lecture notes and code examples. The docs/ecg-6303/chapters/ and docs/ecg-6423/chapters/ folders contain the worked Python/Java/C# code snippets from each chapter.

docs.title: Jupyter notebooks
docs.text:
Both courses use Jupyter for interactive labs.

jupyter notebook

Then navigate to notebooks/ in the course folder. Each chapter's lab exercises are provided as .ipynb files.

Tip: use JupyterLab instead of classic Notebook for a better UI:

pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab

docs.title: Data and audio files
docs.text:
• Speech samples: assets/audio/ in the course folder
  • Image samples: assets/images/ — Kodak, USC-SIPI, BSDS500 subsets
  • Video samples: assets/video/ — Xiph test clips, UVG sequences

Download the full datasets from the links in the Resources page if you want more extensive testing.

docs.title: Recommended IDEs
docs.text:
Language IDE Why Python VS Code, PyCharm, JupyterLab Best for scientific computing MATLAB MATLAB IDE Built-in Java IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse Standard C# Visual Studio, VS Code Standard

VS Code with the Python + Jupyter extensions is the recommended setup for most students.

docs.title: pip install fails with permission error
docs.text: Use a virtual environment (as above) or pip install --user.

docs.title: numpy import fails on macOS M1/M2
docs.text: Use the arm64 Python from python.org, or pip install --upgrade numpy.

docs.title: opencv-python fails on Windows
docs.text: Try pip install opencv-python-headless (no GUI dependencies).

docs.title: librosa import fails
docs.text:
librosa has many dependencies (numba, llvmlite). Sometimes pip install librosa fails; try installing dependencies manually:

pip install numba
pip install soundfile
pip install librosa

docs.title: import errors after installing packages
docs.text: Restart the Python kernel (in Jupyter) or the terminal (in scripts). Package imports are cached at Python startup.

docs.title: Testing the environment
docs.text:
Run this quick test to verify everything is working:

import numpy as np
import scipy
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import librosa
import cv2
from scipy.signal import welch, firwin
from scipy.fft import dct

# Quick test: generate noise, filter, plot
x = np.random.randn(1000)
b = firwin(51, 0.1)
y = scipy.signal.lfilter(b, 1, x)

f, pxx = welch(y, fs=1000, nperseg=256)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.semilogy(f, pxx)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_title("Welch PSD — test")
plt.savefig("test_plot.png")
print("✓ All packages working")

If this runs without errors and produces test_plot.png, the environment is ready.
